docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: from a rotating coil to RMS values

Tools: GeoGebra Classic, then Jupyter + NumPy + matplotlib.

  1. In GeoGebra, create sliders ω and t, draw a unit vector at angle ω t (the coil normal) and the point (t, cos(ω t)) with trace on. The flux through a flat coil of area \(A\) in a uniform field \(B\) is \(\Phi = BA\cos\omega t\); add the point (t, ω sin(ω t)) for the normalized EMF and observe the 90° shift between flux and EMF.
  2. In a notebook, for a coil with \(N = 100\) turns, \(A = 0.01\ \text{m}^2\), \(B = 0.5\) T at 50 Hz, sample one period, compute \(\Phi(t)\) and \(e(t) = -N\, d\Phi/dt\) with np.gradient, and compare with the analytic \(e(t) = NBA\omega \sin\omega t\). Plot both with matplotlib.
  3. Compute the RMS of the sampled EMF as np.sqrt(np.mean(e**2)) over whole periods and compare with \(E_{\text{peak}}/\sqrt{2}\). Repeat for a signal with a 150 Hz component added and check that the squares of the component RMS values add.
  4. Plot the instantaneous power \(p(t) = e(t)^2 / R\) into a resistor and show that its mean equals \(E_{\text{RMS}}^2/R\): this is why RMS values are used for AC power.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
All statements are also in exercises.ipynb; the worked examples run in examples.ipynb.

  1. An aluminium conductor (\(\rho \approx 2.82\cdot10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\text{m}\)) is 100 km long with a 500 mm² cross-section. Compute its resistance and the Joule losses at 1 000 A. (Pen and paper) Answer: \(5.64\ \Omega\); \(5.64\) MW.

    Solution: Exercise 1. 2. A two-conductor line made of the conductor of Exercise 1 delivers 200 MW. Compare the current and the losses at 200 kV and at 400 kV, and state the scaling law. (Pen and paper) Answer: 1 000 A and 11.3 MW vs 500 A and 2.8 MW; losses scale as \(1/V^2\).

    Solution: Exercise 2. 3. For the coil of the lab, compute the peak and RMS EMF by hand. (Pen and paper) Answer: \(157.1\) V and \(111.1\) V.

    Solution: Exercise 3. 4. Compute the energy stored in a 1 H inductor carrying 1 000 A and in a 1 µF capacitor at 230.9 kV. Explain why the current through an inductor and the voltage across a capacitor cannot change instantaneously. (Pen and paper)

    Solution: Exercise 4. 5. Sample \(v(t) = 325 \sin(2\pi 50 t)\) and verify numerically that its RMS is about 230 V. Over a window that is an integer number of periods, how many samples per period does the discrete RMS need to be exact? Over a window that is not an integer number of periods (say 1.4, 10.4 or 40.4 periods), show that adding samples does not reduce the error, and work out how long the window must be for 0.1 % accuracy, or how a power meter avoids the question by synchronising the window to whole periods. One would expect denser sampling to help; it does not, because the error is a window effect, the extra fraction of a period in the mean of \(\sin^2\), which the sampling density cannot remove. (Jupyter: NumPy + matplotlib)

    Solution: Exercise 5.

docs.title: Chapter 7 – Solutions
docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 7. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: coil_emf.py (the rotating coil, RMS values and the sampling study; python coil_emf.py prints every number of the Lab answers and of Exercises 3 and 5) and conductor.py (python conductor.py prints those of Exercises 1, 2 and 4). The notebooks examples.ipynb, lab.ipynb and exercises.ipynb import these modules.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. GeoGebra (not run here; GeoGebra is interactive). Method: two sliders ω (say 1 to 10) and t (0 to 10, animated); the vector Vector((0, 0), (cos(ω t), sin(ω t))) is the coil normal, which makes an angle \(\omega t\) with the field (taken along the \(x\) axis); the point (t, cos(ω t)) with Trace on draws the normalized flux \(\Phi / (BA) = \cos\omega t\) as t runs, and (t, ω sin(ω t)) draws the normalized EMF \(e / (NBA) = -\,d(\cos\omega t)/dt = \omega \sin\omega t\). Expected picture: the EMF trace is zero where the flux trace is at a peak (the normal along the field) and largest where the flux crosses zero (the normal across the field, when the flux changes fastest). The EMF is shifted by a quarter period, \(90^\circ\), with respect to the flux; raising ω raises the EMF amplitude in proportion and leaves the flux amplitude alone. The numeric check in coil_emf.py: \(e(0) = 0\) where \(\Phi(0) = 0.5\) Wb-turn is the maximum, and the mean of \(\Phi(t)\, e(t)\) over a period is zero (the two are orthogonal).

  2. Flux and EMF of the coil. With \(N = 100\), \(A = 0.01\ \text{m}^2\), \(B = 0.5\) T and \(\omega = 2\pi \cdot 50 = 314.16\ \text{rad/s}\) the flux linkage is \(N\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t\) with peak \(0.5\) Wb-turn, and \(e = -N\, d\Phi/dt = NBA\omega \sin\omega t\) with peak \(NBA\omega = 157.08\) V. Sampled at 1 000 points per period, np.gradient reproduces the analytic EMF within \(0.49\) V (\(3.1\cdot10^{-3}\) of the peak); the error is \(1.6\cdot10^{-1}\) with 20 samples per period and \(3.1\cdot10^{-2}\) with 100, so it falls as \(1/n\): np.gradient is second order inside the window but first order at the two end points, where it uses one-sided differences, and the largest error sits there. Plotted together, the two EMF curves coincide and both are shifted by a quarter period with respect to the flux.

    coil_emf.py: flux and EMF
    def sample_period(samples: int = 1000, periods: float = 1.0, freq: float = FREQ) -> np.ndarray:
    """``samples`` instants per period over ``periods`` periods, the end point excluded (t = 0, Δt, 2Δt, ...)."""
    return np.arange(round(samples * periods)) / (samples * freq)


def flux(t: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Flux linkage N B A cos(ωt) in weber-turns."""
    return N_TURNS * B_FIELD * AREA * np.cos(OMEGA * t)


def emf_numeric(t: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The EMF e = −dΦ/dt by central differences (``np.gradient``) on the sampled flux."""
    return -np.gradient(flux(t), t)


def emf_analytic(t: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The EMF e = N B A ω sin(ωt)."""
    return E_PEAK * np.sin(OMEGA * t)

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  3. RMS. Over one period (and over three) the sampled RMS of the EMF is \(111.072\) V \(= 157.08 / \sqrt2\). A 150 Hz component \(40 \sin 3\omega t\) has RMS \(28.284\) V \(= 40/\sqrt2\); the RMS of the sum is \(114.617\) V, and \(\sqrt{111.072^2 + 28.284^2} = 114.617\) V: the squares add. They add because the cross term \(2\,\overline{e_1 e_3}\) vanishes, sinusoids of different frequencies being orthogonal over a whole number of periods of both (here one period of the fundamental holds three of the harmonic).

  4. Power into a resistor. With \(R = 100\ \Omega\) the instantaneous power \(p(t) = e^2/R\) swings between 0 and \(246.74\) W (\(= E_\text{peak}^2/R\)) at 100 Hz, twice the frequency of the EMF, and its mean over a period is \(123.37\) W, exactly \(E_\text{RMS}^2/R = 111.072^2 / 100\). That is the definition of the RMS value: the DC voltage that would heat the same resistor at the same average rate. A DC calculation with \(E_\text{RMS}\) gives the AC average power, which is why ratings and bills are in RMS volts and amperes.

    coil_emf.py: RMS and mean power
    def rms(x: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Root mean square of the samples."""
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(x**2)))


def mean_power(e: np.ndarray, r: float) -> float:
    """Average of p(t) = e(t)² / R over the samples, in watts."""
    return float(np.mean(e**2 / r))

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
\(R = \rho L / A = 2.82\cdot10^{-8} \times 10^5 / (500\cdot10^{-6}) = 5.64\ \Omega\). At \(I = 1\,000\) A the Joule losses are \(P = RI^2 = 5.64 \times 10^6\ \text{W} = 5.64\) MW, in one conductor (conductor.py prints both numbers). Whether 5.64 MW is a lot depends on the power the conductor carries, which depends on the voltage: that is Exercise 2.

conductor.py: losses
def resistance(rho: float = RHO_AL, length: float = LENGTH, area: float = AREA) -> float:
    """R = ρ L / A in ohms."""
    return rho * length / area


def joule_losses(current: float, r: float | None = None) -> float:
    """P = R I² in watts for one conductor (``r`` defaults to the Exercise 1 conductor)."""
    r = resistance() if r is None else r
    return r * current**2


def line_losses(power: float, voltage: float, conductors: int = 2, r: float | None = None) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Current I = P / V and the losses of ``conductors`` conductors each carrying it, in (A, W)."""
    current = power / voltage
    return current, conductors * joule_losses(current, r)

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text: The current that carries \(P = 200\) MW at voltage \(V\) is \(I = P/V\): \(1\,000\) A at 200 kV and \(500\) A at 400 kV. Each of the two conductors dissipates \(RI^2\), so the line loses \(2RI^2 = 2 \times 5.64 \times 10^6 = 11.28\) MW (5.64 % of the power delivered) at 200 kV and \(2 \times 5.64 \times 500^2 = 2.82\) MW (1.41 %) at 400 kV. Substituting \(I = P/V\) gives the scaling law \(P_\text{loss} = 2R P^2 / V^2\): for a fixed power and conductor the losses fall as \(1/V^2\), so doubling the voltage divides them by four. The same law holds for any number of conductors and is the reason transmission runs at hundreds of kilovolts, with transformers (induction, the topic of this chapter) to step the voltage up and down.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text: \(E_\text{peak} = NBA\omega = 100 \times 0.5 \times 0.01 \times 2\pi \times 50 = 0.5 \times 314.16 = 157.1\) V and \(E_\text{RMS} = E_\text{peak}/\sqrt2 = 111.1\) V. The sampled values of the lab are \(157.08\) V and \(111.07\) V.

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text: \(W_L = \tfrac12 L I^2 = \tfrac12 \times 1 \times 1000^2 = 500\) kJ and \(W_C = \tfrac12 C V^2 = \tfrac12 \times 10^{-6} \times (230.9\cdot10^3)^2 = 26.66\) kJ. The energy of an inductor is a function of its current and that of a capacitor a function of its voltage. A jump in the current of an inductor would be a jump in its stored energy, which needs an infinite power \(p = v\,i\) and so an infinite voltage \(v = L\, di/dt\); a jump in the voltage of a capacitor would need an infinite current \(i = C\, dv/dt\). Neither exists in a real circuit, so \(i_L\) and \(v_C\) are continuous: they are the state variables of the circuit, and whatever a switch does, they keep their value across the switching instant. This is why opening a breaker on an inductive line produces an arc (the current insists on continuing) and why a capacitor bank is pre-charged or switched at a voltage zero.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text: Sampling \(v(t) = 325 \sin(2\pi 50 t)\) at 1 000 points over one period gives an RMS of \(229.81\) V \(= 325/\sqrt2\), the nominal 230 V of a European outlet. The number of samples per period is not what limits the accuracy. Over a whole number of periods the discrete RMS of a sinusoid is exact already with 3 samples per period (the error is \(10^{-16}\) with 3, 4, 10 or 100 samples per period over 10 periods), because the discrete mean of \(\sin^2\) over an integer number of equally spaced samples per period is exactly \(1/2\) when there are at least three. Over a window that is not a whole number of periods the error is a window effect: the mean of \(\sin^2\omega t\) over \([0, T]\) is \(\tfrac12 - \sin(2\omega T) / (4\omega T)\), so the relative error of the RMS is at most \(1/(4\omega T) = 1/(8\pi n)\) for a window of \(n\) periods, whatever the sampling. With 1 000 samples per period the error is \(2.7\cdot10^{-2}\) over 1.4 periods, \(3.6\cdot10^{-3}\) over 10.4, \(9.3\cdot10^{-4}\) over 40.4 and \(3.8\cdot10^{-4}\) over 100.4 periods, each just below its bound (\(2.8\cdot10^{-2}\), \(3.8\cdot10^{-3}\), \(9.8\cdot10^{-4}\), \(4.0\cdot10^{-4}\)), and over 10.4 periods it is \(1.5\cdot10^{-3}\) with 10 samples per period, \(3.5\cdot10^{-3}\) with 100 and \(3.6\cdot10^{-3}\) with 1 000: more samples make the discrete sum a better approximation of the continuous integral, which is itself off by the window term. So the answer is: for 0.1 % accuracy with a window of arbitrary length you need the window to hold at least \(1/(8\pi \cdot 0.001) \approx 40\) periods (0.8 s at 50 Hz), and a few samples per period are then enough; or you synchronise the window to whole periods, as power meters do, and 3 samples per period are exact. rms_window_error and rms_window_error_bound in coil_emf.py give the table.

docs.title: Chapter 8. DC circuits and nodal analysis in matrix form
docs.text:
Weeks: 2.5 · Semester: 2 · Prerequisites: Chapter 2, Chapter 3, Chapter 7

Why it matters for ToOp

The DC power flow is nodal analysis of a network of reactances: \(B\theta = P\) has the same structure as \(Gv = i\) for a resistor network. Superposition is why flows can be updated by adding contributions. When a substation is split into busbars A and B, the flow across the coupler is obtained from Kirchhoff's current law alone: it equals the imbalance at busbar A, the sum of the flows into A minus the flows out of A plus the injection assigned to A (_compute_bus_a_imbalance in dc_solver/jax/cross_coupler_flow.py). Chapter 18 shows how ToOp uses that number to update all flows after a split.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Circuit elements; KCL and KVL; series and parallel.
  • Nodal analysis and the nodal admittance (conductance) matrix; mesh analysis. The nodal conductance matrix \(G = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(g) A\) is the weighted Laplacian of Chapter 2 and Chapter 3, revisited here with physical units.
  • Linearity and superposition; Thévenin and Norton equivalents; maximum power transfer.
  • Network topology: graphs of circuits, trees and cotrees, incidence matrix formulation, Tellegen's theorem.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Write the nodal equations of any resistive network directly in matrix form \(Gv = i\).
  • Show that \(G\) is a weighted Laplacian and explain the role of the reference (ground) node.
  • Compute a Thévenin equivalent between two nodes with two linear solves.
  • Compute the current through a coupler joining two parts of a split node from KCL.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Two nodes plus ground. Conductances: 1 S from node 1 to ground, 2 S between nodes 1 and 2, 4 S from node 2 to ground; a 3 A current source feeds node 1. KCL at each node, written by inspection (diagonal: sum of the conductances at the node; off-diagonal: minus the conductance between the nodes):

\[ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 + 4 \end{bmatrix}}_{G} \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_1 = \frac{18}{14} \approx 1.286\ \text{V},\ \ v_2 = \frac{6}{14} \approx 0.429\ \text{V}. \]

This \(G\) is exactly \(A^\top \operatorname{diag}(g) A\) with the ground row and column deleted, where \(A\) is the incidence matrix of the three branches over the nodes \(\{0, 1, 2\}\).

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: a nodal solver you will reuse

Tools: Jupyter + NumPy (+ pandas for the branch table), or Octave.

  1. Write nodal_solve(fr, to, g, inj, n, ground=0) that builds \(A\) and \(G = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(g) A\), deletes the ground row and column, solves for the node voltages and returns them with the branch currents \(g \odot (Av)\). Check it on the worked example.
  2. Use the network of the Chapter 2 lab: 0.5 A injected at node 2, 1 A withdrawn at node 5, and the ground node supplying the balance. Verify KCL at every node and the power balance \(v^\top i = \sum_k g_k (Av)_k^2\).
  3. Superposition: solve for each source separately and check that the voltages add up.
  4. Thévenin: inject 1 A at node 5 and withdraw it at node 0; the voltage difference is the Thévenin resistance between those nodes. Compare with the effective resistance of Chapter 3.
  5. Split a node: in the same network, split node 2 into busbar A (keeping branches (0, 2), (1, 2) and the 0.5 A injection) and busbar B (a new node 6 that takes branch (2, 4)), joined by a coupler branch (2, 6) with a very large conductance (\(10^6\) S). Solve the split network and read the coupler current. Compare it with the imbalance at A computed from the unsplit solution: flows into A over its branches plus the injection at A (expected: both about 0.766 A). This is the quantity computed in dc_solver/jax/cross_coupler_flow.py.
  6. Keep nodal_solve: it becomes the DC power flow in Chapter 16 by replacing conductances with susceptances.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

docs.title: Chapter 8 – Solutions
docs.text:
Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 8. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: nodal.py (the nodal solver and the lab network; python nodal.py prints every number of the Lab answers and of Exercises 4 and 5), wheatstone.py (python wheatstone.py prints those of Exercises 1 and 3) and mesh_nodal.m (Exercise 2, Octave). The notebooks examples.ipynb, lab.ipynb and exercises.ipynb import these modules. The ToOp function of Exercise 6 was read at commit ba1874e.

Node numbers start at 0 and branch \(k\) runs from fr[k] to to[k]; a positive branch current flows that way. The lab network is the one of the Chapter 2 lab: branches \((0,1)\), \((0,2)\), \((1,2)\), \((1,3)\), \((2,4)\), \((3,4)\), \((4,5)\) with conductances \(10, 5, 8, 4, 6, 3, 2\) S.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. nodal_solve. The incidence matrix \(A\) has one row per branch with \(+1\) in the fr column and \(-1\) in the to column; \(A^\top \operatorname{diag}(g) A\) is the weighted Laplacian of the network, singular because its rows sum to zero. Deleting the ground row and column leaves the invertible \(G\) of the chapter; the solver fills the ground voltage with 0 and returns \(g \odot (Av)\) as branch currents. The injection given for the ground node is not used: ground supplies whatever balances the others. On the worked example it returns \(v = (0, 1.2857, 0.4286)\) V \(= (0, 18/14, 6/14)\) and the branch currents \(1.2857\) A through the 1 S branch and \(1.7143\) A through the 2 S and 4 S branches, which add up to the 3 A of the source.

    nodal.py: nodal_solve
    def incidence(fr, to, n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Branch-node incidence matrix A (branches × nodes): +1 at the from node, −1 at the to node."""
    a = np.zeros((len(fr), n))
    a[np.arange(len(fr)), fr] = 1.0
    a[np.arange(len(fr)), to] = -1.0
    return a


def nodal_solve(fr, to, g, inj, n: int, ground: int = 0) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Node voltages and branch currents of a resistive network with current injections.

    Builds A and G = Aᵀ diag(g) A, deletes the ground row and column, solves G_r v_r = i_r and returns the
    full voltage vector (0 at ``ground``) with the branch currents g ⊙ (A v), positive from ``fr`` to ``to``.
    The injection at the ground node is ignored: ground supplies whatever balances the others.
    """
    a = incidence(fr, to, n)
    gmat = a.T @ np.diag(g) @ a
    keep = [k for k in range(n) if k != ground]
    v = np.zeros(n)
    v[keep] = np.linalg.solve(gmat[np.ix_(keep, keep)], np.asarray(inj, float)[keep])
    return v, np.asarray(g) * (a @ v)

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  2. The Chapter 2 network. With \(0.5\) A into node 2, \(1\) A out of node 5 and node 0 grounded, the voltages are \(v = (0, -0.03041, -0.03918, -0.08889, -0.16686, -0.66686)\) V and the branch currents, in branch order, \((0.30409, 0.19591, 0.07018, 0.23392, 0.76608, 0.23392, 1.00000)\) A. KCL: \(A^\top i\) equals the injection at every node to \(10^{-12}\) once the ground injection is written as the \(+0.5\) A it must supply (the two branches leaving node 0 carry \(0.30409 + 0.19591 = 0.5\) A). Power balance: the sources deliver \(v^\top i = 0.5\,(0) + 0.5\,(-0.03918) - 1\,(-0.66686) = 0.647271\) W and the branches dissipate \(\sum_k g_k (Av)_k^2 = \sum_k i_k^2 / g_k = 0.647271\) W, the same number (Exercise 3 proves it must be).

  3. Superposition. Solving with the \(0.5\) A alone and with the \(-1\) A alone and adding the two voltage vectors reproduces the voltages of step 2 to \(3\cdot10^{-17}\) (superposition_check). The solution map \(i \mapsto v = G^{-1} i\) is linear, so it respects sums; this is the property that lets Chapter 17 build flows from one sensitivity per injection and add them.

  4. Thévenin. Injecting 1 A at node 5 and withdrawing it at node 0 gives \(v_5 - v_0 = 0.71189\ \Omega\) (thevenin_resistance, one linear solve: the second solve of the chapter's "two linear solves" is only needed when the open-circuit voltage is wanted too). The Chapter 3 effective resistance \((e_5 - e_0)^\top L^+ (e_5 - e_0)\) with the pseudoinverse of the full Laplacian is \(0.71189\ \Omega\) too, to \(10^{-12}\): they are the same quantity. Sanity check: node 5 hangs off node 4 through the single 2 S branch (\(0.5\ \Omega\)), so the Thévenin resistance must exceed \(0.5\ \Omega\); the rest of the network between node 4 and ground adds \(0.21189\ \Omega\).

    nodal.py: Thévenin and effective resistance
    def thevenin_resistance(fr, to, g, n: int, a: int, b: int) -> float:
    """Thévenin (effective) resistance between nodes a and b: inject 1 A at a, withdraw it at b, read v_a − v_b."""
    inj = np.zeros(n)
    inj[a], inj[b] = 1.0, -1.0
    v, _ = nodal_solve(fr, to, g, inj, n, ground=b)
    return float(v[a] - v[b])


def effective_resistance(fr, to, g, n: int, a: int, b: int) -> float:
    """The Chapter 3 formula (e_a − e_b)ᵀ L⁺ (e_a − e_b) with the pseudoinverse of the full Laplacian."""
    amat = incidence(fr, to, n)
    lap = amat.T @ np.diag(g) @ amat
    e = np.zeros(n)
    e[a], e[b] = 1.0, -1.0
    return float(e @ np.linalg.pinv(lap) @ e)

  5. Split a node. split_node_2 moves branch \((2, 4)\) to a new node 6 (busbar B), keeps \((0, 2)\), \((1, 2)\) and the \(0.5\) A on node 2 (busbar A) and adds the coupler branch \((2, 6)\) with \(10^6\) S. The coupler current is \(0.76608\) A from A to B, across a drop of \(7.7\cdot10^{-7}\) V. From the unsplit solution, the imbalance at A is the flow into A over its two branches plus the injection at A: \(0.19591 + 0.07018 + 0.5 = 0.76608\) A, and the two agree to \(10^{-6}\). They must: in the unsplit network KCL at node 2 says that whatever enters through \((0, 2)\), \((1, 2)\) and the source leaves through \((2, 4)\), and after the split the only way from A to \((2, 4)\) is the coupler. When the coupler is ideal (zero voltage drop) the split network has the same voltages as the unsplit one, so every other current is unchanged and the coupler simply makes the hidden internal current of node 2 visible. This is the number ToOp computes in _compute_bus_a_imbalance (Exercise 6).

    nodal.py: split_node_2
    def split_node_2(coupler_g: float = 1e6) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Split node 2 of the lab network into busbar A (branches (0, 2), (1, 2), the 0.5 A) and busbar B (branch (2, 4)).

    Busbar B is a new node 6; a coupler branch (2, 6) of conductance ``coupler_g`` joins them. Returns the coupler
    current (A to B), the KCL imbalance at A computed from the unsplit solution (flows into A over its branches
    plus the injection at A) and the voltage across the coupler.
    """
    fr, to, g = [*FR, 2], [*TO, 6], [*G, coupler_g]
    fr[FR.index(2)] = 6  # branch (2, 4) now leaves busbar B
    inj = [*INJ, 0.0]
    v, i = nodal_solve(fr, to, g, inj, N + 1)
    _, i0 = nodal_solve(FR, TO, G, INJ, N)
    into_a = sum(i0[k] for k in range(len(FR)) if TO[k] == 2)  # branches (0, 2) and (1, 2) end at A
    return {'coupler': float(i[-1]), 'imbalance_a': float(into_a + INJ[2]), 'coupler_volts': float(v[2] - v[6])}

  6. Keep nodal_solve. With susceptances \(b_k = 1/x_k\) in place of conductances, angles in place of voltages and power injections in place of currents, the same function is the DC power flow \(B\theta = P\) of Chapter 16. Nothing to compute here.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
Number the nodes 0 (bottom, ground), 1 (top), 2 (left) and 3 (right); \(R_1\) joins 1–2, \(R_2\) joins 1–3, \(R_3\) joins 2–0, \(R_4\) joins 3–0 and \(R_5\) is the middle branch 2–3; the source pushes \(I\) into node 1 and takes it from node 0. With \(g_k = 1/R_k\), KCL at the three ungrounded nodes reads

\[ \begin{bmatrix} g_1 + g_2 & -g_1 & -g_2 \\ -g_1 & g_1 + g_3 + g_5 & -g_5 \\ -g_2 & -g_5 & g_2 + g_4 + g_5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} I \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The middle current is \(g_5 (v_2 - v_3)\), zero exactly when \(v_2 = v_3\). Put \(v_2 = v_3 = w\) in the second and third equations: the \(g_5\) terms cancel and they become \(g_1 v_1 = (g_1 + g_3)\, w\) and \(g_2 v_1 = (g_2 + g_4)\, w\), which are compatible only if \(g_1 (g_2 + g_4) = g_2 (g_1 + g_3)\), that is \(g_1 g_4 = g_2 g_3\), or in resistances

\[ R_1 R_4 = R_2 R_3 \qquad \Big(\tfrac{R_1}{R_3} = \tfrac{R_2}{R_4}\Big). \]

Both arms then divide \(v_1\) in the same ratio, \(w = v_1 R_3/(R_1 + R_3) = v_1 R_4/(R_2 + R_4)\), and the condition does not involve \(R_5\) or \(I\): a balanced bridge stays balanced for any middle resistor and any source. Numeric check with bridge_currents: \(R = (100, 200, 50, 100, 1000)\ \Omega\) satisfies \(R_1 R_4 = R_2 R_3 = 10^4\) and gives \(v_2 - v_3 = 0\) and a middle current of \(0\) to \(10^{-12}\); changing \(R_4\) to \(120\ \Omega\) gives \(v_2 - v_3 = -3.839\) V and \(-3.839\) mA through the middle branch.

wheatstone.py: bridge
def bridge_currents(r: list[float], i_src: float = 1.0) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Node voltages and branch currents (R1, R2, R3, R4, R5 order) of the bridge fed by ``i_src`` at node 1."""
    g = 1 / np.asarray(r, float)
    return nodal_solve(BRIDGE_FR, BRIDGE_TO, g, [-i_src, i_src, 0.0, 0.0], 4)


def is_balanced(r: list[float]) -> bool:
    """R1 R4 = R2 R3, the condition for zero current in the middle branch."""
    r1, r2, r3, r4, _ = r
    return bool(np.isclose(r1 * r4, r2 * r3))

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
Resistances \(R_a = 1\ \Omega\) (node 1 to ground), \(R_b = 1/2\ \Omega\) (nodes 1–2), \(R_c = 1/4\ \Omega\) (node 2 to ground). Take mesh 1 as the loop of the current source and \(R_a\), and mesh 2 as the loop \(R_a\)–\(R_b\)–\(R_c\), both clockwise. The source fixes \(I_1 = 3\) A; KVL around mesh 2, \(R_a (I_2 - I_1) + R_b I_2 + R_c I_2 = 0\), gives \(I_2 = R_a I_1 / (R_a + R_b + R_c) = 3 / 1.75 = 12/7 = 1.7143\) A. Then \(v_1 = R_a (I_1 - I_2) = 9/7 = 1.2857\) V and \(v_2 = R_c I_2 = 3/7 = 0.4286\) V, the voltages of the worked example (\(18/14\) and \(6/14\)). The mesh currents are the branch currents of step 1: \(I_1 - I_2 = 1.2857\) A in the 1 S branch and \(I_2 = 1.7143\) A in the series pair. In Octave mesh_nodal solves \(G v = i\) and the mesh system \(R\, I = (I_s, 0)\) and returns both; the Octave test block checks that they agree to \(10^{-12}\). Nodal analysis needs one equation per ungrounded node (2), mesh analysis one per independent loop (2 here, with one trivial because of the current source); for grids with thousands of buses and a current-source model of injections the nodal form wins, which is why power flow is nodal.

mesh_nodal.m
function [v_nodal, v_mesh, i_mesh] = mesh_nodal()
  % The worked example of Chapter 8 solved twice: by nodal analysis (G v = i) and by mesh analysis.
  % Conductances 1 S (node 1 to ground), 2 S (nodes 1-2), 4 S (node 2 to ground); a 3 A source feeds node 1.
  % Mesh 1 holds the source and the 1 ohm resistor, so I1 = 3 A; mesh 2 runs through the 1, 1/2 and 1/4 ohm
  % resistors: KVL gives Ra (I2 - I1) + (Rb + Rc) I2 = 0.
  G = [1 + 2, -2; -2, 2 + 4];
  v_nodal = G \ [3; 0];
  Ra = 1; Rb = 1 / 2; Rc = 1 / 4; Is = 3;
  R = [1, 0; -Ra, Ra + Rb + Rc];
  i_mesh = R \ [Is; 0];
  v_mesh = [Ra * (i_mesh(1) - i_mesh(2)); Rc * i_mesh(2)];
end

%!test
%! [v_nodal, v_mesh, i_mesh] = mesh_nodal();
%! assert(v_nodal, [18 / 14; 6 / 14], 1e-12)
%! assert(v_mesh, v_nodal, 1e-12)
%! assert(i_mesh, [3; 12 / 7], 1e-12)      % 3 A in the source mesh, 1.7143 A through the 2 S and 4 S branches
%! assert(i_mesh(1) - i_mesh(2), v_nodal(1) * 1, 1e-12)   % current in the 1 S branch

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
\(u^\top j = (Av)^\top j = v^\top (A^\top j) = v^\top i\): two lines, using only \(u = Av\) (KVL, the branch voltages are differences of node potentials) and \(A^\top j = i\) (KCL). Nothing relates \(u\) to \(j\): they may come from different circuits on the same graph, and the theorem still holds. For the power balance take \(j = i_\text{branch} = \operatorname{diag}(g)\, Av\) of the same network: \(u^\top j = (Av)^\top \operatorname{diag}(g)\, (Av) = \sum_k g_k (Av)_k^2\), the Joule power, while \(v^\top i\) is the power delivered by the sources (ground included, at potential 0). So \(\sum_k g_k (Av)_k^2 = v^\top i\), which is lab step 2. tellegen_check runs the stronger statement: the voltages of the lab network (\(g = 10, 5, 8, 4, 6, 3, 2\) S) and the currents of a unit-conductance network with the same injections give \(u^\top j = 0.647271\) W \(= v^\top i\); with random conductances for the second network the two sides still agree to \(10^{-12}\).

wheatstone.py: tellegen_check
def tellegen_check(fr, to, g, inj, n: int, g_other) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """uᵀ j against vᵀ i, with u = A v from the network ``g`` and j the branch currents of a network ``g_other``.

    Both networks share the graph and the injections, so j satisfies Aᵀ j = i although it belongs to another
    circuit; Tellegen's theorem says the two numbers agree anyway.
    """
    v, _ = nodal_solve(fr, to, g, inj, n)
    _, j = nodal_solve(fr, to, g_other, inj, n)
    u = incidence(fr, to, n) @ v
    return float(u @ j), float(v @ np.asarray(inj, float))

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text: Let \(L = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(g) A\) be the full Laplacian and \(i\) a balanced injection vector (\(\mathbf 1^\top i = 0\), the ground node's share included). Grounding node \(r\) means solving \(Lv = i\) with \(v_r = 0\); grounding node \(s\) means solving the same \(Lv' = i\) with \(v'_s = 0\). The null space of \(L\) of a connected network is spanned by \(\mathbf 1\) (Chapter 2), so every solution of \(Lv = i\) is \(v + c\mathbf 1\) for one constant \(c\): \(v' = v - v_s \mathbf 1\). All voltages shift by the same constant and \(u = Av' = Av - v_s A\mathbf 1 = Av\) because each row of \(A\) sums to zero, so every branch current \(g \odot u\) is unchanged. Check with nodal_solve (ground 0, then 3): the voltages become \((0.08889, 0.05848, 0.04971, 0, -0.07797, -0.57797)\) V, each exactly \(0.08889\) V \(= -v_3\) above the ground-0 solution, and the branch currents agree to \(2\cdot10^{-16}\). The condition "balanced" matters: the solver ignores the injection at the ground node, so if the injections of the other nodes do not sum to the negative of the ground's, grounding another node changes the problem (a different node then supplies the balance) and the currents do change. That is why INJ in nodal.py lists the \(+0.5\) A of node 0.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
Coupler conductance Coupler current Voltage across the coupler Departure from \(0.76608\) A \(10^6\) S \(0.76608\) A \(7.7\cdot10^{-7}\) V \(< 10^{-6}\) \(10^3\) S \(0.76517\) A \(7.7\cdot10^{-4}\) V \(-0.12\ \%\) \(10\) S \(0.68443\) A \(0.068\) V \(-10.7\ \%\)

The KCL argument of lab step 5 assumes that A and B are at the same potential, so that the split network has the unsplit voltages and only the hidden internal current of node 2 becomes visible. A coupler of finite conductance \(g_c\) is a resistor in series with branch \((2, 4)\): the path from A to node 4 now has resistance \(1/6 + 1/g_c\) instead of \(1/6\ \Omega\), so less current takes it (\(0.684\) A at \(10\) S, where the coupler adds \(0.1\ \Omega\) to \(0.167\ \Omega\)) and more leaves A through \((0, 2)\) and \((1, 2)\); the potentials of every node move, and the "imbalance at A" of the unsplit solution no longer describes the coupler. At \(10^3\) S the extra \(1\) m\(\Omega\) is \(0.6\ \%\) of the path and the error is \(0.12\ \%\); at \(10^6\) S it is invisible. ToOp's update after a split (Chapter 18) uses the unsplit flows and the imbalance formula, which is exact only for a closed, ideal coupler: a closed coupler in a real substation is a busbar section with a negligible impedance, so the assumption holds; an open coupler is the opposite case (the two busbars become two buses with no flow between them), handled as a different topology, not as a weak coupler. split_node_2(coupler_g) prints the table.

docs.title: Exercise 6
docs.text:
_compute_bus_a_imbalance in toop_engine_dc_solver/jax/cross_coupler_flow.py (ToOp commit ba1874e) computes, per timestep,

imbalance_a = sum(flows[branch_to_a]) - sum(flows[branch_from_a]) + bus_a_injection

and returns it as the cross-coupler flow, zeroing it when the substation index is out of range or when the configuration mask puts no branch on busbar A (jnp.all(~substation_configuration)). Term by term against lab step 5:

ToOp Lab step 5 flows (timesteps × branches, "potentially already updated by previous splits") the branch currents \(i = g \odot (Av)\) of the unsplit solution branch_to_a: branches whose flow direction is towards bus A branches \((0, 2)\) and \((1, 2)\), whose to end is node 2: \(0.19591 + 0.07018\) A branch_from_a: branches whose flow direction is away from bus A none here (branch \((2, 4)\) leaves from node 2 but is assigned to busbar B) bus_a_injection: net power injection assigned to bus A the \(0.5\) A kept on busbar A substation_configuration (True = branch on bus A) the choice \(\{(0, 2), (1, 2)\} \to\) A, \(\{(2, 4)\} \to\) B imbalance_a the coupler current \(0.76608\) A from A to B .get(mode='fill', fill_value=0.0) on padded indices substations have different numbers of branches; the padding entries contribute 0

"Towards A" and "away from A" refer to the orientation of each branch (its fr/to convention), not to the sign of the flow, exactly as the lab sums signed currents \(i_k\) with the sign of \(A\). The function works in power (MW) where the lab works in amperes, and over many timesteps at once (the axis=1 sums), but the formula is the KCL of lab step 5 and nothing more: with the flows of the unsplit grid it is exact for a closed ideal coupler (Exercise 5), and Chapter 18 shows how this one number then updates every other flow.

docs.title: Chapter 9. AC steady state and complex power
docs.text:
Weeks: 2.5 · Semester: 2 · Prerequisites: Chapter 1, Chapter 8

Why it matters for ToOp

AC validation reports active and reactive power, current magnitude, voltage magnitude and angle per element (interfaces/ loadflow result schemas). DC limits are derived from current ratings assuming a power factor of 1 (dc_power_factor in grid_helpers/powsybl/loadflow_parameters.py). The DC model that ToOp optimizes on is the small-angle, flat-voltage limit of the transfer formula \(P = V_1 V_2 \sin\delta / X\) derived in this chapter.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Sinusoids, RMS values, phasors; impedance and admittance.
  • Nodal analysis with complex admittances (revisits Chapter 8 with \(Y\) instead of \(G\)).
  • Instantaneous, active, reactive and apparent power; complex power \(S = V I^* = P + jQ\); power factor and its correction.
  • Power transfer between two AC sources through a reactance, \(P = \dfrac{V_1 V_2}{X}\sin\delta\) (the seed of DC power flow in Chapter 16).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Solve single-phase AC circuits with phasors and compute \(P\), \(Q\), \(S\) and the power factor.
  • Derive \(P\) and \(Q\) transferred through a lossless reactance and plot the \(P\)–\(\delta\) curve.
  • Quantify the error of the linearization \(P \approx \delta / X\) (per unit) as a function of \(\delta\).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Bus 1 has voltage \(V_1\angle\delta\), bus 2 has \(V_2\angle 0\), and they are joined by a lossless reactance \(jX\). The current from 1 to 2 is \(I = (V_1 e^{j\delta} - V_2)/(jX)\), and the complex power leaving bus 1 is

\[ S_{12} = V_1 e^{j\delta}\, I^* = \frac{V_1^2 - V_1 V_2 e^{j\delta}}{-jX} = \underbrace{\frac{V_1 V_2}{X}\sin\delta}_{P_{12}} + j\,\underbrace{\frac{V_1^2 - V_1 V_2\cos\delta}{X}}_{Q_{12}} . \]

Active power follows the angle difference; reactive power follows mainly the magnitude difference. With \(V_1 = V_2 = 1\) per unit and small \(\delta\) (in radians), \(\sin\delta \approx \delta\) gives the DC approximation

\[ P_{12} \approx \frac{\delta}{X}. \]

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: the P–δ curve and the DC approximation

Tools: GeoGebra Classic, then Jupyter + NumPy + pandas + matplotlib.

  1. In GeoGebra, enter p(x) = V_1 V_2 sin(x) / X_L and accept the automatic sliders for V_1, V_2 and X_L (or create them with the Slider tool); add q(x) = x / X_L for the linearization. Move the sliders and note the maximum transferable power and the angle where it occurs.
  2. Phasor diagram: points U_1 = V_1 (cos(d) + i sin(d)) and U_2 = V_2 + 0i with a slider d, the difference U_1 - U_2 and the current I_L = (U_1 - U_2) / (X_L i). Check that I_L is perpendicular to U_1 - U_2 and watch how its angle relative to U_1 changes with d.
  3. In a notebook, tabulate with pandas, for \(\delta = 0^\circ, 5^\circ, \dots, 90^\circ\) and \(V_1 = V_2 = 1\) pu, \(X = 0.1\) pu: the exact \(P\), the DC estimate \(\delta/X\) and the relative error. Plot the error with matplotlib. Check: about 0.5% at \(10^\circ\), 4.7% at \(30^\circ\) and 21% at \(60^\circ\).
  4. Repeat with \(V_1 = 1.05\) and \(V_2 = 0.95\) pu and separate the error caused by the angle linearization from the error caused by assuming flat voltage magnitudes.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

  1. A series RL load, \(R = 10\ \Omega\) and \(L = 50\) mH, is fed by 230 V at 50 Hz. Compute \(Z\), \(I\), \(S\) and the power factor, then the capacitance in parallel that raises the power factor to 0.95.   4. From the worked example, show that for \(\delta = 0\) reactive power flows from the bus with the higher voltage magnitude, and explain why the DC approximation ignores \(Q\) altogether. (Pen and paper)

    Solution: Exercise 5.

  6. A branch limit is a current \(I_{\max}\). If the DC model converts it to \(P_{\max} = V I_{\max}\) (power factor 1, as with ToOp's dc_power_factor=1.0) but the branch operates at power factor 0.95, by how much does the DC limit overestimate the admissible active power? (Pen and paper) Answer: about 5.3%.

docs.title: Chapter 9 – Solutions
docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 9. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: ac_transfer.py (power through a reactance, the error table, Exercises 4 and 6), rl_load.py and rl_load.m (Exercise 1), instantaneous_power.py (Exercise 3), ac_nodal.py and ac_nodal.m (Exercise 5). Each Python module prints every number quoted below when run as a script; the worked examples run live in examples.ipynb. The GeoGebra steps were not run here: for them the solution gives the construction and the values it must show, checked numerically.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. GeoGebra: the P–δ curve. p(x) = V_1 V_2 sin(x) / X_L is a sine of amplitude \(V_1 V_2 / X_L\): the maximum transferable power is \(V_1 V_2 / X_L\) and it occurs at \(x = 90^\circ\), whatever the sliders say. With \(V_1 = V_2 = 1\) and \(X_L = 0.1\) the peak is \(10\) pu (transfer_power(1, 1, 0.1, 90.0)); raising either voltage raises the peak in proportion, raising \(X_L\) lowers it, and none of them moves the peak away from \(90^\circ\). The line q(x) = x / X_L is the tangent of p at the origin: it has no maximum, which is the first thing the DC model loses. Beyond \(90^\circ\) the exact curve falls while the tangent keeps growing, so the DC model can predict transfers that no AC steady state can carry. (Construction not run here.)
  2. GeoGebra: the phasor diagram. Dividing a complex number by \(jX_L\) multiplies its magnitude by \(1/X_L\) and rotates it by \(-90^\circ\), so I_L is always perpendicular to U_1 - U_2, lagging it by a quarter turn: phasor_current(1, 1, 0.1, 30.0) is at \(-90.0^\circ\) from \(U_1 - U_2\). As d grows from 0, \(U_1 - U_2\) turns from pointing "upwards" (at \(90^\circ + d/2\), since the chord of two equal phasors is perpendicular to their bisector) and \(I_L\) therefore sits at \(d/2\): the current is in phase with the bisector of the two voltages, halfway between them. Its angle relative to \(U_1\) is \(-d/2\): the current lags the sending voltage by half the angle difference, so the sending end delivers both active power (\(I_L\) has a component along \(U_1\)) and reactive power (\(I_L\) has a component \(90^\circ\) behind \(U_1\)), as the worked example computes. (Construction not run here.)

  3. The error table. error_table() tabulates \(\delta\), the exact \(P = \sin\delta / 0.1\), the DC estimate \(\delta_{\text{rad}} / 0.1\) and the relative error \(\delta / \sin\delta - 1\), which does not depend on \(X\):

    ac_transfer.py (error_table)
    def error_table(v1: float = 1.0, v2: float = 1.0, x: float = 0.1, step_deg: int = 5) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Exact P, DC estimate and relative error for delta = 0, step, ..., 90 degrees.

    The relative error splits exactly into two factors: ``angle_error`` = delta / sin(delta) − 1, which is all
    there is when V1 = V2 = 1, and ``magnitude_error`` = 1 / (V1 V2) − 1, from assuming flat voltages, with
    (1 + total) = (1 + angle)(1 + magnitude).
    """
    delta = np.arange(0, 91, step_deg, dtype=float)
    p_exact, _ = transfer_power(v1, v2, x, delta)
    p_dc = dc_estimate(x, delta)
    magnitude = 1 / (v1 * v2) - 1
    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):  # at delta = 0 both powers are 0: take the limit values
        rel = np.where(delta > 0, p_dc / p_exact - 1, magnitude)
        angle = np.where(delta > 0, np.radians(delta) / np.sin(np.radians(delta)) - 1, 0.0)
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            'delta_deg': delta,
            'p_exact_pu': p_exact,
            'p_dc_pu': p_dc,
            'rel_error_pct': 100 * rel,
            'angle_error_pct': 100 * angle,
            'magnitude_error_pct': np.full_like(delta, 100 * magnitude),
        }
    )

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

    \(\delta\) exact \(P\) (pu) DC \(\delta/X\) (pu) error \(5^\circ\) 0.872 0.873 0.13 % \(10^\circ\) 1.736 1.745 0.51 % \(20^\circ\) 3.420 3.491 2.06 % \(30^\circ\) 5.000 5.236 4.72 % \(45^\circ\) 7.071 7.854 11.07 % \(60^\circ\) 8.660 10.472 20.92 % \(90^\circ\) 10.000 15.708 57.08 %

    The check values hold: 0.51 % at \(10^\circ\), 4.72 % at \(30^\circ\), 20.92 % at \(60^\circ\). The error is always positive (the DC model overestimates the flow, since \(\sin\delta < \delta\)) and grows like \(\delta^2 / 6\) for small angles, which is why the plot of the error against \(\delta\) is a parabola near the origin: doubling the angle quadruples the error. Transmission lines in normal operation run at angle differences of a few degrees, where the error is below one percent. 4. Unequal voltages. With \(V_1 = 1.05\) and \(V_2 = 0.95\) pu the exact power is \(0.9975 \sin\delta / X\) while the DC estimate stays \(\delta / X\), so the total error factor splits exactly as a product:

    \[ 1 + \varepsilon_{\text{total}} = \frac{\delta / X}{V_1 V_2 \sin\delta / X} = \underbrace{\frac{\delta}{\sin\delta}}_{1 + \varepsilon_{\text{angle}}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{V_1 V_2}}_{1 + \varepsilon_{\text{magnitude}}} . \]

    error_table(1.05, 0.95) gives, at \(10^\circ\), \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\), total errors of 0.76 %, 4.98 % and 21.22 %, of which the angle part is 0.51 %, 4.72 % and 20.92 % (the same as in step 3) and the magnitude part is a constant \(1/0.9975 - 1 = 0.25\) %. The magnitude error does not depend on \(\delta\) and is small as long as the voltages are within the usual \(\pm 5\) % band: it is the product \(V_1 V_2\) that matters, and a high and a low voltage largely compensate (\(1.05 \times 0.95 = 0.9975\)). Two low voltages would not: \(0.95^2 = 0.9025\) gives a 10.8 % magnitude error, the situation where the DC model is least trustworthy.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
\(\omega = 2\pi \cdot 50 = 314.16\) rad/s, so \(X_L = \omega L = 15.71\ \Omega\) and \(Z = 10 + j15.71\ \Omega\), \(|Z| = 18.62\ \Omega\) at \(57.5^\circ\). With \(V = 230\angle 0\) V, \(I = V / Z = 12.35\angle{-57.5^\circ}\) A. The complex power is \(S = V I^* = |I|^2 Z = 152.6 \times (10 + j15.71) = 1526 + j2396\) VA, \(|S| = 2841\) VA, and the power factor is \(P / |S| = 10 / 18.62 = 0.537\) lagging. To reach \(\text{pf} = 0.95\) the load must draw only \(Q' = P \tan(\arccos 0.95) = 1526 \times 0.3287 = 502\) var, so a capacitor in parallel must supply \(Q_C = 2396 - 502 = 1895\) var:

\[ C = \frac{Q_C}{\omega V^2} = \frac{1895}{314.16 \times 230^2} = 114.0\ \mu\text{F}. \]

rl_load.py prints these numbers and checks them by recomputing \(S\) with the capacitor in parallel: \(1526 + j501\) VA, pf \(0.950\) (the capacitor leaves \(P\) untouched). The Octave version is rl_load.m:

rl_load.m
function [Z, I, S, pf, C] = rl_load(R, L, V, f, pf_target)
  % Series RL load on a sinusoidal supply: impedance, current, complex power, power factor and the
  % parallel capacitance that raises the power factor to pf_target (Chapter 9, Exercise 1).
  w = 2 * pi * f;
  Z = R + 1i * w * L;
  I = V / Z;
  S = V * conj(I);
  pf = real(S) / abs(S);
  Qc = imag(S) - real(S) * tan(acos(pf_target));
  C = Qc / (w * V^2);
end

%!test
%! [Z, I, S, pf, C] = rl_load(10, 50e-3, 230, 50, 0.95);
%! assert(Z, 10 + 15.708i, 1e-3)
%! assert(abs(I), 12.35, 5e-3)
%! assert([real(S), imag(S)], [1526, 2396], 1)
%! assert(pf, 0.537, 5e-4)
%! assert(C * 1e6, 114, 0.1)
%! Zc = 1 / (1 / Z + 1i * 2 * pi * 50 * C);           % load with the capacitor in parallel
%! Sc = 230 * conj(230 / Zc);
%! assert(real(Sc) / abs(Sc), 0.95, 1e-9)

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text: (GeoGebra construction not run here.) With sliders V_m, ω, φ and an animated t, the point u = V_m (cos(ω t + φ) + i sin(ω t + φ)) is \(u(t) = V_m e^{j(\omega t + \varphi)} = V_m e^{j\varphi}\, e^{j\omega t}\): a fixed complex number \(V_m e^{j\varphi}\) multiplied by a unit rotation. At \(t = 0\) the rotation is \(e^{0} = 1\) and the point is exactly \(V_m e^{j\varphi}\), the phasor: a photograph of the rotating vector when the clock starts. The traced point (t, x(u)) draws \(V_m \cos(\omega t + \varphi)\), the signal: its value at \(t = 0\) is \(V_m \cos\varphi\), the real part of the phasor, and its first positive peak is at \(t = -\varphi / \omega\), earlier for a positive \(\varphi\) (a leading signal). Moving φ rotates the phasor and slides the trace along \(t\) without changing its shape; moving ω changes how fast the vector turns and how compressed the trace is, but not the phasor. That is why phasor analysis can drop \(e^{j\omega t}\) altogether: in a linear circuit at one frequency, every voltage and current rotates at the same rate, and only the photographs at \(t = 0\) differ.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
\[ p(t) = 2VI \cos\omega t \cos(\omega t - \varphi) = VI\cos\varphi + VI\cos(2\omega t - \varphi), \]

by the product-to-sum identity: a constant term \(P = VI\cos\varphi\) and a cosine at twice the supply frequency whose amplitude is \(VI = S\), regardless of \(\varphi\). instantaneous_power.sample_power(230, 10, 36.87) samples one period at 50 Hz with 2 000 points; mean_and_swing returns a mean of 1840.0 W (against \(VI\cos\varphi = 1840.0\) W) and a swing \((\max - \min)/2\) of 2300.0 VA (against \(VI = 2300\) VA). The minimum of \(p(t)\) is \(-460\) W: twice per period the load returns energy to the source, which is what a non-unity power factor means in the time domain. The test also checks that the spectrum of \(p(t) - P\) peaks at the second harmonic. A plot of \(p(t)\) with the mean drawn as a horizontal line shows the 100 Hz ripple around \(P\) (figure in examples.ipynb, not saved).

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
From the worked example, \(Q_{12} = (V_1^2 - V_1 V_2 \cos\delta) / X\). At \(\delta = 0\), \(Q_{12} = V_1 (V_1 - V_2) / X\), which is positive when \(V_1 > V_2\) and negative otherwise: reactive power leaves the bus whose voltage magnitude is higher. transfer_power(1.05, 1.0, 0.1, 0.0) gives \(Q_{12} = +0.525\) pu and transfer_power(1.0, 1.05, 0.1, 0.0) gives \(-0.500\) pu (the two are not opposite numbers because \(Q\) at the sending end also includes the reactive power absorbed by the reactance itself, \(|I|^2 X\)).

The DC approximation makes two assumptions, and each one kills \(Q\) in its own way. First, flat voltages \(V_1 = V_2 = 1\): then \(Q_{12} = (1 - \cos\delta) / X \approx \delta^2 / (2X)\), second order in the angle, while \(P_{12} \approx \delta / X\) is first order. At \(\delta = 10^\circ\) with \(X = 0.1\) pu, \(Q_{12} = 0.152\) pu against \(P_{12} = 1.74\) pu, and a linearization around \(\delta = 0\) keeps only first-order terms, so \(Q\) drops to zero. Second, the DC model does not solve for voltage magnitudes at all: it has no unknown that reactive power could determine. In the AC equations \(Q\) is tied to the magnitudes (as the first part of the exercise shows) and \(P\) to the angles; the DC model keeps the \(P\)–\(\theta\) half and discards the \(Q\)–\(V\) half. The price is that the DC limits ToOp uses must be given in MW, which is Exercise 6.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
Nodes 0 (ground), 1 and 2. The circuit in ac_nodal.py has a voltage source holding node 1 at \(V_1 = 230\angle 0\) V, a current source injecting \(I_2 = 5\angle{-30^\circ}\) A into node 2, an RL branch \(Z_{RL} = 2 + j5\ \Omega\) between nodes 1 and 2 and an RC branch \(Z_{RC} = 10 - j4\ \Omega\) from node 2 to ground. The admittance matrix is \(Y = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(1/Z)\, A\), exactly as in Chapter 8 with \(1/Z\) instead of \(g\). Node 1 has a known voltage, so its row leaves the system and its column goes to the right-hand side: KCL at node 2 alone reads \(Y_{22} V_2 = I_2 - Y_{21} V_1\), giving \(V_2 = 225.14\angle{-22.8^\circ}\) V. The product \(Y V\) then returns the net injection at every node; at node 1 it is the current the voltage source must supply, \(I_1 = 16.71\angle 7.4^\circ\) A, which is also the RL branch current, and the RC branch carries \(20.90\angle{-1.0^\circ}\) A.

The power balance is Tellegen's theorem in complex form: \(\sum_k V_k I_k^* = \sum_b |I_b|^2 Z_b\). Both sides are \(4927.9 - j351.9\) VA: the sources deliver 4 928 W, all dissipated in the two resistors, and the circuit as a whole is slightly capacitive (the RC branch's \(-j4\ \Omega\) with its larger current outweighs the \(+j5\ \Omega\) of the RL branch). The test checks the balance to \(10^{-9}\). The same circuit in Octave, with Y \ I replaced by the one-unknown division, is ac_nodal.m:

ac_nodal.m
function [V, Iinj, Ib, Sin, Sabs] = ac_nodal(fr, to, z, V1, I2)
  % Complex nodal analysis of the three-node circuit of Chapter 9, Exercise 5: node 1 is ground, node 2
  % is held at V1 by a voltage source, node 3 receives the current I2; branches have impedances z between
  % nodes fr and to (indices from 1). Returns the node voltages, the net injections Y * V (the second one
  % is the current of the voltage source), the branch currents and the injected and absorbed complex power.
  m = numel(fr);
  A = zeros(m, 3);
  A(sub2ind([m 3], 1:m, fr)) = 1;
  A(sub2ind([m 3], 1:m, to)) = -1;
  Y = A' * diag(1 ./ z) * A;
  V = [0; V1; (I2 - Y(3, 2) * V1) / Y(3, 3)];
  Iinj = Y * V;
  Ib = (V(fr) - V(to)) ./ z(:);
  Sin = sum(V(2:3) .* conj(Iinj(2:3)));
  Sabs = sum(abs(Ib).^2 .* z(:));
end

%!test
%! [V, Iinj, Ib, Sin, Sabs] = ac_nodal([2 3], [3 1], [2 + 5i, 10 - 4i], 230, 5 * exp(-1i * pi / 6));
%! assert(V(1), 0)
%! assert(V(2), 230)
%! assert(Sin, Sabs, 1e-9)                              % Tellegen: injected equals absorbed
%! assert(abs(Ib(1)), abs(Iinj(2)), 1e-9)               % the voltage source current flows through RL
%! assert(Iinj(1) + Iinj(2) + Iinj(3), 0, 1e-9)         % KCL over the whole circuit

docs.title: Exercise 6
docs.text:
The branch can carry at most \(|S| = V I_{\max}\). At power factor 0.95 the admissible active power is \(P_{\text{adm}} = 0.95\, V I_{\max}\), while the DC model allows \(P_{\max} = V I_{\max}\). The overestimate, relative to what the branch can really carry, is

\[ \frac{P_{\max}}{P_{\text{adm}}} - 1 = \frac{1}{0.95} - 1 = 5.26\ \% \]

(dc_limit_overestimate(0.95)), or 5 % if measured against \(P_{\max}\) itself. A DC flow at exactly 100 % of the limit therefore corresponds to a current 5.3 % above the rating once the reactive part is added, which is one of the reasons ToOp's DC results are checked with an AC power flow before they are trusted (Chapter 19).

docs.title: Chapter 10. Three-phase systems and the per-unit system
docs.text:
Weeks: 1.5 · Semester: 2 · Prerequisites: Chapter 9

Why it matters for ToOp

Limits are converted between current and power with \(P = \sqrt{3}\, V_{LL} I\): the PowSyBl preprocessing computes p_limit as current limit × limit voltage × 1e-3 × sqrt(3) (dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_helpers.py). The cascade relay model uses phase voltages \(V_{LL}/\sqrt{3}\) to compute impedances (contingency/pandapower/cascade/detection/switch_preparation.py). Network data is converted to per unit, and the phase-shift distribution factors are scaled by the base power, base_mva * (np.pi / 180) * psdf (dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/psdf.py, with the base from get_base_mva in dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_backend.py). ToOp's AC metrics also report voltage-angle differences (max_va_diff_n_0, docs/topology_optimizer/metrics.md); why the angle across an open breaker matters for closing it (synchro-check) is left to Chapter 20.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Balanced three-phase sources and loads; wye and delta; line vs phase quantities; three-phase power \(S_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}\, V_{LL} I_L\), \(P = \sqrt{3}\, V_{LL} I_L \cos\varphi\).
  • The operator \(a = e^{j2\pi/3}\) (revisits the roots of unity of Chapter 1); per-phase equivalent circuit.
  • Per-unit system: base quantities, change of base, per-unit transformer models.
  • Symmetrical components (awareness level; used for faults, not by ToOp).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Draw the phasor diagram of a balanced three-phase set and derive \(|V_{LL}| = \sqrt{3}\,|V_{\text{ph}}|\) and the \(30^\circ\) shift.
  • Convert current limits to power limits and back at a given voltage and power factor.
  • Convert impedances to per unit and change the base of a per-unit value.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• Courses and videos:
  • NPTEL Fundamentals of Electrical Engineering (IIT Kharagpur, Das) https://nptel.ac.in/courses/108105112. Lectures 47–50 "Three phase circuits".
  • NPTEL Power System Analysis (IIT Kharagpur, Sinha) https://nptel.ac.in/courses/108105067. Lecture 2 "Introduction to Single Line Diagram" (per-unit system, change of base, a worked example) and, at awareness level, Lecture 26 "Symmetrical Component Analysis".
  • Free texts: Kuphaldt Vol. II, Ch. 10 "Polyphase AC Circuits"; MIT 6.061 notes Ch. 3 (polyphase networks) and Ch. 4 (symmetrical components); Overbye, ECEN 615 Lecture 3 slides (per unit, Ybus) https://overbye.engr.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/146/2022/09/Lecture-3.pdf.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
With a three-phase base power \(S_{\text{base}}\) and a line-to-line base voltage \(V_{\text{base}}\):

\[ Z_{\text{base}} = \frac{V_{\text{base}}^2}{S_{\text{base}}}, \qquad I_{\text{base}} = \frac{S_{\text{base}}}{\sqrt{3}\, V_{\text{base}}}, \qquad z_{\text{pu}} = \frac{Z}{Z_{\text{base}}}, \qquad z_{\text{pu,new}} = z_{\text{pu,old}} \left(\frac{V_{\text{base,old}}}{V_{\text{base,new}}}\right)^2 \frac{S_{\text{base,new}}}{S_{\text{base,old}}}. \]
  • A 380 kV line rated 1 000 A carries at most \(P = \sqrt{3} \cdot 380\ \text{kV} \cdot 1000\ \text{A} \approx 658\) MW at unity power factor.
  • A 220 kV line of 100 km with \(x = 0.4\ \Omega/\text{km}\) has \(X = 40\ \Omega\). On a 100 MVA base, \(Z_{\text{base}} = 220^2/100 = 484\ \Omega\), so \(x_{\text{pu}} = 40/484 \approx 0.0826\), and \(I_{\text{base}} \approx 262\) A.
  • A transformer with \(x = 0.10\) pu on its own 50 MVA rating has \(x = 0.10 \cdot 100/50 = 0.20\) pu on a 100 MVA system base (same voltage base).

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: three-phase phasors and a per-unit branch table

Tools: GeoGebra Classic, then Jupyter + pandas + NumPy.

  1. In GeoGebra, define V_a = 1 + 0i, V_b = V_a (cos(-120°) + i sin(-120°)) and V_c = V_a (cos(120°) + i sin(120°)), and draw them with Vector(V_a) and so on. Add V_ab = V_a - V_b and check abs(V_ab) and arg(V_ab): \(\sqrt{3}\) and \(30^\circ\).
  2. Add a slider φ and balanced currents I_a = V_a (cos(-φ) + i sin(-φ)), and likewise for I_b and I_c. Check that I_a + I_b + I_c = 0 for every φ (no neutral current), and read the power factor angle between each voltage and its current.
  3. In a notebook, build a pandas DataFrame of branches with columns name, v_kv, length_km, r_ohm_per_km, x_ohm_per_km, i_max_a, for example a 380 kV line of 150 km (0.03, 0.30 Ω/km, 2 000 A), a 220 kV line of 100 km (0.06, 0.40 Ω/km, 1 000 A) and a 110 kV cable of 20 km (0.05, 0.12 Ω/km, 600 A). Add columns for \(Z_{\text{base}}\), \(r_{\text{pu}}\), \(x_{\text{pu}}\) on a 100 MVA base and the limit in MW at unity power factor.
  4. Compare your MW column with the formula used in ToOp's powsybl_helpers.py (value * limit_voltage * 1e-3 * math.sqrt(3)) and state the units each factor assumes.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
All statements are also in exercises.ipynb; the worked examples run in examples.ipynb.

  1. A balanced wye load has \(Z_Y = 30 + j40\ \Omega\) per phase on a 400 V (line-to-line) supply. Compute the line current, total \(P\) and \(Q\), and the equivalent delta impedance \(Z_\Delta = 3 Z_Y\). (Pen and paper)

    Solution: Exercise 1.

  2. Verify numerically that the instantaneous total power of a balanced three-phase set is constant in time, unlike single-phase power. (Jupyter: NumPy + matplotlib)

    Solution: Exercise 2.

  3. The cascade relay model computes a phase voltage \(V_{LL}/\sqrt{3}\), an impedance magnitude \(|Z| = V_{\text{ph}}/I\) and an angle \(\operatorname{atan2}(Q, P)\) (get_complex_impedance in contingency/pandapower/cascade/detection/switch_preparation.py). Compute \(R\) and \(X\) seen by a relay at 380 kV with \(I = 1\,000\) A, \(P = 600\) MW and \(Q = 200\) Mvar. (Pen and paper) Answer: \(|Z| \approx 219.4\ \Omega\), \(R \approx 208.1\ \Omega\), \(X \approx 69.4\ \Omega\).

    Solution: Exercise 3.

  4. A 1 600 MVA transformer has \(x = 0.15\) pu on its own rating. Express it on a 100 MVA base, and explain why the per-unit value does not depend on which side's voltage base is used when bases are chosen through the turns ratio. (Pen and paper)

    Solution: Exercise 4.

  5. Symmetrical components (awareness): with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & a^2 & a \\ 1 & a & a^2 \end{bmatrix}\), compute \(V_{012} = A^{-1} V_{abc}\) for a set where phase b has dropped to 0.9 pu. (Octave) Answer: \(|V_1| \approx 0.967\), \(|V_0| = |V_2| \approx 0.033\) pu.

    Solution: Exercise 5.

docs.title: Chapter 10 – Solutions
docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 10. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: per_unit.py (bases, change of base, the branch table and the MW limit of the lab, Exercise 4), three_phase.py (balanced phasors, the wye load, instantaneous power, the relay impedance and the symmetrical components of Exercises 1, 2, 3 and 5) and sym_components.m (Exercise 5 in Octave, as the statement asks). Each Python module prints every number quoted below when run as a script; the worked examples run live in examples.ipynb. The GeoGebra steps were not run here: for them the solution gives the construction and the values it must show, checked numerically.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. GeoGebra: line and phase voltages. With \(V_a = 1\), \(V_b = e^{-j120^\circ}\) and \(V_c = e^{j120^\circ}\), the difference \(V_{ab} = V_a - V_b = 1 - (-\tfrac12 - j\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}) = \tfrac32 + j\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) has magnitude \(\sqrt{9/4 + 3/4} = \sqrt3\) and argument \(\arctan(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} / \tfrac32) = 30^\circ\): abs(V_ab) shows 1.7321 and arg(V_ab) shows \(30^\circ\) (three_phase.line_voltages(balanced_set())). The geometry is the isosceles triangle \(V_a\), \(V_b\), \(V_{ab}\) with a \(120^\circ\) apex: the base is \(2 \sin 60^\circ = \sqrt3\) times the side, and the base is tilted \(30^\circ\) from \(V_a\), halfway between \(V_a\) and \(-V_b\). The same holds for \(V_{bc}\) and \(V_{ca}\), each \(120^\circ\) further on, so line voltages are also a balanced set, \(\sqrt3\) larger and \(30^\circ\) ahead of the phase voltages. (Construction not run here.)
  2. GeoGebra: balanced currents. I_a = V_a (cos(-φ) + i sin(-φ)) and its two companions form a balanced set rotated by \(-\varphi\), so \(I_a + I_b + I_c = (1 + a^2 + a)\, e^{-j\varphi} = 0\) for every φ: the neutral carries nothing (numerically \(4 \times 10^{-16}\) for \(\varphi = 30^\circ\)). The angle between each voltage and its current is the same \(\varphi\) in all three phases (balanced_set()[1] / balanced_set(1, -phi)[1] is at \(\varphi\)), which is why one power factor describes the whole load and why the per-phase equivalent circuit of a balanced system loses nothing. (Construction not run here.)

  3. The per-unit branch table. per_unit.branch_table() adds the columns to the branch list:

    per_unit.py (branch table)
    BRANCHES = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        'name': ['380 kV line', '220 kV line', '110 kV cable'],
        'v_kv': [380.0, 220.0, 110.0],
        'length_km': [150.0, 100.0, 20.0],
        'r_ohm_per_km': [0.03, 0.06, 0.05],
        'x_ohm_per_km': [0.30, 0.40, 0.12],
        'i_max_a': [2000.0, 1000.0, 600.0],
    }
)


def branch_table(branches: pd.DataFrame = BRANCHES, s_mva: float = S_BASE_MVA) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add Z_base, the per-unit resistance and reactance on ``s_mva`` and the MW limit at unity power factor."""
    out = branches.copy()
    out['z_base_ohm'] = out.v_kv**2 / s_mva
    out['r_pu'] = out.r_ohm_per_km * out.length_km / out.z_base_ohm
    out['x_pu'] = out.x_ohm_per_km * out.length_km / out.z_base_ohm
    out['p_limit_mw'] = out.i_max_a * out.v_kv * 1e-3 * math.sqrt(3)
    return out

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

    Branch \(Z_{\text{base}}\) (\(\Omega\)) \(r_{\text{pu}}\) \(x_{\text{pu}}\) limit (MW) 380 kV line, 150 km, 2 000 A 1 444 0.0031 0.0312 1 316.4 220 kV line, 100 km, 1 000 A 484 0.0124 0.0826 381.1 110 kV cable, 20 km, 600 A 121 0.0083 0.0198 114.3

    Two things the table teaches. First, the 380 kV line is 45 \(\Omega\) of reactance and the cable 2.4 \(\Omega\), yet in per unit the cable is "closer" to the line than the ohms suggest, because the base impedance falls with the square of the voltage: per unit measures a branch against what its own voltage level can carry. Second, the 220 kV line reproduces the worked example (\(x_{\text{pu}} = 0.0826\)). 4. ToOp's formula. value * limit_voltage * 1e-3 * math.sqrt(3) is \(\sqrt3\, V_{LL} I\) with value in ampere and limit_voltage in kilovolt: A × kV = kVA, and 1e-3 turns kVA into MVA, so the result is the three-phase apparent power in MVA at the current limit, used as a MW limit at unity power factor (the dc_power_factor of Chapter 9). The p_limit_mw column uses the same product in the same units and agrees to machine precision (test_toop_formula_matches_table). The factor \(\sqrt3\) is there because the limit is a line current and the voltage a line-to-line value; with phase voltages it would be \(3 V_{\text{ph}} I\).

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
The phase voltage is \(V_{\text{ph}} = 400 / \sqrt3 = 230.94\) V and \(|Z_Y| = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50\ \Omega\) at \(53.13^\circ\), so the line current (equal to the phase current in a wye) is \(I_L = 230.94 / 50 = 4.619\) A, lagging its phase voltage by \(53.13^\circ\). The total power is three times the per-phase power:

\[ S = 3\, |I_L|^2 Z_Y = 3 \times 21.33 \times (30 + j40) = 1920 + j2560\ \text{VA}, \qquad |S| = 3200\ \text{VA} = \sqrt3 \times 400 \times 4.619 . \]

\(P = 1920\) W, \(Q = 2560\) var, power factor \(0.6\) lagging. The equivalent delta impedance is \(Z_\Delta = 3 Z_Y = 90 + j120\ \Omega\): a delta branch sees the line voltage, \(\sqrt3\) times larger, and carries the phase current, \(1/\sqrt3\) of the line current, so it must be 3 times the wye impedance to draw the same power (three_phase.wye_load).

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text: For a balanced load, \(p_a(t) = VI\cos\varphi + VI\cos(2\omega t - \varphi)\) as in Chapter 9, Exercise 3, and \(p_b\), \(p_c\) are the same expression with \(\omega t\) shifted by \(\mp 120^\circ\), so their pulsating terms are shifted by \(\mp 240^\circ\), that is by \(\pm 120^\circ\): three equal cosines \(120^\circ\) apart, which add to zero, as the phasors of lab step 2 do. What remains is \(p_a + p_b + p_c = 3 VI \cos\varphi\), constant. three_phase.instantaneous_power(230, 10, 30) samples one period: each phase power swings by \(\pm 2300\) W around its mean while the total stays at \(5975.6\) W to nine digits (min and max are both 5 975.6 W, against \(3 \times 230 \times 10 \times \cos 30^\circ = 5975.6\) W). This is the mechanical reason for three-phase transmission: a three-phase generator delivers constant torque, a single-phase one pulsates at 100 Hz. The figure in examples.ipynb shows the three pulsating curves and the flat total (not saved).

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
\(V_{\text{ph}} = 380 / \sqrt3 = 219.39\) kV, so \(|Z| = V_{\text{ph}} / I = 219\,393 / 1000 = 219.4\ \Omega\). The angle is \(\operatorname{atan2}(200, 600) = 18.43^\circ\), hence

\[ R = 219.4 \cos 18.43^\circ = 208.1\ \Omega, \qquad X = 219.4 \sin 18.43^\circ = 69.4\ \Omega \]

(three_phase.relay_impedance(380, 1000, 600, 200)). Two remarks on the model. The impedance angle is the angle of \(S = P + jQ\), which is the angle of \(V I^*\) and therefore of \(V/I\): \(\operatorname{atan2}(Q, P)\) is exactly the impedance angle, and it is positive (inductive) for a lagging load. And the magnitude uses the phase voltage because a distance relay measures phase voltage over phase current; using \(V_{LL}\) would overstate \(|Z|\) by \(\sqrt3\), the same factor as in lab step 4.

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
Change of base at the same voltage: \(x = 0.15 \times 100 / 1600 = 0.009375\) pu, under one percent. The transformer looks small on the system base because 100 MVA is a small load for a 1 600 MVA unit; the ohms did not change.

Why the side does not matter: let the ratio be \(380/110\) kV with bases \(V_{\text{HV}} = 380\) kV and \(V_{\text{LV}} = 110\) kV, chosen through the turns ratio, and the same \(S_{\text{base}}\) on both sides. An ohmic reactance \(X_{\text{HV}}\) on the high-voltage side is \(X_{\text{LV}} = X_{\text{HV}} (110/380)^2\) referred to the low-voltage side (Chapter 11, Exercise 1), while the base impedances are in the ratio \(Z_{\text{base,HV}} / Z_{\text{base,LV}} = (380/110)^2\): 90.25 \(\Omega\) against 7.5625 \(\Omega\) on 1 600 MVA, a ratio of 11.934 = \((380/110)^2\) (per_unit.main). Dividing, \(X_{\text{HV}} / Z_{\text{base,HV}} = X_{\text{LV}} / Z_{\text{base,LV}}\): the referral factor and the base factor are the same \((V_{\text{HV}}/V_{\text{LV}})^2\) and cancel. In per unit the ideal transformer disappears from the circuit; test_exercise_4_change_of_base_is_independent_of_side checks the two routes to 0.009375. The argument fails as soon as the voltage bases are not in the turns ratio (an off-nominal tap, say): then a residual ratio stays in the model, which is what ToOp's \(x/\rho\) in Chapter 11 accounts for.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
With \(a = e^{j120^\circ}\) and \(V_{abc} = (1,\ 0.9 a^2,\ a)\), \(A^{-1} = \tfrac13 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & a^2 & a \end{bmatrix}\) gives

\[ V_0 = \tfrac13 (1 + 0.9 a^2 + a) = -\tfrac{0.1}{3} a^2, \quad V_1 = \tfrac13 (1 + 0.9 a^3 + a^3) = \tfrac{2.9}{3}, \quad V_2 = \tfrac13 (1 + 0.9 a^4 + a^2) = -\tfrac{0.1}{3} a, \]

using \(a^3 = 1\) and \(1 + a + a^2 = 0\): \(|V_1| = 0.9667\) and \(|V_0| = |V_2| = 0.0333\) pu. The 10 % dip of one phase is mostly a 3.3 % loss of positive sequence plus equal 3.3 % zero and negative sequences, which is how protection sees an unbalance. sym_components.m is the Octave solution the statement asks for; three_phase.symmetrical_components gives the same numbers in Python and examples.ipynb runs it.

sym_components.m
function [V012, A] = sym_components(Vabc)
  % Symmetrical components V012 = A \ Vabc of a three-phase set, with a = exp(2i pi / 3) and
  % A = [1 1 1; 1 a^2 a; 1 a a^2] (Chapter 10, Exercise 5). Vabc is a column of three phasors.
  a = exp(2i * pi / 3);
  A = [1 1 1; 1 a^2 a; 1 a a^2];
  V012 = A \ Vabc(:);
end

%!test
%! a = exp(2i * pi / 3);
%! V012 = sym_components([1; a^2; a]);                 % balanced set: positive sequence only
%! assert(abs(V012), [0; 1; 0], 1e-12)
%! V012 = sym_components([1; 0.9 * a^2; a]);           % phase b at 0.9 pu
%! assert(abs(V012), [0.0333; 0.9667; 0.0333], 5e-5)
%! [V012, A] = sym_components([1; 0.9 * a^2; a]);
%! assert(A * V012, [1; 0.9 * a^2; a], 1e-12)          % the transform inverts

docs.title: Chapter 11. Transformers, phase-shifting transformers, machines and HVDC
docs.text:
Weeks: 3 · Semester: 2 · Prerequisites: Chapter 10

Why it matters for ToOp

PST tap optimization is one of ToOp's four action types. The solver models PSTs through the phase-shift distribution factor (dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/psdf.py) and writes the angle of the selected tap, read from a per-tap table, into the nodal injection vector (dc_solver/jax/pst.py); per-tap susceptances cover PSTs whose reactance changes with the tap. The PowSyBl importer flags a PST as linear in DC when its reactance is the same at every tap (get_linear_pst in dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_helpers.py). How tap tables enter the sensitivity updates is taught in Chapter 18. Transformer ratios enter the DC reactance as \(x/\rho\) (get_trafos in the same file). In the pandapower backend, three-winding transformers are represented around an auxiliary star bus and their outage is a multi-outage (get_trafo3w_multioutage in dc_solver/preprocess/pandapower/pandapower_backend.py); the PowSyBl backend asserts that there are none (dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_backend.py). HVDC converter stations (LCC and VSC) and batteries are fixed injections (_get_injections in powsybl_backend.py).

Awareness: HVDC setpoints exist in the action-set schema (HVDCRange with min_power and max_power in interfaces/stored_action_set.py), but the field is documented as "currently not implemented yet in the solver", and preprocessing always writes hvdc_ranges=[] (dc_solver/preprocess/network_data.py). Other topology optimization tools may optimize them.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Magnetic circuits; ideal and real transformers; equivalent circuits; T vs π models.
  • Tap changers and off-nominal turns ratios; phase-shifting transformers (symmetric and asymmetric; tap tables; linear vs non-linear steps). The phase shift is a multiplication by \(e^{j\alpha}\) (revisits Chapter 1); ToOp's tap tables are detailed in Chapter 18.
  • Three-winding transformers and the star equivalent.
  • Synchronous generator at awareness level: voltage and reactive power control (PV behavior).
  • Power electronics, HVDC (LCC and VSC), SVCs and batteries at awareness level; HVDC links as controllable pairs of injections.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Refer impedances across an ideal transformer and build the star equivalent of a three-winding transformer.
  • Draw the phasor diagram of symmetric and quadrature PSTs and compute the phase shift and magnitude change of a tap step.
  • Show with the DC model that the flow through a PST branch in a meshed network is affine in the phase shift \(\alpha\), and compute its slope.
