docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Buses 1 and 2 are joined by two parallel paths: line \(a\) (reactance \(x_a\)) in series with an ideal PST that advances the voltage on its side by \(\alpha\), and line \(b\) (reactance \(x_b\)). Bus 1 injects \(P\) and bus 2 withdraws it. In the DC model, with \(\theta_{12} = \theta_1 - \theta_2\) and \(\alpha\) in radians,

\[ F_a = \frac{\theta_{12} + \alpha}{x_a}, \qquad F_b = \frac{\theta_{12}}{x_b}, \qquad F_a + F_b = P \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_a = \frac{x_b}{x_a + x_b}\,P + \frac{\alpha}{x_a + x_b}. \]

The flow is affine in \(\alpha\): a base share of \(P\) plus a loop flow \(\alpha/(x_a + x_b)\) that circulates through both lines. With \(x_a = 0.1\) pu, \(x_b = 0.3\) pu and \(P = 1\) pu, \(F_a = 0.75\) pu at \(\alpha = 0\) and each degree adds \((\pi/180)/0.4 \approx 0.0436\) pu, 4.36 MW on a 100 MVA base; this is why ToOp scales its PSDF by base_mva * (np.pi / 180). With a single line and no parallel path, the PST could not change the flow at all. The sign of \(\alpha\) here is a modeling choice; ToOp's sign conventions are covered in Chapters 17 and 18.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: phase shifters as phasors and as loop flows

Tools: GeoGebra Classic, then Jupyter + NumPy + matplotlib (reusing nodal_solve from the Chapter 8 lab).

  1. In GeoGebra, let U = 1 + 0i be the input voltage and k a slider in \([-0.2, 0.2]\). A quadrature booster adds a voltage perpendicular to the input: W_q = U + k i U. A symmetric PST rotates the input: W_s = U (cos(α) + i sin(α)) with α = arg(W_q). Compare abs(W_q) and abs(W_s) and explain why the symmetric design keeps the magnitude.
  2. Add a slider φ for the step angle and the general series voltage W_g = U + k (cos(φ) + i sin(φ)). Check arg(W_g) against the formula of Chapter 1, Exercise 4.
  3. In a notebook, compute \(F_a\) and \(F_b\) of the worked example for \(\alpha\) from \(-10^\circ\) to \(10^\circ\), plot them and check the slope. At which \(\alpha\) does line \(b\) carry no flow, and when does its flow reverse?
  4. Model the PST as an equivalent pair of injections: \(-\alpha/x_a\) at bus 1 and \(+\alpha/x_a\) at bus 2, plus \(\alpha/x_a\) added back to line \(a\)'s flow. Verify with nodal_solve that this gives the same flows as the direct formula.
  5. Put a PST on branch (1, 3) of the Chapter 2 network (with susceptances instead of conductances) and compute the change of every branch flow per degree by finite differences. This column of sensitivities is what ToOp's PSDF stores.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
All statements are also in exercises.ipynb; the worked examples run in examples.ipynb.

  1. An ideal 380/110 kV transformer feeds a 10 Ω impedance on its 110 kV side. What impedance is seen from the 380 kV side? (Pen and paper) Answer: \(10 \cdot (380/110)^2 \approx 119.3\ \Omega\).

    Solution: Exercise 1.

  2. ToOp replaces a transformer's reactance \(x\) by \(x/\rho\) in the DC model (get_trafos in dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_helpers.py, commented as equivalent to PowSyBl's dc_use_transformer_ratio = True). For \(\rho = 1.05\), by what percentage does the branch susceptance change, and does the transformer attract more or less flow in a meshed network? (Pen and paper)

    Solution: Exercise 2.

  3. A three-winding transformer has pairwise short-circuit reactances \(x_{12} = 0.10\), \(x_{13} = 0.25\) and \(x_{23} = 0.20\) pu on a common base. Compute the star equivalent \(x_1 = (x_{12} + x_{13} - x_{23})/2\) and its cyclic permutations, and explain why an outage of this transformer removes three branches at once. (Pen and paper) Answer: \(x_1 = 0.075\), \(x_2 = 0.025\), \(x_3 = 0.175\) pu.

    Solution: Exercise 3.

  4. Build two tap tables with pandas for a PST with taps \(-16 \dots 16\): one with constant \(x\) and \(\alpha\) from the atan2 formula of Chapter 1 (1% per step at \(90^\circ\)), one where \(x\) grows by 1% per tap away from neutral. Apply the same test as get_linear_pst in DC mode (np.allclose on x) to each. Is \(\alpha\) exactly proportional to the tap number in the first table? (Jupyter: pandas + NumPy)

    Solution: Exercise 4.

  5. Draw the phasor diagram of a symmetric PST and a quadrature booster with the same phase shift in GeoGebra, and measure the output magnitude of each. (GeoGebra)

    Solution: Exercise 5.

  6. An HVDC link between buses 1 and 3 of a three-bus AC ring is a pair of injections \(-P_{dc}\) at bus 1 and \(+P_{dc}\) at bus 3. With nodal_solve, show that every AC branch flow is affine in \(P_{dc}\) and find the setpoint that unloads the most loaded AC line. Why would optimizing \(P_{dc}\) be a continuous action, unlike a busbar split? (Jupyter: NumPy + matplotlib)

    Solution: Exercise 6.

docs.title: Chapter 11 – Solutions
docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 11. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: dc_nodal.py (the nodal_solve of the Chapter 8 lab, with susceptances), pst_flows.py (the worked example, lab steps 3 to 5), pst_phasors.py (lab steps 1 and 2, Exercise 5), trafo_equivalents.py and trafo_equivalents.m (Exercises 1 to 3), tap_tables.py (Exercise 4) and hvdc_ring.py (Exercise 6). Each Python module prints every number quoted below when run as a script; the worked examples run live in examples.ipynb. The GeoGebra steps were not run here: for them the solution gives the construction and the values it must show, checked numerically.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. GeoGebra: quadrature booster against symmetric PST. W_q = U + k i U adds a voltage perpendicular to U, so \(W_q = U(1 + jk)\): its argument is \(\alpha = \arctan k\) and its magnitude \(|U|\sqrt{1 + k^2}\), always larger than \(|U|\). W_s = U (cos(α) + i sin(α)) is \(U e^{j\alpha}\), a pure rotation: abs(W_s) stays at 1 for every k. pst_phasors.quadrature_booster and symmetric_pst give, for \(k = 0.05\), \(0.1\) and \(0.2\), shifts of \(2.862^\circ\), \(5.711^\circ\) and \(11.310^\circ\) with \(|W_q| = 1.0012\), \(1.0050\) and \(1.0198\), and \(|W_s| = 1.0000\) in each case. The symmetric design keeps the magnitude because its series voltage is not perpendicular to the input but to the bisector of input and output: the triangle \(U\), \(W_s\), \(W_s - U\) is isosceles, so the output lies on the same circle as the input. A quadrature booster is cheaper (one series winding fed from a quadrature voltage) and its small magnitude change, second order in \(k\), is accepted. (Construction not run here.)
  2. GeoGebra: the general series voltage. W_g = U + k (cos(φ) + i sin(φ)) with \(U = 1\) has argument \(\operatorname{atan2}(k\sin\varphi,\ 1 + k\cos\varphi)\), the formula of Chapter 1, Exercise 4, and magnitude \(\sqrt{(1 + k\cos\varphi)^2 + (k\sin\varphi)^2}\). pst_phasors.series_voltage(1, 0.05, phi) against phase_shift_deg(0.05, phi): at \(\varphi = 90^\circ\) both give \(2.862^\circ\) with \(|W_g| = 1.0012\) (the quadrature booster of step 1), at \(\varphi = 60^\circ\) both give \(2.419^\circ\) with \(|W_g| = 1.0259\): a step angle below \(90^\circ\) buys less shift and more magnitude change for the same winding. The two values \(2.86^\circ\) and \(2.42^\circ\) are those of Chapter 1 (\(n = 5\) taps of 1 %). (Construction not run here.)

  3. \(F_a\) and \(F_b\) against \(\alpha\). pst_flows.two_path_flows evaluates the closed formula:

    \(\alpha\) \(F_a\) (pu) \(F_b\) (pu) \(-10^\circ\) 0.3137 0.6863 \(-5^\circ\) 0.5318 0.4682 \(0^\circ\) 0.7500 0.2500 \(5^\circ\) 0.9682 0.0318 \(10^\circ\) 1.1863 \(-0.1863\)

    Both lines are straight: \(F_a\) rises by \(0.0436\) pu per degree (slope_per_degree, \((\pi/180)/0.4\)) and \(F_b = P - F_a\) falls by the same amount; the sum is always 1 pu. Line \(b\) carries nothing when \(F_a = P\), that is when \(\theta_{12} = 0\): then \(F_a = \alpha / x_a = P\) gives \(\alpha = x_a P = 0.1\) rad \(= 5.73^\circ\) (alpha_for_zero_flow_b). Beyond it \(F_b\) is negative: the PST pushes more than the whole transfer through line \(a\) and the surplus comes back through line \(b\), a loop flow in the literal sense. At \(10^\circ\) line \(a\) carries 119 % of the transfer. 4. The PST as a pair of injections. With the PST removed, line \(a\) is a plain reactance and the network has injections \(P - \alpha/x_a\) at bus 1 and \(-(P - \alpha/x_a)\) at bus 2; nodal_solve gives \(\theta_{12} = (P - \alpha/x_a) / (1/x_a + 1/x_b)\) and the flows \(\theta_{12}/x_a\), \(\theta_{12}/x_b\). Adding \(\alpha/x_a\) back to line \(a\) gives \((\theta_{12} + \alpha)/x_a\), the PST branch's true flow:

    pst_flows.py (injections and PSDF)
    def two_path_by_injections(alpha_deg: float, p: float = P, x_a: float = X_A, x_b: float = X_B) -> tuple:
    """F_a and F_b from ``nodal_solve`` with the PST replaced by injections −α/x_a at bus 1 and +α/x_a at bus 2.

    The plain two-line network is solved with the modified injections; the PST's own branch then gets α/x_a
    added back, because the angle across its reactance is θ12 + α, not θ12.
    """
    shift = np.radians(alpha_deg) / x_a
    inj = np.array([p - shift, -p + shift])
    _, flows = nodal_solve([0, 0], [1, 1], [1 / x_a, 1 / x_b], inj, 2)
    return flows[0] + shift, flows[1]


def psdf_column(
    fr: np.ndarray, to: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, pst_branch: int, inj: np.ndarray, n: int, step_deg: float = 1.0
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Change of every branch flow per degree of a PST on ``pst_branch``, by finite differences.

    The DC model is linear, so the difference quotient is exact whatever the step and the injections; the
    column is what ToOp's PSDF stores for that transformer (before its base_mva × π/180 scaling).
    """
    shift = np.radians(step_deg) * b[pst_branch]
    inj_pst = np.array(inj, dtype=float)
    inj_pst[fr[pst_branch]] -= shift
    inj_pst[to[pst_branch]] += shift
    _, base = nodal_solve(fr, to, b, inj, n)
    _, shifted = nodal_solve(fr, to, b, inj_pst, n)
    shifted[pst_branch] += shift
    return (shifted - base) / step_deg

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

    two_path_by_injections agrees with two_path_flows to \(10^{-12}\) at every angle tested (the test runs \(-10^\circ\), \(-3^\circ\), \(0^\circ\), \(4.5^\circ\) and \(10^\circ\)). The equivalence is exact in the DC model because the PST equation \(F_a = (\theta_{12} + \alpha)/x_a\) is linear: the term \(\alpha/x_a\) is a constant flow entering bus 2 and leaving bus 1 through branch \(a\), and a constant flow through a branch is indistinguishable, for the rest of the network, from an injection pair at its ends. This is why ToOp can keep one nodal matrix for all taps and move the PST angle into the injection vector (dc_solver/jax/pst.py). 5. A PSDF column. psdf_column(FR, TO, B, 3, INJ, 6) puts the PST on branch (1, 3) of the Chapter 2 network (branch index 3) and takes the difference quotient of the flows for a step of one degree:

    Branch base flow (pu) change per degree (pu) (0, 1) 0.3041 \(+0.00612\) (0, 2) 0.1959 \(-0.00612\) (1, 2) 0.0702 \(-0.01470\) (1, 3) 0.2339 \(+0.02082\) (2, 4) 0.7661 \(-0.02082\) (3, 4) 0.2339 \(+0.02082\) (4, 5) 1.0000 \(0\)

    The column is a circulation: it adds up to zero at every node (test_psdf_column_is_exact_and_step_independent checks \(A^\top \Delta F = 0\)), so it changes no injection, only the split of the flows among parallel paths. The PST pushes \(0.0208\) pu per degree through its own branch and on through (3, 4); the same amount returns through (2, 4), then back to node 1 partly through (1, 2) (\(0.0147\)) and partly around node 0 (\(0.0061\) through (0, 2) and (0, 1)). Branch (4, 5) does not react: node 5 is a leaf, so KCL fixes its flow at the 1 pu withdrawn there, whatever any PST does. The column is the same for a step of \(0.01^\circ\) and the same for zero injections (the test checks both), which is the point: in the linear DC model the sensitivity does not depend on the operating point, so ToOp computes it once in preprocessing (dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/psdf.py) and scales it by base_mva * (np.pi / 180) to get MW per degree, \(2.08\) MW per degree on 100 MVA for branch (1, 3) here.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
An impedance \(Z\) on the low-voltage side draws \(I_2 = V_2 / Z\); the ideal transformer carries \(V_1 = (380/110) V_2\) and \(I_1 = (110/380) I_2\), so from the high-voltage side

\[ Z' = \frac{V_1}{I_1} = \left(\frac{380}{110}\right)^2 \frac{V_2}{I_2} = \left(\frac{380}{110}\right)^2 Z = 11.934 \times 10 = 119.3\ \Omega \]

(trafo_equivalents.referred_impedance(10, 380, 110) gives \(119.34\ \Omega\)). Impedances scale with the square of the ratio because voltage goes up by the ratio and current down by it. This is also why per-unit values do not depend on the side (Chapter 10, Exercise 4): the base impedance scales by the same square.

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text: The DC susceptance of a branch is \(b = 1/x\). Replacing \(x\) by \(x/\rho\) gives \(b' = \rho / x = \rho\, b\), a change of \(\rho - 1 = +5\) % for \(\rho = 1.05\) (susceptance_change). A larger susceptance means a stiffer branch, so in a meshed network the transformer attracts more flow: in the two-path example with the transformer (\(x = 0.1\)) in parallel with a line (\(x = 0.3\)), its share of a 1 pu transfer rises from \(0.7500\) to \(0.7590\) (flow_share_with_ratio), a change of \(+1.2\) %, less than 5 % because the parallel path dilutes it: \(\rho b_t / (\rho b_t + b_\ell)\) against \(b_t / (b_t + b_\ell)\). A \(\rho\) below 1 would do the opposite. The sign of the effect depends on which side the reactance is referred to: PowSyBl's dc_use_transformer_ratio = True and ToOp's get_trafos make the same choice, which is what the comment in the code records.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
\[ x_1 = \frac{0.10 + 0.25 - 0.20}{2} = 0.075, \qquad x_2 = \frac{0.10 + 0.20 - 0.25}{2} = 0.025, \qquad x_3 = \frac{0.25 + 0.20 - 0.10}{2} = 0.175\ \text{pu}, \]

and indeed \(x_1 + x_2 = x_{12}\), \(x_1 + x_3 = x_{13}\), \(x_2 + x_3 = x_{23}\): each pairwise short-circuit test sees the two star branches in series, which is where the formula comes from (trafo_equivalents.star_equivalent; the Octave version is trafo_equivalents.m). A star branch can come out negative in real units when one winding sits between the other two; it is still a valid branch of the equivalent, only not a physical reactance.

The star node is not a busbar: it is a fictitious point inside one tank. A fault or a maintenance outage of the transformer removes the whole unit, so the three branches that meet at the star node disappear together, and leaving the star node connected to one of them would create a dangling node with no injection. That is why the pandapower backend turns the outage of a three-winding transformer into a multi-outage of three branches (get_trafo3w_multioutage), and why the PowSyBl backend simply refuses networks that contain one.

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
tap_tables.constant_x_table() builds taps \(-16 \dots 16\) with \(x = 0.1\) pu throughout and \(\alpha(n) = \operatorname{atan2}(0.01 n \sin 90^\circ,\ 1 + 0.01 n \cos 90^\circ) = \arctan(0.01 n)\); growing_x_table() keeps the same \(\alpha\) and sets \(x = 0.1\,(1 + 0.01 |n|)\), \(0.116\) pu at the end taps. is_linear_pst applies np.allclose(x, x[0]): True for the first table, False for the second. ToOp treats the first as linear in DC (one PSDF column, the angle in the injection vector) and needs per-tap susceptances for the second, as the chapter's ToOp note says.

\(\alpha\) is not exactly proportional to the tap number in the first table: \(\arctan\) grows more slowly than its argument. The shift per tap is \(0.5729^\circ\) at tap 1 and only \(0.5681^\circ\) at tap 16, where \(\alpha = 9.090^\circ\) against \(16 \times 0.5729^\circ = 9.167^\circ\) if it were proportional, a shortfall of \(0.08^\circ\) (0.8 %). It is proportional to third order, \(\alpha \approx 0.01 n - (0.01 n)^3/3\), which is why the first few taps look linear and the end taps do not. Since ToOp reads the angle of the selected tap from a table instead of multiplying a step by a tap number, this non-linearity costs it nothing; "linear" in get_linear_pst refers to the reactance, not to the angle.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text: (GeoGebra construction not run here.) Draw \(U = 1\), then for the quadrature booster the series voltage \(k\, jU\) perpendicular to \(U\) and the output \(W_q = U + jkU\); for the symmetric PST the output \(W_s = e^{j\alpha} U\) on the unit circle. The two outputs have the same argument when \(k = \tan\alpha\), so \(|W_q| = \sqrt{1 + \tan^2\alpha} = 1/\cos\alpha\) and \(|W_s| = 1\) (pst_phasors.quadrature_magnitude_for_shift): for \(\alpha = 5^\circ\), \(10^\circ\) and \(20^\circ\) the quadrature output measures \(1.0038\), \(1.0154\) and \(1.0642\) pu, the symmetric one \(1.0000\). In the diagram the symmetric PST's series voltage \(W_s - U\) is the chord of the unit circle, perpendicular to the bisector of the angle \(\alpha\) (so it is at \(90^\circ + \alpha/2\) from \(U\), not at \(90^\circ\)), and its length \(2\sin(\alpha/2)\) is slightly shorter than the quadrature booster's \(\tan\alpha\).

docs.title: Exercise 6
docs.text:
hvdc_ring.py uses the ring \(x_{12} = 0.10\), \(x_{23} = 0.15\), \(x_{13} = 0.20\) pu with a generator at bus 1 feeding loads of 0.6 pu at bus 2 and 0.4 pu at bus 3. The HVDC link is inj[0] -= p_dc, inj[2] += p_dc before nodal_solve (bus 1 is the slack, so the withdrawal at bus 1 is absorbed by the balance anyway). At \(P_{dc} = 0\) the AC flows are \(0.6444\) pu on L1-2, \(0.0444\) on L2-3 and \(0.3556\) on L1-3, and L1-2 is the most loaded line. Because the DC model is linear, \(F(P_{dc}) = F(0) + P_{dc}\, d\) with \(d = F(1) - F(0) = (-0.4444, -0.4444, -0.5556)\): every unit the link carries is a unit that no longer travels over the AC ring, \(0.444\) of it along the path 1–2–3 and \(0.556\) along L1-3, in inverse proportion to the path reactances (\(0.25\) and \(0.20\)). The test checks the affine law at three setpoints and the script at nine: the largest deviation is \(2 \times 10^{-16}\).

Unloading the most loaded line can mean two things. The flow on L1-2 reaches zero at \(P_{dc} = 0.6444/0.4444 = 1.45\) pu, but by then L1-3 carries \(-0.45\) pu backwards, so the line that was relieved has handed the problem to its neighbour. The sensible target is the setpoint that minimizes the largest AC flow, a one-variable linear program (best_setpoint, solved with scipy.optimize.linprog): \(P_{dc} = 0.775\) pu, where L1-2 carries \(+0.300\) pu, L2-3 \(-0.300\) pu and L1-3 \(-0.075\) pu. The maximum AC loading falls from \(0.644\) to \(0.300\) pu, and moving the setpoint \(0.1\) pu either way makes it worse again (the test checks both sides). The figure in examples.ipynb shows the three straight lines crossing and the setpoint where \(|F_{12}| = |F_{23}|\).

The HVDC setpoint is a continuous action: \(P_{dc}\) can take any value between the converter limits and every flow responds linearly and smoothly, so the optimization is a small linear program with a unique, interior optimum, as above. A busbar split is a discrete choice among configurations (Chapter 19 counted them): there is no "half a split", the flows jump from one topology to the next, and the problem becomes combinatorial. That difference is why ToOp's action-set schema reserves HVDCRange with min_power and max_power for the continuous variable, even though the solver does not optimize it yet, while busbar splits and PST taps are enumerated.

docs.title: Chapter 12. The power grid and its operation
docs.text:
Weeks: 1.5 · Semester: 2 · Prerequisites: Chapter 9

Why it matters for ToOp

ToOp is built by transmission system operators (Elia in Belgium, 50Hertz in Germany) for their operational processes: day-ahead congestion forecasts, border lines with neighboring TSOs, transformers to distribution grids, control and observation areas (importer/pypowsybl_import/, AreaSettings).

Topology optimization is one of the cheapest remedial actions an operator has: switching busbars costs almost nothing, while redispatch and countertrading cost hundreds of millions of euros per quarter in Germany alone (see the lab). Knowing who pays for congestion, and when in the planning timeline a topology can still be changed, explains why ToOp optimizes what it optimizes.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Generation, transmission, distribution; voltage levels; synchronous areas.
  • Roles: TSOs, DSOs, regulators, ENTSO-E; European grid codes (System Operation Guideline).
  • Electricity markets at awareness level: zonal markets, market coupling, nodal prices (LMP), redispatch.
  • Congestion: why it appears (renewables far from load, cross-border flows) and what it costs.
  • Remedial actions and their cost ranking: topology changes (busbar splitting, line switching), phase-shifter taps, redispatch, countertrading, curtailment.
  • Operational planning timeline: day-ahead congestion forecast (DACF), intraday, real time. The coordinated European processes (common grid models, capacity calculation, remedial action optimization) are covered in Chapter 21.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Describe the roles of TSOs, DSOs, regulators and ENTSO-E, and place DACF, intraday and real-time operation on a timeline.
  • Compute the dispatch, nodal prices, congestion rent and redispatch cost of a two-node market with a line limit.
  • Load public congestion-management and generation data with pandas and quantify the cost of congestion per MWh.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• Courses and videos:
  • Kirschen (University of Washington), lectures on his textbook Fundamentals of Power System Economics https://labs.ece.uw.edu/real/videos.html. Lectures 01–02 (introduction, organization of electricity markets) and 11 "Effect of transmission network" (markets with transmission constraints, locational marginal prices, financial transmission rights) cover the market part of this chapter.
  • PowerWorld Training playlist (vendor training, free on YouTube), "M1: Electricity Market Concepts" https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_HrmtpKBlPg.
  • MIT OCW 15.031J Energy Decisions, Markets, and Policies, Lecture 17 "(Yesterday's &) Today's Electric Power System" (Schmalensee) https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-031j-energy-decisions-markets-and-policies-spring-2012/resources/lecture-17-yesterday2019s-todays-electric-power-system/: grid architecture, transmission, baseload and peaking units, market models.
  • DelftX Smart Grids: Analysis, Automation and Data (TU Delft, Palensky, Rueda Torres et al.; free to audit) https://www.edx.org/learn/smart-grids/delft-university-of-technology-smart-grids-the-basics: how grids are monitored and operated, power flow, substation automation.
  • Coursera Electric Power Systems (University at Buffalo, Grinberg; introductory; paid, with a free trial; no free audit shown) https://www.coursera.org/learn/electric-power-systems.
  • MIT OCW 6.061 Introduction to Electric Power Systems (Kirtley), notes and problem sets (no videos) https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-061-introduction-to-electric-power-systems-spring-2011/.
  • Regulation: Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/1485, System Operation Guideline (SO GL): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/1485/oj/eng.
  • Data:
  • ENTSO-E Transparency Platform (load, generation, cross-border physical flows, congestion management data for all European bidding zones): https://transparency.entsoe.eu/.
  • SMARD, the Bundesnetzagentur's electricity market data portal (German generation, consumption, prices and quarterly congestion-management reports): https://www.smard.de/en; data download center https://www.smard.de/en/downloadcenter/download-market-data.
  • SMARD, "Congestion management in Q1 2026: lower volume of measures and costs" (volumes and estimated costs of redispatch and countertrading): https://www.smard.de/page/en/topic-article/5892/221272/lower-volume-of-measures-and-costs.
  • Textbooks:
  • von Meier, Electric Power Systems: A Conceptual Introduction (Berkeley), 2nd ed. 2024. The best qualitative entry point. NOT ON IA.
  • Kirschen, Power Systems: Fundamental Concepts and the Transition to Sustainability (Wiley 2024). NOT ON IA.
  • Kirschen & Strbac, Fundamentals of Power System Economics (6 syllabi, the markets reference). NOT ON IA.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: what congestion costs

Tools: Jupyter + pandas + matplotlib (Chapter 30).

  1. Read the SMARD congestion-management article for Q1 2026 (Resources). Put the reported figures in a small pandas DataFrame (quarter, total volume of measures in GWh, estimated cost in million euros, of which curtailment of renewables in GWh) for Q1 2025 and Q1 2026. Compute the average cost per MWh of congestion management and its change between the two quarters. The article reports 9,035 GWh and about 882 million euros for Q1 2025, and 8,248 GWh and about 784 million euros for Q1 2026.
  2. From the SMARD download center, export one winter week of hourly German electricity generation by source and total consumption as CSV. Inspect the header, delimiter and number format before parsing it with pandas.read_csv. Plot wind generation and consumption on the same axes, and plot the residual load (consumption minus wind and solar) as a duration curve.
  3. Mark the hours with high wind and low residual load. In a short paragraph, explain why these are the hours in which north–south transmission corridors congest, and which remedial actions (from the Topics list) an operator would try first.
  4. Optional: on the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform, look up the cross-border physical flows of Belgium or Germany for the same week and relate them to your plot.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
All statements are also in exercises.ipynb; the worked examples run in examples.ipynb.

  1. Two-node market, pen and paper. Node A has a generator with marginal cost 20 €/MWh and 1,000 MW capacity; node B has a generator with 60 €/MWh and 1,000 MW capacity and a load of 800 MW. The line A–B is limited to 500 MW. (a) Find the nodal-pricing dispatch, both nodal prices and the congestion rent. (b) A zonal market ignores the line limit: find its dispatch and price, then the redispatch needed to respect the limit and its cost. Hint: (a) 500 MW from A, 300 MW from B, prices 20 and 60 €/MWh, rent 20,000 €/h; (b) 800 MW from A, redispatch 300 MW at a cost of 12,000 €/h.

    Solution: Exercise 1.

  2. (GeoGebra) Build the two-node market of Exercise 1 with sliders for the line limit and the load at B. Plot the redispatch cost and the congestion rent as functions of the line limit, and explain the kink.

    Solution: Exercise 2.

  3. Draw the operational planning timeline from two days ahead to real time. Place the day-ahead congestion forecast, intraday updates and real-time operation, and mark where a ToOp run fits and how much time it has.

    Solution: Exercise 3.

  4. (Jupyter: pandas + matplotlib) With the week of SMARD data from the lab, compute the daily share of wind and solar in consumption and the maximum hourly ramp of residual load. Which day would you expect to be the hardest for the grid operator, and why?

    Solution: Exercise 4.

  5. Rank busbar splitting, phase-shifter tap changes, redispatch, countertrading and renewable curtailment by cost and by speed of activation. For each, say whether a market participant is involved.

    Solution: Exercise 5.

docs.title: Chapter 12 – Solutions
docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 12. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: congestion_cost.py (Lab step 1), smard_api.py and smard_week.py (Lab steps 2–3, Exercise 4) and two_node_market.py (Exercises 1–2). Each module's main() prints every number quoted below. The SMARD numbers are those of the week of Monday 12 to Sunday 18 January 2026, fetched from the portal's JSON API on 16 October 2026 by smard_api.py and saved next to it as smard_live_week_2026-01-12_generation.csv and smard_live_week_2026-01-12_consumption.csv, in the layout of the download center's CSV export, so everything below runs offline; the two synthetic samples smard_generation_sample.csv and smard_consumption_sample.csv remain as a fully known test input for the parser. Lab step 4 needs a personal ENTSO-E API token and is marked "not run here".

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. The SMARD article for Q1 2026. The article (read on 16 October 2026) reports the total volume of congestion management measures (redispatch with operational and reserve plants, and countertrading), their estimated cost, and the share of the redispatch volume that curtailed renewable plants. In a DataFrame indexed by quarter:

    quarter volume (GWh) cost (M€) curtailment of renewables (GWh) €/MWh Q1 2025 9,035 882 2,153 97.62 Q1 2026 8,248 784 2,215 95.05

    The average cost is \(1000 \times \text{cost}_{\text{M€}} / \text{volume}_{\text{GWh}}\), about 98 €/MWh in Q1 2025 and 95 €/MWh in Q1 2026, a change of −2.57 €/MWh (−2.6 %). The volume fell by 787 GWh (−8.7 %) and the cost by 98 M€ (−11.1 %), so the unit cost fell slightly: fewer MWh were moved, and each one cost a little less. The article's breakdown shows where the money went (redispatch of conventional plants 423 → 282 M€, compensation of curtailed renewables 71 → 55 M€, reserve plants 355 → 430 M€, countertrading 33 → 17 M€; both columns add up to the totals). For scale: 95 €/MWh is above the marginal cost of most plants in the merit order, which is why a switching action that avoids a MWh of redispatch is worth having even when it costs an hour of an operator's attention.

    congestion_cost.py
    """Average cost of German congestion management per MWh from SMARD's quarterly figures (Chapter 12, Lab step 1).

The figures are those of the SMARD article "Congestion management in Q1 2026: lower volume of measures and costs"
(read on 16 October 2026): total volume of measures (redispatch with operational and reserve plants, and
countertrading), estimated total cost, and the part of the redispatch volume that curtailed renewable plants. The
cost breakdown of the same article is kept in a second table; its rows add up to the totals.
"""

import pandas as pd

QUARTERS = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        'quarter': ['Q1 2025', 'Q1 2026'],
        'volume_gwh': [9035.0, 8248.0],
        'cost_meur': [882.0, 784.0],
        'curtailment_gwh': [2153.0, 2215.0],
    }
).set_index('quarter')

COST_BREAKDOWN_MEUR = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        'Q1 2025': [423.0, 71.0, 355.0, 33.0],
        'Q1 2026': [282.0, 55.0, 430.0, 17.0],
    },
    index=[
        'redispatch, conventional plants',
        'compensation, curtailed renewables',
        'reserve plants',
        'countertrading',
    ],
)


def cost_per_mwh(table: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Average cost of congestion management in euros per MWh of measures: million euros over GWh, times 1000."""
    return 1000.0 * table['cost_meur'] / table['volume_gwh']


def changes(table: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Absolute and relative change of each column, unit cost included, between the first and the last quarter."""
    with_unit = table.assign(eur_per_mwh=cost_per_mwh(table))
    first, last = with_unit.iloc[0], with_unit.iloc[-1]
    return pd.DataFrame({'first': first, 'last': last, 'change': last - first, 'change_pct': 100 * (last / first - 1)})


def main() -> None:
    """Print the unit cost of each quarter, the changes between them and the cost breakdown."""
    pd.set_option('display.width', 119)
    print(QUARTERS.assign(eur_per_mwh=cost_per_mwh(QUARTERS)).round(2))
    print()
    print(changes(QUARTERS).round(2))
    print()
    print(
        COST_BREAKDOWN_MEUR.assign(
            change_pct=(100 * (COST_BREAKDOWN_MEUR['Q1 2026'] / COST_BREAKDOWN_MEUR['Q1 2025'] - 1))
        ).round(1)
    )
    print('breakdown totals:', COST_BREAKDOWN_MEUR.sum().to_dict())


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  2. One winter week as CSV. The week is Monday 12 to Sunday 18 January 2026. The SMARD download center writes one CSV per table (generation by source; consumption), and the first two lines of each file show everything the parser needs: a semicolon as delimiter, a UTF-8 byte-order mark before the first header cell, two timestamp columns (Start date, End date) in Berlin local time, - where a value is missing (the whole Nuclear column, since April 2023), and every value column named <source> [MWh] Calculated resolutions. Dates and numbers follow the language of the portal: the English export writes Jan 12, 2026 12:00 AM and 53,862.40, the German one (Datum von, Netzlast [MWh] Berechnete Auflösungen) writes 12.01.2026 00:00 and 53.862,40. The parser for the English file is pandas.read_csv(path, sep=';', thousands=',', decimal='.', na_values=['-'], encoding='utf-8-sig') followed by pandas.to_datetime(..., format='%b %d, %Y %I:%M %p') on the start column; the German file needs thousands='.', decimal=',' and format='%d.%m.%Y %H:%M'. smard_week.read_smard picks the layout from the first header cell and returns English column names either way (the two real exports of this week were parsed with it and agree value for value); the load column of the consumption table is called grid load.

    The download center is a form, but the numbers behind the portal's charts come from a JSON API that needs no login, and smard_api.fetch_week uses it: index_hour.json lists the available weeks (Mondays 00:00 Berlin time, in milliseconds since the epoch; 616 weeks from 29 December 2014 on the fetch date) and one <filter>_DE_hour_<timestamp>.json per source gives the 168 hourly values in MWh. The filter ids are those of the Bundesnetzagentur's description of the API (410 grid load, 4359 residual load, 4387 pumped-storage consumption; 1223 lignite, 1224 nuclear, 1225 wind offshore, 1226 hydropower, 1227 other conventional, 1228 other renewable, 4066 biomass, 4067 wind onshore, 4068 photovoltaics, 4069 hard coal, 4070 pumped storage, 4071 natural gas); nuclear answers 404, which the module turns into the - column of the export. smard_api.save_week writes the two tables in the export layout: the saved files are identical to the download center's English export of the same week except for the byte-order mark and the line endings. SMARD revises recent data, so a later fetch can differ from the saved files in the last decimals.

    Numbers of the week: consumption from 45.7 GW (Sunday 18 January 03:00) to 75.8 GW (Monday 12 January 10:00); wind, offshore plus onshore, from 9.1 GW (Saturday 17 January 13:00) to 38.2 GW (Friday 16 January 04:00); photovoltaics up to 20.6 GW (Friday 16 January 12:00); wind and solar together supplied 37.7 % of the week's consumption. The residual load recomputed as consumption − wind offshore − wind onshore − photovoltaics matches SMARD's own Residual load column to 0.01 MWh, the rounding of the file, which is the check to run on any download. Plots (described, not saved): wind and consumption never cross in this week, but they move against each other, wind rising through the nights of Tuesday to Wednesday and Thursday to Friday while consumption falls to about 51.5 GW; the residual load runs from 60.5 GW (Wednesday 14 January 18:00, the evening peak with little wind) down to 13.5 GW (Friday 16 January 02:00). Its duration curve (duration_curve, the 168 hourly values sorted from largest to smallest) falls from 60.5 GW at hour 1 through 38.2 GW at the median hour 84 to 13.5 GW at hour 168: in a real January week the thermal fleet is never idle, unlike in the synthetic sample, whose right tail drops towards zero.

    smard_api.py
    """Fetch one week of hourly SMARD generation and consumption through the public JSON API (Chapter 12).

The download center of SMARD (https://www.smard.de) is a form, but the data behind its charts is a JSON API that
needs no login: ``.../chart_data/{filter}/{region}/index_hour.json`` lists the weeks available for a filter (ms
since the epoch, each a Monday 00:00 Berlin time) and ``.../chart_data/{filter}/{region}/{filter}_{region}_hour_
{timestamp}.json`` returns ``{"meta_data": ..., "series": [[timestamp, value], ...]}``, one value per hour of that
week in MWh. The filter ids are the ones documented by the Bundesnetzagentur (github.com/bundesAPI/smard-api) and
were checked against the data: the residual-load filter equals grid load minus wind and solar to 0.01 MWh, and the
values are those of the CSV export of the same week. A filter without data in the week (nuclear, since April 2023)
answers 404 and becomes a column of NaN, where the export prints ``-``.

``fetch_week`` returns the two tables with the columns of the CSV export, so every function of ``smard_week``
processes them unchanged; ``save_week`` writes them in the export layout next to this file, and ``load_week``
reads them back, so the lab runs offline on the saved week of 12–18 January 2026.
"""

import json
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from smard_week import LOAD, read_smard, report, to_smard_csv

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
BASE_URL = 'https://www.smard.de/app/chart_data'
REGION = 'DE'
TIMEOUT_S = 30
TIMEZONE = 'Europe/Berlin'
GENERATION_FILTERS = {
    'Biomass': 4066,
    'Hydropower': 1226,
    'Wind offshore': 1225,
    'Wind onshore': 4067,
    'Photovoltaics': 4068,
    'Other renewable': 1228,
    'Nuclear': 1224,
    'Lignite': 1223,
    'Hard coal': 4069,
    'Fossil gas': 4071,
    'Hydro pumped storage': 4070,
    'Other conventional': 1227,
}
CONSUMPTION_FILTERS = {LOAD: 410, 'Hydro pumped storage': 4387, 'Residual load': 4359}
LIVE_WEEK = pd.Timestamp('2026-01-12')  # the Monday of the week saved next to this file


class SmardUnavailableError(ConnectionError):
    """The SMARD API could not be reached: no network, a timeout or a server error."""


def fetch_json(url: str, timeout: float = TIMEOUT_S) -> dict | None:
    """The JSON document at ``url``, or ``None`` when SMARD answers 404 (no data for that filter and week)."""
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout) as response:  # noqa: S310 -- https URL under BASE_URL
            return json.load(response)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
        error.close()  # the error carries the response body, a file that would otherwise stay open
        if error.code == 404:
            return None
        raise SmardUnavailableError(f'SMARD answered HTTP {error.code} for {url}') from error
    except (urllib.error.URLError, TimeoutError, OSError) as error:
        raise SmardUnavailableError(
            f'cannot reach SMARD ({error}); check the network connection, then retry'
        ) from error


def to_berlin(timestamps_ms) -> pd.DatetimeIndex:
    """Epoch milliseconds as naive Berlin local timestamps, the clock the SMARD exports use."""
    return pd.to_datetime(list(timestamps_ms), unit='ms', utc=True).tz_convert(TIMEZONE).tz_localize(None)


def week_timestamp(monday: pd.Timestamp) -> int:
    """Epoch milliseconds of ``monday`` 00:00 Berlin time, the key under which SMARD files that week."""
    if monday.weekday() != 0 or monday != monday.normalize():
        raise ValueError(f'{monday} is not a Monday at 00:00')
    return int(monday.tz_localize(TIMEZONE).timestamp() * 1000)


def available_weeks(filter_id: int = 410, region: str = REGION) -> pd.DatetimeIndex:
    """The Mondays of every week SMARD has for a filter, oldest first."""
    index = fetch_json(f'{BASE_URL}/{filter_id}/{region}/index_hour.json')
    if index is None:
        raise SmardUnavailableError(f'SMARD has no hourly index for filter {filter_id} in {region}')
    return to_berlin(index['timestamps'])


def fetch_series(filter_id: int, monday: pd.Timestamp, region: str = REGION) -> pd.Series | None:
    """The hourly values (MWh) of one filter for the week of ``monday``, or ``None`` when SMARD has none."""
    stamp = week_timestamp(monday)
    data = fetch_json(f'{BASE_URL}/{filter_id}/{region}/{filter_id}_{region}_hour_{stamp}.json')
    if data is None:
        return None
    timestamps, values = zip(*data['series'], strict=True)
    return pd.Series(values, index=to_berlin(timestamps), dtype=float)


def fetch_table(filters: dict[str, int], monday: pd.Timestamp, region: str = REGION) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One export table: a column per filter, in the given order, NaN for filters without data."""
    series = {name: fetch_series(filter_id, monday, region) for name, filter_id in filters.items()}
    table = pd.DataFrame({name: s for name, s in series.items() if s is not None}).reindex(columns=list(filters))
    table.index.name = 'start'
    return table


def fetch_week(monday: pd.Timestamp = LIVE_WEEK, region: str = REGION) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Generation by source and consumption for the week of ``monday``, in the layout of the SMARD exports."""
    return fetch_table(GENERATION_FILTERS, monday, region), fetch_table(CONSUMPTION_FILTERS, monday, region)


def live_paths(monday: pd.Timestamp = LIVE_WEEK, folder: Path = HERE) -> tuple[Path, Path]:
    """Where the generation and consumption tables of the week of ``monday`` are saved."""
    day = monday.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
    return folder / f'smard_live_week_{day}_generation.csv', folder / f'smard_live_week_{day}_consumption.csv'


def save_week(gen: pd.DataFrame, cons: pd.DataFrame, folder: Path = HERE) -> tuple[Path, Path]:
    """Write the two tables in the export layout (``smard_week.to_smard_csv``) and return their paths."""
    paths = live_paths(gen.index[0], folder)
    for path, table in zip(paths, (gen, cons), strict=True):
        path.write_text(to_smard_csv(table), encoding='utf-8', newline='\n')
    return paths


def load_week(monday: pd.Timestamp = LIVE_WEEK, folder: Path = HERE) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """The saved tables of the week of ``monday``, read with ``smard_week.read_smard``."""
    gen_path, cons_path = live_paths(monday, folder)
    return read_smard(gen_path), read_smard(cons_path)


def live_or_saved(monday: pd.Timestamp = LIVE_WEEK) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame, str]:
    """The week from the API when SMARD answers, otherwise the saved copy; the third item says which."""
    try:
        gen, cons = fetch_week(monday)
    except SmardUnavailableError as error:
        print(f'{error}; using the saved week')
        gen, cons = load_week(monday)
        return gen, cons, 'saved'
    return gen, cons, 'api'


def main() -> None:
    """Fetch the live week, save it next to this file and print the numbers quoted in the solutions."""
    gen, cons = fetch_week(LIVE_WEEK)
    weeks = available_weeks()
    print(f'SMARD has {len(weeks)} weeks of hourly data, {weeks[0].date()} to {weeks[-1].date()}')
    print('no data (NaN):', [c for c in gen.columns if gen[c].isna().all()])
    gen_path, cons_path = save_week(gen, cons)
    print('saved', gen_path.name, 'and', cons_path.name)
    saved_gen, saved_cons = load_week(LIVE_WEEK)
    print('saved files reproduce the API week:', saved_gen.equals(gen.round(2)) and saved_cons.equals(cons.round(2)))
    report(gen, cons)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

    smard_week.py
    """Parse a week of SMARD generation and consumption exports and derive the residual load (Chapter 12).

The SMARD download center writes one CSV per table (generation by source; consumption), with a semicolon as
delimiter, a UTF-8 byte-order mark, two timestamp columns for the start and the end of each interval, ``-`` where
a value is missing (nuclear, since April 2023) and every value column named ``<source> [MWh] Calculated
resolutions``. Dates and numbers follow the language of the portal: the English export writes
``Jan 12, 2026 12:00 AM`` and ``12,345.67``; the German export (``Datum von``, German column names, suffix
``Berechnete Auflösungen``) writes ``12.01.2026 00:00`` and ``12.345,67``. ``read_smard`` tells the two apart by the
first header cell and returns the English short names either way; both layouts were checked against the real
exports of the week of 12 January 2026. ``to_smard_csv`` writes the English layout.

The committed samples ``smard_generation_sample.csv`` and ``smard_consumption_sample.csv`` are synthetic:
``write_samples`` builds a plausible winter week (a weekday daily cycle, a lower weekend, a wind front passing
mid-week, short solar days) in exactly this layout, so that the parsing code can be exercised and tested without a
download. ``smard_api`` fetches a real week through the SMARD JSON API and saves it in the same layout.
"""

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
GENERATION_CSV = HERE / 'smard_generation_sample.csv'
CONSUMPTION_CSV = HERE / 'smard_consumption_sample.csv'
WEEK_START = pd.Timestamp('2026-01-12 00:00')  # a Monday
HOURS = 7 * 24
SUFFIX = ' [MWh] Calculated resolutions'
GENERATION_COLUMNS = [
    'Biomass',
    'Hydropower',
    'Wind offshore',
    'Wind onshore',
    'Photovoltaics',
    'Other renewable',
    'Nuclear',
    'Lignite',
    'Hard coal',
    'Fossil gas',
    'Hydro pumped storage',
    'Other conventional',
]
LOAD = 'grid load'  # the consumption table's name for the total load, in the order of the export
CONSUMPTION_COLUMNS = [LOAD, 'Hydro pumped storage', 'Residual load']
RENEWABLE_VARIABLE = ['Wind offshore', 'Wind onshore', 'Photovoltaics']
GERMAN_NAMES = {
    'Biomasse': 'Biomass',
    'Wasserkraft': 'Hydropower',
    'Wind Offshore': 'Wind offshore',
    'Wind Onshore': 'Wind onshore',
    'Photovoltaik': 'Photovoltaics',
    'Sonstige Erneuerbare': 'Other renewable',
    'Kernenergie': 'Nuclear',
    'Braunkohle': 'Lignite',
    'Steinkohle': 'Hard coal',
    'Erdgas': 'Fossil gas',
    'Pumpspeicher': 'Hydro pumped storage',
    'Sonstige Konventionelle': 'Other conventional',
    'Netzlast': LOAD,
    'Residuallast': 'Residual load',
}
# The two languages of the portal, keyed by the first header cell: the end column, the date format, the thousands
# and decimal marks, the suffix of every value column and the column names to translate.
LAYOUTS = {
    'Start date': ('End date', '%b %d, %Y %I:%M %p', ',', '.', SUFFIX, {}),
    'Datum von': ('Datum bis', '%d.%m.%Y %H:%M', '.', ',', ' [MWh] Berechnete Auflösungen', GERMAN_NAMES),
}


def synthetic_week() -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Generation by source and consumption, hourly MWh, for one synthetic winter week.

    The shapes are deterministic formulas of the hour of the week: consumption has a daytime hump and an evening
    peak, scaled down at the weekend; onshore wind is a bell-shaped front centred on Wednesday night on top of a
    slow swell; offshore wind follows onshore at a smaller scale; photovoltaics is a short daytime arc whose
    height changes from day to day; the thermal fleet covers what is left above a must-run floor.
    """
    t = np.arange(HOURS)
    hour, day = t % 24, t // 24
    weekend = np.where(day >= 5, 0.86, 1.0)
    load = weekend * (
        47000 + 13000 * np.exp(-(((hour - 12) / 5.0) ** 2)) + 4000 * np.exp(-(((hour - 18.5) / 2.0) ** 2))
    )
    wind_on = np.maximum(500.0, 8000 + 30000 * np.exp(-(((t - 80) / 30.0) ** 2)) + 6000 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 40))
    wind_off = np.minimum(9000.0, 1500 + 0.22 * wind_on)
    solar_day = np.array([0.6, 1.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.9, 0.7, 0.4])[day]
    solar = 11000 * solar_day * np.maximum(0.0, np.sin(np.pi * (hour - 8) / 9.0)) * ((hour >= 8) & (hour <= 17))
    biomass, hydro, other_ren = np.full(HOURS, 4800.0), np.full(HOURS, 1600.0), np.full(HOURS, 150.0)
    residual = load - wind_on - wind_off - solar
    pumped = np.maximum(0.0, residual - 45000) * 0.15
    thermal = np.maximum(residual - pumped - biomass - hydro - other_ren, 7000.0)
    gen = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            'Biomass': biomass,
            'Hydropower': hydro,
            'Wind offshore': wind_off,
            'Wind onshore': wind_on,
            'Photovoltaics': solar,
            'Other renewable': other_ren,
            'Nuclear': np.full(HOURS, np.nan),  # no nuclear generation in Germany since April 2023: SMARD prints '-'
            'Lignite': 0.45 * thermal,
            'Hard coal': 0.20 * thermal,
            'Fossil gas': 0.30 * thermal,
            'Hydro pumped storage': pumped,
            'Other conventional': 0.05 * thermal,
        },
        index=pd.date_range(WEEK_START, periods=HOURS, freq='h'),
    )
    cons = pd.DataFrame({LOAD: load, 'Hydro pumped storage': 1.1 * pumped, 'Residual load': residual}, index=gen.index)
    return gen, cons


def english_stamp(t: pd.Timestamp) -> str:
    """A timestamp as the English export writes it, ``Jan 5, 2026 1:00 AM``: day and hour without a leading zero."""
    return f'{t:%b} {t.day}, {t.year} {t.hour % 12 or 12}:{t.minute:02d} {"AM" if t.hour < 12 else "PM"}'


def to_smard_csv(table: pd.DataFrame) -> str:
    """Serialize a table in the layout of the English SMARD export: start and end columns, ``-`` for NaN."""
    lines = ['Start date;End date;' + ';'.join(f'{c}{SUFFIX}' for c in table.columns)]
    for start, row in zip(table.index, table.itertuples(index=False), strict=True):
        cells = ['-' if np.isnan(v) else f'{v:,.2f}' for v in row]
        lines.append(';'.join([english_stamp(start), english_stamp(start + pd.Timedelta(hours=1)), *cells]))
    return '\n'.join(lines) + '\n'


def write_samples(folder: Path = HERE) -> tuple[Path, Path]:
    """Write the two sample CSV files into ``folder`` and return their paths."""
    gen, cons = synthetic_week()
    paths = (folder / GENERATION_CSV.name, folder / CONSUMPTION_CSV.name)
    for path, table in zip(paths, (gen, cons), strict=True):
        path.write_text(to_smard_csv(table), encoding='utf-8', newline='\n')
    return paths


def read_smard(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a SMARD CSV export (English or German) into a frame indexed by the start of each interval.

    The first header cell selects the layout (``Start date`` or ``Datum von``); the byte-order mark of a real
    download is skipped, ``-`` becomes NaN, the end column is dropped, the ``[MWh] ...`` suffix is removed and
    German column names are translated, so the result has the same short English names whatever the language.
    """
    with open(path, encoding='utf-8-sig') as file:
        first_cell = file.readline().split(';', 1)[0]
    if first_cell not in LAYOUTS:
        raise ValueError(f'{path}: not a SMARD export, the header starts with {first_cell!r}')
    end, date_format, thousands, decimal, suffix, names = LAYOUTS[first_cell]
    table = pd.read_csv(path, sep=';', thousands=thousands, decimal=decimal, na_values=['-'], encoding='utf-8-sig')
    table.index = pd.to_datetime(table.pop(first_cell), format=date_format)
    table.index.name = 'start'
    table = table.drop(columns=[end])
    table.columns = [names.get(c.removesuffix(suffix), c.removesuffix(suffix)) for c in table.columns]
    return table


def residual_load(gen: pd.DataFrame, cons: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Consumption minus wind (onshore and offshore) and photovoltaics, hour by hour."""
    return (cons[LOAD] - gen[RENEWABLE_VARIABLE].sum(axis=1)).rename('residual')


def duration_curve(series: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    """The values of a series sorted from largest to smallest, indexed by the number of hours at or above each."""
    values = np.sort(series.to_numpy())[::-1]
    return pd.Series(values, index=np.arange(1, len(values) + 1), name=series.name)


def critical_hours(gen: pd.DataFrame, cons: pd.DataFrame, q: float = 0.75) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Hours with wind above its ``q`` quantile and residual load below its ``1 - q`` quantile.

    These are the hours in which the north–south corridors of the German grid congest: much wind in the north,
    little demand left for the thermal plants of the south.
    """
    wind = gen[['Wind offshore', 'Wind onshore']].sum(axis=1).rename('wind')
    residual = residual_load(gen, cons)
    mask = (wind >= wind.quantile(q)) & (residual <= residual.quantile(1 - q))
    return pd.DataFrame({'wind': wind, 'consumption': cons[LOAD], 'residual': residual})[mask]


def daily_summary(gen: pd.DataFrame, cons: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Per day: share of wind and solar in consumption, maximum hourly ramp of the residual load, its minimum."""
    renewable = gen[RENEWABLE_VARIABLE].sum(axis=1)
    load = cons[LOAD]
    residual = residual_load(gen, cons)
    by_day = pd.Grouper(freq='D')
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            'weekday': load.groupby(by_day).first().index.day_name(),
            'share_pct': 100 * renewable.groupby(by_day).sum() / load.groupby(by_day).sum(),
            'max_ramp_mw_h': residual.diff().abs().groupby(by_day).max(),
            'min_residual_mw': residual.groupby(by_day).min(),
        }
    )


def report(gen: pd.DataFrame, cons: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    """Print the numbers that the solutions of Lab steps 2–3 and Exercise 4 quote for a week of data."""
    pd.set_option('display.width', 119)
    print('generation columns:', list(gen.columns))
    print('consumption columns:', list(cons.columns), 'rows:', len(cons))
    residual = residual_load(gen, cons)
    print(f'residual load matches the SMARD column to {np.abs(residual - cons["Residual load"]).max():.3f} MWh')
    load = cons[LOAD]
    wind = gen[['Wind offshore', 'Wind onshore']].sum(axis=1)
    for name, series in (
        ('consumption', load),
        ('wind', wind),
        ('solar', gen['Photovoltaics']),
        ('residual', residual),
    ):
        print(f'{name} {series.min():,.0f} ({series.idxmin()}) to {series.max():,.0f} MWh/h ({series.idxmax()})')
    print(f'wind and solar supplied {100 * gen[RENEWABLE_VARIABLE].sum().sum() / load.sum():.1f} % of the week')
    curve = duration_curve(residual)
    print(
        f'duration curve: {curve.iloc[0]:,.0f} at 1 h, {curve.iloc[83]:,.0f} at 84 h, {curve.iloc[-1]:,.0f} at 168 h'
    )
    crit = critical_hours(gen, cons)
    print(f'wind at or above {wind.quantile(0.75):,.0f} and residual at or below {residual.quantile(0.25):,.0f}:')
    print(f'{len(crit)} critical hours, from {crit.index.min()} to {crit.index.max()}')
    print(crit.round(0))
    ramp = residual.diff()
    print(f'largest ramp {ramp[ramp.abs().idxmax()]:+,.0f} MW in the hour ending {ramp.abs().idxmax()}')
    print(daily_summary(gen, cons).round({'share_pct': 1, 'max_ramp_mw_h': 0, 'min_residual_mw': 0}))


def main() -> None:
    """Print the numbers of the committed synthetic samples."""
    report(read_smard(GENERATION_CSV), read_smard(CONSUMPTION_CSV))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  3. High wind, low residual load. critical_hours marks the hours whose wind is in the top quarter of the week (at or above 25.5 GW) and whose residual load is in the bottom quarter (at or below 31.0 GW): 19 hours in the week of 12 January 2026, all at night, in three runs: Monday 12 January 05:00; Tuesday 13 January 22:00 to Wednesday 14 January 05:00 (8 hours); and Thursday 15 January 21:00 to Friday 16 January 06:00 (10 hours). The extreme is Friday 02:00, with 38.1 GW of wind against 51.5 GW of consumption and 13.5 GW of residual load. The pattern is that of a windy January week: the wind blows day and night, but demand drops at night, so the hours of least residual load are the small hours.

    Why these hours congest the north–south corridors: German wind capacity, offshore and onshore, sits in the north, while the large loads and much of the remaining thermal and hydro capacity sit in the south and west. When wind is high the northern injections exceed the northern load, and the surplus has to cross the few 380 kV corridors to the south. When at the same time the residual load is low, the southern thermal plants that would otherwise feed the south are out of the market (prices are low), so the south imports even more. The corridor flows then reach their limits; the market result is physically infeasible. Operators try the cheapest remedies first: switching actions (busbar splitting, line switching) and phase-shifter taps, which redirect flow at no fuel cost; then redispatch (curtail northern wind or conventional plants, start southern plants, paid at cost) and countertrading with neighbours; renewable curtailment is in principle the last step but, as the Q1 figures show (2,215 GWh in one quarter), it is routine in these hours.

  4. Cross-border flows (optional). Not run here: the RESTful API of the Transparency Platform only answers requests that carry a personal security token (without one, the endpoint below returns HTTP 401 with an acknowledgement document whose reason is "Authentication failed."). To get a token: register at https://transparency.entsoe.eu/ (Sign In → register, then confirm the address through the e-mail you receive); send an e-mail to transparency@entsoe.eu with "RESTful API access" as subject and the registered address in the body; access is granted within three working days; then My Account → Generate a new token shows it (the helpdesk article "How to get security token", https://transparencyplatform.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/12845911031188-How-to-get-security-token, has the screenshots). The production endpoint is https://web-api.tp.entsoe.eu/api, and the physical flows are the A11 document (Aggregated energy data report), listed as 12.1.G Cross-Border Physical Flows under Transmission in the platform's Postman reference (https://documenter.getpostman.com/view/7009892/2s93JtP3F6), one request per neighbour and direction:

    https://web-api.tp.entsoe.eu/api?securityToken=<token>&documentType=A11
    &out_Domain=10Y1001A1001A83F&in_Domain=10YNL----------L
    &periodStart=202601112300&periodEnd=202601182300

    out_Domain is the area the energy leaves and in_Domain the one it enters (here Germany to the Netherlands; swap the two for the opposite direction, the net export is the difference), each an EIC code: Germany 10Y1001A1001A83F, Netherlands 10YNL----------L, Belgium 10YBE----------2, France 10YFR-RTE------C, Austria 10YAT-APG------L, Czech Republic 10YCZ-CEPS-----N, Poland 10YPL-AREA-----S, Switzerland 10YCH-SWISSGRIDZ, western Denmark 10YDK-1--------W. The period is UTC in yyyyMMddHHmm, so the Berlin week of 12 January 00:00 starts at 11 January 23:00 UTC; the timestamps of the answer are UTC too. The answer is XML with one <Point> per time step (position, quantity in MW; the step, PT60M or PT15M, is in the <resolution> element); pandas.read_xml or the entsoe-py package (EntsoePandasClient.query_crossborder_flows) turns it into a series. On the website the same data item, Cross-Border Physical Flows (item 12.1.G), has an export function, one border at a time. What to look for: in the 19 hours of step 3 Germany should be exporting strongly towards the Netherlands, Poland, the Czech Republic and Austria, and part of that export is north–south transit through the neighbours ("loop flows"), which is exactly the cross-border congestion the coordinated processes of Chapter 21 are meant to manage.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
(a) Nodal pricing. The cheap generator at A can send at most 500 MW over the line, so it is dispatched at 500 MW; the remaining 300 MW of the 800 MW load are generated at B. The price at each node is the cost of the generator that would serve one more MW there: 20 €/MWh at A (its generator has 500 MW spare but cannot reach B) and 60 €/MWh at B. The congestion rent is the price difference times the flow:

\[ R = (\lambda_B - \lambda_A)\, F = (60 - 20) \times 500 = 20{,}000 \text{ €/h}. \]

It is what the load pays (800 × 60 = 48,000 €/h) minus what the generators receive (500 × 20 + 300 × 60 = 28,000 €/h), and accrues to the owner of the line (or to the holders of its financial transmission rights).

(b) Zonal market. Without the limit the merit order dispatches the cheap generator for the whole load, 800 MW from A, 0 from B, at a single price of 20 €/MWh. The line would carry 800 MW, 300 MW too many. The operator buys 300 MW down at A and 300 MW up at B; in cost-based redispatch it pays B's cost and recovers A's saved fuel, a net cost of

\[ 300 \times (60 - 20) = 12{,}000 \text{ €/h}, \]

which falls on the grid tariff instead of on the market price. The final physical dispatch (500, 300) is the same as in (a); what differs is who pays: in the nodal market the load at B pays 60 €/MWh and the rent goes to the grid, in the zonal market the load pays 20 €/MWh and the grid pays 12,000 €/h. two_node_market.nodal() and two_node_market.zonal() reproduce these numbers.

two_node_market.py
"""Nodal and zonal clearing of a two-node market with one line limit (Chapter 12, Exercises 1 and 2).

Node A has a cheap generator, node B an expensive one and the load. Under nodal pricing the line limit is part of
the market clearing; under zonal pricing it is ignored and the operator restores it afterwards by redispatch.
Costs are in euros per MWh, powers in MW, so every money figure is in euros per hour.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np

COST_A, COST_B = 20.0, 60.0  # marginal costs in euros per MWh
CAP_A, CAP_B = 1000.0, 1000.0  # generator capacities in MW
LOAD_B, LIMIT = 800.0, 500.0  # load at node B and line limit of the exercise, MW


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Nodal:
    """Result of a nodal market clearing: dispatch, nodal prices, flow and congestion rent."""

    gen_a: float
    gen_b: float
    price_a: float
    price_b: float
    flow: float
    rent: float


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Zonal:
    """Result of a zonal clearing followed by redispatch: dispatch and price, then the redispatch and its cost."""

    gen_a: float
    gen_b: float
    price: float
    redispatch_mw: float
    redispatch_cost: float


def nodal(limit: float = LIMIT, load: float = LOAD_B) -> Nodal:
    """Clear the two-node market with the line limit enforced.

    The cheap generator at A serves as much of the load as the line (and its own capacity) allows; the rest comes
    from B. The price at B is the cost of the last generator serving B, the price at A the cost of generator A
    while it has spare capacity. The congestion rent is the price difference times the flow.

    Args:
        limit: Transfer limit of the line A–B in MW.
        load: Load at node B in MW; it must not exceed the generation reachable at B.
    """
    flow = min(load, CAP_A, limit)
    gen_b = load - flow
    if gen_b > CAP_B:
        raise ValueError('the load at B cannot be served')
    price_b = COST_B if gen_b > 0 else COST_A
    price_a = COST_A if flow < CAP_A else price_b
    return Nodal(flow, gen_b, price_a, price_b, flow, (price_b - price_a) * flow)


def zonal(limit: float = LIMIT, load: float = LOAD_B) -> Zonal:
    """Clear the market as one zone, then redispatch to bring the line flow back within its limit.

    The zonal clearing stacks the generators by cost and ignores the line. The flow it implies is all of A's
    output; whatever exceeds the limit is moved from A to B, and the operator pays the cost difference for each
    MW moved (cost-based redispatch).
    """
    gen_a = min(load, CAP_A)
    gen_b = load - gen_a
    price = COST_B if gen_b > 0 else COST_A
    moved = max(0.0, gen_a - limit)
    return Zonal(gen_a, gen_b, price, moved, moved * (COST_B - COST_A))


def sweep(limits: np.ndarray, load: float = LOAD_B) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Redispatch cost and congestion rent for each line limit, the two curves of Exercise 2."""
    cost = np.array([zonal(lim, load).redispatch_cost for lim in limits])
    rent = np.array([nodal(lim, load).rent for lim in limits])
    return cost, rent


def main() -> None:
    """Print the solution of Exercise 1 and the kink of Exercise 2."""
    n = nodal()
    print(f'nodal   : A {n.gen_a:.0f} MW at {n.price_a:.0f} EUR/MWh, B {n.gen_b:.0f} MW at {n.price_b:.0f} EUR/MWh')
    print(f'          flow {n.flow:.0f} MW, congestion rent {n.rent:,.0f} EUR/h')
    z = zonal()
    print(f'zonal   : A {z.gen_a:.0f} MW, B {z.gen_b:.0f} MW, one price {z.price:.0f} EUR/MWh')
    print(f'          redispatch {z.redispatch_mw:.0f} MW, cost {z.redispatch_cost:,.0f} EUR/h')
    limits = np.array([0.0, 200.0, 400.0, 500.0, 600.0, 799.0, 800.0, 1000.0])
    cost, rent = sweep(limits)
    print('limit MW        ' + ' '.join(f'{v:8.0f}' for v in limits))
    print('redispatch EUR/h' + ' '.join(f'{v:8.0f}' for v in cost))
    print('rent EUR/h      ' + ' '.join(f'{v:8.0f}' for v in rent))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
GeoGebra construction not run here; the same functions are evaluated in Python by two_node_market.sweep, and the GeoGebra sliders only change the two parameters \(L\) (line limit) and \(D\) (load at B). With \(c_A = 20\), \(c_B = 60\) and the generator at A large enough,

\[ \text{redispatch cost}(L) = (c_B - c_A)\,\max(0,\, D - L), \qquad \text{rent}(L) = \begin{cases} (c_B - c_A)\, L & L < D \\ 0 & L \ge D \end{cases} \] limit (MW) 0 200 400 500 600 799 800 1,000 redispatch cost (€/h) 32,000 24,000 16,000 12,000 8,000 40 0 0 congestion rent (€/h) 0 8,000 16,000 20,000 24,000 31,960 0 0

The kink is at \(L = D = 800\) MW. Below it the line is congested: every extra MW of capacity saves 40 €/h of redispatch, so the cost falls with slope \(-(c_B - c_A)\), and the rent grows with slope \(+(c_B - c_A)\) because one more MW flows at the full 40 €/MWh price difference. At \(L = D\) the congestion disappears: the redispatch cost reaches zero and stays there (a kink, continuous but with a slope change from −40 to 0), while the rent does not decline gradually but jumps from 31,960 €/h to 0, because the price difference itself collapses from 40 €/MWh to zero the moment the constraint stops binding. Moving the load slider moves the kink: it is always at the load (or at the capacity of A, if that is smaller). In GeoGebra, define L and D as sliders, cost(x) = 40 max(0, D − x), rent(x) = If(x < D, 40 x, 0), and watch the kink follow D.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
The planning timeline, from two days ahead (D-2) to real time, with the time a topology optimization has at each stage:

flowchart LR
    A["D-2<br/>two-day-ahead congestion forecast<br/>(D2CF): expected grid, outages, forecasts"]
    B["D-1 ~12:00<br/>day-ahead market coupling clears<br/>(zonal prices, scheduled exchanges)"]
    C["D-1 afternoon/evening<br/>DACF: common grid model for every hour of D<br/>N-1 analysis, remedial actions chosen"]
    D["D, every hour<br/>intraday congestion forecast (IDCF):<br/>updated forecasts and schedules, actions revised"]
    E["real time<br/>state estimation every few seconds<br/>only pre-validated actions, operator decides"]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> E
Stage When What is fixed What can still change Time for a ToOp run D2CF D-2 planned outages, load and renewable forecasts everything about the dispatch hours; results are indicative day-ahead market D-1, around noon zonal dispatch and exchanges the grid topology and remedial actions – DACF D-1 afternoon to evening one grid model per hour of D, N-1 results topology (bus splits, line switching), PST taps, then redispatch an hour or more per batch of 24 hourly models: this is where ToOp runs IDCF D, hourly forecasts updated with the latest measurements the same actions, re-checked tens of minutes per update real time D, continuously the actual state (state estimator) switching actions already validated, redispatch activation none for optimization; seconds for the operator to act

A ToOp run belongs to the DACF and to the intraday updates: it needs a converged grid model (the common grid model built after the market result) and an N-1 analysis to improve, and its output, a list of proposed splittings with their security metrics and switching distances, must be validated (AC check, operator judgement) before it can be executed. At D-1 evening the engine has hours for 24 hourly cases; intraday it must answer in tens of minutes; in real time nothing is optimized any more, the operator only applies actions that were already studied. This is why the chapters on the solver stress speed per topology (Chapter 31): the budget is set by the timeline, not by the algorithm.

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
Numbers of the week of 12–18 January 2026 (smard_week.daily_summary on the tables that smard_api fetched). The daily share of wind and solar in consumption is the ratio of daily sums, the ramp is the largest absolute hour-to-hour change of the residual load within the day:

day wind + solar share (%) max residual ramp (MW/h) min residual load (MW) Monday 12 Jan 36.6 7,293 26,538 Tuesday 13 Jan 36.9 8,012 22,590 Wednesday 14 Jan 37.0 6,846 19,161 Thursday 15 Jan 43.1 7,283 20,101 Friday 16 Jan 43.4 8,963 13,452 Saturday 17 Jan 28.0 3,819 35,323 Sunday 18 Jan 37.5 4,821 27,611

Friday 16 January is the hardest day on every count. It has the highest share (43.4 %), the lowest residual load of the week (13.5 GW at 02:00, with 38 GW of wind in the night: 7 of the 19 critical hours of Lab step 3 fall on it) and the largest ramp, +9.0 GW in the hour ending 15:00, when the week's highest solar arc (20.6 GW at noon) fades while the evening demand builds up: the operator who spent the night managing north–south flows with the thermal fleet near its floor must bring that fleet back by 9 GW within one hour the same afternoon. Thursday is the runner-up, with 43.1 % and the start of the same windy night. Saturday is the opposite case: the week's weakest wind (9.1 GW at 13:00), a 28 % share, the highest residual-load floor (35.3 GW) and the smallest ramps; congestion is not the problem that day, the thermal fleet simply carries the load. In general the day of minimum residual load is the hard one for congestion (the question of this chapter) and the day of maximum ramp the hard one for balancing; in this week both fall on the same day, a windy night followed by a sunny afternoon, which is the combination operators plan for most carefully.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
Ranking from cheapest to most expensive, and from fastest to slowest to activate; the two orders are nearly reversed, which is the whole point of putting topology first in the remedial-action list:

Remedial action Cost per MW relieved Speed of activation Market participant involved Busbar splitting, line switching lowest: no fuel, only switching wear and operator time; the risk is a worse N-1 state afterwards minutes (remote switching), but only after an N-1 check of the new topology, so hours of preparation in the DACF no: entirely within the TSO Phase-shifter tap change very low: no fuel, mechanical wear of the tap changer one tap every few seconds to minutes; also coordinated with neighbours when the PST sits on a border no (TSO, or two TSOs for a border PST) Redispatch (conventional plants) high: the cost difference between the plants moved, about 95 €/MWh on average in Q1 2026 (Lab step 1) from a quarter of an hour (gas, hydro) to several hours (coal start-up); it is planned day-ahead and intraday yes: the plant operators, compensated at cost Countertrading high: the price difference between the two zones, paid on the intraday market roughly the intraday gate closure, an hour or less yes: traders in both zones Renewable curtailment high per MWh and the most visible: lost zero-cost energy, compensation of the plant owner (55 M€ for 2,215 GWh in Q1 2026) fast once instructed (minutes), but legally the last resort after conventional measures yes: the renewable plant operators, compensated

The German figures of Lab step 1 show the asymmetry: topology changes and PST taps cost almost nothing per MWh and do not appear in the cost table at all, while the three market-based measures cost 784 M€ in a quarter. That is why an engine that finds a switching action for a congestion, instead of paying for redispatch, pays for itself after a few hours of operation.

docs.title: Chapter 13. Substations, grid models and data formats
docs.text:
Weeks: 2 · Semester: 2 · Prerequisites: Chapter 3, Chapter 12

Why it matters for ToOp

Busbar splitting and reassignment are physical switching operations inside substations. ToOp maps node-breaker models (busbars, couplers, bays, breakers, disconnectors) to a bus-branch model and back (docs/interfaces/asset_topology.md, importer/network_graph/), enumerates coupler states that realize an electrical split (dc_solver/preprocess/preprocess_switching.py), and scores the switching effort as a Hamming distance (docs/dc_solver/switching_distance.md, dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/switching_distance.py). It reads UCTE-DEF, CGMES and XIIDM files and exports UCTE and PowerFactory DGS.

This chapter is taught in semester 2, before the network matrices of Chapter 14 and the bus-split factors of Chapter 18, which assume that you can read a station as a graph of busbars and couplers.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Substation arrangements: single and double busbar, breaker-and-a-half, ring; busbar couplers, sections, bays, breakers vs disconnectors.
  • Node-breaker vs bus-breaker vs bus-branch models; topology processing (revisits connected components from Chapter 3).
  • Electrical vs physical switching. The electrical topology says which branch is on which electrical busbar (ToOp allows at most a two-way split, bus A and bus B); the physical topology says how every coupler and bay switch is set. Optimization works on the electrical topology; operators pay for the physical switching.
  • Switching distance in ToOp's code. For a station with \(n\) couplers, make_separation_set enumerates all \(2^n\) open/closed coupler states (it raises an error for \(n > 20\)), builds the busbar graph for each state, and keeps the states whose graph has exactly two connected components. Each kept state gives a candidate (bus A, bus B) assignment of assets and its coupler state. The distance to a target electrical topology is the minimum Hamming distance over these candidates, checked for both labelings of A and B, and reported as a reassignment distance plus a coupler distance (per_station_switching_distance). make_optimal_separation_set removes candidates that duplicate another one (or its A/B mirror) and, for tables with at least clip_at_size rows (default 100), also those within clip_hamming_distance of another.
  • "Topo-vect" (two nodes per substation) as the solver's view of a station.
  • Data formats: UCTE-DEF, CGMES / CIM, PowSyBl IIDM/XIIDM, pandapower JSON, MATPOWER. PowerWorld Simulator keeps cases in its own .pwb (binary) and .aux (text) files, which ToOp does not read.
  • Merging models from several TSOs (boundaries, tie lines); single-line diagrams.
  • Forward link: state estimation and topology errors (a breaker status that is wrong in the model) are treated in Chapter 22.
