docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A station has four physical busbars \(b_1,\dots,b_4\) connected in a chain by three closed couplers \(c_{12}, c_{23}, c_{34}\). Opening a set of couplers splits the chain into connected components. With \(n = 3\) there are \(2^3 = 8\) coupler states:

  • all closed: one component (skipped; this is the unsplit station);
  • exactly one coupler open: two components, 3 states (\(\{b_1\}|\{b_2 b_3 b_4\}\), \(\{b_1 b_2\}|\{b_3 b_4\}\), \(\{b_1 b_2 b_3\}|\{b_4\}\));
  • two or three couplers open: three or four components (discarded).

Each of the three kept states defines a candidate: two Boolean rows \(a_A, a_B \in \{0,1\}^m\) over the \(m\) assets, where \(a_A\) marks the assets whose bays connect to a busbar of the first component and \(a_B\) those of the second. For a target electrical topology \(t \in \{0,1\}^m\) the code computes

\[ d(t, a) = \min\left(\lVert a_A \oplus \bar t \rVert_1 + \lVert a_B \oplus t \rVert_1,\; \lVert a_A \oplus t \rVert_1 + \lVert a_B \oplus \bar t \rVert_1\right), \]

where \(\oplus\) is exclusive or and the minimum accounts for swapping the names A and B. Because the bus A and bus B rows are compared separately, an asset connected to both busbars, or to neither, is counted correctly, and a singly connected asset that changes busbar counts twice (one connection opened, one closed). ToOp keeps the candidate with the smallest reassignment distance and reports its coupler distance (the Hamming distance between the candidate's coupler state and the current one) separately.

coupler_splits.py
"""Which coupler states split a four-busbar substation into exactly two electrical nodes (Chapter 13)."""

import itertools

import networkx as nx

COUPLERS = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]  # busbar pairs joined by a coupler


def two_node_configurations(couplers: list[tuple[int, int]], n_busbars: int) -> list[tuple[tuple[bool, ...], list]]:
    """Enumerate the open/closed states of the couplers that leave exactly two connected groups of busbars.

    Returns ``(is_open, parts)`` pairs: the state of each coupler (``True`` = open) and the two groups.
    """
    found = []
    for is_open in itertools.product([True, False], repeat=len(couplers)):
        g = nx.Graph()
        g.add_nodes_from(range(n_busbars))
        g.add_edges_from(c for c, o in zip(couplers, is_open, strict=True) if not o)
        parts = list(nx.connected_components(g))
        if any(is_open) and len(parts) == 2:
            found.append((is_open, parts))
    return found


def main() -> None:
    """Print the splits of a four-busbar substation whose couplers form a chain."""
    for is_open, parts in two_node_configurations(COUPLERS, 4):
        print(is_open, parts)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

docs.title: Documentation vs code: known discrepancies
docs.text:
• docs/dc_solver/switching_distance.md says the two-cluster assignments are enumerated with "a graph algorithm involving edge cuts". The code in make_separation_set (dc_solver/preprocess/preprocess_switching.py) brute-forces all \(2^n\) coupler states with itertools.product and a connected-components test, with a hard limit of 20 couplers.
  • The same document says a multi-connected asset keeps the busbar "with the most other branches connected to it". The helper used during station preparation, fix_multi_connected_without_coupler (grid_helpers/asset_topology_helpers.py), documents and implements removing the connection to the busbar with the lower index.
  • docs/topology_optimizer/metrics.md states that the AC solver counts switching_distance slightly differently from the DC solver and calls it a bug.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: from a node-breaker station to a switching distance

Tools: ToOp notebooks (set up in Chapter 0), pypowsybl, NetworkX (Chapter 3).

  1. Work through notebooks/example_asset_topology_analysis.ipynb: inspect a voltage level's node-breaker graph and single-line diagram, and identify busbars, couplers and bays.
  2. For one bus group, list its couplers and busbars, and enumerate by hand (or with the snippet from the worked example) the coupler states that give exactly two electrical busbars.
  3. Call prepare_for_separation_set and make_optimal_separation_set (dc_solver/preprocess/preprocess_switching.py) on the same bus group and check that the separation set matches your enumeration.
  4. Choose a target electrical assignment of the station's branches and compute its switching distance with per_station_switching_distance (dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/switching_distance.py). Verify the reassignment and coupler distances by hand.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab_toop.ipynb (needs ToOp).

  1. Draw a double-busbar, single-breaker substation with four line bays and one coupler. Give its node-breaker, bus-breaker and bus-branch representations, and list which switches change when one line moves to the other busbar.

    Solution: Exercise 1.

  2. Explain why a disconnector must not interrupt load current and how that constrains the sequence of switching operations for a busbar reassignment.

    Solution: Exercise 2.

  3. (Jupyter: Python + NetworkX) Generalize the worked example to a ring of \(n\) busbars with \(n\) couplers. Count the two-component coupler states for \(n = 3,\dots,12\), compare with the closed form \(\binom{n}{2}\), and time the brute force as \(n\) grows toward ToOp's limit of 20.

    Solution: Exercise 3.

  4. (Jupyter: NumPy) Given the candidates as a Boolean array of shape (candidates, 2, assets) and a target vector, compute the reassignment distance of the worked example with and without the A/B swap in one vectorized expression. Construct an example where ignoring the swap overstates the distance.

    Solution: Exercise 4.

  5. (pypowsybl) Create pypowsybl.network.create_four_substations_node_breaker_network(), list its voltage levels and switches, and for one voltage level classify the switches into breakers and disconnectors.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
The lab names the interactive ToOp notebook notebooks/example_asset_topology_analysis.ipynb. Its widgets and single-line diagrams need a browser session and are not run here; the same materialization of a node-breaker network into ToOp's bus groups, without widgets, is what station_toop.four_substations_bus_groups does, with the functions the notebook itself imports (get_node_breaker_master_asset_topology, materialize_runtime_bus_groups_from_network_state). The network is pypowsybl's four-substations node-breaker example, the one Exercise 5 also uses.

  1. Node-breaker graph of a voltage level. The five voltage levels of the example become five bus groups. Four of them (S1VL1, S2VL1, S3VL1, S4VL1) have a single busbar section and no coupler: ToOp logs "No couplers found in the substation" and they cannot be split. S1VL2, the 400 kV level of substation S1, is a double busbar:

    busbar int_id bays closed onto it S1VL2_BBS1 0 TWT (branch), GH1, GH2, GH3, SHUNT S1VL2_BBS2 1 LCC1, LD2, LD3, LD4, VSC1

    joined by the coupler S1VL2_COUPLER (a breaker, closed, between int_ids 0 and 1, with a disconnector on each side). Every bay is a breaker plus one busbar disconnector per busbar section (the 33 switches of Exercise 5). In the single-line diagram the two horizontal busbar sections, the coupler between them and the ten bays hanging from them are exactly these objects; the bus-branch model sees one bus (the coupler is closed) with one branch and nine injections.

  2. Coupler states by hand. S1VL2 has one coupler and two busbars, so \(2^1 = 2\) states: coupler closed, one electrical busbar (the current state, skipped); coupler open, two electrical busbars \(\{\text{BBS1}\} \mid \{\text{BBS2}\}\). One candidate. For the worked example's chain of four busbars and three closed couplers, coupler_splits.two_node_configurations lists the three states with exactly one coupler open: open \(c_{01}\) gives \(\{b_0\} \mid \{b_1 b_2 b_3\}\), open \(c_{12}\) gives \(\{b_0 b_1\} \mid \{b_2 b_3\}\), open \(c_{23}\) gives \(\{b_0 b_1 b_2\} \mid \{b_3\}\). With six line bays L0, L1 on \(b_0\), L2 on \(b_1\), L3 on \(b_2\) and L4, L5 on \(b_3\) (reassignment_distance.ASSET_BUSBAR), the candidates are A = {L0 L1} | B = {L2 L3 L4 L5}, A = {L0 L1 L2} | B = {L3 L4 L5} and A = {L0 L1 L2 L3} | B = {L4 L5}.

  3. ToOp's separation set. station_toop.separation runs prepare_for_separation_set (nothing to fix: StationProblems is empty for both stations) and make_optimal_separation_set. For S1VL2 the separation set has shape (1, 2, 1): one configuration, two busbars, one branch asset (the table covers the branches, TWT on bus A, so [[1], [0]]), with coupler_states = [[True]] (the coupler must be open), busbar_a = [{0}] and coupler_distance = [1], since the coupler is closed today. For the chain station the set has three configurations, in ToOp's order the same three splits as the hand enumeration (the script checks every row against coupler_splits, mirror images allowed, and prints same candidates as coupler_splits: True):

    coupler state (True = open) busbars in A bus A bus B \(c_{01}\) open {0} L0 L1 L2 L3 L4 L5 \(c_{12}\) open {0, 1} L0 L1 L2 L3 L4 L5 \(c_{23}\) open {0, 1, 2} L0 L1 L2 L3 L4 L5

    make_optimal_separation_set removes nothing: the three rows are distinct even up to the A/B mirror, and with fewer than clip_at_size = 100 rows no Hamming clipping applies.

  4. Switching distance of a target. All couplers are closed today (current_coupler_state = [F, F, F]). station_toop.switching_distance calls per_station_switching_distance; the pure NumPy reassignment_distance.reassignment_distance gives the same reassignment count in every case:

    target (True = on bus B) best configuration inverted reassignment coupler L3 L4 L5 on B 1 (\(c_{12}\) open) no 0 1 L3 L4 on B, L5 on A 1 (\(c_{12}\) open) no 2 1 L0 L1 L2 on B (the mirror of the first) 1 (\(c_{12}\) open) yes 0 1

    By hand: the first target is the second candidate, so no bay changes busbar, and the only physical operation is opening \(c_{12}\), one coupler switching. In the second target L5 must leave the group of \(b_3\) for the other side: its connection to a bus-B busbar is opened and a connection to a bus-A busbar is closed, two reassignment operations, plus the coupler. The third target is the first one with the names A and B exchanged; without the swap it would cost 12 (every one of the six bays on both rows), with it ToOp reports invert = True and distance 0, which is the reason the minimum over both labelings exists.

    station_toop.py
    """ToOp's separation set and switching distance for two stations (Chapter 13, Lab steps 1–4).

Runs with ToOp's interpreter only. The first station is the worked example's chain of four busbars and three
couplers with six line bays (the same station as ``reassignment_distance.py``), built here as a ``RuntimeBusGroup``
by hand. The second is voltage level S1VL2 of pypowsybl's four-substations node-breaker network, the double-busbar
level with one coupler, materialized with the same ToOp functions as ``notebooks/example_asset_topology_analysis``.
"""

import sys
import tempfile
from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path

import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import pypowsybl as pp
from reassignment_distance import ASSET_BUSBAR, ASSET_NAMES, N_BUSBARS, asset_table, candidates, reassignment_distance
from toop_engine_dc_solver.preprocess.helpers.switching_distance import per_station_switching_distance
from toop_engine_dc_solver.preprocess.preprocess_switching import (
    OptimalSeparationSetInfo,
    make_optimal_separation_set,
    prepare_for_separation_set,
)
from toop_engine_grid_helpers.powsybl.example_grids import create_default_network_masks
from toop_engine_grid_helpers.powsybl.powsybl_asset_topo import materialize_runtime_bus_groups_from_network_state
from toop_engine_grid_helpers.powsybl.powsybl_station_to_graph import get_node_breaker_master_asset_topology
from toop_engine_interfaces.asset_topology.assets_runtime import (
    RuntimeBranchAsset,
    RuntimeBusbar,
    RuntimeBusbarCoupler,
)
from toop_engine_interfaces.asset_topology.runtime_topology import RuntimeAssetConnection, RuntimeBusGroup
from toop_engine_interfaces.messages.preprocess.preprocess_commands import AreaSettings, CgmesImporterParameters

CHAIN_COUPLERS = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]


def chain_station() -> RuntimeBusGroup:
    """The worked example as a ToOp bus group: busbars b0..b3, closed breakers c01, c12, c23, six line bays."""
    busbars = [RuntimeBusbar(grid_model_id=f'b{i}', int_id=i) for i in range(N_BUSBARS)]
    couplers = [
        RuntimeBusbarCoupler(
            grid_model_id=f'c{a}{b}', coupler_type='BREAKER', busbar_from_id=a, busbar_to_id=b, open=False
        )
        for a, b in CHAIN_COUPLERS
    ]
    branches = [RuntimeAssetConnection(asset=RuntimeBranchAsset(grid_model_id=name)) for name in ASSET_NAMES]
    return RuntimeBusGroup(
        bus_group_id='chain',
        busbars=busbars,
        couplers=couplers,
        branch_connections=branches,
        injection_connections=[],
        branch_switching_table=asset_table(ASSET_BUSBAR, N_BUSBARS),
        injection_switching_table=np.zeros((N_BUSBARS, 0), dtype=bool),
    )


def four_substations_bus_groups(folder: Path) -> list[RuntimeBusGroup]:
    """The runtime bus groups of pypowsybl's four-substations network, one per voltage level.

    The network is saved as XIIDM into ``folder`` because ToOp's importer parameters name a grid file; every
    substation is marked relevant so that each voltage level becomes a bus group.
    """
    net = pp.network.create_four_substations_node_breaker_network()
    grid = folder / 'four_substations.xiidm'
    net.save(str(grid))
    masks = create_default_network_masks(net)
    masks = replace(
        masks,
        relevant_subs=np.ones(len(net.get_buses()), dtype=bool),
        busbar_for_nminus1=np.ones(len(net.get_busbar_sections()), dtype=bool),
    )
    parameters = CgmesImporterParameters(
        area_settings=AreaSettings(control_area=[''], view_area=[''], nminus1_area=[''], cutoff_voltage=1),
        data_folder=folder,
        grid_model_file=grid,
    )
    master = get_node_breaker_master_asset_topology(network=net, network_masks=masks, importer_parameters=parameters)
    return materialize_runtime_bus_groups_from_network_state(network=net, master_data=master)


def separation(group: RuntimeBusGroup) -> OptimalSeparationSetInfo:
    """Prepare a bus group and build its optimal separation set, as ToOp's preprocessing does."""
    branch_ids = [c.asset.grid_model_id for c in group.branch_connections]
    injection_ids = [c.asset.grid_model_id for c in group.injection_connections]
    simplified, _problems = prepare_for_separation_set(group, branch_ids, injection_ids)
    return make_optimal_separation_set(simplified)


def switching_distance(
    info: OptimalSeparationSetInfo, current_coupler_state: np.ndarray, target: np.ndarray
) -> tuple[int, bool, int, int]:
    """Best configuration, whether A and B were swapped, reassignment distance and coupler distance of a target."""
    best, invert, reassignment, coupler = per_station_switching_distance(
        jnp.asarray(target, dtype=bool),
        jnp.asarray(current_coupler_state, dtype=bool),
        jnp.asarray(info.separation_set),
        jnp.asarray(info.coupler_states),
    )
    return int(best), bool(invert), int(reassignment), int(coupler)


def describe_group(group: RuntimeBusGroup) -> str:
    """One line per busbar, coupler and asset of a bus group."""
    lines = [f'bus group {group.bus_group_id} (voltage level {group.voltage_level_id})']
    lines += [f'  busbar {b.grid_model_id} (int_id {b.int_id})' for b in group.busbars]
    lines += [
        f'  coupler {c.grid_model_id} {c.coupler_type} b{c.busbar_from_id}-b{c.busbar_to_id} open={c.open}'
        for c in group.couplers
    ]
    for row, busbar in zip(group.asset_switching_table, group.busbars, strict=True):
        assets = [a.grid_model_id for a, on in zip(group.assets, row, strict=True) if on]
        lines.append(f'  on {busbar.grid_model_id}: {assets}')
    return '\n'.join(lines)


def main(folder: Path) -> None:
    """Print the bus groups of the four-substations network, the separation sets and the switching distances."""
    groups = four_substations_bus_groups(folder)
    for group in groups:
        print(describe_group(group))
    s1vl2 = next(g for g in groups if g.voltage_level_id == 'S1VL2')
    info = separation(s1vl2)
    print(
        'S1VL2 separation set',
        info.separation_set.astype(int).tolist(),
        'coupler states',
        info.coupler_states.astype(int).tolist(),
    )
    print('S1VL2 busbar A', info.busbar_a, 'coupler distance', np.asarray(info.coupler_distance).tolist())

    chain = chain_station()
    info = separation(chain)
    print('chain: configurations', info.separation_set.shape[0], 'coupler states (True = open):')
    for state, group_a, row in zip(info.coupler_states, info.busbar_a, info.separation_set, strict=True):
        a = [n for n, on in zip(ASSET_NAMES, row[0], strict=True) if on]
        b = [n for n, on in zip(ASSET_NAMES, row[1], strict=True) if on]
        print(f'  open {state.astype(int).tolist()} busbars A {sorted(group_a)}: A = {a}, B = {b}')
    mine = candidates(CHAIN_COUPLERS, ASSET_BUSBAR)
    same = all(any((row == c).all() or (row[::-1] == c).all() for c in mine) for row in info.separation_set)
    print('chain: same candidates as coupler_splits:', same)
    closed = np.zeros(len(CHAIN_COUPLERS), dtype=bool)
    for label, target in (
        ('L3 L4 L5 on B', np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1], dtype=bool)),
        ('L3 L4 on B (L5 moves)', np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0], dtype=bool)),
        ('L0 L1 L2 on B (mirror)', np.array([1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0], dtype=bool)),
    ):
        best, invert, reassignment, coupler = switching_distance(info, closed, target)
        numpy_best = int(reassignment_distance(mine, target).min())
        print(f'target {label}: best {best}, invert {invert}, reassignment {reassignment}, coupler {coupler}')
        print(f'  numpy reassignment_distance: {numpy_best}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main(Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()))

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
The station: two busbars BB1 and BB2, four line bays L1–L4 and one coupler bay. In a double-busbar, single-breaker arrangement each line bay has one circuit breaker CB and two busbar disconnectors, DS-1 towards BB1 and DS-2 towards BB2 (plus a line disconnector on the line side, which plays no part here); the coupler bay has a breaker CB-C with a disconnector on each side. Take L1, L2 on BB1 and L3, L4 on BB2 with the coupler closed.

Node-breaker. Every conductor segment is a node and every switch is an edge between two nodes. Per line bay: node \(n_\text{line}\) (the line end), edge CB to node \(n_\text{bay}\) (the busbar-side segment), edge DS-1 from \(n_\text{bay}\) to BB1 and edge DS-2 from \(n_\text{bay}\) to BB2, one of them closed. The coupler bay is the path BB1 – DS – \(n_c\) – CB-C – \(n_c'\) – DS – BB2. In total 2 busbar nodes, 4 × 2 bay nodes, 2 coupler nodes and 4 × 3 + 3 = 15 switches (plus the four line disconnectors if drawn), exactly the pattern of S1VL2 in Exercise 5.

flowchart LR
    BB1((BB1)) ---|DS-1 closed| n1["bay 1"] ---|CB| L1
    BB2((BB2)) -.-|DS-2 open| n1
    BB1 ---|DS-1 closed| n2["bay 2"] ---|CB| L2
    BB2 -.-|DS-2 open| n2
    BB1 -.-|DS-1 open| n3["bay 3"] ---|CB| L3
    BB2 ---|DS-2 closed| n3
    BB1 -.-|DS-1 open| n4["bay 4"] ---|CB| L4
    BB2 ---|DS-2 closed| n4
    BB1 ---|DS| c1["coupler"] ---|CB-C closed| c2["bay"] ---|DS| BB2

Bus-breaker. Disconnectors are resolved: each bay is attached to the busbar whose disconnector is closed, and only the breakers remain as switches. Two buses, BB1 with L1 and L2 and BB2 with L3 and L4, each line behind its breaker, and the coupler breaker between the two buses. This is the view pypowsybl's bus-breaker voltage levels keep and the one ToOp's RuntimeBusGroup encodes: a branch_switching_table with a row per busbar (here [[1, 1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1, 1]]) and the list of couplers with their open/closed state.

Bus-branch. Closed breakers disappear too, and busbars joined by a closed coupler merge: one bus with the four lines (the unsplit station). With the coupler open there are two buses, {L1, L2} and {L3, L4}, which is what a power flow or ToOp's DC solver sees, and nothing else: the bus-branch model cannot tell which physical busbar a line is on, only which electrical node.

Moving L3 from BB2 to BB1. With the coupler closed (BB1 and BB2 at the same potential), close DS-1 of bay 3, then open DS-2 of bay 3: two switch operations in the node-breaker model, none in the bus-branch model (the electrical topology is unchanged while the coupler is closed). ToOp counts exactly these two, one connection closed and one opened, as a reassignment distance of 2 (Exercise 4); if the coupler were open it would first have to be closed, and that operation counts in the coupler distance. If the goal is a split with L3 on the BB1 side, the coupler is opened afterwards (one more operation, the coupler distance of Lab step 4).

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
A disconnector (isolator) is a slow, air-insulated knife switch without an arc-quenching chamber. Opening a circuit that carries load current draws an arc; a circuit breaker extinguishes it with SF₆, vacuum or oil and a fast mechanism, a disconnector cannot, so the arc would persist, re-strike and flash over to earth or to the other phases. Disconnectors are therefore rated to open and close only de-energized circuits or circuits that carry no current to interrupt, and their task is isolation (a visible gap for maintenance) and selection (which busbar a bay uses), not switching. Interlocks in the substation enforce this: a busbar disconnector cannot be operated unless either its bay breaker is open or a parallel path at the same potential exists.

For a busbar reassignment under load the parallel path is the coupler. The sequence is "make before break":

  1. Close the coupler breaker (if it was open): BB1 and BB2 are now one electrical node at the same voltage.
  2. Close the disconnector of the bay towards the new busbar: it closes between two points at the same potential, so no current flows through it at the moment of closing and nothing has to be interrupted.
  3. Open the disconnector towards the old busbar: the bay current it carried diverts through the new disconnector, the new busbar and the coupler, so again it interrupts no load current (only a small circulating current, within the rating of the disconnector).
  4. Repeat for every bay that moves; then, if the intention is to split the station, open the coupler breaker, the one device in the sequence that interrupts a real current.

Consequences for the switching distance: a bay reassignment always costs two disconnector operations (ToOp's reassignment distance of 2 per moved asset), the coupler must be closed during the move, and a split is only completed by a breaker, so the coupler distance is counted separately. It also fixes the order in time: the reassignments come first and the coupler opens last, which is why a target split cannot be reached with fewer operations than ToOp's reassignment plus coupler count.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
A ring of \(n\) busbars with \(n\) couplers (busbar \(i\) joined to busbar \(i + 1 \bmod n\)) stays connected with one coupler open (a chain) and falls into exactly two groups when exactly two couplers are open; a third open coupler makes three groups. Hence the two-component states are the ways of choosing the two open couplers, \(\binom{n}{2}\). ring_splits.count_two_component_states runs the brute force of the worked example (coupler_splits.two_node_configurations over all \(2^n\) states) and closed_form gives \(\binom{n}{2}\); they agree for every \(n\) from 3 to 16 (the test checks 3–10):

\(n\) states \(2^n\) two-component states \(\binom{n}{2}\) seconds 3 8 3 3 0.000 4 16 6 6 0.000 6 64 15 15 0.001 8 256 28 28 0.003 10 1,024 45 45 0.015 12 4,096 66 66 0.073 14 16,384 91 91 0.307 16 65,536 120 120 1.333

The times are from one run on the maintainer's laptop and vary by machine, but the growth does not: each extra coupler doubles the number of states and the time, while the number of useful states grows only quadratically. Extrapolating the last row, \(n = 20\) takes about \(1.33 \times 2^4 \approx 21\) s and \(n = 30\) about six hours. That is why make_separation_set refuses stations with more than 20 couplers: a brute force over coupler states is affordable for the handful of couplers a real station has, and the limit guards against a mis-modelled station (for example, every bay disconnector counted as a coupler) rather than against a real design.

ring_splits.py
"""Two-component coupler states of a ring of busbars, by brute force and in closed form (Chapter 13, Exercise 3).

A ring of n busbars joined by n couplers falls into exactly two connected groups when exactly two couplers are
open, so the count is n choose 2. The brute force of ``coupler_splits.two_node_configurations`` visits all 2**n
coupler states, which is what bounds ToOp's enumeration to 20 couplers.
"""

import time
from math import comb

from coupler_splits import two_node_configurations


def ring_couplers(n: int) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """The n couplers of a ring of n busbars: busbar i joined to busbar (i + 1) mod n."""
    return [(i, (i + 1) % n) for i in range(n)]


def count_two_component_states(n: int) -> int:
    """Brute-force count of the coupler states of a ring of n busbars that leave exactly two components."""
    return len(two_node_configurations(ring_couplers(n), n))


def closed_form(n: int) -> int:
    """The binomial coefficient n choose 2: the two-component states open exactly two of the n couplers of the ring."""
    return comb(n, 2)


def timed_count(n: int) -> tuple[int, float]:
    """The brute-force count for a ring of n busbars and the wall-clock seconds it took."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    count = count_two_component_states(n)
    return count, time.perf_counter() - start


def main(n_max: int = 16) -> None:
    """Print count, closed form and time for n = 3 .. n_max, then extrapolate the time to ToOp's limit of 20."""
    print(' n  states  count  C(n,2)  seconds')
    last = 0.0
    for n in range(3, n_max + 1):
        count, seconds = timed_count(n)
        print(f'{n:2d}  {2**n:6d}  {count:5d}  {closed_form(n):6d}  {seconds:7.3f}')
        last = seconds
    print(f'doubling per coupler: about {last * 2 ** (20 - n_max):.0f} s for n = 20 on this machine')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
With the candidates as a Boolean array cands of shape (candidates, 2, assets) and the target t (True = on bus B), the distance of every candidate, with and without the swap, is one expression each:

direct  = (cands[:, 0] ^ ~t).sum(axis=1) + (cands[:, 1] ^ t).sum(axis=1)
swapped = (cands[:, 0] ^ t).sum(axis=1) + (cands[:, 1] ^ ~t).sum(axis=1)
distance = np.minimum(direct, swapped)

Bus A is compared with the complement of the target (the assets that should not be on B) and bus B with the target; broadcasting does it for all candidates at once. For the worked example's station (six bays, candidates A = {L0 L1} | B = {L2 L3 L4 L5}, A = {L0 L1 L2} | B = {L3 L4 L5}, A = {L0 L1 L2 L3} | B = {L4 L5}) and the target "L3 L4 L5 on bus B" the distances are [2, 0, 2] with or without the swap: the second candidate is the target, and the neighbours differ by one bay, which counts twice (one connection to open, one to close).

Where ignoring the swap overstates. Take the mirror target "L0 L1 L2 on bus B", the same split with the names of the two buses exchanged. Without the swap the distances are [10, 12, 10]: bus A of the second candidate disagrees with \(\bar t\) on all six assets and bus B disagrees with \(t\) on all six, although not a single bay has to move. With the swap they are [2, 0, 2] again. The names A and B are arbitrary labels of the two electrical nodes, so a distance that depends on them would make the engine pay twelve switching operations for renaming; this is what the invert flag of per_station_switching_distance records (Lab step 4). In general, without the swap the distance of a candidate to its own mirror is \(2m\) for \(m\) assets, the maximum possible, instead of 0.

reassignment_distance.py
"""Vectorized reassignment distance of the worked example's station, with and without the A/B swap (Chapter 13).

The station is the chain of four busbars and three couplers of the worked example, with six line bays: lines 0
and 1 on busbar 0, line 2 on busbar 1, line 3 on busbar 2, lines 4 and 5 on busbar 3. A candidate is a pair of
Boolean rows (bus A, bus B) over the assets; a target is one Boolean row, True meaning "on bus B". The distance of
a candidate is the number of asset-busbar connections that differ, counted on bus A against the complement of the
target and on bus B against the target; ToOp also tries the target with A and B swapped and keeps the smaller sum.
"""

import numpy as np
from coupler_splits import COUPLERS, two_node_configurations

N_BUSBARS = 4
ASSET_BUSBAR = np.array([0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3])  # busbar of each of the six line bays
ASSET_NAMES = [f'L{i}' for i in range(len(ASSET_BUSBAR))]


def asset_table(asset_busbar: np.ndarray = ASSET_BUSBAR, n_busbars: int = N_BUSBARS) -> np.ndarray:
    """Boolean table of shape (busbars, assets): True where the asset's bay is closed onto that busbar."""
    return np.arange(n_busbars)[:, None] == asset_busbar[None, :]


def candidates(couplers: list[tuple[int, int]] = COUPLERS, asset_busbar: np.ndarray = ASSET_BUSBAR) -> np.ndarray:
    """All two-component coupler states as a Boolean array of shape (candidates, 2, assets).

    Row 0 of each candidate marks the assets whose busbar lies in the first component, row 1 those in the second.
    """
    n_busbars = int(asset_busbar.max()) + 1
    table = asset_table(asset_busbar, n_busbars)
    out = []
    for _, parts in two_node_configurations(couplers, n_busbars):
        out.append(np.stack([table[sorted(part)].any(axis=0) for part in parts]))
    return np.array(out)


def reassignment_distance(cands: np.ndarray, target: np.ndarray, allow_swap: bool = True) -> np.ndarray:
    """Reassignment distance of every candidate to a target, one vectorized expression.

    Args:
        cands: Boolean array (candidates, 2, assets), bus A first, bus B second.
        target: Boolean array (assets,), True for the assets that should end on bus B.
        allow_swap: Also compare with the roles of A and B exchanged and keep the smaller distance, as ToOp does.
    """
    direct = (cands[:, 0] ^ ~target).sum(axis=1) + (cands[:, 1] ^ target).sum(axis=1)
    if not allow_swap:
        return direct
    swapped = (cands[:, 0] ^ target).sum(axis=1) + (cands[:, 1] ^ ~target).sum(axis=1)
    return np.minimum(direct, swapped)


def describe(cand: np.ndarray) -> str:
    """The two busbar groups of a candidate as asset names, for printing."""
    a = ' '.join(n for n, on in zip(ASSET_NAMES, cand[0], strict=True) if on)
    b = ' '.join(n for n, on in zip(ASSET_NAMES, cand[1], strict=True) if on)
    return f'A = {{{a}}}, B = {{{b}}}'


def main() -> None:
    """Print the candidates, the distances to two targets, and the example where ignoring the swap overstates."""
    cands = candidates()
    print('candidates (bus A | bus B):')
    for k, cand in enumerate(cands):
        print(f'  {k}: {describe(cand)}')
    target = np.array([False, False, False, True, True, True])  # L3, L4, L5 on bus B
    print('target: L3 L4 L5 on bus B')
    print('  with swap   ', reassignment_distance(cands, target))
    print('  without swap', reassignment_distance(cands, target, allow_swap=False))
    mirror = ~target  # the same split, with the names of the two buses exchanged
    print('mirror target: L0 L1 L2 on bus B')
    print('  with swap   ', reassignment_distance(cands, mirror))
    print('  without swap', reassignment_distance(cands, mirror, allow_swap=False))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
pypowsybl.network.create_four_substations_node_breaker_network() has four substations and five voltage levels, all node-breaker: S1VL1 (225 kV) and S1VL2 (400 kV) in S1, and S2VL1, S3VL1, S4VL1 (400 kV). net.get_switches() lists 59 switches with their kind, open and retained flags; net.get_node_breaker_topology(vl) adds the two nodes of each switch and which nodes are busbar sections:

voltage level breakers disconnectors S1VL1 2 2 S1VL2 11 22 S2VL1 3 3 S3VL1 5 5 S4VL1 3 3

The single-busbar levels have one breaker and one disconnector per bay. S1VL2 is the double busbar of the Lab: four_substations.classify_switches separates its 33 switches by kind and by the node they touch (a disconnector that touches a busbar-section node is a busbar selector):

kind role count BREAKER bay breaker (S1VL2_<asset>_BREAKER) 10 BREAKER coupler (S1VL2_COUPLER) 1 DISCONNECTOR busbar disconnector (S1VL2_BBS1_<asset>_DISCONNECTOR, S1VL2_BBS2_<asset>_DISCONNECTOR) 20 DISCONNECTOR coupler disconnector (S1VL2_BBS1_COUPLER_DISCONNECTOR, S1VL2_BBS2_COUPLER_DISCONNECTOR) 2

Ten bays (TWT, GH1–GH3, LD2–LD4, SHUNT, LCC1, VSC1), each with a breaker and two busbar disconnectors, one per busbar section, and the coupler bay with its breaker and two disconnectors: the textbook double-busbar, single-breaker arrangement of Exercise 1, and the only level of the example that ToOp can split (Lab step 3). All eleven breakers are retained, so pypowsybl keeps them as switches in its bus-breaker view, while the disconnectors are resolved into the bus a bay belongs to.

four_substations.py
"""Voltage levels and switches of pypowsybl's four-substations node-breaker network (Chapter 13, Exercise 5).

Every voltage level of this example is modelled node-breaker, so each one has a list of switches with a kind
(``BREAKER`` or ``DISCONNECTOR``), an open flag and the two nodes it joins. In the bay of an asset, the breaker
interrupts current and the busbar disconnectors select the busbar; in a double-busbar level the coupler is a breaker
between the two busbar sections, with a disconnector on each side.
"""

import pandas as pd
import pypowsybl as pp

VOLTAGE_LEVEL = 'S1VL2'  # the only double-busbar level of the example: two busbar sections and a coupler


def network() -> pp.network.Network:
    """The four-substations node-breaker example shipped with pypowsybl."""
    return pp.network.create_four_substations_node_breaker_network()


def voltage_levels(net: pp.network.Network) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Id, substation, nominal voltage and topology kind of every voltage level."""
    return net.get_voltage_levels(attributes=['substation_id', 'nominal_v', 'topology_kind'])


def switch_counts(net: pp.network.Network) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Number of switches per voltage level and kind."""
    return net.get_switches().groupby(['voltage_level_id', 'kind']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)


def classify_switches(net: pp.network.Network, voltage_level: str = VOLTAGE_LEVEL) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The switches of one voltage level with a ``role`` column.

    Roles: ``coupler`` (the breaker between the two busbar sections), ``coupler disconnector`` (its busbar
    selectors), ``bay breaker`` (the breaker of an asset bay) and ``busbar disconnector`` (the selector of an asset
    bay onto one busbar section). The role follows from the kind and from the node the switch touches: a switch
    touching a busbar-section node is a selector.
    """
    topo = net.get_node_breaker_topology(voltage_level)
    busbar_nodes = set(topo.nodes.index[topo.nodes['connectable_type'] == 'BUSBAR_SECTION'])
    switches = topo.switches.copy()
    on_busbar = switches['node1'].isin(busbar_nodes) | switches['node2'].isin(busbar_nodes)
    is_coupler = switches.index.str.contains('COUPLER')
    role = pd.Series('bay breaker', index=switches.index)
    role[(switches['kind'] == 'DISCONNECTOR') & on_busbar & ~is_coupler] = 'busbar disconnector'
    role[(switches['kind'] == 'DISCONNECTOR') & is_coupler] = 'coupler disconnector'
    role[(switches['kind'] == 'BREAKER') & is_coupler] = 'coupler'
    return switches.assign(role=role)


def main() -> None:
    """Print the voltage levels, the switch counts and the classification of the switches of S1VL2."""
    pd.set_option('display.width', 119)
    net = network()
    print(voltage_levels(net))
    print()
    print(switch_counts(net))
    print()
    classified = classify_switches(net)
    print(classified[['kind', 'open', 'retained', 'node1', 'node2', 'role']])
    print()
    print(classified.groupby(['kind', 'role']).size())


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Chapter 14. Network component models and network matrices
docs.text:
Weeks: 2 · Semester: 3 · Prerequisites: Chapter 11, Chapter 12

Why it matters for ToOp

The two backends turn grid elements into branch susceptances and injections (dc_solver/preprocess/pandapower/pandapower_backend.py, dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_backend.py): lines, two- and three-winding transformers, PSTs, Ward and extended Ward equivalents, dangling (boundary) lines, tie lines (\(x = x_1 + x_2\)), HVDC as injections. The matrices built here reappear as \(B_\text{bus} = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(b)\, A\) in get_susceptance_matrices (dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/ptdf.py), the starting point of every DC computation in ToOp.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Transmission line parameters; short, medium (\(\pi\)) and long line models.
  • Transformer models with off-nominal tap and phase shift in the branch admittance matrix.
  • Generators, loads (constant P, constant Z), shunts.
  • Bus admittance matrix \(Y_\text{bus}\): construction by inspection and via the connection matrices \(C_f, C_t\) (revisits the incidence matrix and Laplacian of Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 with complex weights); sparsity; loss of symmetry with phase shifters.
  • Network equivalents: Ward / extended Ward (Kron reduction as a Schur complement), boundary nodes (X-nodes), tie lines.
  • Tools: MATPOWER in GNU Octave (loadcase, ext2int, makeYbus, define_constants); pandapower's internal ppc and its PYPOWER port of makeYbus.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Build \(Y_\text{bus}\) of a small network by inspection and with \(C_f^\top Y_f + C_t^\top Y_t + [Y_\text{sh}]\), including off-nominal taps and phase shifters.
  • Reproduce MATPOWER's makeYbus (Octave) or pandapower's makeYbus (NumPy) for IEEE 14 to machine precision.
  • Explain why a phase shifter makes \(Y_\text{bus}\) non-symmetric and how a Ward equivalent is a Schur complement of \(Y_\text{bus}\).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Branch model. MATPOWER (and pandapower, which ports it) models every line, transformer and phase shifter as a \(\pi\) section with series admittance \(y_s = 1/(r_s + j x_s)\) and total charging susceptance \(b_c\), in series with an ideal transformer of complex ratio \(N = \tau e^{j\theta_\text{shift}}\) at the from end:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} i_f \\ i_t \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \left(y_s + j\frac{b_c}{2}\right)\frac{1}{\tau^2} & -\,y_s \frac{1}{\tau e^{-j\theta_\text{shift}}} \\ -\,y_s \frac{1}{\tau e^{j\theta_\text{shift}}} & y_s + j\frac{b_c}{2} \end{bmatrix}}_{Y_\text{br} = \begin{bmatrix} y_{ff} & y_{ft} \\ y_{tf} & y_{tt} \end{bmatrix}} \begin{bmatrix} v_f \\ v_t \end{bmatrix}. \]

With \(y_{ft} \neq y_{tf}\) whenever \(\theta_\text{shift} \neq 0\), a phase shifter breaks the symmetry of \(Y_\text{bus}\).

Assembly. Stack the four entries of all \(n_l\) branches into vectors \(Y_{ff}, Y_{ft}, Y_{tf}, Y_{tt}\) and let \(C_f, C_t \in \{0,1\}^{n_l \times n_b}\) mark the from and to bus of each branch. With \([\cdot]\) the diagonal matrix of a vector,

\[ Y_f = [Y_{ff}]\,C_f + [Y_{ft}]\,C_t, \qquad Y_t = [Y_{tf}]\,C_f + [Y_{tt}]\,C_t, \qquad Y_\text{bus} = C_f^\top Y_f + C_t^\top Y_t + [Y_\text{sh}]. \]

For plain lines (\(\tau = 1\), \(\theta_\text{shift} = 0\)) this reduces to a complex weighted Laplacian of Chapter 3 plus diagonal terms,

\[ Y_\text{bus} = A^\top [y_s]\, A + \left[(C_f + C_t)^\top \tfrac{j b_c}{2}\right] + [Y_\text{sh}], \qquad A = C_f - C_t . \]

Dropping resistances, charging and shunts leaves \(Y_\text{bus} = -j\,A^\top \operatorname{diag}(1/x)\, A\), whose imaginary part (up to sign) is the DC matrix \(B_\text{bus} = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(b)\, A\), \(b = 1/x\), of Chapter 16.

Octave + MATPOWER. Rebuild \(Y_\text{bus}\) for IEEE 14 and compare with makeYbus:

ybus_check.m
function err = ybus_check(casename)
  % Rebuild the bus admittance matrix of a MATPOWER case from the branch model, Ybus = Cf' (Yff Cf + Yft Ct)
  % + Ct' (Ytf Cf + Ytt Ct) + Ysh, and return the largest difference against makeYbus (Chapter 14).
  define_constants;
  mpc = ext2int(loadcase(casename));
  [Ybus, Yf, Yt] = makeYbus(mpc);

  nb = size(mpc.bus, 1);  nl = size(mpc.branch, 1);
  Cf = sparse(1:nl, mpc.branch(:, F_BUS), 1, nl, nb);
  Ct = sparse(1:nl, mpc.branch(:, T_BUS), 1, nl, nb);
  stat = mpc.branch(:, BR_STATUS);
  ys = stat ./ (mpc.branch(:, BR_R) + 1j * mpc.branch(:, BR_X));
  bc = stat .* mpc.branch(:, BR_B);
  tap = ones(nl, 1);  k = find(mpc.branch(:, TAP));  tap(k) = mpc.branch(k, TAP);
  tap = tap .* exp(1j * pi / 180 * mpc.branch(:, SHIFT));
  Ytt = ys + 1j * bc / 2;  Yff = Ytt ./ (tap .* conj(tap));
  Yft = -ys ./ conj(tap);  Ytf = -ys ./ tap;
  Ysh = (mpc.bus(:, GS) + 1j * mpc.bus(:, BS)) / mpc.baseMVA;
  D = @(v) spdiags(v, 0, numel(v), numel(v));
  Y2 = Cf.' * (D(Yff) * Cf + D(Yft) * Ct) + Ct.' * (D(Ytf) * Cf + D(Ytt) * Ct) + D(Ysh);
  err = full(max(max(abs(Ybus - Y2))));   % expect round-off only
end

%!test
%! if isempty(which('makeYbus')), disp('MATPOWER not on the path, test skipped'); return; end
%! assert(ybus_check('case14') < 1e-12)
%! assert(ybus_check('case57') < 1e-12)

The same construction in NumPy against pandapower.pypower.makeYbus.makeYbus(baseMVA, bus, branch) on the ppc of pandapower.networks.case14() reproduces pandapower's matrix exactly; note that pandapower stores TAP = 1 for lines, while MATPOWER case files use TAP = 0.

Lab: IEEE 14 admittance matrix, two ways

Tools: Jupyter + NumPy + pandapower, or Octave + MATPOWER (either path is fine; doing both is better).

  1. Load IEEE 14 (pandapower.networks.case14() and run pandapower.runpp once to populate net._ppc, or loadcase('case14') in Octave). Build \(C_f\), \(C_t\), \(Y_f\), \(Y_t\) and \(Y_\text{bus}\) from the branch and bus tables as in the worked example.

  3. Plot the sparsity pattern of \(Y_\text{bus}\) with matplotlib.pyplot.spy (Octave: spy). Identify the transformer branches from their off-nominal taps and check the symmetry of \(Y_\text{bus}\) numerically.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
All statements are also in exercises.ipynb; the worked examples run in examples.ipynb.

  1. Build \(Y_\text{bus}\) by inspection for a three-bus ring with series impedances \(j0.1\), \(j0.2\), \(j0.25\) p.u. and charging \(b_c = 0.02\) p.u. on each line. Check that every row sums to the bus's total shunt admittance.

    Solution: Exercise 1.

  2. A transformer with ratio \(\tau = 1.05\) and no phase shift connects buses 1 and 2 with \(x = 0.1\) p.u. Write its \(Y_\text{br}\) and draw the equivalent \(\pi\) circuit implied by it. Why is the \(\pi\) circuit asymmetric?

    Solution: Exercise 2.

  3. (Octave + MATPOWER) For case14, compute \(B_\text{bus} = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(1/x)\, A\) ignoring taps and compare it with the first output of makeBdc(mpc). Explain every entry that differs.

    Solution: Exercise 3.

  4. (Jupyter: NumPy) Kron reduction: partition the buses of IEEE 14 into kept and eliminated sets, compute the Ward-type equivalent \(Y_{kk} - Y_{ke} Y_{ee}^{-1} Y_{ek}\), and show that it reproduces the kept-bus voltages for a current injection pattern with zero injection at the eliminated buses.

    Solution: Exercise 4.

  5. (Jupyter: NumPy + matplotlib) For a 300 km line with given per-km parameters, compare the exact long-line ABCD parameters with the nominal \(\pi\) model as a function of length, and plot the relative error of the series admittance.

    Solution: Exercise 5.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. Ybus from the tables. ybus_numpy.case14_ppc() loads pandapower.networks.case14(), runs one power flow and returns net._ppc: 14 buses, 20 branches, baseMVA = 100. connection_matrices builds \(C_f\) and \(C_t\) (20 × 14, one 1 per row, from the F_BUS and T_BUS columns, already 0-based in the ppc), branch_admittances the four entries of every branch from BR_R, BR_X, BR_B, TAP and SHIFT,

    \[ y_{tt} = y_s + j\tfrac{b_c}{2}, \quad y_{ff} = \frac{y_{tt}}{\tau^2}, \quad y_{ft} = -\frac{y_s}{\tau e^{-j\theta}}, \quad y_{tf} = -\frac{y_s}{\tau e^{j\theta}}, \]

    and build_ybus assembles \(Y_f = [Y_{ff}] C_f + [Y_{ft}] C_t\), \(Y_t = [Y_{tf}] C_f + [Y_{tt}] C_t\) and \(Y_\text{bus} = C_f^\top Y_f + C_t^\top Y_t + [Y_\text{sh}]\) with \(Y_\text{sh} = (G_s + jB_s)/\text{baseMVA}\) from the bus table (only bus 9 has a shunt, 19 Mvar). The Octave path is ybus_check.m unchanged.

  2. Comparison. max_difference(ppc) gives \(\max |Y_\text{bus} - Y_\text{bus}^\text{makeYbus}| = 0\) exactly: both codes do the same floating-point operations in the same order. Octave: ybus_check('case14') returns \(1.8 \times 10^{-15}\) and ybus_check('case57') \(1.4 \times 10^{-14}\), round-off from the sparse products.

  3. Sparsity, taps, symmetry. matplotlib.pyplot.spy(Ybus) shows 54 nonzeros of 196 (28 %): the 14 diagonal entries and two per branch (figure described, not saved; with 20 branches and 14 buses the pattern is the adjacency of the IEEE 14 graph plus the diagonal). The transformers are the branches with TAP different from 1: branches 15, 16, 17 of the ppc (0-based), i.e. 4–7 with \(\tau = 0.978\), 4–9 with \(\tau = 0.969\) and 5–6 with \(\tau = 0.932\) (1-based bus numbers), none with a phase shift. \(\lVert Y_\text{bus} - Y_\text{bus}^\top \rVert_F = 0\): an off-nominal tap scales \(y_{ff}\) by \(1/\tau^2\) and both off-diagonals by \(1/\tau\), so the matrix stays symmetric; only a phase shift breaks the symmetry.

  4. A 5° phase shift. with_shift(branch, 15, 5.0) puts \(\theta = 5°\) on the 4–7 transformer. Rebuilt, \(\lVert Y_\text{bus} - Y_\text{bus}^\top \rVert_F = 1.2053\), coming from the single pair \(Y_{4,7} = -0.4261 + 4.8709j\) and \(Y_{7,4} = +0.4261 + 4.8709j\): the two entries have the same modulus 4.8895 (\(= 1/(x\tau)\)) and opposite real parts, since \(y_{ft} = -y_s e^{j\theta}/\tau\) and \(y_{tf} = -y_s e^{-j\theta}/\tau\) are complex conjugates up to the common factor \(-y_s/\tau\). The norm is \(\sqrt{2}\,|Y_{4,7} - Y_{7,4}| = \sqrt{2} \times 2 \times 0.4261 = 1.2053\), i.e. \(2\sqrt{2}\,\sin 5° / (x \tau)\).

    ybus_numpy.py
    """Ybus of IEEE 14 from the connection matrices, checked against pandapower's makeYbus (Chapter 14, Lab).

Every branch is a pi section with series admittance ys = 1/(r + jx), total charging bc and an ideal transformer of
complex ratio tap = tau·exp(j·shift) at the from end. Its four entries are Yff = (ys + j·bc/2)/|tap|²,
Yft = −ys/conj(tap), Ytf = −ys/tap and Ytt = ys + j·bc/2. With Cf and Ct marking the from and to bus of each
branch, Yf = diag(Yff) Cf + diag(Yft) Ct, Yt = diag(Ytf) Cf + diag(Ytt) Ct and Ybus = Cfᵀ Yf + Ctᵀ Yt + diag(Ysh).
pandapower keeps a MATPOWER-style ``ppc`` after a power flow; it stores TAP = 1 for lines where MATPOWER files
write 0, so the tap column can be used as it is.
"""

import numpy as np
import pandapower as pp
import pandapower.networks as pn
from pandapower.pypower.idx_brch import BR_B, BR_R, BR_STATUS, BR_X, F_BUS, SHIFT, T_BUS, TAP
from pandapower.pypower.idx_bus import BS, GS
from pandapower.pypower.makeYbus import makeYbus


def case14_ppc() -> dict:
    """The internal MATPOWER-style case of pandapower's IEEE 14, populated by one power flow."""
    net = pn.case14()
    pp.runpp(net)
    return net._ppc  # noqa: SLF001  (pandapower exposes the ppc only as a private attribute)


def connection_matrices(branch: np.ndarray, n_bus: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Cf and Ct, shape (branches, buses): a one in the column of the from bus and of the to bus of each branch."""
    n_branch = branch.shape[0]
    cf, ct = np.zeros((n_branch, n_bus)), np.zeros((n_branch, n_bus))
    cf[np.arange(n_branch), branch[:, F_BUS].real.astype(int)] = 1
    ct[np.arange(n_branch), branch[:, T_BUS].real.astype(int)] = 1
    return cf, ct


def branch_admittances(branch: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """The four entries Yff, Yft, Ytf, Ytt of every branch, out-of-service branches set to zero."""
    status = branch[:, BR_STATUS].real
    ys = status / (branch[:, BR_R] + 1j * branch[:, BR_X])
    bc = status * branch[:, BR_B].real
    tau = np.where(branch[:, TAP].real == 0, 1.0, branch[:, TAP].real)
    tap = tau * np.exp(1j * np.pi / 180 * branch[:, SHIFT].real)
    ytt = ys + 1j * bc / 2
    yff = ytt / (tap * np.conj(tap))
    yft = -ys / np.conj(tap)
    ytf = -ys / tap
    return yff, yft, ytf, ytt


def build_ybus(bus: np.ndarray, branch: np.ndarray, base_mva: float) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Ybus, Yf and Yt (dense) assembled as Ybus = Cfᵀ Yf + Ctᵀ Yt + diag(Ysh)."""
    n_bus = bus.shape[0]
    cf, ct = connection_matrices(branch, n_bus)
    yff, yft, ytf, ytt = branch_admittances(branch)
    yf = np.diag(yff) @ cf + np.diag(yft) @ ct
    yt = np.diag(ytf) @ cf + np.diag(ytt) @ ct
    ysh = (bus[:, GS] + 1j * bus[:, BS]) / base_mva
    return cf.T @ yf + ct.T @ yt + np.diag(ysh), yf, yt


def max_difference(ppc: dict) -> float:
    """Largest absolute entry of Ybus (this module) minus Ybus (pandapower's makeYbus)."""
    ybus, _, _ = build_ybus(ppc['bus'], ppc['branch'], ppc['baseMVA'])
    reference, _, _ = makeYbus(ppc['baseMVA'], ppc['bus'], ppc['branch'])
    return float(np.abs(ybus - reference.toarray()).max())


def transformer_branches(branch: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Indices of the branches with an off-nominal tap or a phase shift."""
    tap, shift = branch[:, TAP].real, branch[:, SHIFT].real
    return np.flatnonzero(((tap != 0) & (tap != 1)) | (shift != 0))


def asymmetry(matrix: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Frobenius norm of Y − Yᵀ, zero for a symmetric matrix."""
    return float(np.linalg.norm(matrix - matrix.T))


def with_shift(branch: np.ndarray, index: int, degrees: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """A copy of the branch table with a phase shift (degrees) on one branch."""
    shifted = branch.copy()
    shifted[index, SHIFT] = degrees
    return shifted


def main() -> None:
    """Print the numbers of Lab steps 1–4 for IEEE 14."""
    ppc = case14_ppc()
    bus, branch, base_mva = ppc['bus'], ppc['branch'], ppc['baseMVA']
    ybus, _, _ = build_ybus(bus, branch, base_mva)
    print(f'{bus.shape[0]} buses, {branch.shape[0]} branches, baseMVA {base_mva}')
    print(f'max |Ybus - makeYbus| = {max_difference(ppc):.3e}')
    nnz = int(np.count_nonzero(ybus))
    print(f'nonzeros {nnz} of {ybus.size} ({100 * nnz / ybus.size:.0f} %)')
    print(f'  {bus.shape[0]} diagonal + 2 x {(nnz - bus.shape[0]) // 2} off-diagonal')
    trafos = transformer_branches(branch)
    for k in trafos:
        f, t = int(branch[k, F_BUS].real), int(branch[k, T_BUS].real)
        tap, x = branch[k, TAP].real, branch[k, BR_X].real
        print(f'transformer branch {k}: buses {f + 1}-{t + 1} (1-based), tap {tap:.4f}, x {x:.5f}')
    print(f'||Ybus - Ybus^T|| = {asymmetry(ybus):.3e} (symmetric despite the taps)')
    shifted, _, _ = build_ybus(bus, with_shift(branch, int(trafos[0]), 5.0), base_mva)
    f, t = int(branch[trafos[0], F_BUS].real), int(branch[trafos[0], T_BUS].real)
    print(f'with a 5 degree shift on branch {trafos[0]}: ||Ybus - Ybus^T|| = {asymmetry(shifted):.4f}')
    print(f'  Y[{f + 1},{t + 1}] = {shifted[f, t]:.4f}, Y[{t + 1},{f + 1}] = {shifted[t, f]:.4f}')
    print(f'  same modulus {abs(shifted[f, t]):.4f}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
Series admittances: \(1/j0.1 = -j10\) (line 1–2), \(1/j0.2 = -j5\) (line 2–3), \(1/j0.25 = -j4\) (line 1–3). Each line adds \(y_s + jb_c/2 = y_s + j0.01\) to the diagonal entry of both its buses and \(-y_s\) to the two off-diagonal entries between them. Bus 1 has lines 1–2 and 1–3, bus 2 has 1–2 and 2–3, bus 3 has 2–3 and 1–3:

\[ Y_\text{bus} = \begin{bmatrix} -j13.98 & j10 & j4 \\ j10 & -j14.98 & j5 \\ j4 & j5 & -j8.98 \end{bmatrix}, \]

for example \(Y_{11} = -j10 - j4 + 2 \times j0.01 = -j13.98\). Every row sums to \(j0.02\): the series admittances cancel between the diagonal and the off-diagonal entries of the same row, and what remains is the total charging connected to the bus, two half-lines of \(j0.01\) each. In general \(\sum_k Y_{ik}\) is the total shunt admittance at bus \(i\) (charging plus explicit shunts), zero for a lossless network without charging, which is why \(B_\text{bus}\) of the DC power flow is singular. small_ybus.ring3_ybus() and row_sums reproduce the matrix and the row sums of \(j0.02\).

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
With \(y_s = 1/(j0.1) = -j10\), \(\tau = 1.05\) and \(\theta = 0\),

\[ Y_\text{br} = \begin{bmatrix} y_s/\tau^2 & -y_s/\tau \\ -y_s/\tau & y_s \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -j9.0703 & j9.5238 \\ j9.5238 & -j10 \end{bmatrix}. \]

A \(\pi\) circuit with series admittance \(y_\text{se}\) and shunts \(y_1\), \(y_2\) has \(Y = \begin{bmatrix} y_\text{se} + y_1 & -y_\text{se} \\ -y_\text{se} & y_\text{se} + y_2 \end{bmatrix}\), so matching the entries:

\[ y_\text{se} = \frac{y_s}{\tau} = -j9.5238, \qquad y_1 = y_s\left(\frac{1}{\tau^2} - \frac{1}{\tau}\right) = +j0.4535, \qquad y_2 = y_s\left(1 - \frac{1}{\tau}\right) = -j0.4762 . \]

The shunt at the tapped (from) side is capacitive (\(+j\)) and the one at the other side inductive (\(-j\)); they nearly cancel (\(y_1 + y_2 = y_s (1/\tau - 1)^2 = -j0.0227\)). The circuit is asymmetric because the ideal transformer sits at one end: seen from bus 1 the reactance is scaled by \(\tau^2\), seen from bus 2 it is not, so the two driving-point admittances \(y_s/\tau^2\) and \(y_s\) differ while the transfer admittance is the geometric mean \(y_s/\tau\) of the two. A symmetric \(\pi\) would need \(y_1 = y_2\), i.e. \(\tau = 1\). The "negative" shunt is a mathematical artefact of forcing a transformer into a \(\pi\) template, not a physical capacitor; it is nevertheless what every power-flow program stores. small_ybus.transformer_ybr(1.05, 0.1) and pi_equivalent print these values.

small_ybus.py
"""Ybus of a three-bus ring by inspection and the branch matrix of a tapped transformer (Chapter 14, Exercises 1–2).

By inspection, the diagonal entry of a bus is the sum of the admittances of everything connected to it (series
admittances of its lines plus half the charging of each line plus shunts) and the off-diagonal entry between two
buses is minus the series admittance of the line joining them. For a transformer with ratio tau at the from end,
Ybr = [[ys/tau², −ys/tau], [−ys/tau, ys]], whose pi equivalent has series admittance ys/tau, a from-side shunt of
ys (1/tau² − 1/tau) and a to-side shunt of ys (1 − 1/tau).
"""

import numpy as np

RING_LINES = [(0, 1, 0.1j), (1, 2, 0.2j), (0, 2, 0.25j)]  # (from, to, series impedance in p.u.)
RING_BC = 0.02  # total charging susceptance of each line, p.u.


def ring3_ybus(lines: list[tuple[int, int, complex]] = RING_LINES, bc: float = RING_BC) -> np.ndarray:
    """Ybus of the three-bus ring, filled in by inspection line by line."""
    ybus = np.zeros((3, 3), dtype=complex)
    for f, t, z in lines:
        ys = 1 / z
        ybus[f, f] += ys + 1j * bc / 2
        ybus[t, t] += ys + 1j * bc / 2
        ybus[f, t] -= ys
        ybus[t, f] -= ys
    return ybus


def row_sums(ybus: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The sum of each row: with no shunt elements it is the total charging admittance connected to the bus."""
    return ybus.sum(axis=1)


def transformer_ybr(tau: float, x: float, shift_deg: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray:
    """Branch admittance matrix of a transformer with ratio tau·exp(j·shift) at the from end and reactance x."""
    ys = 1 / (1j * x)
    tap = tau * np.exp(1j * np.deg2rad(shift_deg))
    return np.array([[ys / (tap * np.conj(tap)), -ys / np.conj(tap)], [-ys / tap, ys]])


def pi_equivalent(ybr: np.ndarray) -> tuple[complex, complex, complex]:
    """Series admittance, from-side shunt and to-side shunt of the pi circuit with the same branch matrix.

    Valid when the two off-diagonal entries are equal (no phase shift): a pi circuit cannot represent a phase
    shifter, whose Ybr is not symmetric.
    """
    series = -ybr[0, 1]
    return series, ybr[0, 0] - series, ybr[1, 1] - series


def main() -> None:
    """Print the ring's Ybus with its row sums and the transformer's Ybr with its pi equivalent."""
    np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)
    ybus = ring3_ybus()
    print('three-bus ring Ybus =')
    print(ybus)
    print('row sums =', row_sums(ybus), '  (expected j bc = 0.02j at every bus)')
    ybr = transformer_ybr(1.05, 0.1)
    print('transformer tau = 1.05, x = 0.1: Ybr =')
    print(ybr)
    series, shunt_from, shunt_to = pi_equivalent(ybr)
    print(f'pi equivalent: series {series:.4f}, shunt at from {shunt_from:.4f}, shunt at to {shunt_to:.4f}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
bdc_check.m builds \(A = C_f - C_t\), \(B_\text{plain} = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(1/x)\, A\) and subtracts it from the first output of makeBdc(mpc). For case14 the difference is zero everywhere except at the buses of the three transformers, where MATPOWER uses \(b = 1/(x\tau)\) instead of \(1/x\) (makeBdc: b = b ./ tap):

branch \(\tau\) \(x\) \(1/x\) \(1/(x\tau)\) difference 4–7 0.978 0.20912 4.7819 4.8895 0.10757 4–9 0.969 0.55618 1.7980 1.8555 0.05752 5–6 0.932 0.25202 3.9679 4.2574 0.28951

The eleven entries that differ (1-based) are exactly the ones these branches touch: \((5,5)\) and \((6,6)\) by \(+0.28951\), \((5,6)\) and \((6,5)\) by \(-0.28951\); \((4,7)\) and \((7,4)\) by \(-0.10757\), \((7,7)\) by \(+0.10757\); \((4,9)\) and \((9,4)\) by \(-0.05752\), \((9,9)\) by \(+0.05752\); and \((4,4)\) by \(+0.10757 + 0.05752 = 0.16509\), the sum of its two transformers. The largest difference is 0.28951 (the 5–6 transformer, with the smallest \(\tau\)), and for case9, which has no taps, the two matrices are identical (\(0\)). Nothing else differs: phase shifts, if there were any, would not appear in \(B_\text{bus}\) at all but in the injection vectors Pbusinj and Pfinj (the third and fourth outputs; here zero), because in the DC model a shift adds a constant to the angle difference rather than a term to the matrix. The lesson for get_susceptance_matrices in ToOp: \(b = 1/x\) is the DC model of a line, and the tap ratio of a transformer enters the DC susceptance as \(1/(x\tau)\), a correction of a few percent that MATPOWER applies and a plain Laplacian forgets.

bdc_check.m
function [maxdiff, rows, cols, diffs] = bdc_check(casename)
  % Compare the plain DC matrix A' diag(1/x) A, which ignores taps, with the first output of MATPOWER's makeBdc,
  % and return the largest difference with the list of entries that differ (Chapter 14, Exercise 3).
  define_constants;
  mpc = ext2int(loadcase(casename));
  Bbus = makeBdc(mpc);

  nb = size(mpc.bus, 1);  nl = size(mpc.branch, 1);
  Cf = sparse(1:nl, mpc.branch(:, F_BUS), 1, nl, nb);
  Ct = sparse(1:nl, mpc.branch(:, T_BUS), 1, nl, nb);
  A = Cf - Ct;
  b = mpc.branch(:, BR_STATUS) ./ mpc.branch(:, BR_X);
  Bplain = A' * spdiags(b, 0, nl, nl) * A;
  D = Bbus - Bplain;
  [rows, cols, diffs] = find(abs(D) > 1e-9 .* ones(size(D)) & D ~= 0);
  diffs = full(D(sub2ind(size(D), rows, cols)));
  maxdiff = full(max(max(abs(D))));
end

%!test
%! if isempty(which('loadcase')), disp('MATPOWER not on the path, test skipped'); return; end
%! define_constants;
%! [maxdiff, rows, cols, diffs] = bdc_check('case14');
%! mpc = ext2int(loadcase('case14'));
%! k = find(mpc.branch(:, TAP));
%! assert(numel(k), 3);                                  % three transformers in IEEE 14
%! buses = unique([mpc.branch(k, F_BUS); mpc.branch(k, T_BUS)]);
%! assert(all(ismember(rows, buses)) && all(ismember(cols, buses)));   % only their buses differ
%! expected = max(abs(1 ./ mpc.branch(k, BR_X) .* (1 ./ mpc.branch(k, TAP) - 1)));
%! assert(maxdiff, expected, 1e-9);                      % the largest difference is b/tau - b of one transformer
%! assert(bdc_check('case9') < 1e-12);                   % no taps: the two matrices are identical

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
Partition the nodal equations \(I = Y V\) into kept (\(k\)) and eliminated (\(e\)) buses:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} I_k \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Y_{kk} & Y_{ke} \\ Y_{ek} & Y_{ee} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V_k \\ V_e \end{bmatrix} \;\Rightarrow\; V_e = -Y_{ee}^{-1} Y_{ek} V_k, \qquad I_k = \left(Y_{kk} - Y_{ke} Y_{ee}^{-1} Y_{ek}\right) V_k . \]

The Schur complement \(Y_\text{red} = Y_{kk} - Y_{ke} Y_{ee}^{-1} Y_{ek}\) is the Ward-type equivalent: an admittance matrix on the kept buses alone that gives the same \(V_k\) for every injection with \(I_e = 0\). kron_reduction.KEEP keeps buses 1–5 of IEEE 14 (the 132 kV part) and eliminates 6–14. Checks (kron_reduction.main()): with a deterministic pseudo-random complex injection at the kept buses, \(\max |V_k^\text{full} - V_k^\text{reduced}| = 3.5 \times 10^{-13}\), round-off; the reduced matrix is symmetric (the original is). Only buses 4 and 5 are neighbours of the eliminated set (through the transformers 4–7, 4–9 and 5–6), so the reduction changes only the block \(\{4, 5\}\): \(Y_{4,5}\) goes from \(-6.841 + 21.579j\) to \(-7.101 + 23.060j\), and the diagonals of 4 and 5 move with it, while the entries of buses 1–3 are untouched. In general the elimination creates a fictitious branch between every pair of kept buses that share an eliminated neighbour (fill-in), which is why equivalents of a large external network are dense. The equivalent is only valid for the injection pattern it assumes: adding 1 p.u. of current at the eliminated bus 9 moves the kept voltages by 2.47 p.u. relative to the reduced solution. A Ward equivalent therefore carries, besides \(Y_\text{red}\), equivalent injections at the boundary buses that stand for the eliminated loads and generators, and an extended Ward adds a fictitious generator to hold the boundary voltage.

kron_reduction.py
"""Kron reduction of the IEEE 14 admittance matrix onto a set of kept buses (Chapter 14, Exercise 4).

Partition the buses into kept (k) and eliminated (e). With zero current injection at the eliminated buses the
nodal equations I = Y V reduce to I_k = (Y_kk − Y_ke Y_ee⁻¹ Y_ek) V_k: the Schur complement is the Ward-type
equivalent, an admittance matrix on the kept buses alone that gives the same kept-bus voltages for any such
injection pattern. Eliminated buses leave fictitious branches between every pair of kept buses they connected, so the
equivalent fills in where the original was sparse.
"""

import numpy as np
from ybus_numpy import build_ybus, case14_ppc

KEEP = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])  # buses 1–5 (1-based): the 132 kV part of IEEE 14 and the transformer buses


def kron_reduce(ybus: np.ndarray, keep: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Schur complement Y_kk − Y_ke Y_ee⁻¹ Y_ek of the admittance matrix onto the kept buses."""
    eliminate = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(ybus.shape[0]), keep)
    y_kk = ybus[np.ix_(keep, keep)]
    y_ke = ybus[np.ix_(keep, eliminate)]
    y_ek = ybus[np.ix_(eliminate, keep)]
    y_ee = ybus[np.ix_(eliminate, eliminate)]
    return y_kk - y_ke @ np.linalg.solve(y_ee, y_ek)


def kept_voltages_full(ybus: np.ndarray, keep: np.ndarray, injection_kept: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Kept-bus voltages from the full network, with the given currents at the kept buses and zero elsewhere."""
    current = np.zeros(ybus.shape[0], dtype=complex)
    current[keep] = injection_kept
    return np.linalg.solve(ybus, current)[keep]


def kept_voltages_reduced(ybus: np.ndarray, keep: np.ndarray, injection_kept: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Kept-bus voltages from the Kron-reduced matrix alone."""
    return np.linalg.solve(kron_reduce(ybus, keep), injection_kept)


def main() -> None:
    """Print the reduced matrix of IEEE 14 onto buses 1–5 and the voltage check."""
    np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True, linewidth=119)
    ppc = case14_ppc()
    ybus, _, _ = build_ybus(ppc['bus'], ppc['branch'], ppc['baseMVA'])
    reduced = kron_reduce(ybus, KEEP)
    print(f'kept buses (1-based): {KEEP + 1}, eliminated: {np.setdiff1d(np.arange(14), KEEP) + 1}')
    print(
        'nonzeros: full block Y_kk', np.count_nonzero(ybus[np.ix_(KEEP, KEEP)]), ', reduced', np.count_nonzero(reduced)
    )
    print('reduced matrix (imaginary part):')
    print(reduced.imag)
    print('new coupling between buses 4 and 5 (zero in Y_kk):', f'{ybus[3, 4]:.3f} -> {reduced[3, 4]:.3f}')
    rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
    injection = rng.normal(size=len(KEEP)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=len(KEEP))
    v_full = kept_voltages_full(ybus, KEEP, injection)
    v_reduced = kept_voltages_reduced(ybus, KEEP, injection)
    print(f'max |V_full - V_reduced| at the kept buses = {np.abs(v_full - v_reduced).max():.2e}')
    with_injection_elsewhere = np.zeros(14, dtype=complex)
    with_injection_elsewhere[KEEP] = injection
    with_injection_elsewhere[8] = 1.0  # one ampere at bus 9: the equivalent no longer applies
    v_bad = np.linalg.solve(ybus, with_injection_elsewhere)[KEEP]
    print(f'with a current at an eliminated bus the mismatch is {np.abs(v_bad - v_reduced).max():.3f}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
The statement leaves the per-km parameters to you; long_line.py uses a typical single-circuit 400 kV line at 50 Hz: \(r = 0.028\ \Omega/\text{km}\), \(L = 0.9\) mH/km (\(x = 0.2827\ \Omega/\text{km}\)), \(C = 12.5\) nF/km (\(b = 3.927\ \mu\text{S/km}\)), \(g = 0\). Then \(\gamma = \sqrt{zy} = 5.21 \times 10^{-5} + j1.055 \times 10^{-3}\) per km (wavelength \(2\pi/\beta = 5956\) km) and \(Z_c = \sqrt{z/y} = 268.7 - j13.3\ \Omega\). For a length \(l\),

\[ A = D = \cosh \gamma l, \qquad B = Z_c \sinh \gamma l, \qquad C = \frac{\sinh \gamma l}{Z_c}, \qquad AD - BC = 1 , \]

and at 300 km \(A = 0.9504 + 0.0049j\), \(B = 8.12 + 83.43j\ \Omega\), \(C = -1.9 \times 10^{-6} + 1.159 \times 10^{-3}j\) S. The exact equivalent \(\pi\) has \(Z' = B = Z \,\sinh(\gamma l)/(\gamma l)\) and \(Y'/2 = (A - 1)/B = (Y/2) \tanh(\gamma l/2)/(\gamma l/2)\), against the nominal \(Z = zl = 8.40 + 84.82j\ \Omega\) and \(Y = yl = 1.178 \times 10^{-3}j\) S: the exact series impedance is 1.7 % smaller and the shunt 0.8 % larger. The relative error of the nominal series admittance \(1/Z\) is \(|\gamma l / \sinh(\gamma l) - 1| \approx |\gamma l|^2/6\):

length (km) 50 100 200 300 400 500 error of \(1/Z\) (%) 0.05 0.19 0.75 1.69 3.04 4.80

The plot (described, not saved) is a parabola: the error grows with the square of the length, 1.67 % from the rule of thumb at 300 km against 1.69 % exact, and crosses 1 % at about 230 km. That is the usual textbook boundary between "medium" lines, where the nominal \(\pi\) is adequate, and "long" lines, where the exact \(\pi\) (or the ABCD form) is needed. For the branch tables of Chapter 14 the practical consequence is that the \(r\), \(x\), \(b_c\) of a long line in a MATPOWER or pandapower case should already be the equivalent \(\pi\) values, which is what grid data from TSOs normally contains.

long_line.py
"""Exact long-line (ABCD) parameters against the nominal pi model as a function of length (Chapter 14, Exercise 5).

For a line with series impedance z and shunt admittance y per km, the propagation constant is gamma = sqrt(z y)
and the characteristic impedance Zc = sqrt(z / y). Over a length l the exact two-port has A = D = cosh(gamma l),
B = Zc sinh(gamma l) and C = sinh(gamma l) / Zc, and the exact equivalent pi has series impedance
Z' = Z sinh(gamma l) / (gamma l) and half-shunts (Y/2) tanh(gamma l / 2) / (gamma l / 2), where Z = z l and
Y = y l are the nominal-pi values. The relative error of the nominal series admittance is
|gamma l / sinh(gamma l) − 1|.
"""

import numpy as np

# a typical single-circuit 400 kV overhead line at 50 Hz
R_PER_KM = 0.028  # ohm/km
X_PER_KM = 2 * np.pi * 50 * 0.9e-3  # ohm/km, from 0.9 mH/km
B_PER_KM = 2 * np.pi * 50 * 12.5e-9  # S/km, from 12.5 nF/km
LENGTH_KM = 300.0


def abcd(length_km: float, r: float = R_PER_KM, x: float = X_PER_KM, b: float = B_PER_KM) -> np.ndarray:
    """The exact ABCD matrix of a lossy line of the given length."""
    z, y = r + 1j * x, 1j * b
    gamma, zc = np.sqrt(z * y), np.sqrt(z / y)
    gl = gamma * length_km
    return np.array([[np.cosh(gl), zc * np.sinh(gl)], [np.sinh(gl) / zc, np.cosh(gl)]])


def nominal_pi(
    length_km: float, r: float = R_PER_KM, x: float = X_PER_KM, b: float = B_PER_KM
) -> tuple[complex, complex]:
    """Series impedance Z = z l and total shunt admittance Y = y l of the nominal pi model."""
    return (r + 1j * x) * length_km, 1j * b * length_km


def exact_pi(
    length_km: float, r: float = R_PER_KM, x: float = X_PER_KM, b: float = B_PER_KM
) -> tuple[complex, complex]:
    """Series impedance and total shunt admittance of the exact equivalent pi, from the ABCD parameters."""
    m = abcd(length_km, r, x, b)
    series = m[0, 1]  # B = Z'
    shunt_half = (m[0, 0] - 1) / m[0, 1]  # (A - 1) / B = Y'/2
    return series, 2 * shunt_half


def series_admittance_error(
    length_km: np.ndarray, r: float = R_PER_KM, x: float = X_PER_KM, b: float = B_PER_KM
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Relative error |Z/Z' − 1| of the nominal series admittance 1/Z against the exact 1/Z', elementwise."""
    gl = np.sqrt((r + 1j * x) * 1j * b) * np.asarray(length_km, dtype=float)
    return np.abs(gl / np.sinh(gl) - 1)


def main() -> None:
    """Print the ABCD parameters at 300 km, the nominal and exact pi values and the error at several lengths."""
    z, y = R_PER_KM + 1j * X_PER_KM, 1j * B_PER_KM
    gamma, zc = np.sqrt(z * y), np.sqrt(z / y)
    print(f'z = {z:.4f} ohm/km, y = {y.imag:.3e}j S/km, Zc = {zc:.1f} ohm, gamma = {gamma:.3e} /km')
    print(f'wavelength 2 pi / Im(gamma) = {2 * np.pi / gamma.imag:.0f} km')
    m = abcd(LENGTH_KM)
    print(f'ABCD at {LENGTH_KM:.0f} km: A = {m[0, 0]:.4f}, B = {m[0, 1]:.2f} ohm, C = {m[1, 0]:.3e} S')
    print(f'  AD - BC = {np.linalg.det(m):.6f}')
    (z_nom, y_nom), (z_ex, y_ex) = nominal_pi(LENGTH_KM), exact_pi(LENGTH_KM)
    print(f'nominal pi: Z = {z_nom:.2f} ohm, Y = {y_nom.imag:.3e}j S')
    print(f'exact pi:   Z = {z_ex:.2f} ohm, Y = {y_ex.imag:.3e}j S')
    error_300 = 100 * series_admittance_error(LENGTH_KM)
    print(f'relative error of the series admittance at {LENGTH_KM:.0f} km: {error_300:.2f} %')
    lengths = np.array([50.0, 100.0, 200.0, 300.0, 400.0, 500.0])
    errors = series_admittance_error(lengths)
    print('length km   ' + ' '.join(f'{v:7.0f}' for v in lengths))
    print('error %     ' + ' '.join(f'{100 * v:7.2f}' for v in errors))
    print(f'quadratic rule of thumb |gamma l|^2 / 6 at 300 km: {100 * abs(gamma * LENGTH_KM) ** 2 / 6:.2f} %')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Chapter 15. AC power flow
docs.text:
Weeks: 2.5 · Semester: 3 · Prerequisites: Chapter 6, Chapter 14

Why it matters for ToOp

The final word on every candidate topology is an AC N-1 analysis (contingency/ac_loadflow_service/, pandapower and pypowsybl runners). ToOp's AC-only metrics (voltage jump after a contingency, voltage-angle difference across open breakers, non-converging load flows) come from here, and so does the AC–DC mismatch correction applied to DC flows (Chapter 17).

Two AC settings shape everything downstream:

  • Distributed slack. ToOp's PowSyBl parameter sets (grid_helpers/powsybl/loadflow_parameters.py) use OpenLoadFlow with distributed_slack=True: POWSYBL_LOADFLOW_PARAM_PF balances with BalanceType.PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P_MAX, while CGMES_DISTRIBUTED_SLACK and UCTE_DISTRIBUTED_SLACK use BalanceType.PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P with slackDistributionFailureBehavior = LEAVE_ON_SLACK_BUS. docs/dc_solver/loadflow_parameters.md justifies the distributed slack by the smaller AC–DC mismatch it produces. The DC solver itself, in contrast, uses a single slack bus (Chapter 17).
  • Initialization and fallbacks. On import, find_converging_loadflow_params (importer/pypowsybl_import/preprocessing.py) tries POWSYBL_LOADFLOW_PARAM_PF and then CGMES_DISTRIBUTED_SLACK, each with the voltage initializations PREVIOUS_VALUES, DC_VALUES and UNIFORM_VALUES, and keeps the first combination whose AC load flow converges. If none converges it raises an error, unless fail_on_non_convergence is off, in which case it logs a warning and continues with CGMES_DISTRIBUTED_SLACK. The PowSyBl DC backend (dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_backend.py) runs its own AC load flow (default parameters CGMES_DISTRIBUTED_SLACK); if it does not converge, the AC–DC mismatch is set to zero.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Power balance equations in polar and rectangular form; bus types (PQ, PV, slack).
  • Newton–Raphson power flow: mismatch vector, Jacobian blocks, iteration (revisits Chapter 6 on a real system).
  • Gauss–Seidel; fast decoupled load flow (the \(B'\) and \(B''\) matrices, MATPOWER makeB).
  • Reactive power limits and PV→PQ switching; voltage control.
  • Distributed slack: participation factors and how they change the Jacobian; OpenLoadFlow balance types.
  • Initialization (flat, DC, previous values); convergence failures and what they indicate (voltage collapse, islands, bad data); why the initialization can decide which solution you get.
  • Tools: MATPOWER runpf and mpoption in Octave; pandapower.runpp; pypowsybl.loadflow.run_ac; optionally PowerWorld Simulator, the commercial tool used in the labs of several surveyed courses (Appendix A).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Power flow equations. With \(V_i = |V_i| e^{j\theta_i}\), \(Y_\text{bus} = G + jB\) and \(\theta_{ik} = \theta_i - \theta_k\), the complex injections are \(S = [V]\,\overline{Y_\text{bus} V}\), or per bus

\[ P_i = \sum_{k} |V_i||V_k|\left(G_{ik}\cos\theta_{ik} + B_{ik}\sin\theta_{ik}\right), \qquad Q_i = \sum_{k} |V_i||V_k|\left(G_{ik}\sin\theta_{ik} - B_{ik}\cos\theta_{ik}\right). \]

Newton–Raphson. The unknowns are \(\theta\) at all non-slack buses and \(|V|\) at PQ buses. Each iteration solves

\[ \begin{bmatrix} J_{11} & J_{12} \\ J_{21} & J_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \Delta\theta \\ \Delta|V| \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} P^\text{spec} - P(\theta, |V|) \\ Q^\text{spec} - Q(\theta, |V|) \end{bmatrix}, \qquad J_{11} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial \theta},\; J_{12} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial |V|},\; J_{21} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \theta},\; J_{22} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial |V|}, \]

keeping the rows of \(P\) for non-slack buses and of \(Q\) for PQ buses. For \(k \neq i\):

\[ \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial \theta_k} = |V_i||V_k|(G_{ik}\sin\theta_{ik} - B_{ik}\cos\theta_{ik}),\quad \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial |V_k|} = |V_i|(G_{ik}\cos\theta_{ik} + B_{ik}\sin\theta_{ik}), \] \[ \frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial \theta_k} = -|V_i||V_k|(G_{ik}\cos\theta_{ik} + B_{ik}\sin\theta_{ik}),\quad \frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial |V_k|} = |V_i|(G_{ik}\sin\theta_{ik} - B_{ik}\cos\theta_{ik}), \]

and on the diagonal

\[ \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial \theta_i} = -Q_i - B_{ii}|V_i|^2,\quad \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial |V_i|} = \frac{P_i}{|V_i|} + G_{ii}|V_i|,\quad \frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial \theta_i} = P_i - G_{ii}|V_i|^2,\quad \frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial |V_i|} = \frac{Q_i}{|V_i|} - B_{ii}|V_i|. \]

The same blocks in matrix form, as in the dSbus_dV function of MATPOWER and of its PYPOWER port in pandapower (pandapower.pypower.dSbus_dV), with \(I = Y_\text{bus} V\) and \(E = [V/|V|]\) (a diagonal matrix):

\[ \frac{\partial S}{\partial \theta} = j[V]\,\overline{\left([I] - Y_\text{bus}[V]\right)}, \qquad \frac{\partial S}{\partial |V|} = [V]\,\overline{Y_\text{bus} E} + \overline{[I]}\,E, \]

with \(J_{11}, J_{21}\) the real and imaginary parts of \(\partial S/\partial\theta\) and \(J_{12}, J_{22}\) those of \(\partial S/\partial|V|\). Check your implementation against finite differences before trusting it:

ac_jacobian.py
"""Complex power injections and the four Jacobian blocks of the AC power flow, in matrix form (Chapter 15)."""

import numpy as np


def injections(theta: np.ndarray, vm: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Complex nodal injections S = [V] conj(Y V) for angles ``theta`` (rad), magnitudes ``vm`` and Ybus ``y``."""
    v = vm * np.exp(1j * theta)
    return v * np.conj(y @ v)


def jacobian_blocks(theta: np.ndarray, vm: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, ...]:
    """dP/dtheta, dP/dV, dQ/dtheta, dQ/dV (J11, J12, J21, J22) for every bus, before removing slack and PV rows."""
    v = vm * np.exp(1j * theta)
    i = y @ v
    e = np.diag(v / vm)
    ds_dth = 1j * np.diag(v) @ np.conj(np.diag(i) - y @ np.diag(v))
    ds_dvm = np.diag(v) @ np.conj(y @ e) + np.diag(np.conj(i)) @ e
    return ds_dth.real, ds_dvm.real, ds_dth.imag, ds_dvm.imag


def main() -> None:
    """Print the injections and J11 of a two-bus example: a line of 0.01 + j0.1 pu between a source and a load."""
    y_line = 1 / (0.01 + 0.1j)
    y = np.array([[y_line, -y_line], [-y_line, y_line]])
    theta, vm = np.array([0.0, -0.05]), np.array([1.0, 0.98])
    print(np.round(injections(theta, vm, y), 4))
    print(np.round(jacobian_blocks(theta, vm, y)[0], 4))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

test_ac_jacobian.py, next to it in the chapter's src folder, does exactly that: central differences of injections on a random three-bus state, column by column.

Distributed slack. Replace the slack bus's unknown \(P\) by a scalar mismatch \(\Delta\) shared by the participating generators, \(P_{g,i} = P_{g,i}^0 + k_i \Delta\) with \(\sum_i k_i = 1\). The unknown vector gains \(\Delta\), the \(P\) equation of the former slack bus is kept, the Jacobian gains the column \(-k\) (the derivative of \(P(\theta, |V|) - P^0 - k\Delta\) with respect to \(\Delta\)), and the angle reference stays at one bus. In OpenLoadFlow, the balance type selects \(k\) (proportional to \(P_\text{max}\), to the target \(P\), and so on).

Octave + MATPOWER.

matpower_pf.m
function [results, results_fd] = matpower_pf(casename)
  % Solve a MATPOWER case with Newton-Raphson (enforcing reactive limits) and with the XB fast decoupled
  % method, and return both result structs (Chapter 15).
  mpc = loadcase(casename);
  mpopt = mpoption('pf.alg', 'NR', 'pf.enforce_q_lims', 1, 'verbose', 0, 'out.all', 0);
  results = runpf(mpc, mpopt);                   % results.success is 1 if converged
  mpopt = mpoption(mpopt, 'pf.alg', 'FDXB');     % fast decoupled, XB version
  results_fd = runpf(mpc, mpopt);
end

%!test
%! if isempty(which('runpf')), disp('MATPOWER not on the path, test skipped'); return; end
%! [r, rfd] = matpower_pf('case14');
%! assert(r.success == 1 && rfd.success == 1)
