docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: Newton–Raphson from scratch, then break it

Tools: Jupyter + NumPy + matplotlib + pandapower; optionally Octave + MATPOWER, pypowsybl and PowerWorld Simulator.

  1. Implement Newton–Raphson for a 5-bus grid (reuse Chapter 6 code and the \(Y_\text{bus}\) of Chapter 14), with the Jacobian of the worked example. Plot the mismatch norm per iteration on a log scale and confirm quadratic convergence.
  2. Run pandapower.runpp on the same data (or runpf in Octave) and compare voltage magnitudes and angles.
  3. Break convergence on purpose: scale the load until the solver fails, remove a reactive source, or open a line that islands a load. Record the iteration history each time and classify the failure.
  4. Compare flat start, DC-angle start and a start from a previous solution on a heavily loaded case: count iterations and check whether all starts converge to the same voltages.
  5. Optional: with pypowsybl.network.create_ieee14(), run pypowsybl.loadflow.run_ac with Parameters(distributed_slack=False) and with distributed_slack=True, and tabulate how generator active powers and the largest branch flows change.
  6. Optional (Windows): build the 5-bus grid of step 1 in the PowerWorld Simulator demo, with the same MVA base, solve it, and compare bus voltages and branch flows with your solver. The demo is limited to 13 buses, so IEEE 14 does not fit. Then repeat one failure of step 3 and compare how Simulator reports it with your iteration history.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
All statements are also in exercises.ipynb; the worked examples run in examples.ipynb.

  1. For a two-bus system (slack bus 1 at \(1\angle 0\), PQ bus 2 with load \(P + jQ\), line reactance \(X\)), write the power flow equations and the \(2 \times 2\) Jacobian, and do two Newton iterations by hand for \(X = 0.1\), \(P = 1\), \(Q = 0.5\) p.u.

    Solution: Exercise 1.

  2. (GeoGebra) Two-bus power transfer: with sliders for \(|V_1|\), \(|V_2|\), \(X\) and \(\delta\), plot \(P = |V_1||V_2|\sin\delta / X\) and \(Q_2 = (|V_1||V_2|\cos\delta - |V_2|^2)/X\). Find the maximum transfer and explain what happens to Newton–Raphson near \(\delta = 90^\circ\).

    Solution: Exercise 2.

  3. (Jupyter: NumPy) Verify the polar Jacobian formulas of the worked example against central finite differences on IEEE 14, then time the dense and scipy.sparse versions.

    Solution: Exercise 3.

  4. (Octave + MATPOWER) Solve case118 with pf.alg set to NR, FDXB and GS; tabulate iterations and time, and explain the ranking with the cost per iteration of each method.

    Solution: Exercise 4.

  5. Explain why a DC power flow can give a solution for a topology whose AC power flow diverges. List three physical causes and the symptom each leaves in the iteration history.

    Solution: Exercise 5.

  6. (pypowsybl) Repeat the distributed-slack comparison of the lab with BalanceType.PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P and BalanceType.PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P_MAX. Which generators pick up the losses in each case?

docs.title: Lab

1. Newton–Raphson for a five-bus grid. CASE5 is a five-bus grid in MATPOWER column order: slack bus 1 at 1.06 pu, PV bus 2 at 1.045 pu generating 40 MW, loads 20 + j10, 45 + j15, 40 + j5 and 60 + j10 MVA at buses 2 to 5, and seven lines with \(r/x = 1/3\) and line charging. make_ybus builds \(Y_\text{bus}\) from the branch table (series admittance, half the charging at each end, taps and bus shunts), specified returns the bus types and the injections \(P^\text{spec}, Q^\text{spec}\) in pu, and newton_pf iterates with the four blocks of ac_jacobian.jacobian_blocks, keeping the \(P\) rows of the non-slack buses and the \(Q\) rows of the PQ buses. From a flat start the mismatch infinity norm goes \(4.9 \times 10^{-1} \to 3.3 \times 10^{-2} \to 7.2 \times 10^{-5} \to 5.1 \times 10^{-10}\) pu: the exponent doubles at each step, which is the quadratic convergence of Chapter 6. Three iterations reach \(10^{-8}\). The solution is \(\theta = (0, -2.768, -4.977, -5.309, -6.129)^\circ\) and \(|V| = (1.06, 1.045, 1.0223, 1.0215, 1.0156)\) pu. On a log scale the four points lie on a curve that bends down, not on a straight line: a straight line would be linear convergence.

    nr_power_flow.py
    """Newton-Raphson power flow of a five-bus grid, its failure modes and its initializations (Chapter 15, Lab 1-4).

The grid is a MATPOWER-style case dict (``CASE5``), so the same data feed the Newton-Raphson solver of this module,
``pandapower`` (through ``pandapower.converter.from_ppc``) and, saved as a case file, MATPOWER's ``runpf``.
Column indices follow the MATPOWER manual: bus table (bus number, type, Pd, Qd, Gs, Bs, ..., Vm), branch table
(from, to, r, x, b, ..., ratio, angle, status), generator table (bus, Pg, Qg, Qmax, Qmin, Vg, ...).
"""

import numpy as np
import pandapower as pp
from ac_jacobian import injections, jacobian_blocks

PQ, PV, SLACK = 1, 2, 3
# fmt: off
CASE5 = {
    'version': '2',
    'baseMVA': 100.0,
    # bus_i type Pd   Qd   Gs Bs area Vm    Va baseKV zone Vmax Vmin
    'bus': np.array([
        [1, 3,  0.0,  0.0, 0, 0, 1, 1.06, 0, 230, 1, 1.1, 0.9],
        [2, 2, 20.0, 10.0, 0, 0, 1, 1.045, 0, 230, 1, 1.1, 0.9],
        [3, 1, 45.0, 15.0, 0, 0, 1, 1.0, 0, 230, 1, 1.1, 0.9],
        [4, 1, 40.0,  5.0, 0, 0, 1, 1.0, 0, 230, 1, 1.1, 0.9],
        [5, 1, 60.0, 10.0, 0, 0, 1, 1.0, 0, 230, 1, 1.1, 0.9],
    ], dtype=float),
    # bus Pg   Qg Qmax Qmin  Vg    mBase status Pmax Pmin (+ 11 cost/ramp columns MATPOWER expects)
    'gen': np.array([
        [1,  0.0, 0, 300, -300, 1.06,  100, 1, 300, 0] + [0] * 11,
        [2, 40.0, 0, 300, -300, 1.045, 100, 1, 300, 0] + [0] * 11,
    ], dtype=float),
    # f t  r     x     b     rateA rateB rateC ratio angle status angmin angmax
    'branch': np.array([
        [1, 2, 0.02, 0.06, 0.06, 250, 250, 250, 0, 0, 1, -360, 360],
        [1, 3, 0.08, 0.24, 0.05, 250, 250, 250, 0, 0, 1, -360, 360],
        [2, 3, 0.06, 0.18, 0.04, 250, 250, 250, 0, 0, 1, -360, 360],
        [2, 4, 0.06, 0.18, 0.04, 250, 250, 250, 0, 0, 1, -360, 360],
        [2, 5, 0.04, 0.12, 0.03, 250, 250, 250, 0, 0, 1, -360, 360],
        [3, 4, 0.01, 0.03, 0.02, 250, 250, 250, 0, 0, 1, -360, 360],
        [4, 5, 0.08, 0.24, 0.05, 250, 250, 250, 0, 0, 1, -360, 360],
    ], dtype=float),
}
# fmt: on


def make_ybus(ppc: dict) -> np.ndarray:
    """Dense bus admittance matrix (pu) of a case dict: series branches, line charging, taps and bus shunts."""
    n = len(ppc['bus'])
    y = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=complex)
    for f, t, r, x, b, *_rest, ratio, angle, status in ppc['branch'][:, :11]:
        if not status:
            continue
        i, k = int(f) - 1, int(t) - 1
        ys = 1 / (r + 1j * x)
        tap = (ratio if ratio else 1.0) * np.exp(1j * np.deg2rad(angle))
        y[i, i] += (ys + 1j * b / 2) / abs(tap) ** 2
        y[k, k] += ys + 1j * b / 2
        y[i, k] -= ys / np.conj(tap)
        y[k, i] -= ys / tap
    y[np.diag_indices(n)] += (ppc['bus'][:, 4] + 1j * ppc['bus'][:, 5]) / ppc['baseMVA']
    return y


def specified(ppc: dict) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Bus types, specified injections P and Q (pu, generation minus load) and the voltage set points."""
    bus, gen = ppc['bus'], ppc['gen']
    types = bus[:, 1].astype(int)
    p = -bus[:, 2] / ppc['baseMVA']
    q = -bus[:, 3] / ppc['baseMVA']
    vset = np.ones(len(bus))
    for g in gen[gen[:, 7] > 0]:
        i = int(g[0]) - 1
        p[i] += g[1] / ppc['baseMVA']
        q[i] += g[2] / ppc['baseMVA']
        vset[i] = g[5]
    return types, p, q, vset


def newton_pf(
    ybus: np.ndarray,
    types: np.ndarray,
    p_spec: np.ndarray,
    q_spec: np.ndarray,
    theta0: np.ndarray,
    vm0: np.ndarray,
    tol: float = 1e-8,
    max_iter: int = 20,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, list[float], bool]:
    """Polar Newton-Raphson: angles, magnitudes, the mismatch infinity norm per iteration and a converged flag.

    Unknowns are the angles of the non-slack buses and the magnitudes of the PQ buses; the Jacobian blocks come
    from ``ac_jacobian.jacobian_blocks``. The history has one entry per evaluated mismatch, the first one at the
    starting point. A singular Jacobian (an island without a slack) raises ``numpy.linalg.LinAlgError``.
    """
    theta, vm = theta0.astype(float).copy(), vm0.astype(float).copy()
    non_slack = np.flatnonzero(types != SLACK)
    pq = np.flatnonzero(types == PQ)
    history = []
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        s = injections(theta, vm, ybus)
        mismatch = np.concatenate([(p_spec - s.real)[non_slack], (q_spec - s.imag)[pq]])
        history.append(float(np.abs(mismatch).max()))
        if history[-1] < tol:
            return theta, vm, history, True
        j11, j12, j21, j22 = jacobian_blocks(theta, vm, ybus)
        jac = np.block(
            [
                [j11[np.ix_(non_slack, non_slack)], j12[np.ix_(non_slack, pq)]],
                [j21[np.ix_(pq, non_slack)], j22[np.ix_(pq, pq)]],
            ]
        )
        step = np.linalg.solve(jac, mismatch)
        theta[non_slack] += step[: len(non_slack)]
        vm[pq] += step[len(non_slack) :]
    return theta, vm, history, False


def flat_start(ppc: dict) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Zero angles, set-point magnitudes at the slack and PV buses, 1 pu at the PQ buses."""
    types, _, _, vset = specified(ppc)
    vm = np.where(types == PQ, 1.0, vset)
    return np.zeros(len(types)), vm


def dc_start(ppc: dict) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Angles of the DC power flow (b = 1/x, slack angle 0) with the magnitudes of the flat start."""
    types, p, _, _ = specified(ppc)
    n = len(types)
    bbus = np.zeros((n, n))
    for f, t, _r, x in ppc['branch'][:, :4]:
        i, k = int(f) - 1, int(t) - 1
        bbus[[i, k], [i, k]] += 1 / x
        bbus[[i, k], [k, i]] -= 1 / x
    keep = types != SLACK
    theta = np.zeros(n)
    theta[keep] = np.linalg.solve(bbus[np.ix_(keep, keep)], p[keep])
    return theta, flat_start(ppc)[1]


def solve(
    ppc: dict, start: tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] | None = None, **kwargs
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, list[float], bool]:
    """Newton-Raphson on a case dict from ``start`` (default: flat start)."""
    types, p, q, _ = specified(ppc)
    theta0, vm0 = start if start is not None else flat_start(ppc)
    return newton_pf(make_ybus(ppc), types, p, q, theta0, vm0, **kwargs)


def scaled_loads(ppc: dict, factor: float) -> dict:
    """A copy of the case with every load (P and Q) multiplied by ``factor``."""
    out = {k: (v.copy() if isinstance(v, np.ndarray) else v) for k, v in ppc.items()}
    out['bus'][:, 2:4] *= factor
    return out


def without_branches(ppc: dict, rows: list[int]) -> dict:
    """A copy of the case with the branches in ``rows`` (0-based) removed."""
    out = {k: (v.copy() if isinstance(v, np.ndarray) else v) for k, v in ppc.items()}
    out['branch'] = np.delete(out['branch'], rows, axis=0)
    return out


def pv_to_pq(ppc: dict, bus: int) -> dict:
    """A copy of the case where the generator at ``bus`` (1-based) no longer holds its voltage: Qg is fixed at 0."""
    out = {k: (v.copy() if isinstance(v, np.ndarray) else v) for k, v in ppc.items()}
    out['bus'][bus - 1, 1] = PQ
    return out


def pandapower_net(ppc: dict, f_hz: float = 50.0) -> pp.pandapowerNet:
    """The same case as a pandapower network: per-unit branch data become ohms and nF on the bus voltage base."""
    net = pp.create_empty_network(sn_mva=ppc['baseMVA'], f_hz=f_hz)
    for bus_i, _type, pd, qd, *_rest in ppc['bus']:
        b = pp.create_bus(net, vn_kv=ppc['bus'][int(bus_i) - 1, 9], index=int(bus_i) - 1)
        if pd or qd:
            pp.create_load(net, b, p_mw=pd, q_mvar=qd)
    types = ppc['bus'][:, 1].astype(int)
    for g in ppc['gen'][ppc['gen'][:, 7] > 0]:
        bus = int(g[0]) - 1
        if types[bus] == SLACK:
            pp.create_ext_grid(net, bus, vm_pu=g[5])
        elif types[bus] == PV:
            pp.create_gen(net, bus, p_mw=g[1], vm_pu=g[5])
        else:
            pp.create_sgen(net, bus, p_mw=g[1], q_mvar=g[2])
    for f, t, r, x, b, *_rest in ppc['branch']:
        z_base = ppc['bus'][int(f) - 1, 9] ** 2 / ppc['baseMVA']  # ohm
        c_nf = b / z_base / (2 * np.pi * f_hz) * 1e9
        pp.create_line_from_parameters(
            net,
            int(f) - 1,
            int(t) - 1,
            length_km=1.0,
            r_ohm_per_km=r * z_base,
            x_ohm_per_km=x * z_base,
            c_nf_per_km=c_nf,
            max_i_ka=1.0,
        )
    return net


def pandapower_solution(ppc: dict) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Voltage angles (rad) and magnitudes (pu) of ``pandapower.runpp`` on the same case."""
    net = pandapower_net(ppc)
    pp.runpp(net, tolerance_mva=1e-10, init='flat')
    return np.deg2rad(net.res_bus.va_degree.to_numpy()), net.res_bus.vm_pu.to_numpy()


def max_loading(ppc: dict, step: float = 0.05, limit: float = 10.0) -> float:
    """The largest load multiple (in steps of ``step``) for which Newton-Raphson from a flat start converges."""
    factor = 1.0
    while factor + step <= limit and solve(scaled_loads(ppc, factor + step))[3]:
        factor += step
    return factor


def main() -> None:
    """Print every number quoted in the Lab solutions of steps 1-4."""
    theta, vm, hist, ok = solve(CASE5)
    print('Step 1: mismatch inf-norm per iteration (pu):', ' '.join(f'{h:.1e}' for h in hist), 'converged', ok)
    print('  angles (deg):', np.round(np.rad2deg(theta), 4), ' magnitudes (pu):', np.round(vm, 5))
    th_pp, vm_pp = pandapower_solution(CASE5)
    dv, dth = np.abs(vm - vm_pp).max(), np.rad2deg(np.abs(theta - th_pp)).max()
    print(f'Step 2: pandapower  max |dV| = {dv:.1e} pu, max |dtheta| = {dth:.1e} deg')
    lam = max_loading(CASE5)
    print(f'Step 3a: loads can be scaled by {lam:.2f}; at {lam + 0.05:.2f} the iteration fails:')
    th_f, vm_f, hist_f, ok_f = solve(scaled_loads(CASE5, lam + 0.05))
    print('  mismatch history:', ' '.join(f'{h:.1e}' for h in hist_f), 'converged', ok_f, ' |V| =', np.round(vm_f, 3))
    _, vm_l, hist_l, _ = solve(scaled_loads(CASE5, lam))
    print(f'  at {lam:.2f}: {len(hist_l) - 1} iterations, lowest |V| = {vm_l.min():.3f} pu')
    no_q = pv_to_pq(CASE5, 2)
    lam_q = max_loading(no_q)
    _, vm_q, hist_q, ok_q = solve(no_q)
    print(f'Step 3b: bus 2 as PQ (no voltage support): nominal load converges={ok_q} in {len(hist_q) - 1} iterations,')
    print(f'  |V2| = {vm_q[1]:.4f};', end='')
    print(f'  the largest load multiple drops from {lam:.2f} to {lam_q:.2f}')
    try:
        solve(without_branches(CASE5, [4, 6]))
        print('Step 3c: islanding bus 5 did not raise')
    except np.linalg.LinAlgError as err:
        print('Step 3c: lines 2-5 and 4-5 removed, bus 5 islanded with its load:', err)
    heavy = scaled_loads(CASE5, lam)
    previous = solve(scaled_loads(CASE5, lam - 0.1))[:2]
    for name, start in (('flat', flat_start(heavy)), ('DC angles', dc_start(heavy)), ('previous solution', previous)):
        th_s, vm_s, hist_s, ok_s = solve(heavy, start)
        print(f'Step 4: {name:18s} {len(hist_s) - 1} iterations, converged={ok_s}, |V| = {np.round(vm_s, 4)}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  2. pandapower on the same data. pandapower_net builds the same grid with create_line_from_parameters: the per-unit branch data become ohms through \(Z_\text{base} = V_\text{base}^2 / S_\text{base} = 230^2/100 = 529\ \Omega\), and the line charging \(b\) becomes a capacitance \(C = b / (Z_\text{base}\, 2\pi f)\) in nF. runpp with tolerance_mva=1e-10 agrees with step 1 to \(5.5 \times 10^{-11}\) pu in magnitude and \(1.3 \times 10^{-9}\) degrees in angle; test_nr_power_flow.py also checks that make_ybus equals pandapower's internal Ybus entry by entry. With Octave, save CASE5 as a case file and call matpower_pf (worked example) on it; the voltages must agree to the same precision (not run here).

  3. Breaking convergence. Three failures, three signatures:
    • Loads scaled up (max_loading): with every load multiplied by 5.20 the iteration still converges, in 7 iterations, with the lowest voltage at 0.643 pu. At 5.25 it never does: the mismatch falls from 3.0 to \(8.7 \times 10^{-3}\) in five iterations and then wanders between \(10^{-2}\) and \(10^{-1}\) for the remaining fifteen, with \(|V| = (1.06, 1.045, 0.618, 0.622, 0.578)\) at iteration 20. This is the nose of the P–V curve: beyond the maximum loadability the equations have no solution, so Newton has nothing to converge to and the iterates oscillate around the point where the two solution branches merged. The Jacobian becomes singular exactly at the nose (Exercise 2).
    • A reactive source removed (pv_to_pq(CASE5, 2)): the generator at bus 2 no longer holds 1.045 pu and injects \(Q = 0\). The nominal case still converges (4 iterations, \(|V_2| = 1.032\) pu), but the largest load multiple drops from 5.20 to 2.95. Symptom: convergence on light load with low voltages and an earlier nose; near the limit the \(Q\) rows of the mismatch dominate.
    • An islanded load (without_branches(CASE5, [4, 6]), lines 2–5 and 4–5 removed): bus 5 keeps its load but has no path to a voltage source. The rows and columns of bus 5 in the reduced Jacobian are zero, so numpy.linalg.solve raises LinAlgError: Singular matrix at the first iteration. Symptom: no history at all, a singular or ill-conditioned matrix. Production solvers detect islands first (Chapter 3) and either drop them or give each one a slack.
  4. Initializations. On the case with the loads scaled by 5.20, the flat start and the DC-angle start both need 7 iterations, and the solution of the case scaled by 5.10 needs 4. All three end at the same voltages, \(|V| = (1.06, 1.045, 0.6696, 0.6741, 0.6427)\) pu. Here the DC angles do not help, because the angles are not the problem (they stay below 30°): it is the voltage magnitudes, which the DC start leaves at 1 pu, that are far from the 0.64–0.67 pu solution. A previous solution gets both right and halves the work. On a heavily loaded case there is a second, low-voltage solution of the same equations; a start below the nose would converge to it, which is why PREVIOUS_VALUES and DC_VALUES are tried in order on import (find_converging_loadflow_params).

  5. Distributed slack with pypowsybl. On the stock IEEE 14 nothing changes between Parameters(distributed_slack=False) and True: the generator targets (232.4 + 40 MW) already include the 13.4 MW of losses, so the remaining slack mismatch is \(-0.007\) MW and there is nothing to distribute. With every load raised by 10 % (compare(1.1)) the picture is:

    Generator (target) single slack proportional to P proportional to Pmax B1-G (232.4 MW) 232.4 257.27 246.97 B2-G (40 MW) 40.0 44.28 54.57 B3-G, B6-G, B8-G (0 MW) 0 0 0 slack mismatch left 29.15 MW \(-0.27\) MW \(-0.91\) MW largest flow change vs single slack – 3.8 MW (L1-2) 12.9 MW (L1-2)

    With a single slack OpenLoadFlow leaves the 29.1 MW on the slack bus and reports it as slack_bus_results[0].active_power_mismatch; the slack generator's p keeps its target. With the slack distributed, the 29.1 MW go to the generators in the ratio 232.4 : 40 (PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P) or equally (PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P_MAX, both units have max_p = 9999 MW); the three synchronous condensers with a 0 MW target never participate. The largest base-case flow, on line 1–2, is 177.4 MW with a single slack, 173.6 MW and 164.5 MW with the two distributed settings: how the losses are shared changes the flows by up to 13 MW on a 260 MW system, which is the AC–DC mismatch argument of ToOp's loadflow_parameters.md.

    powsybl_slack.py
    """Single versus distributed slack on IEEE 14 with pypowsybl (Chapter 15, Lab step 5 and Exercise 6).

pypowsybl reports a generator's active power with the receptor sign convention (negative when generating), so
the module negates it to print MW produced. Branch flows ``p1`` are the active power entering at side 1.
"""

import pandas as pd
import pypowsybl as pyp
import pypowsybl.loadflow as lf

BALANCE = {
    'single slack': lf.Parameters(distributed_slack=False),
    'proportional to P': lf.Parameters(
        distributed_slack=True, balance_type=lf.BalanceType.PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P
    ),
    'proportional to Pmax': lf.Parameters(
        distributed_slack=True, balance_type=lf.BalanceType.PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P_MAX
    ),
}


def solve_ieee14(parameters: lf.Parameters, load_factor: float = 1.0) -> tuple[pd.Series, pd.Series, float]:
    """Generator outputs (MW), branch flows ``p1`` (MW) and the remaining slack mismatch of an AC load flow.

    The stock case is balanced (the generator targets already include the losses), so ``load_factor`` scales every
    load to create a mismatch for the slack to absorb.
    """
    net = pyp.network.create_ieee14()
    loads = net.get_loads()
    net.update_loads(id=loads.index, p0=loads['p0'] * load_factor, q0=loads['q0'] * load_factor)
    result = lf.run_ac(net, parameters)[0]
    if result.status != lf.ComponentStatus.CONVERGED:
        raise RuntimeError(f'load flow did not converge: {result.status}')
    gens = -net.get_generators()['p']
    flows = pd.concat([net.get_lines()['p1'], net.get_2_windings_transformers()['p1']])
    return gens, flows, result.slack_bus_results[0].active_power_mismatch


def compare(load_factor: float = 1.0, cases: dict[str, lf.Parameters] = BALANCE) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Generator outputs and the five largest base-case branch flows, one column per slack setting."""
    gens, flows = {}, {}
    for name, parameters in cases.items():
        gens[name], flows[name], _ = solve_ieee14(parameters, load_factor)
    gens, flows = pd.DataFrame(gens), pd.DataFrame(flows)
    top = flows.abs().max(axis=1).nlargest(5).index
    return gens, flows.loc[top]


def main() -> None:
    """Print the tables of Lab step 5 and Exercise 6."""
    pd.set_option('display.width', 120)
    targets = pyp.network.create_ieee14().get_generators()['target_p']
    for load_factor in (1.0, 1.1):
        print(f'== loads scaled by {load_factor} ==')
        gens, flows = compare(load_factor)
        gens.insert(0, 'target_p', targets)
        print('generator active power (MW)')
        print(gens.round(3))
        print('total generation (MW):', gens.drop(columns='target_p').sum().round(3).to_dict())
        print('five largest base-case flows p1 (MW)')
        print(flows.round(3))
        print(
            'largest change of any branch flow against the single slack (MW):',
            flows.sub(flows['single slack'], axis=0).abs().max().round(3).to_dict(),
        )
        print(
            'remaining slack mismatch (MW):',
            {k: round(solve_ieee14(v, load_factor)[2], 3) for k, v in BALANCE.items()},
        )


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  6. PowerWorld Simulator (optional, Windows). Not run here. Method: create the five buses with the 230 kV nominal voltage, enter each line with its per-unit \(R\), \(X\) and \(B\) (Simulator takes per-unit values on the system base, 100 MVA), set bus 1 as the slack at 1.06 pu, the bus 2 generator at 40 MW with 1.045 pu voltage setpoint and unlimited reactive power, the loads as constant power, and Single Solution – Full Newton. Expected outcome: the bus voltages and angles of step 1 to four decimals, and the line flows of net.res_line to 0.1 MW. For the failure of step 3, scale the loads with Load Scaling to 525 %: Simulator stops after its maximum number of iterations and reports the largest mismatch and its bus, the same stalling of the mismatch that your history shows; for the islanded load it removes the island before solving (the bus turns grey) and reports it in the message log, where your solver raised on the singular Jacobian.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
With \(V_1 = 1\angle 0\), \(V_2 = v\angle\delta\) and \(Y_\text{bus} = \begin{bmatrix} -j/X & j/X \\ j/X & -j/X \end{bmatrix}\) (\(G = 0\), \(B_{21} = 1/X\), \(B_{22} = -1/X\)), the injections at bus 2 from the general formulas of the worked example are

\[ P_2 = \frac{v}{X}\sin\delta, \qquad Q_2 = \frac{v^2 - v\cos\delta}{X}, \]

and the specified values are \(P_2^\text{spec} = -P\), \(Q_2^\text{spec} = -Q\) (a load). The Jacobian is

\[ J = \begin{bmatrix} \partial P_2/\partial\delta & \partial P_2/\partial v \\ \partial Q_2/\partial\delta & \partial Q_2/\partial v \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{X}\begin{bmatrix} v\cos\delta & \sin\delta \\ v\sin\delta & 2v - \cos\delta \end{bmatrix}. \]

Flat start \(\delta = 0\), \(v = 1\), with \(X = 0.1\), \(P = 1\), \(Q = 0.5\):

  • Iteration 1. \(P_2 = Q_2 = 0\), mismatch \((-1, -0.5)\), \(J = \operatorname{diag}(10, 10)\), step \((-0.1, -0.05)\): \(\delta = -0.1\) rad (\(-5.730^\circ\)), \(v = 0.95\).
  • Iteration 2. \(P_2 = 9.5\sin(-0.1) = -0.9484\), \(Q_2 = (0.9025 - 0.95\cos 0.1)/0.1 = -0.4275\), mismatch \((-0.0516, -0.0725)\), \(J = \begin{bmatrix} 9.4525 & -0.9983 \\ -0.9484 & 9.0500 \end{bmatrix}\), step \((-0.0064, -0.0087)\): \(\delta = -0.1064\) rad (\(-6.095^\circ\)), \(v = 0.9413\).

The exact solution, from \(v^4 + (2QX - 1)v^2 + X^2(P^2 + Q^2) = 0\) (exact_solution), is \(v = 0.9412\), \(\delta = -0.1064\) rad (\(-6.099^\circ\)): two iterations are within \(10^{-4}\). The mismatch norms of the first five iterations, \(1.0,\ 7.2 \times 10^{-2},\ 8.9 \times 10^{-4},\ 1.3 \times 10^{-7},\ 2.9 \times 10^{-15}\), double their exponent each time.

two_bus.py
"""Two-bus power flow: Newton-Raphson by hand and the power transfer curve (Chapter 15, Exercises 1 and 2).

Slack bus 1 at 1 pu and zero angle, PQ bus 2 with load P + jQ behind a lossless line of reactance X. With
v = |V2| and d = theta_2, the injections at bus 2 are P2 = (v / X) sin d and Q2 = (v² - v cos d) / X, and the
specified values are -P and -Q (a load), so the solution has d < 0.
"""

import numpy as np


def injections_2bus(d: float, v: float, x: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """(P2, Q2) at the load bus for angle ``d`` (rad), magnitude ``v`` and line reactance ``x``."""
    return np.array([v * np.sin(d) / x, (v**2 - v * np.cos(d)) / x])


def jacobian_2bus(d: float, v: float, x: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """The 2 x 2 Jacobian [[dP2/dd, dP2/dv], [dQ2/dd, dQ2/dv]]."""
    return np.array([[v * np.cos(d) / x, np.sin(d) / x], [v * np.sin(d) / x, (2 * v - np.cos(d)) / x]])


def newton_steps(p: float, q: float, x: float, n_steps: int = 2) -> list[dict]:
    """The first ``n_steps`` Newton iterations from the flat start, with mismatch, Jacobian, step and new state."""
    d, v = 0.0, 1.0
    out = []
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        mismatch = np.array([-p, -q]) - injections_2bus(d, v, x)
        jac = jacobian_2bus(d, v, x)
        step = np.linalg.solve(jac, mismatch)
        d, v = d + step[0], v + step[1]
        out.append({'mismatch': mismatch, 'jacobian': jac, 'step': step, 'state': np.array([d, v])})
    return out


def exact_solution(p: float, q: float, x: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Closed form (angle in rad, magnitude): the high-voltage root of v⁴ + (2QX - 1) v² + X²(P² + Q²) = 0."""
    b = 2 * q * x - 1
    c = x**2 * (p**2 + q**2)
    v = np.sqrt((-b + np.sqrt(b**2 - 4 * c)) / 2)
    return float(-np.arcsin(p * x / v)), float(v)


def transfer(v1: float, v2: float, x: float, delta: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """P = |V1||V2| sin(delta) / X and Q2 = (|V1||V2| cos(delta) - |V2|²) / X for the angles ``delta`` (rad)."""
    return v1 * v2 * np.sin(delta) / x, (v1 * v2 * np.cos(delta) - v2**2) / x


def main() -> None:
    """Exercise 1 (two iterations, exact solution) and Exercise 2 (maximum transfer, Jacobian at 90 degrees)."""
    x, p, q = 0.1, 1.0, 0.5
    for k, it in enumerate(newton_steps(p, q, x), start=1):
        print(
            f'iteration {k}: mismatch {np.round(it["mismatch"], 4)}, Jacobian {np.round(it["jacobian"], 4).tolist()}'
        )
        d, v = it['state']
        print(f'  step {np.round(it["step"], 4)} -> theta2 = {d:.4f} rad ({np.rad2deg(d):.3f} deg), |V2| = {v:.4f}')
    d, v = exact_solution(p, q, x)
    print(f'exact: theta2 = {d:.4f} rad ({np.rad2deg(d):.3f} deg), |V2| = {v:.4f}')
    more = newton_steps(p, q, x, 5)
    print('mismatch inf-norm per iteration:', ' '.join(f'{np.abs(it["mismatch"]).max():.1e}' for it in more))
    delta = np.deg2rad(np.linspace(0, 90, 7))
    pt, qt = transfer(1.0, 1.0, x, delta)
    print('delta (deg):', np.round(np.rad2deg(delta)).astype(int), ' P:', np.round(pt, 3), ' Q2:', np.round(qt, 3))
    for deg in (60, 85, 89, 90):
        print(f'dP/d(delta) at {deg} deg: {np.cos(np.deg2rad(deg)) / x:.4f} pu/rad')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
GeoGebra construction (not run here): four sliders V1, V2 in \([0.9, 1.1]\), X in \([0.05, 0.5]\) and d in \([0°, 180°]\); the functions P(x) = V1 V2 sin(x) / X and Q2(x) = (V1 V2 cos(x) - V2²) / X plotted against the angle, and the point (d, P(d)) moving on the curve. \(Q_2\) as written in the statement is the reactive power received at bus 2 (minus the injection of Exercise 1). The numbers below are from two_bus.transfer with \(|V_1| = |V_2| = 1\), \(X = 0.1\):

\(\delta\) 0° 15° 30° 45° 60° 75° 90° \(P\) (pu) 0 2.588 5.000 7.071 8.660 9.659 10.000 \(Q_2\) (pu) 0 \(-0.341\) \(-1.340\) \(-2.929\) \(-5.000\) \(-7.412\) \(-10.000\)

The maximum transfer is \(P_\max = |V_1||V_2|/X = 10\) pu at \(\delta = 90^\circ\) (the slider past 90° brings \(P\) down again: the same power is reached twice, once on each side). At that point the line absorbs \(|V_1||V_2|/X\) of reactive power. The derivative \(\partial P/\partial\delta = |V_1||V_2|\cos\delta / X\) is \(5.0\) pu/rad at 60°, \(0.87\) at 85°, \(0.17\) at 89° and \(0\) at 90°: the \(P\)–\(\delta\) row of the Jacobian vanishes, the matrix is singular and the Newton step \(\Delta\delta = \Delta P / (\partial P/\partial\delta)\) blows up. For a specified \(P\) slightly below \(P_\max\) the two solutions (\(\delta\) and \(180^\circ - \delta\)) are close, the Jacobian is nearly singular, and Newton converges slowly or jumps between them; for \(P > P_\max\) there is no solution and the mismatch stalls, as in Lab step 3.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
jacobian_timing.case_state takes the converged state and the sparse Ybus of pandapower's case14 and case118 (from net._ppc['internal']). finite_difference_error compares every column of the four blocks with central differences of injections (\(h = 10^{-6}\)): the largest difference is \(7.7 \times 10^{-9}\) on IEEE 14 and \(2.5 \times 10^{-8}\) on IEEE 118, the round-off level of a central difference, so the formulas are right. jacobian_blocks_sparse is the same matrix expression with scipy.sparse.diags and a CSR Ybus. Timings (best of three, this laptop):

Case buses nonzeros of \(Y_\text{bus}\) dense sparse IEEE 14 14 54 0.030 ms 0.79 ms IEEE 118 118 476 0.98 ms 0.88 ms

On 14 buses the dense version is 25 times faster: the matrices have 196 entries and the sparse machinery's fixed cost dominates. At 118 buses the two break even, and beyond that the dense cost grows with \(n^2\) memory and \(n^3\) products while the sparse one grows with the number of branches. The real saving of sparsity is in the linear solve of each iteration, not in building the blocks.

jacobian_timing.py
"""Polar Jacobian of IEEE 14 and IEEE 118 against finite differences; dense versus sparse (Chapter 15, Exercise 3).

The bus admittance matrix comes from pandapower's internal ``Ybus`` after ``runpp``; the state is the converged
one, read from the same internal structure.
"""

import timeit

import numpy as np
import pandapower as pp
import pandapower.networks as pn
import scipy.sparse as sps
from ac_jacobian import injections, jacobian_blocks


def case_state(name: str) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, sps.csr_matrix]:
    """Converged angles (rad), magnitudes (pu) and the sparse Ybus (pu) of a pandapower network case."""
    net = getattr(pn, name)()
    pp.runpp(net)
    v = np.asarray(net._ppc['internal']['V'])
    return np.angle(v), np.abs(v), sps.csr_matrix(net._ppc['internal']['Ybus'])


def jacobian_blocks_sparse(theta: np.ndarray, vm: np.ndarray, y: sps.spmatrix) -> tuple[sps.csr_matrix, ...]:
    """The same four blocks as ``ac_jacobian.jacobian_blocks``, with sparse diagonals and a sparse Ybus."""
    v = vm * np.exp(1j * theta)
    i = y @ v
    diag_v, diag_i, e = sps.diags(v), sps.diags(i), sps.diags(v / vm)
    ds_dth = 1j * diag_v @ (diag_i - y @ diag_v).conj()
    ds_dvm = diag_v @ (y @ e).conj() + diag_i.conj() @ e
    return ds_dth.real.tocsr(), ds_dvm.real.tocsr(), ds_dth.imag.tocsr(), ds_dvm.imag.tocsr()


def finite_difference_error(theta: np.ndarray, vm: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, h: float = 1e-6) -> float:
    """Largest difference between the analytic blocks and central differences of ``injections``, column by column."""
    j11, j12, j21, j22 = jacobian_blocks(theta, vm, y)
    n = len(theta)
    worst = 0.0
    for k in range(n):
        d = np.zeros(n)
        d[k] = h
        ds = (injections(theta + d, vm, y) - injections(theta - d, vm, y)) / (2 * h)
        worst = max(worst, np.abs(j11[:, k] - ds.real).max(), np.abs(j21[:, k] - ds.imag).max())
        ds = (injections(theta, vm + d, y) - injections(theta, vm - d, y)) / (2 * h)
        worst = max(worst, np.abs(j12[:, k] - ds.real).max(), np.abs(j22[:, k] - ds.imag).max())
    return worst


def time_both(theta: np.ndarray, vm: np.ndarray, y: sps.csr_matrix, number: int = 50) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Milliseconds per evaluation of the dense and of the sparse Jacobian blocks (best of three runs)."""
    y_dense = y.toarray()
    dense = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: jacobian_blocks(theta, vm, y_dense), number=number, repeat=3)) / number
    sparse = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: jacobian_blocks_sparse(theta, vm, y), number=number, repeat=3)) / number
    return 1e3 * dense, 1e3 * sparse


def main() -> None:
    """Finite-difference error and timings for IEEE 14 and IEEE 118."""
    for name in ('case14', 'case118'):
        theta, vm, y = case_state(name)
        err = finite_difference_error(theta, vm, y.toarray())
        dense, sparse = time_both(theta, vm, y)
        print(f'{name}: {len(theta)} buses, {y.nnz} nonzeros in Ybus, max |analytic - central difference| = {err:.1e}')
        print(f'  dense blocks {dense:.3f} ms, sparse blocks {sparse:.3f} ms per evaluation')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
pf_algorithms runs runpf with pf.alg set to NR, FDXB and GS at pf.tol = 1e-8 and returns results.iterations and results.et. Octave 11.3 with MATPOWER 8.1, after one warm-up call (the first runpf of a session loads MATPOWER's classes and is several times slower):

Case NR FDXB GS case14 2 iterations, 0.098 s 6 iterations, 0.184 s 103 iterations, 0.355 s case118 3 iterations, 0.120 s 8 iterations, 0.195 s 2111 iterations, 10.4 s

Gauss–Seidel needs pf.gs.max_it raised to 5000 on case118 (2111 iterations are more than the default limit). The ranking follows from the cost per iteration against the number of iterations. Newton–Raphson converges quadratically (2–3 iterations) but each iteration builds the Jacobian and factorizes a new \((2n - n_{PV} - 2)\) matrix. The fast decoupled method factorizes \(B'\) and \(B''\) once, then does two cheap forward–backward substitutions per iteration, but its convergence is linear (the decoupling \(\partial P/\partial|V| \approx 0\), \(\partial Q/\partial\theta \approx 0\) is an approximation of the Jacobian), hence 6–8 iterations. Gauss–Seidel costs one sweep through the buses per iteration, no factorization at all, and converges linearly with a rate that worsens with the size of the system: 103 iterations on 14 buses, 2111 on 118. On small cases the wall time is dominated by MATPOWER's setup, which is why FDXB does not beat NR here; its advantage shows in repeated solves of large cases (contingency analysis), where the factorizations are reused.

pf_algorithms.m
function t = pf_algorithms(casename, algs)
  % Iterations, wall time and success of runpf with each power flow algorithm on one case
  % (Chapter 15, Exercise 4). Returns a struct array with fields alg, iterations, time, success.
  if nargin < 2, algs = {'NR', 'FDXB', 'GS'}; end
  mpc = loadcase(casename);
  t = struct('alg', {}, 'iterations', {}, 'time', {}, 'success', {});
  for k = 1:numel(algs)
    mpopt = mpoption('pf.alg', algs{k}, 'pf.tol', 1e-8, 'pf.gs.max_it', 5000, 'verbose', 0, 'out.all', 0);
    r = runpf(mpc, mpopt);
    t(k) = struct('alg', algs{k}, 'iterations', r.iterations, 'time', r.et, 'success', r.success);
  end
end

%!test
%! if isempty(which('runpf')), disp('MATPOWER not on the path, test skipped'); return; end
%! t = pf_algorithms('case14');
%! assert(all([t.success] == 1))
%! assert(t(1).iterations < t(2).iterations && t(2).iterations < t(3).iterations)

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
The DC power flow \(P = B_\text{bus}\theta\) is linear: for any connected topology (with the slack in the component) \(\tilde B\) is a nonsingular grounded Laplacian (Chapter 16), so there is exactly one solution for every injection vector, however large. The AC equations are nonlinear and have a solution only inside a bounded region of the injection space; outside it Newton–Raphson has nothing to find. Three physical causes, with the symptom each leaves in the mismatch history (all three appear in Lab step 3):

  1. Active power beyond the transfer limit. A corridor asked to carry more than \(|V_f||V_t|/X\) (Exercise 2), because a topology change lengthened the path or a line outage left one line with the load of two. The DC model happily reports a flow of 150 % of the limit; in AC the \(P\)–\(\delta\) curve has no point there. Symptom: the mismatch decreases for a few iterations, then stalls or oscillates around \(10^{-2}\)–\(10^{-1}\) while angles across the corridor approach 90° (Lab 3, loads × 5.25).
  2. Reactive power deficit, voltage collapse. Loads with reactive demand far from any voltage-controlled bus, after losing a generator, a shunt capacitor or a line that carried reactive support. The DC model ignores \(Q\) and fixes \(|V| = 1\), so it sees nothing. Symptom: the \(Q\) rows dominate the mismatch, the voltage magnitudes sink iteration after iteration (0.6 pu and below), PV buses hit their reactive limits and switch to PQ, sometimes flip-flopping between the two types; the limit of the loading comes much earlier than with the reactive source present (Lab 3, bus 2 without voltage control: 2.95 instead of 5.20).
  3. Topology or data that make the Jacobian singular or ill-conditioned. An island without a generator (the DC solve fails too, but only if the island is noticed), an island with generation but no slack, a branch with near-zero reactance, a wrong tap or a load entered in the wrong unit. Symptom: a singular-matrix error or a huge first step (voltages of 10 pu, angles of hundreds of degrees) followed by divergence, visible from the first iteration (Lab 3, bus 5 islanded). Note that ToOp's DC solver accepts the topology and the AC validation rejects it, which is what the "non-converging load flows" metric of the AC stage counts.

docs.title: Exercise 6
docs.text:
Same run as Lab step 5 (powsybl_slack.compare(1.1)), reading the pick-up above target per generator:

Balance type B1-G B2-G B3-G, B6-G, B8-G PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P \(+24.87\) MW \(+4.28\) MW 0 PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P_MAX \(+14.57\) MW \(+14.57\) MW 0

With PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P the 29.1 MW of extra load and losses are shared in proportion to the active power targets, 232.4 : 40 = 5.81 : 1, so the large unit at bus 1 takes 85 % of it. With PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P_MAX the weights are the max_p values, 9999 MW for every generator in pypowsybl's IEEE 14, so the two generating units take half each. In both cases the synchronous condensers at buses 3, 6 and 8, which have a 0 MW target, pick up nothing: OpenLoadFlow leaves units that produce no active power out of the distribution. This is why ToOp's CGMES and UCTE parameter sets, with PROPORTIONAL_TO_GENERATION_P, make the AC flows follow the dispatch pattern, while the P_MAX variant of POWSYBL_LOADFLOW_PARAM_PF moves more of the balance to the units with the largest ratings whatever their current output.

docs.title: Chapter 16. DC power flow
docs.text:
Weeks: 1.5 · Semester: 3 · Prerequisites: Chapter 14, Chapter 15

Why it matters for ToOp

The whole GPU solver is a DC power flow. get_susceptance_matrices builds \(B_\text{bus} = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(b)\, A\) and \(B_f = \operatorname{diag}(b)\, A\) with \(b = 1/x\) (dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/ptdf.py); a single slack bus is required because distributed slack cannot be combined with bus-split factors; an AC–DC mismatch term corrects DC flows (dc_solver/jax/cross_coupler_flow.py). The base-case DC flows are computed by run_initial_loadflow (dc_solver/preprocess/convert_to_jax.py) and stored as unsplit_flow.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Assumptions: flat voltage magnitudes, small angle differences, \(r \ll x\), reactive power ignored.
  • \(P = B_\text{bus}\,\theta\), branch flows \(F = B_f\,\theta\); slack elimination (revisits the grounded Laplacian of Chapter 2 and the DC circuits of Chapter 8 with susceptances instead of conductances).
  • Phase shifters as equivalent injections; sign conventions.
  • Accuracy of the DC approximation and when it fails; hot-start DC and AC–DC corrections.
  • The time axis: one topology, many injection snapshots (see the note below).
  • Tools: MATPOWER makeBdc and rundcpf in Octave; pandapower.rundcpp; pypowsybl.loadflow.run_dc.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
From AC to DC. For a branch from \(f\) to \(t\) with reactance \(x\), tap ratio \(\tau\) and phase shift \(\theta_\text{shift}\), the AC active flow is \(p_f = \frac{|V_f||V_t|}{x\tau}\sin(\theta_f - \theta_t - \theta_\text{shift})\) when \(r = 0\). With \(|V| \approx 1\) and small angles (MATPOWER manual, eq. 3.23),

\[ p_f \approx b\,(\theta_f - \theta_t - \theta_\text{shift}), \qquad b = \frac{1}{x\tau}. \]

Matrix form. With the branch–bus incidence matrix \(A = C_f - C_t\) and \(b\) the vector of branch susceptances,

\[ F = B_f\,\theta + P_{f,\text{shift}}, \qquad B_f = \operatorname{diag}(b)\,A, \qquad P = B_\text{bus}\,\theta + P_\text{bus,shift}, \qquad B_\text{bus} = A^\top \operatorname{diag}(b)\,A, \]

where the shift terms are \(P_{f,\text{shift}} = -\operatorname{diag}(b)\,\theta_\text{shift}\) and \(P_\text{bus,shift} = A^\top P_{f,\text{shift}}\): a phase shifter acts like a pair of opposite injections at its terminals plus a direct flow on its own branch. \(B_\text{bus}\) is singular (its rows sum to zero), so fix \(\theta_s = 0\) at the slack bus \(s\), delete row and column \(s\), and solve

\[ \tilde B\, \tilde\theta = \tilde P - \tilde P_\text{bus,shift}, \qquad F = B_f\,\theta + P_{f,\text{shift}}. \]

The slack bus absorbs the imbalance \(P_s = -\sum_{i \ne s} P_i\).

dc_power_flow.py
"""DC power flow of a branch list: nodal susceptance matrix, angles and branch flows (Chapter 16)."""

import numpy as np


def dc_power_flow(frm: np.ndarray, to: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, p: np.ndarray, slack: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Branch flows (from -> to, same unit as ``p``) for reactances ``x`` and nodal injections ``p``."""
    n, m = len(p), len(frm)
    a = np.zeros((m, n))
    a[np.arange(m), frm] = 1.0
    a[np.arange(m), to] = -1.0
    b = 1.0 / x
    bbus = a.T @ np.diag(b) @ a
    keep = np.arange(n) != slack
    theta = np.zeros(n)
    theta[keep] = np.linalg.solve(bbus[np.ix_(keep, keep)], p[keep])
    return np.diag(b) @ a @ theta


def main() -> None:
    """Three-bus ring: 100 MW from bus 0 to bus 2 split in inverse proportion to the path reactances."""
    frm, to = np.array([0, 1, 0]), np.array([1, 2, 2])
    x = np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.2])
    p = np.array([100.0, 0.0, -100.0])
    print(dc_power_flow(frm, to, x, p, slack=0))  # [50. 50. 50.]


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

Sign conventions. ToOp's PSDF (dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/psdf.py) corresponds to a branch flow \(b_k(\theta_f - \theta_t + \varphi_k)\), i.e. \(\varphi_k\) enters with the opposite sign of MATPOWER's \(\theta_\text{shift}\); the PowSyBl backend negates the grid model's shift angle in get_shift_angles (dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_backend.py) under the comment # TODO find out where this minus comes from..., and also negates PowSyBl's p1 in get_basecase_dc_branch_flows because "Powsybl's p1 convention is opposite to the solver's from-node to to-node orientation". Always check the orientation of flows and angles before comparing two tools.

The multi-timestep axis

Most ToOp arrays carry a leading time axis: nodal_injections has shape (n_timesteps, n_bus), unsplit_flow has shape (n_timesteps, n_branches), and the N-1 matrix has shape (n_timesteps, n_failures, n_branches_monitored) (dc_solver/jax/types.py, dc_solver/jax/contingency_analysis.py). The PTDF has no time axis: one topology is evaluated against several injection snapshots, and a flow is one matrix–vector product per snapshot. The metrics aggregate over time in different ways (dc_solver/jax/aggregate_results.py): overload energy takes the worst failure and then sums over timesteps, while the critical-branch count reports only the worst timestep. Harmonizing grid models of different timesteps into one joint optimization (dc_solver/preprocess/harmonize.py) is commented out "until we decide to take up the multi-timestep optimization again", and the example notebook runs with one timestep.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: how wrong is the DC power flow?

Tools: Jupyter + NumPy + pandas + matplotlib + pandapower; ToOp notebooks. Optionally Octave + MATPOWER.

  1. Run notebooks/example1_dc_loadflow_example.ipynb (IEEE 57 in PowSyBl format). Inspect static_information.dynamic_information.unsplit_flow and explain its shape.
  2. On pandapower.networks.case57() (or case14()), compute DC flows with the function of the worked example, then run pandapower.rundcpp and compare with net.res_line.p_from_mw and net.res_trafo.p_hv_mw. Find and explain any systematic difference (per-unit base, taps, phase shifts, orientation).
  3. Run pandapower.runpp on the same network. Put DC and AC flows in a pandas DataFrame and plot the relative error per branch against AC loading and against \(r/x\).
  4. Compare your DC flows with ToOp's unsplit_flow for the same grid, taking the orientation conventions of the worked example into account.
  5. Optional: repeat step 2 with MATPOWER's rundcpf on case57 in Octave.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
All statements are also in exercises.ipynb; the worked examples run in examples.ipynb.

  1. Starting from \(p_f = \frac{|V_f||V_t|}{x}\sin(\theta_f - \theta_t)\), bound the relative error of the DC flow for \(|\theta_f - \theta_t| \le 10^\circ\) and \(|V| \in [0.95, 1.05]\) p.u.

    Solution: Exercise 1.

  2. Show that the flows of a DC power flow do not depend on which bus is the slack when the injections sum to zero, and that the voltage angles do.

    Solution: Exercise 2.

  3. (Jupyter: NumPy) Build \(B_\text{bus}\) and \(B_f\) for IEEE 14 from the branch table, solve the DC power flow with a sparse factorization (scipy.sparse.linalg.splu), and reuse the factorization for 1,000 random balanced injection vectors stacked as a (n_timesteps, n_bus) array. Compare the time with 1,000 separate solves.

    Solution: Exercise 3.

  4. (Octave + MATPOWER) For case14, verify that Bbus from makeBdc equals \(A^\top \operatorname{diag}(b) A\) with \(b = 1/(x\tau)\), and that Pfinj is zero unless a branch has a nonzero SHIFT. Add a 3° shift to one transformer and check the equivalent-injection formula.

    Solution: Exercise 4.

  5. (Jupyter: NumPy) Implement ToOp's PSDF column \(\text{PSDF}_{\ell k} = b_k(\delta_{\ell k} - \text{PTDF}_{\ell f_k} + \text{PTDF}_{\ell t_k})\) (in radians, before ToOp's conversion to MW per degree) and confirm it against a DC power flow with a phase shift \(\varphi_k\) modeled as equivalent injections. Then state which sign convention for the grid model's angle would make the minus in get_shift_angles necessary.

    Solution: Exercise 5.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. ToOp's example notebook. toop57.py does what example1_dc_loadflow_example.ipynb does: case57_data_powsybl(folder) writes the grid and masks, load_grid(..., pandapower=False) preprocesses them and run_initial_loadflow fills unsplit_flow. Its shape is (1, 82) = (n_timesteps, n_branches): one injection snapshot and 82 branches (64 lines and 18 two-winding transformers, because case57_data_powsybl extends pypowsybl's IEEE 57 with a phase-shifting transformer and its auxiliary line and bus), on 72 nodes (the example also adds busbars, create_busbar_b_in_ieee). nodal_injections has the matching shape (1, 72). The first axis is the time axis of the note in the chapter: a second snapshot would add a row to both arrays and leave the PTDF alone. branch_names are node-pair labels ('B1 ## B2 ## ') and repeat for parallel branches (80 distinct names for 82 branches); branch_ids are the pypowsybl ids and are unique.

    toop57.py
    """ToOp's base-case DC flows (``unsplit_flow``) on its IEEE 57 example against pypowsybl (Chapter 16, Lab steps 1, 4).

Run it with ToOp's interpreter (its container or virtual environment)::

    python toop57.py /tmp/case57

It writes ToOp's extended IEEE 57 case in PowSyBl format into that folder, as
``notebooks/example1_dc_loadflow_example.ipynb`` does, loads it, runs the initial load flow and compares
``unsplit_flow`` with ``pypowsybl.loadflow.run_dc`` on the saved grid.
"""

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import jax
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pypowsybl as pyp
from fsspec.implementations.dirfs import DirFileSystem
from toop_engine_dc_solver.example_grids import CGMES_DISTRIBUTED_SLACK, case57_data_powsybl
from toop_engine_dc_solver.preprocess.convert_to_jax import load_grid, run_initial_loadflow
from toop_engine_interfaces.folder_structure import PREPROCESSING_PATHS
from toop_engine_interfaces.messages.preprocess.preprocess_commands import PreprocessParameters

jax.config.update('jax_enable_x64', True)


def load(folder: Path):
    """Write the example case into ``folder`` and preprocess it; return static information and network data."""
    case57_data_powsybl(folder)
    _, si, network_data = load_grid(
        DirFileSystem(str(folder)),
        pandapower=False,
        parameters=PreprocessParameters(action_set_filter_bsdf_lodf=False),
    )
    si, _ = run_initial_loadflow(si)
    return si, network_data


def toop_flows(si, network_data) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """ToOp's ``unsplit_flow`` of timestep 0 next to the backend's DC flows and AC-DC mismatch, by branch id (MW)."""
    ids = list(network_data.branch_ids)
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            'name': list(network_data.branch_names),
            'unsplit_flow': np.asarray(si.dynamic_information.unsplit_flow)[0],
            'basecase_dc': np.asarray(network_data.basecase_dc_branch_flows)[0],
            'ac_dc_mismatch': np.asarray(network_data.ac_dc_mismatch)[0],
        },
        index=ids,
    )


def powsybl_flows(folder: Path) -> pd.Series:
    """``p1`` of every line and transformer after ``run_dc`` with ToOp's parameters on the saved grid (MW)."""
    net = pyp.network.load(str(folder / PREPROCESSING_PATHS['grid_file_path_powsybl']))
    pyp.loadflow.run_dc(net, CGMES_DISTRIBUTED_SLACK)
    return pd.concat([net.get_lines()['p1'], net.get_2_windings_transformers()['p1']]).rename('powsybl_p1')


def compare(folder: Path) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, object]:
    """ToOp flows next to pypowsybl's ``p1``; ``unsplit + p1`` is zero when the orientations are opposite."""
    si, network_data = load(folder)
    frame = toop_flows(si, network_data)
    frame['powsybl_p1'] = powsybl_flows(folder).reindex(frame.index)
    frame['unsplit + p1'] = frame['unsplit_flow'] + frame['powsybl_p1']
    frame['unsplit - basecase_dc'] = frame['unsplit_flow'] - frame['basecase_dc']
    return frame, si


def main() -> None:
    """Shape of ``unsplit_flow`` and the agreement with pypowsybl's DC flows."""
    folder = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 'case57')
    pd.set_option('display.width', 140)
    frame, si = compare(folder)
    di = si.dynamic_information
    shape = np.asarray(di.unsplit_flow).shape
    print(f'unsplit_flow shape {shape} = (n_timesteps, n_branches): {di.n_timesteps} timestep(s), ', end='')
    print(f'{di.n_branches} branches, {di.n_nodes} nodes')
    print(f'nodal_injections shape {np.asarray(di.nodal_injections).shape}; ', end='')
    print(f'{frame.index.nunique()} distinct branch ids, {frame["name"].nunique()} distinct names')
    print(f'max |unsplit_flow - basecase_dc_branch_flows| = {frame["unsplit - basecase_dc"].abs().max():.2e} MW')
    print(f'max |unsplit_flow + p1| = {frame["unsplit + p1"].abs().max():.4f} MW (p1 has the opposite orientation)')
    mism = frame['ac_dc_mismatch'].abs()
    print(
        f'AC-DC mismatch stored for alpha: mean |m| {mism.mean():.2f} MW, max {mism.max():.2f} MW on {mism.idxmax()}'
    )
    print(frame.loc[frame['unsplit_flow'].abs().nlargest(5).index].round(3))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  2. DC flows against rundcpp on case57. dc_vs_ac.dc_case reads pandapower's internal MATPOWER-style branch table (net._ppc['branch']: from, to, BR_X, TAP, SHIFT and the flow PF in MW) after rundcpp, and the injections as -net.res_bus.p_mw, which are balanced because the DC model has no losses. The case has 80 branches, 15 of them transformers with a tap ratio, no phase shift, slack at bus 0. With \(b = 1/x\) the worked example's function differs from rundcpp by up to 1.286 MW, all of it on transformers (the largest on trafo 12, tap 0.895: \(-30.29\) against \(-31.57\) MW). With \(b = 1/(x\tau)\) the difference is \(2.2 \times 10^{-13}\) MW. That is the systematic difference to find: MATPOWER's and pandapower's DC model divide the series susceptance by the tap ratio (manual eq. 3.23), and a tap of 0.895 changes the branch susceptance by 12 %. The per-unit base is pandapower's sn_mva (100 MVA), already applied inside _ppc; the orientation is pandapower's own, from bus to to bus for lines and hv to lv for transformers, which is why res_line.p_from_mw and res_trafo.p_hv_mw are the columns to compare. Had the case contained a shift, SHIFT would have appeared as the extra term \(P_{f,\text{shift}}\) of the worked example (Exercise 4).

    dc_vs_ac.py
    """DC flows of a pandapower case against ``rundcpp`` and ``runpp`` (Chapter 16, Lab steps 2 and 3).

The branch table (from, to, x, tap, shift) comes from the internal MATPOWER-style structure that pandapower builds
for its own solvers (``net._ppc``), so the per-unit base is pandapower's ``sn_mva`` and the orientation is
pandapower's (lines: from bus to to bus; transformers: hv bus to lv bus).
"""

import numpy as np
import pandapower as pp
import pandapower.networks as pn
import pandas as pd
from dc_power_flow import dc_power_flow

F_BUS, T_BUS, BR_R, BR_X, TAP, SHIFT, PF = 0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 13


def branch_table(net: pp.pandapowerNet) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Branches of a solved network: from, to, r, x, tap, shift (deg) and the DC flow pandapower computed (MW)."""
    br = net._ppc['branch'].real
    names = [f'line {i}' for i in net.line.index] + [f'trafo {i}' for i in net.trafo.index]
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            'from': br[:, F_BUS].astype(int),
            'to': br[:, T_BUS].astype(int),
            'r': br[:, BR_R],
            'x': br[:, BR_X],
            'tap': np.where(br[:, TAP] == 0, 1.0, br[:, TAP]),
            'shift': br[:, SHIFT],
            'p_pandapower': br[:, PF],
        },
        index=names,
    )
    table['kind'] = ['line'] * len(net.line) + ['trafo'] * len(net.trafo)
    return table


def dc_case(name: str) -> tuple[pp.pandapowerNet, pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray, int]:
    """Run ``rundcpp`` on ``pandapower.networks.<name>()``: the net, the branch table, injections (MW) and slack."""
    net = getattr(pn, name)()
    pp.rundcpp(net)
    table = branch_table(net)
    p = -net.res_bus.p_mw.to_numpy()  # res_bus is a demand: minus it is the net injection, balanced in DC
    return net, table, p, int(net.ext_grid.bus.iloc[0])


def own_dc_flows(table: pd.DataFrame, p: np.ndarray, slack: int, with_taps: bool = True) -> np.ndarray:
    """DC flows (MW) with the worked example's function, with or without the tap ratio in b = 1/(x tau)."""
    x = table['x'].to_numpy() * (table['tap'].to_numpy() if with_taps else 1.0)
    return dc_power_flow(table['from'].to_numpy(), table['to'].to_numpy(), x, p, slack)


def dc_ac_frame(name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per branch: DC flow, AC flow, AC loading (%), r/x and the relative DC error against the AC flow."""
    net, table, p, slack = dc_case(name)
    table['p_dc'] = own_dc_flows(table, p, slack)
    pp.runpp(net)
    table['p_ac'] = np.concatenate([net.res_line.p_from_mw.to_numpy(), net.res_trafo.p_hv_mw.to_numpy()])
    table['loading_ac'] = np.concatenate(
        [net.res_line.loading_percent.to_numpy(), net.res_trafo.loading_percent.to_numpy()]
    )
    table['losses_ac'] = np.concatenate([net.res_line.pl_mw.to_numpy(), net.res_trafo.pl_mw.to_numpy()])
    table['r_over_x'] = table['r'] / table['x']
    table['abs_error'] = (table['p_dc'] - table['p_ac']).abs()
    table['rel_error'] = table['abs_error'] / table['p_ac'].abs()
    return table


def main() -> None:
    """Print the comparison of Lab steps 2 and 3 for case57."""
    pd.set_option('display.width', 140)
    _, table, p, slack = dc_case('case57')
    n_tap = int((table['tap'] != 1).sum())
    print(
        f'case57: {len(table)} branches, {n_tap} with a tap ratio, shifts {table["shift"].unique()}, slack bus {slack}'
    )
    no_tap, with_tap = own_dc_flows(table, p, slack, with_taps=False), own_dc_flows(table, p, slack)
    ref = table['p_pandapower'].to_numpy()
    err_no_tap, err_tap = np.abs(no_tap - ref).max(), np.abs(with_tap - ref).max()
    print(f'Step 2: max |own - rundcpp| ignoring taps: {err_no_tap:.3f} MW; with b = 1/(x tau): {err_tap:.1e} MW')
    worst = int(np.abs(no_tap - ref).argmax())
    tap = table['tap'].iloc[worst]
    print(f'  largest tap effect on {table.index[worst]} (tap {tap:.3f}): {no_tap[worst]:.2f} vs {ref[worst]:.2f} MW')
    print(f'  for the Octave comparison (step 5): first five rundcpp flows {np.round(ref[:5], 4)}, ', end='')
    print(f'sum |F| {np.abs(ref).sum():.4f}, max |F| {np.abs(ref).max():.4f} MW')
    frame = dc_ac_frame('case57')
    err = frame['abs_error']
    print(f'Step 3: AC losses {frame["losses_ac"].sum():.2f} MW of {-p[p < 0].sum():.1f} MW of load; ', end='')
    print(f'mean |DC - AC| {err.mean():.2f} MW, max {err.max():.2f} MW on {err.idxmax()}')
    heavy = frame[frame['p_ac'].abs() > 10]
    rel = 100 * heavy['rel_error']
    print(
        f'  branches above 10 MW: median relative error {rel.median():.1f} %, max {rel.max():.1f} % ({rel.idxmax()})'
    )
    print(f'  correlation of |DC - AC| with |AC flow|: {err.corr(frame["p_ac"].abs()):.2f}; ', end='')
    print(f'of the relative error with r/x (branches above 10 MW): {heavy["rel_error"].corr(heavy["r_over_x"]):.2f}')
    lines = frame[frame['kind'] == 'line']
    n_trafo_r = int((frame.loc[frame['kind'] == 'trafo', 'r'] > 0).sum())
    print(f'  r/x of the lines: {lines["r_over_x"].min():.2f} to {lines["r_over_x"].max():.2f}; ', end='')
    print(f'transformers with r > 0: {n_trafo_r}')
    print('  five worst absolute errors:')
    print(frame.nlargest(5, 'abs_error')[['kind', 'p_dc', 'p_ac', 'loading_ac', 'r_over_x', 'rel_error']].round(3))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  3. DC against AC. dc_ac_frame('case57') adds runpp's flows and losses. The AC solution loses 30.29 MW of the 695.8 MW of load; the DC flows miss the AC ones by 1.56 MW on average and by 10.18 MW at most, on line 14 (139.4 MW DC against 149.6 MW AC). Among the branches above 10 MW the median relative error is 5.3 % and the largest 27.5 % (line 21, a lightly loaded line whose AC flow is far from its DC value). The absolute error correlates with the magnitude of the AC flow (coefficient 0.62): the heavier the branch, the more losses and voltage drop it carries, and both are absent from the DC model. The relative error does not correlate with \(r/x\) on this case (coefficient \(-0.02\)): the lines of case57 have \(r/x\) between 0 and 1.09, and the transformers have \(r = 0\); the error is set by the voltage profile (0.94 to 1.06 pu, Exercise 1) and by how the 30 MW of losses are routed to the slack, not by the resistance of each branch. On a case with a wide spread of \(r/x\) (distribution grids) the second plot would show the trend the exercise expects. The five worst absolute errors are all lines carrying 30 to 150 MW. A scatter of rel_error against |p_ac| is a funnel: large relative errors only on small flows; against r_over_x it is a cloud.

  4. ToOp's unsplit_flow. On ToOp's extended IEEE 57, unsplit_flow equals network_data.basecase_dc_branch_flows to \(1.6 \times 10^{-13}\) MW (the default ac_dc_interpolation = 0 adds no mismatch) and equals minus pypowsybl's p1 from run_dc with the same CGMES_DISTRIBUTED_SLACK parameters on the saved grid, to \(10^{-4}\) MW: get_basecase_dc_branch_flows negates p1 because PowSyBl's convention is opposite to the solver's from-node to to-node orientation. The largest flows are \(-271.2\) MW on L8-9-1, 113.9 MW on L7-8-1, \(-73.2\) MW on T7-29-1, 70.9 MW on L6-8-1 and \(-50.1\) MW on L1-17-1. The backend also stores the AC–DC mismatch \(m = F^{AC} - F^{DC}\) per branch: 1.51 MW on average, 8.23 MW at most, again on L8-9-1, the heaviest branch, the same pattern as step 3. Note that the grid is not pandapower's case57 of step 2 (different dispatch, extra elements), so the two sets of flows are not comparable branch by branch; the test test_toop57_toop.py checks both relations under make test-toop.
  5. Octave + MATPOWER. [pf, Bbus, Bf] = matpower_dcpf('case57') (Octave 11.3, MATPOWER 8.1) gives 80 flows whose first five are 97.8996, 94.8996, 58.4379, 13.8948 and 12.7802 MW, with \(\sum|F| = 1919.4868\) MW and \(\max|F| = 177.2260\) MW; dc_vs_ac.main() prints the same five numbers and the same two sums from rundcpp. pandapower's case57 is converted from MATPOWER's, and both apply the tap ratio, so the two agree to the fourth decimal.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
With \(\Delta\theta = \theta_f - \theta_t\), the AC active flow of a lossless branch is \(p_f = |V_f||V_t|\sin(\Delta\theta)/x\) and the DC flow is \(p_f^{DC} = \Delta\theta/x\). Their ratio does not depend on \(x\):

\[ \frac{p_f^{DC}}{p_f} = \frac{\Delta\theta}{|V_f||V_t|\sin\Delta\theta}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{p_f^{DC} - p_f}{p_f} = \frac{1}{|V_f||V_t|}\cdot\frac{\Delta\theta}{\sin\Delta\theta} - 1 . \]

Both factors are monotone on the given ranges: \(\Delta\theta/\sin\Delta\theta\) grows from 1 at \(\Delta\theta \to 0\) to \(1/\operatorname{sinc}(10^\circ) = 1/0.99493 = 1.0051\) at \(10^\circ\), and \(1/(|V_f||V_t|)\) lies between \(1/1.05^2 = 0.9070\) and \(1/0.95^2 = 1.1080\). Hence

\[ -9.30\,\% = \frac{1}{1.05^2} - 1 \;\le\; \varepsilon \;\le\; \frac{1.0051}{0.95^2} - 1 = +11.37\,\% . \]

The angle contributes only \(+0.51\) % at \(10^\circ\); the voltage magnitudes contribute about \(\pm 10\) %, which is why the DC approximation is a flat-voltage approximation before it is a small-angle one, and why a voltage profile of 0.94–1.06 pu produces the errors of Lab step 3 even with \(r = 0\). Measured against the DC flow instead (\((p_f - p_f^{DC})/p_f^{DC} = |V_f||V_t|\operatorname{sinc}\Delta\theta - 1\)) the bounds are \(-10.2\) % and \(+10.25\) %. dc_approximation.error_bounds evaluates \(\varepsilon\) on the four voltage corners and 1,001 angles and returns the same two numbers.

dc_approximation.py
"""Error of the DC branch flow and independence of the slack (Chapter 16, Exercises 1 and 2)."""

import numpy as np
from dc_power_flow import dc_power_flow


def relative_error(vf: float, vt: float, dtheta: float) -> float:
    """(p_DC - p_AC) / p_AC for a lossless branch: |Vf||Vt| sin(d) / d is the AC flow per unit of DC flow."""
    return dtheta / (vf * vt * np.sin(dtheta)) - 1


def error_bounds(v_lo: float = 0.95, v_hi: float = 1.05, max_deg: float = 10.0) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Smallest and largest relative error over |V| in [v_lo, v_hi] at both ends and 0 < |d| <= max_deg."""
    d = np.deg2rad(np.linspace(1e-6, max_deg, 1001))
    errors = [relative_error(vf, vt, d) for vf in (v_lo, v_hi) for vt in (v_lo, v_hi)]
    return float(np.min(errors)), float(np.max(errors))


def angles_and_flows(
    frm: np.ndarray, to: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, p: np.ndarray, slack: int
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Bus angles (rad, slack at 0) and branch flows of a DC power flow, both for the chosen slack."""
    n, m = len(p), len(frm)
    a = np.zeros((m, n))
    a[np.arange(m), frm], a[np.arange(m), to] = 1.0, -1.0
    bbus = a.T @ np.diag(1 / x) @ a
    keep = np.arange(n) != slack
    theta = np.zeros(n)
    theta[keep] = np.linalg.solve(bbus[np.ix_(keep, keep)], p[keep])
    return theta, dc_power_flow(frm, to, x, p, slack)


def main() -> None:
    """Exercise 1 bounds and the slack comparison of Exercise 2 on the four-bus grid of the tests."""
    lo, hi = error_bounds()
    print(f'Exercise 1: relative error of the DC flow between {100 * lo:+.2f} % and {100 * hi:+.2f} %')
    sinc = np.sin(np.deg2rad(10)) / np.deg2rad(10)
    print(f'  sinc(10 deg) = {sinc:.5f}; 1/0.95^2 - 1 = {1 / 0.95**2 - 1:+.4f}; 1/1.05^2 - 1 = {1 / 1.05**2 - 1:+.4f}')
    print(f'  angle alone at 10 deg (|V| = 1): {100 * relative_error(1, 1, np.deg2rad(10)):+.2f} %')
    frm, to = np.array([0, 0, 1, 2]), np.array([1, 2, 3, 3])
    x = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.1, 0.2])
    p = np.array([0.8, 0.2, -0.5, -0.5])  # pu, like the reactances
    th0, f0 = angles_and_flows(frm, to, x, p, slack=0)
    th3, f3 = angles_and_flows(frm, to, x, p, slack=3)
    print('Exercise 2: flows (pu) with slack 0:', np.round(f0, 4), ' with slack 3:', np.round(f3, 4))
    print('  angles (deg) slack 0:', np.round(np.rad2deg(th0), 3), ' slack 3:', np.round(np.rad2deg(th3), 3))
    print('  difference of the angle vectors (constant):', np.round(np.rad2deg(th3 - th0), 3))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
\(B_\text{bus} = A^\top\operatorname{diag}(b)A\) is a weighted Laplacian of a connected graph: symmetric, positive semidefinite, with the one-dimensional null space spanned by \(\mathbf 1\) (every row sums to zero), and its range is the set of vectors orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1\), that is, the balanced injections. For a balanced \(P\) the equation \(B_\text{bus}\theta = P\) therefore has solutions, and they form the line \(\theta^\star + c\,\mathbf 1\). Choosing a slack \(s\) and deleting its row and column picks the one solution with \(\theta_s = 0\), which is \(\theta^{(s)} = \theta^\star - \theta^\star_s\,\mathbf 1\) (the reduced matrix is nonsingular, Chapter 2). Two slacks \(s\) and \(r\) give \(\theta^{(r)} - \theta^{(s)} = (\theta^\star_s - \theta^\star_r)\,\mathbf 1\): the angle vectors differ by a constant, so the angles depend on the slack. The flows do not, because \(F = \operatorname{diag}(b)A\theta\) and every row of \(A\) has one \(+1\) and one \(-1\), so \(A\,\mathbf 1 = 0\) and \(F^{(r)} - F^{(s)} = \operatorname{diag}(b)A\,c\,\mathbf 1 = 0\). The flow of a branch is a difference of two angles, and the slack choice only adds the same constant to both. If the injections do not sum to zero there is no solution of the full system; the reduced system then assigns the imbalance to the slack bus, \(P_s = -\sum_{i\ne s}P_i\), and the flows do depend on where the imbalance is absorbed (Chapter 17).

Numerically (dc_approximation.main), on the four-bus ring with \(P = (0.8, 0.2, -0.5, -0.5)\) pu, slack 0 and slack 3 give the same flows \((0.3333, 0.4667, 0.5333, -0.0333)\) pu while the angles move from \((0, -1.910, -5.348, -4.966)^\circ\) to \((4.966, 3.056, -0.382, 0)^\circ\): a shift of \(4.966^\circ\) on every bus.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
dc_sparse_solve.susceptance_matrices assembles \(A\) as a sparse (20, 14) incidence matrix from the branch table of pandapower's case14 (with \(b = 1/(x\tau)\): three transformers have taps), then \(B_f = \operatorname{diag}(b)A\) and \(B_\text{bus} = A^\top B_f\), 54 nonzeros. The slack row and column are dropped, splu factorizes the (13, 13) matrix once, and flows_many solves all right-hand sides in one call: lu.solve(p[:, keep].T) takes the (13, 1000) block and \(F = (B_{f,\text{red}}\,\Theta)^\top\) has shape (1000, 20), the layout of ToOp's unsplit_flow. The snapshots are the base case plus Gaussian noise of 10 MW per bus, rebalanced at the slack; snapshot 0 is the base case itself and matches rundcpp to \(7.5 \times 10^{-14}\) MW. The block solve and 1,000 separate spsolve calls agree exactly (difference 0.0). Time (best of several runs): 0.53 ms for the factorization plus the block solve against 38–42 ms for the separate solves, a factor of 70–80. The separate solves pay a symbolic and numeric factorization per call plus Python overhead; the block solve pays one factorization and then one triangular sweep per snapshot in compiled code. This is the PTDF idea in disguise: one topology, one factorization, many injection vectors.

dc_sparse_solve.py
"""Sparse DC power flow of IEEE 14 for many injection snapshots at once (Chapter 16, Exercise 3).

Bbus and Bf are assembled as ``scipy.sparse`` matrices from the branch table that pandapower builds for ``case14``,
factorized once with ``splu`` and reused for a ``(n_timesteps, n_bus)`` block of balanced injections.
"""

import timeit

import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sps
import scipy.sparse.linalg as spla
from dc_vs_ac import dc_case


def susceptance_matrices(
    frm: np.ndarray, to: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, n_bus: int
) -> tuple[sps.csc_matrix, sps.csr_matrix]:
    """Sparse Bbus = Aᵀ diag(b) A and Bf = diag(b) A for branch susceptances ``b``."""
    m = len(frm)
    rows = np.concatenate([np.arange(m), np.arange(m)])
    a = sps.csr_matrix(
        (np.concatenate([np.ones(m), -np.ones(m)]), (rows, np.concatenate([frm, to]))), shape=(m, n_bus)
    )
    bf = sps.diags(b) @ a
    return (a.T @ bf).tocsc(), bf.tocsr()


def flows_many(lu: spla.SuperLU, bf_reduced: sps.csr_matrix, p: np.ndarray, keep: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Flows ``(n_timesteps, n_branches)`` for the injections ``p`` ``(n_timesteps, n_bus)`` with one factorization."""
    theta = lu.solve(p[:, keep].T)  # (n_bus - 1, n_timesteps), every snapshot in one call
    return (bf_reduced @ theta).T


def flows_one_by_one(
    bbus_reduced: sps.csc_matrix, bf_reduced: sps.csr_matrix, p: np.ndarray, keep: np.ndarray
) -> np.ndarray:
    """The same flows with a separate ``spsolve`` (and therefore a separate factorization) per snapshot."""
    return np.array([bf_reduced @ spla.spsolve(bbus_reduced, row[keep]) for row in p])


def main(n_timesteps: int = 1000) -> None:
    """Build IEEE 14, draw balanced snapshots, time the two approaches and check that they agree."""
    _, table, p0, slack = dc_case('case14')
    n_bus = int(max(table['from'].max(), table['to'].max())) + 1
    b = 1 / (table['x'].to_numpy() * table['tap'].to_numpy())
    bbus, bf = susceptance_matrices(table['from'].to_numpy(), table['to'].to_numpy(), b, n_bus)
    keep = np.arange(n_bus) != slack
    bbus_r, bf_r = bbus[keep][:, keep], bf[:, keep]
    rng = np.random.default_rng(16)
    p = p0 + rng.normal(scale=10.0, size=(n_timesteps, n_bus))
    p[0] = p0  # snapshot 0 is the base case itself
    p[:, slack] -= p.sum(axis=1)  # the slack balances every snapshot
    print(f'IEEE 14: Bbus {bbus.shape} with {bbus.nnz} nonzeros, Bf {bf.shape}; injections {p.shape}')
    lu = spla.splu(bbus_r)
    many = flows_many(lu, bf_r, p, keep)
    single = flows_one_by_one(bbus_r, bf_r, p, keep)
    base_err = np.abs(many[0] - table['p_pandapower'].to_numpy()).max()
    print(f'max |block solve - separate solves| = {np.abs(many - single).max():.1e} MW; ', end='')
    print(f'snapshot 0 (the base case) matches rundcpp to {base_err:.1e} MW')
    t_many = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: flows_many(spla.splu(bbus_r), bf_r, p, keep), number=1, repeat=5))
    t_single = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: flows_one_by_one(bbus_r, bf_r, p, keep), number=1, repeat=3))
    print(f'{n_timesteps} snapshots: one factorization + block solve {1e3 * t_many:.2f} ms; ', end='')
    print(f'{n_timesteps} separate solves {1e3 * t_single:.1f} ms; ratio {t_single / t_many:.0f}x')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
makebdc_shift('case14', 8, 3) (Octave 11.3, MATPOWER 8.1) rebuilds \(A\) from F_BUS and T_BUS, takes \(b = 1/(x\tau)\) with \(\tau = 1\) where TAP is zero, and compares with makeBdc: the largest entry difference of \(B_\text{bus}\) is \(0\). Pfinj of the unmodified case is zero in every entry (no branch has a SHIFT). After setting SHIFT = 3 on branch 8 (the transformer 4–7, \(x = 0.2091\), \(\tau = 0.978\)), exactly one entry of Pfinj is nonzero, \(\text{Pfinj}_8 = -b_8 \cdot 3\pi/180 = -4.8897 \times 0.05236 = -0.25601\) pu (\(-25.6\) MW), and Pbusinj equals \(A^\top\,\text{Pfinj}\) (an injection of \(-0.256\) pu at bus 4 and \(+0.256\) pu at bus 7): both checks hold to \(5.6 \times 10^{-17}\). This is the equivalent-injection formula of the worked example, \(P_{f,\text{shift}} = -\operatorname{diag}(b)\,\theta_\text{shift}\) and \(P_\text{bus,shift} = A^\top P_{f,\text{shift}}\), with MATPOWER's sign: a positive SHIFT reduces the flow from \(f\) to \(t\).

makebdc_shift.m
function [err_bbus, pfinj0, pfinj, err_shift] = makebdc_shift(casename, branch_row, shift_deg)
  % Check makeBdc against A' diag(b) A with b = 1/(x tau), and Pfinj against -b * shift (rad), after adding a
  % phase shift to one branch (Chapter 16, Exercise 4). Returns the largest entry differences and both Pfinj.
  define_constants;
  mpc = ext2int(loadcase(casename));
  [Bbus, ~, ~, pfinj0] = makeBdc(mpc);
  nb = size(mpc.bus, 1); nl = size(mpc.branch, 1);
  tau = mpc.branch(:, TAP); tau(tau == 0) = 1;
  b = 1 ./ (mpc.branch(:, BR_X) .* tau);
  A = sparse([1:nl 1:nl], [mpc.branch(:, F_BUS); mpc.branch(:, T_BUS)], [ones(nl, 1); -ones(nl, 1)], nl, nb);
  err_bbus = full(max(max(abs(Bbus - A' * diag(b) * A))));
  mpc.branch(branch_row, SHIFT) = shift_deg;
  [~, ~, Pbusinj, pfinj] = makeBdc(mpc);
  expected = zeros(nl, 1); expected(branch_row) = -b(branch_row) * shift_deg * pi / 180;
  err_shift = max(abs(pfinj - expected));
  err_shift = max(err_shift, full(max(abs(Pbusinj - A' * expected))));   % the bus injections are A' Pfinj
end

%!test
%! if isempty(which('makeBdc')), disp('MATPOWER not on the path, test skipped'); return; end
%! [err_bbus, pfinj0, pfinj, err_shift] = makebdc_shift('case14', 8, 3);
%! assert(err_bbus < 1e-9)
%! assert(all(pfinj0 == 0))
%! assert(err_shift < 1e-12)
%! assert(sum(pfinj ~= 0), 1)
