docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
python ieee14_flow_based.py runs the six steps on the base topology and on two topology actions. The functions named below are in that module.

  1. IEEE 14 and its nodal PTDF. load_ieee14() reads buses, lines, transformers, generators and loads from pypowsybl.network.create_ieee14() and ptdf_matrix() builds \(H\) as in Chapter 17 with bus 1 as slack. Two details decide whether H @ p matches pypowsybl's DC flows: the per-unit base of the reactances, which pypowsybl gives in ohms (a line between two nominal voltages \(V_1\), \(V_2\) uses \(V_1 V_2 / S_\text{base}\); a transformer uses the square of its side-2 voltage, where its ohms are expressed), and the transformer ratio. pypowsybl's default DC load flow keeps the off-nominal ratios \(\rho = (U_{1,\text{rated}}/V_1)/(U_{2,\text{rated}}/V_2)\) (0.978, 0.969 and 0.932 for the three transformers), which multiplies their reactance by \(\rho\) in the DC equations; with Parameters(distributed_slack=False, dc_use_transformer_ratio=False) the textbook model applies and H @ p reproduces every pypowsybl flow to \(2.6 \times 10^{-13}\) MW. The injection vector must be balanced: the data have 272.4 MW of generation set points against 259 MW of load, and in a lossless DC model the slack generator at bus 1 produces 219.0 MW, not its 232.4 MW set point. The net positions at the reference point are then \(NP_A = 87.7\), \(NP_B = -34.3\), \(NP_C = -53.4\) MW (zones A = {1–5}, B = {6, 11, 12, 13}, C = {7, 8, 9, 10, 14}), summing to zero.
  2. Zones and GLSKs. glsk(grid, 'generation') spreads a zone's net position over its generators in proportion to target_p: zone A gets (0.853, 0.147, 0, 0, 0) over buses 1–5 (232.4 and 40 MW at buses 1 and 2; the 0 MW generators at buses 3, 6 and 8 get no weight). Zones B and C have no generation in the base case, so the generation GLSK falls back to flat there: 0.25 on each of buses 6, 11, 12, 13 and 0.2 on each of buses 7, 8, 9, 10, 14. glsk(grid, 'flat') is flat in all three zones. Every column sums to one.

  3. Zonal PTDF and the pypowsybl cross-check. \(\text{PTDF}_z = H\,G\). For zone A with the generation GLSK, pypowsybl_zone_factors() builds the same zone with create_zone_from_injections_and_shift_keys('A', ['B1-G', 'B2-G'], [0.853, 0.147]), runs the DC sensitivity analysis with the parameters of step 1 and reads get_sensitivity_matrix(): the 20 factors agree with the NumPy column to \(5.6 \times 10^{-17}\) (the zone factor is the shift-key-weighted sum of the injection factors, and the injection factors are the PTDF columns). A few rows, zones (A, B, C):

    Branch Generation GLSK Flat GLSK L1-2-1 (−0.123, −0.633, −0.652) (−0.573, −0.633, −0.652) L1-5-1 (−0.024, −0.367, −0.348) (−0.227, −0.367, −0.348) L2-3-1 (0.004, −0.122, −0.138) (−0.152, −0.122, −0.138) T5-6-1 (−0.001, −0.600, −0.294) (−0.007, −0.600, −0.294)

    The B and C columns are identical because both GLSKs are flat there. The A column changes a lot: with 85 % of zone A's shift key on the slack bus, whose PTDF column is zero, the generation GLSK makes zone A almost invisible to the 135 kV lines, while the flat GLSK puts 60 % of every MW on buses 2–5 and loads L1-2 and L1-5. The slack choice does not matter for zone-to-zone PTDFs (differences of columns) but it does for a single zone's column, which is why only zone-to-zone values have a physical meaning. 4. CNECs, \(F_0\) and RAM. cnec_table() makes 40 CNECs (20 branches, both directions) with \(F_\max = \max(1.3\,|F_\text{ref}|,\ 20)\) MW (16 of them sit on the 20 MW floor), FRM \(= 0.05\,F_\max\), \(F_0 = F_\text{ref} - \text{PTDF}_z\,NP_\text{ref}\) and \(\text{RAM}^\pm = F_\max - \text{FRM} \mp F_0\). The four smallest margins:

    CNEC \(F_\text{ref}\) \(F_\max\) \(F_0\) RAM L3-4-1− −24.2 31.4 −36.1 −6.2 L7-8-1− 0.0 20.0 −10.7 8.3 L9-10-1− 6.2 20.0 −5.3 13.7 L10-11-1− −2.8 20.0 −3.6 15.4

    The negative RAM of L3-4-1 in the negative direction means that the point of zero net positions is outside the domain: with no exchange at all the line would carry 36 MW from bus 4 to bus 3, above its 31.4 MW stand-in limit. The market must trade (zone A exporting, as it does at the reference point) to keep this line within its limit. Every RAM is positive at the reference point by construction, since \(|F_\text{ref}| \le F_\max/1.3\) and \(F_\max - \text{FRM} = 0.95\,F_\max\). 5. The domain. With \(NP_C = -NP_A - NP_B\) each CNEC is a half-plane \((\text{PTDF}_A - \text{PTDF}_C)\,NP_A + (\text{PTDF}_B - \text{PTDF}_C)\,NP_B \le \text{RAM}\) (half_planes()). domain_vertices() intersects the boundary lines pairwise and keeps the points that satisfy all 40 constraints: a pentagon with vertices (52.3, −76.3), (70.7, −83.1), (107.8, −47.4), (79.9, 9.5), (41.4, 23.7), whose edges belong to L10-11-1 (both directions), T4-7-1+, T5-6-1+ and L3-4-1− (binding_cnecs()). The reference point (87.7, −34.3) is inside. The domain is small and thin because the 12 kV branches have 20 MW limits and sensitivities to zones B and C of 0.25 to 0.6: ten to twenty MW of exchange fill them. exchanges() measures how far the reference point can move in each zone-to-zone direction before a CNEC binds, the flow-based counterpart of an available transfer capacity:

    Direction Extra exchange Binding CNEC A→B 16.5 MW T5-6-1+ B→A 44.9 MW L3-4-1− A→C 13.7 MW T4-7-1+ C→A 40.0 MW L3-4-1− B→C 27.9 MW T4-7-1+ C→B 32.4 MW T5-6-1+

    Exports from zone A are limited by the two transformers that feed zones B and C; imports into A are limited by L3-4 in its negative direction. The plot is a matplotlib polygon through the vertices with the reference point marked and the five binding CNECs as edge labels (not saved by the module; lab.ipynb leaves the figure to you). 6. A topology action. topology_action(grid, f_max, 'L13-14-1') opens line 13–14, keeps the limits of the surviving branches (limits are properties of the lines, not of the topology), and rebuilds PTDF, CNECs and domain. The new pentagon is bounded by L6-13-1+, T4-7-1+, T5-6-1+, L3-4-1− and L10-11-1−. Overlaying the two polygons and comparing the exchanges:

    Direction Base L13-14 open Change A→B 16.5 18.3 +1.8 B→A 44.9 41.8 −3.0 A→C 13.7 9.6 −4.0 C→A 40.0 39.8 −0.2 B→C 27.9 15.6 −12.3 C→B 32.4 25.9 −6.5

    Only A→B gains: the line 13–14 was the parallel path between zones B and C, so every exchange that used it loses capacity, B→C most of all. The N-1 check of Chapter 19 (security_metrics(), LODF over every non-bridge outage, loading against the same \(F_\max\)) says: base topology worst N-0 loading 76.9 % (that is \(1/1.3\), by construction), worst N-1 loading 300 % on L3-4-1 after the outage of L2-3-1, N-1 overload energy 382.8 MW; with L13-14 open the N-0 worst rises to 81.1 %, the worst N-1 case is the same 300 % and the overload energy grows to 414.7 MW. The stand-in limits of step 4 make the base topology itself N-1 insecure, so the check is a comparison: the action makes N-1 security worse and would not pass. The module also tries line 3–4, the action that enlarges four of the six margins: it leaves no domain at all. Bus 3 becomes radial, so L2-3-1 carries the whole 94.2 MW load of bus 3 whatever the net positions (zonal PTDFs exactly zero), above its 91.1 MW limit: \(\text{RAM} = -7.7\) MW with zero sensitivity is a constraint no exchange can satisfy. In N-0 the line is at 103.4 %, so this action fails before any N-1 case is run (its N-1 energy, 285.4 MW, would be better). A remedial action is only a candidate when the base case stays within limits; the flow-based domain then tells the market how much room the action leaves.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
The TATL is a temporary admissible loading: the line may carry up to 1 250 A for 15 minutes after the contingency, provided the flow is brought back under the PATL (1 000 A) within that time. verdict() in curative_timing.py encodes the three conditions.

  • 1 180 A after the contingency, split active after 10 minutes, 940 A afterwards: the flow is under the TATL, the action arrives before the 15 minutes run out and leaves 940 A < 1 000 A. The curative action is sufficient; no preventive action is needed, and the market keeps the capacity.
  • Activation takes 20 minutes: the line would stay at 1 180 A for 20 minutes, 5 minutes beyond the TATL duration. A preventive action (or a faster curative one) is needed to bring the post-contingency flow under the PATL, or at least to a level the TATL duration covers.
  • Post-contingency flow 1 300 A: above the TATL, so the line is not allowed to carry it even for a second; the protection would trip it. Only a preventive action helps, since there is no time window in which to act.

A boundary case: 1 250 A and exactly 15 minutes pass (the TATL is inclusive in CRAC conventions); a curative action that leaves 1 020 A does not pass, because the end state must respect the PATL.

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
The GeoGebra construction (not run here): five lines \(a_k\,NP_A + b_k\,NP_B = \text{RAM}_k\), the inequality side of each shaded, the intersection filled, a slider on one RAM. domain_2d.py holds one such set, with the zonal PTDFs given relative to the balancing zone C (so \(a_k = \text{PTDF}_{A,k}\), \(b_k = \text{PTDF}_{B,k}\)):

CNEC \(\text{PTDF}_A\) \(\text{PTDF}_B\) RAM (MW) \(s = \text{PTDF}_A - \text{PTDF}_B\) RAM / \(s\) 1 0.5 0.1 200 0.4 500 2 −0.3 0.4 180 −0.7 relieved 3 −0.4 −0.5 250 0.1 2 500 4 0.2 −0.6 220 0.8 275 5 0.6 −0.4 150 1.0 150

An A→B exchange of \(e\) MW is the point \(NP = (e, -e, 0)\); CNEC \(k\) sees \(s_k e\) with \(s_k = a_k - b_k\) and allows \(e \le \text{RAM}_k / s_k\) when \(s_k > 0\) (a CNEC with \(s_k < 0\) is relieved). The largest exchange is 150 MW, bound by CNEC 5. The domain itself is the pentagon with vertices (−612.9, −9.7), (−117.6, −405.9), (7.1, −364.3), (365.4, 173.1) and (269.6, 652.2); it contains the origin. Moving the slider: with RAM\(_5\) = 200 MW the exchange is 200 MW, still bound by CNEC 5; from RAM\(_5\) = 275 MW on, CNEC 4 takes over at 275 MW and raising RAM\(_5\) further (300, 400 MW) changes nothing. That is the general picture: enlarging the margin of the binding CNEC moves the boundary until the next CNEC binds, and a remedial action that only relieves one element has a bounded payoff.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
glsk_sensitivity.compare() rebuilds the worked example with the zone A shift keys (0.6, 0.4), (1.0, 0.0) and (0.0, 1.0):

GLSK A Branch \(F_\text{ref}\) \(\text{PTDF}_{A-B}\) \(F_0\) RAM (0.6, 0.4) 0–1 / 0–2 / 1–3 / 2–3 / 1–2 137.5 / 162.5 / 62.5 / 37.5 / 25.0 0.188 / 0.412 / 0.362 / 0.138 / 0.225 90.6 / 59.4 / −28.1 / 3.1 / −31.2 99.4 / 130.6 / 218.1 / 186.9 / 221.2 (1.0, 0.0) same same 0.438 / 0.562 / 0.312 / 0.188 / 0.125 28.1 / 21.9 / −15.6 / −9.4 / −6.2 161.9 / 168.1 / 205.6 / 199.4 / 196.2 (0.0, 1.0) same same −0.188 / 0.188 / 0.438 / 0.062 / 0.375 184.4 / 115.6 / −46.9 / 21.9 / −68.8 5.6 / 74.4 / 236.9 / 168.1 / 258.8

The reference flows are the same column three times: they come from the nodal injections, \(F_\text{ref} = H\,p\), and the GLSK plays no part in them. The zonal PTDFs, \(F_0 = F_\text{ref} - \text{PTDF}_z\,NP_\text{ref}\) and the margins all change, and so does the capacity the market sees: 317 MW of extra A→B exchange (branch 0–2 binding) with (0.6, 0.4), 299 MW with (1.0, 0.0), 396 MW with (0.0, 1.0). Note the change of sign of the zone-to-zone PTDF of branch 0–1 when zone A's export is assumed to come from bus 1: the same exchange then relieves the branch that the other GLSKs load. The GLSK is a forecast of where in the zone the generators will react to the market; if the real dispatch differs, the flow on each CNEC differs from the forecast by \((\text{PTDF}_{\text{true}} - \text{PTDF}_{\text{GLSK}})\,\Delta NP\). This forecast error, together with load, renewable and topology forecast errors between D-2 and real time, is what the flow reliability margin covers (CACM Art. 22); the FRM is estimated statistically from the observed differences between forecast and realized flows on each CNEC.

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
ToOp artifact CRAC element What ToOp lacks nminus1_definition.json, contingencies (Contingency(id, elements=[GridElement]), plus BASECASE) Contingencies: a named list of network elements that trip together Nothing structural; BASECASE is the preventive state. The line_for_nminus1 mask (and trafo_*, generator_for_nminus1 etc.) is the list of elements turned into single contingencies monitored_elements and the line_for_reward mask The network elements of the CNECs A CNEC in a CRAC is one element in one state (after one contingency, at one instant); ToOp monitors every reward element after every contingency, the full product branch_limits.max_mw_flow (N-0) and max_mw_flow_n_1 Thresholds of the CNECs: PATL for the preventive instant, TATL for the outage instant Only MW thresholds (a CRAC also takes A and % of \(I_\max\)), only two instants: preventive (N-0 flows against max_mw_flow) and outage (N-1 flows against max_mw_flow_n_1). No auto and curative instants, no TATL durations action_set.json local_actions (busbar assignments) and disconnectable_branches Network actions: switch pairs (open/close) and terminal connections All are preventive; the ORAO summary writes them under preventive-actions-list the fact that every action may be applied Usage rules Only "available everywhere, preventive". No onContingencyState, onFlowConstraint, onInstant rules, so no action can be reserved for one contingency or triggered by one CNEC

Three CRAC features with no representation in ToOp: (1) curative and automatic remedial actions, with their instants, TATL durations and the flow-based idea that a curative action restores the PATL after the TATL window (Exercise 1); (2) range actions, PST tap and HVDC set-point optimization as part of the remedial action search (ToOp's pst_ranges are only read by the DC solver as fixed data, and it has no redispatching or countertrading, hence no costs); (3) CNEC-specific usage rules and thresholds (per-instant, per-contingency limits in A or %, voltage and angle CNECs, loop-flow and RAM-based objectives). Smaller gaps: a CRAC names contingencies with several elements and busbar outages explicitly, while ToOp's multi-outages and busbar outages are preprocessing options.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
orao_switches_toop.py imports and preprocesses data/grid_node_breaker/grid.xiidm exactly as the Chapter 22 Lab does (cutoff voltage 10 kV; one relevant substation, VL2, survives preprocessing with ten actions, the unsplit one included). Two findings change the exercise as stated:

  • run_pipeline (the cell of example2_small_grid_toop.ipynb) fails on Windows outside the container: the DC optimizer names its TensorBoard folder after datetime.now(), and the colons of the time are not valid in a Windows path (WinError 123). So the DC optimization stage was not run here. Instead the module writes a res.json that lists every single action as a candidate and calls perform_ac_analysis, the same function the notebook runs after the DC stage, so that the orao_summary.json files come from ToOp's own writer.
  • No topology of this grid is accepted. ToOp's evaluate_acceptance requires at most as many non-converging load flows as the unsplit grid and at least 5 % less AC overload_energy_n_1. The unsplit grid has an AC overload energy of 16.34 MW with 3 non-converging cases; the best split (action 5, 25.38 MW) is worse, the unsplit action 0 is rejected for lack of improvement, and a scan of the 80 split-plus-one-disconnection and 8 disconnection-only candidates (run once, not kept as a test) finds every one rejected on convergence or overload energy. The exercise's "accepted topology" does not exist for this grid; perform_ac_analysis writes the ORAO summary of every assessed topology anyway, so the table below is that of the best split.

The ORAO summary is a dictionary forced-actions → preventive-actions-list → actions, each action {"type": "SWITCH", "id": "Open VL2_BREAKER", "switchId": "VL2_BREAKER", "open": true}. Joined with net.get_switches() (switch_table()) and with the bays of the action set (bay_breakers(), flag_disconnectors()):

Switch Operation Kind Voltage level Bay breaker Needs breaker VL2_BREAKER open BREAKER (coupler) VL2 – no L12_DISCONNECTOR_4_0 open DISCONNECTOR VL2 L12_BREAKER yes L12_DISCONNECTOR_4_2 close DISCONNECTOR VL2 L12_BREAKER yes

Action 5 moves line L1's bay from busbar BBS2_1 to BBS2_3 and opens the coupler between them. The list contains the two disconnector operations of the bay but not its breaker: a disconnector cannot make or break load current (Chapter 20), so the switching sequence must open L12_BREAKER first, then open the busbar disconnector 4_0, close 4_2 and close the breaker again; the coupler VL2_BREAKER, a breaker, can be opened under load as the last step. The ORAO list is a target state, not a sequence: the ordering and the bay breakers are what the operator or OpenRAO's switch sequence has to add. (ToOp's logs call the result "Accepted Topology" while printing the rejection reason; the verdict is the return value of evaluate_acceptance, None when accepted.)

docs.title: Exercise 6
docs.text:
time_coupling.py builds a 24 × 4 table of hourly overload energies (a daily load shape with topology 0 the unsplit grid, topology 1 best in the morning, 2 best in the evening, 3 mediocre everywhere; overload_table() prints it). (a) The single topology with the smallest total, the way ToOp scores one topology on all timesteps of a run, is topology 1 with 262.5 MW. (b) The dynamic program best_sequence(table, c) minimizes \(\sum_h E[h, t_h] + c \cdot \#\{h : t_h \ne t_{h-1}\}\) over sequences: for each hour and topology, the best cost of ending there is its own overload plus the cheaper of staying in the same topology or coming from the best previous one plus \(c\); a back-pointer array recovers the sequence (test_time_coupling.py checks it against brute force on a six-hour day).

Switching cost \(c\) Sequence Overload Switches Total cost 0 2 at hour 0, then 1 for hours 1–12, then 2 196.5 2 196.5 5 1 for hours 0–12, 2 for hours 13–23 199.2 1 204.2 10 same 199.2 1 209.2 20 same 199.2 1 219.2 63.5 topology 1 all day 262.5 0 262.5

The one-switch plan costs \(199.2 + c\) and the fixed plan 262.5, so they coincide at \(c^\star = 63.3\) MW per change (63.5 on the 0.5 MW grid of break_even()): a switching cost of about a quarter of the day's overload energy makes the single topology optimal. Below it, a planner who may switch once a day saves 63 MW of overload energy. ToOp's choice of one topology per run is the \(c \to \infty\) end of this trade-off; it is the right choice when switching between hours is operationally expensive or unverified, and it is why a time-coupled RAO (OpenRAO's MARMOT) needs a switching cost or a limit on the number of changes to be meaningful.

docs.title: Chapter 22. Import and preprocessing: from grid model to search space
docs.text:
Weeks: 2.5 · Semester: 4 · Prerequisites: Chapter 13, Chapter 16, Chapter 18, Chapter 19

Why it matters for ToOp

Most "the optimizer found nothing" reports are import or preprocessing problems: no relevant substation survived the rules, the action set is empty, nothing is monitored, or the base case has no congestion (each shows up as a zero in static_information_stats.json). The search space the GPU explores is decided long before the optimizer starts:

  • Import (importer/pypowsybl_import/preprocessing.py, convert_file): load UCTE, CGMES or XIIDM, find a converging AC load flow, apply white and black lists, compute the masks that encode policy (importer/pypowsybl_import/powsybl_masks.py), add artificial border limits, and write the processed grid folder (interfaces/folder_structure.py).
  • Preprocessing (dc_solver/preprocess/preprocess.py, load_grid in dc_solver/preprocess/convert_to_jax.py): bridges, relevant-node filters, PTDF and PSDF, node and branch reduction, N-2-safe disconnectable branches, action enumeration and filtering (dc_solver/preprocess/action_set.py), physical station realization (dc_solver/preprocess/preprocess_station_realisations.py), bus-B columns, and optional busbar outages.
  • Artifacts you can inspect: masks/*.npy, nminus1_definition.json, action_set.json, static_information_stats.json (DynamicInformationStats in interfaces/messages/preprocess/preprocess_results.py) and static_information.hdf5.

Every other optimizer, not only ToOp, needs the same pipeline: a grid model is not a search space until someone decides what may switch, what is watched and which states are valid.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• The processed grid folder contract. One folder per timestep; file names come from PREPROCESSING_PATHS and NETWORK_MASK_NAMES (interfaces/folder_structure.py), never hard-coded. The importer writes the grid snapshot, masks, load flow parameters, initial asset topology, auxiliary data and the first N-1 definition; load_grid adds the solver artifacts and refreshes the N-1 definition (docs/quickstart.md, packages/contingency_analysis_pkg/README.md).
  • Areas and masks. AreaSettings: control_area (where switching may happen), view_area (monitored branches), nminus1_area (failed elements), cutoff_voltage (default 220 kV; equipment below it is ignored). Masks: relevant_subs, *_for_nminus1, *_for_reward, *_disconnectable, *_overload_weight, *_n0_n1_max_diff_factor, border flags. Branches without operational limits are dropped from the reward mask (get_element_has_limits_mask); the slack is removed from the relevant substations.
  • Relevant-station rules.
    • Import, CGMES and XIIDM path: RelevantStationRules with min_busbars = 2, min_connected_branches = 4, min_connected_elements = 4 (interfaces/messages/preprocess/preprocess_commands.py, importer/pypowsybl_import/cgmes/powsybl_masks_cgmes.py).
    • Import, UCTE path: a bus with more than one busbar and switches in its voltage level (get_switchable_buses_ucte in importer/pypowsybl_import/ucte/powsybl_masks_ucte.py).
    • Preprocessing, always: at least 4 connected non-bridge branches, an asset topology for the node, no materially split station, no asset connected to two busbars (double connection), and at least one action left after filtering (filter_relevant_nodes_*, remove_relevant_subs_without_actions in dc_solver/preprocess/preprocess.py).
  • Graph preprocessing (revisits Chapter 3). Bridges are excluded from the N-1 and disconnectable masks (their LODF denominator is zero, Chapter 17); filter_disconnectable_branches_nminus2 keeps only disconnectable branches whose removal does not island the grid under any N-1 outage (find_n_minus_2_safe_branches in dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/find_bridges.py).
  • Dimension reduction. reduce_node_dimension keeps nodes of relevant substations, of monitored, outaged, PST and busbar-outage branches, multi-outage nodes, the slack, and everything within two branches of them; the other nodes collapse into one REDUCED_NODE column per timestep that carries their precomputed flow contribution \(\text{PTDF}_{\cdot,\text{insig}}\,p_\text{insig}\) with unit injection (dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/reduce_node_dimension.py). reduce_branch_dimension drops branches that are neither monitored, outaged, nor at a relevant substation. add_bus_b_columns_to_ptdf then appends one column per relevant substation, a copy of its bus A column with zero injection (get_extended_ptdf in dc_solver/preprocess/helpers/ptdf.py), ready for the BSDF of Chapter 18.
  • Action enumeration. For a station with \(d\) branches, make_action_repo enumerates the \(2^{d-1}\) assignments that are distinct up to swapping A and B, keeps the representation with fewer branches on B (or closer to a starting configuration), and removes assignments that isolate a single branch; at most \(2^{d-1} - d\) actions remain, the unsplit one included. Above action_set_clip (default \(2^{23}\)) a random subset is drawn instead (enumerate_branch_actions_for_sub, make_action_repo in dc_solver/preprocess/action_set.py).
  • Validity filters. Bridge lookup: every split must leave at least two non-bridge branches on each busbar (filter_splits_by_bridge_lookup, cheap). BSDF/LODF: apply the split, then check that the BSDF, every LODF of the N-1 outages and every multi-outage MODF are well defined, i.e. no N-1 case islands the split grid (is_valid_bsdf_lodf, filter_splits_by_bsdf, costly, on by default). Reassignment limits cap the Hamming distance to the starting configuration (ReassignmentLimits).
  • Physical realization. Electrical actions are mapped to physical busbars and couplers (enumerate_station_realisations; docs/dc_solver/install_time.md); infeasible actions are dropped. Master data (structural, keyed by bus_group_id) vs runtime asset topology (current coupler states) (docs/dc_solver/preprocessing.md, Chapter 13).
  • PSTs. Parallel PST groups (PowSyBl only) share the unordered bus pair, nominal voltage, tap range, number of steps and the full step table (_build_pst_group_labels and _identify_pst_buckets in dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_helpers.py; mask built by dc_solver/preprocess/parallel_pst_groups.py). The DC flag pst_linear means the reactance is constant across taps (get_linear_pst); tap-dependent susceptances are handled in the solver (dc_solver/jax/pst.py).
  • Limits. get_p_max converts current limits with \(P = \sqrt{3}\,V I\), takes permanent_limit for N-0 and the N-1 limit (falling back to the permanent limit) for N-1, prefers loadflow_based_n0/n1 limits where present, and fills a missing limit with 99 999 MW. Loadflow-based border and DSO-transformer limits (importer/pypowsybl_import/loadflow_based_current_limits.py, LimitAdjustmentParameters): \(I_\text{new} = \operatorname{clip}\big(f I_\text{lf},\ \min(I_\text{old}, I_\text{lf} + m I_\text{old}),\ I_\text{old}\big)\) with \(f = 1.2\) (N-0) or \(1.4\) (N-1) and \(m = 0.05\). On the UCTE path, DACF/PRDx white lists scale an element's operational limits by a percentage and add a separate N-1 limit where the N-0 and N-1 percentages differ; black-listed elements are removed from the N-1, reward and disconnectable masks and from the relevant substations (importer/pypowsybl_import/dacf_whitelists.py, importer/pypowsybl_import/network_analysis.py, importer/pypowsybl_import/powsybl_masks.py).
  • Model assembly. Network reduction around the areas with PowSyBl's reduce_by_ids_and_depths (importer/pypowsybl_import/network_reduction.py, off by default); UCTE–CGMES merge as a separate utility (docs/importer/pypowsybl/merge_ucte_with_cgmes.md, importer/pypowsybl_import/merge_ucte_cgmes/).
  • Data quality in real grid models.
    • Missing or implausible limits (see above).
    • Islands: the PowSyBl backend keeps only the main connected and synchronous component (_get_nodes in dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_backend.py).
    • Zero or low impedance: on UCTE import, lines inside one voltage level of the hard-coded area prefix D8 with \(x \le 0.05\ \Omega\) become breakers, and branches across switches are removed (importer/pypowsybl_import/network_analysis.py).
    • Non-converging base case: the importer tries two parameter sets with three voltage initializations (previous values, DC values, uniform) before failing or continuing with fail_on_non_convergence=False (find_converging_loadflow_params).
    • Unsupported elements: the PowSyBl backend asserts that there are no three-winding transformers and no shunt compensators with active power; batteries and LCC/VSC converters enter as injections.
    • Silent no-ops: unknown keyword arguments to the Pydantic parameter models are ignored (the models in interfaces/messages/preprocess/preprocess_commands.py keep Pydantic's default extra="ignore").
  • State estimation and topology errors (awareness). Measurements \(z = h(x) + e\); weighted least squares \(\min_x J(x) = \sum_i (z_i - h_i(x))^2/\sigma_i^2\) solved by Gauss–Newton with gain matrix \(G = H^\top W H\) (revisits Chapter 6 and the normal equations of Chapter 4); observability; bad data detection with the chi-square test on \(J\) and the largest normalized residual; a wrong breaker status appears as a cluster of bad data around one station. The grid models ToOp imports are the output of this process, errors included.
  • Search-space diagnostics. The status_update_fn of load_grid receives NetworkDataStats (nodes, branches, relevant substations, actions, disconnectable branches, PSTs) before every stage (interfaces/status_update.py, get_network_data_stats in dc_solver/preprocess/network_data.py). The final DynamicInformationStats gives the "optimizer found nothing" checklist: n_relevant_subs == 0, n_actions == 0, n_monitored_branches == 0, and overload_energy_n0 == overload_energy_n1 == 0.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Run ToOp's import and preprocessing on a node-breaker grid, inspect every artifact of the processed grid folder, and explain each count in static_information_stats.json.
  • Trace the size of the search space through the preprocessing stages and predict how area settings, relevance rules, clipping and validity filters change it.
  • Compute by hand the number of enumerated actions of a station and the effect of random clipping.
  • Diagnose an empty or degenerate search space from the artifacts, and name the data-quality problems (limits, islands, impedances, convergence, topology errors) that cause it.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
How big is the action space of one station? The code enumerates integers \(0 \dots 2^{d-1}-1\) as bit patterns, so each A/B assignment appears once; it flips patterns with more than \(d/2\) branches on B and drops patterns with exactly one branch on either busbar.

action_count.py
"""How many busbar assignments ToOp keeps for a substation with d branches (Chapter 22)."""

import numpy as np


def assignments(d: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Assignments of d branches to two busbars (one row each, True = busbar B), up to a swap, no branch alone."""
    r = np.arange(2 ** (d - 1))
    repo = ((r[:, None] >> np.arange(d)) & 1).astype(bool)
    flip = repo.sum(axis=1) > d / 2
    repo[flip] = ~repo[flip]
    on_b = repo.sum(axis=1)
    return repo[(on_b != 1) & (on_b != d - 1)]


def n_actions(d: int) -> int:
    """Count the distinct assignments, the unsplit configuration included."""
    return len(np.unique(assignments(d), axis=0))


def main() -> None:
    """Compare the enumeration with the closed form 2^(d-1) - d (the unsplit configuration included)."""
    print([(d, n_actions(d), 2 ** (d - 1) - d) for d in range(4, 9)])
    # [(4, 4, 4), (5, 11, 11), (6, 26, 26), (7, 57, 57), (8, 120, 120)]


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

For \(d = 4\) the three splits are the 2|2 partitions; for \(d = 5\) they are the \(\binom{5}{2} = 10\) partitions 2|3. Random clipping starts when \(2^{d-1} > 2^{23}\), i.e. at \(d = 25\) branches. np.random.choice draws with replacement and duplicates are removed, so for \(d = 25\) the expected number of distinct actions is \(N\,(1 - e^{-k/N}) \approx 6.6\) million for \(N = 2^{24}\) possible assignments and \(k = 2^{23}\) draws, not \(2^{23}\). The draw uses NumPy's global random state with no explicit seed, so two preprocessing runs of such a station can give different action sets.

docs.title: Documentation vs code: known discrepancies
docs.text:
• docs/dc_solver/preprocessing.md lists the preprocess() stages in a different order from the code (bridges are computed before the relevant-node filters), omits three logged stages (assert_network_data, compute_separation_set, preprocess_bb_outage) and three relevance filters, says a relevant node needs "4 branches" where the code requires 4 non-bridge branches, and says nodes "more than one hop away" are merged while get_significant_nodes expands two hops.
  • The same page lists initial_topology/asset_topology_runtime.json and initial_topology/asset_topology.json as importer artifacts; a real convert_file run writes only asset_topology_master_data.json and the original grid file (no source file of packages/importer_pkg/src uses the other two PREPROCESSING_PATHS keys).
  • enumerate_branch_actions_for_sub documents clip_to_n_actions as defaulting to \(2^{20}\); the default is \(2^{23}\).
  • dc_solver/preprocess/parallel_pst_groups.py and PowsyblBackend._get_parallel_pst_groups say the parallel PST groups are identified during importing; they are built when the PowSyBl backend loads the transformers (_build_pst_group_labels in dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_helpers.py).
  • The PowsyblBackend class docstring assumes no HVDC lines and no batteries, but _get_injections includes batteries and LCC/VSC converters.
  • AreaSettings docstrings call the artificial limits border_limit_n0/border_limit_n1 and say flows are limited to the current N-0 flows; the code names them loadflow_based_n0/loadflow_based_n1 and applies the factor-and-clip rule above. Step 3 of the LimitAdjustmentParameters docstring states the comparison the wrong way round.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: from a node-breaker grid file to a search space

Tools: ToOp container and notebooks (Chapter 0), Jupyter with NumPy, pandas and matplotlib (Chapter 30).

  1. Import and preprocess. Copy data/grid_node_breaker/grid.xiidm into a fresh working folder (running ToOp in place rewrites tracked files). Build importer parameters with prepare_importer_parameters and set area_settings.cutoff_voltage = 10; run run_preprocessing(importer_parameters, data_folder, PreprocessParameters(), is_pandapower_net=False) as run_pipeline does in notebooks/example2_small_grid_toop.ipynb (these helpers live in optimizer/benchmark/benchmark_utils.py).
  2. Inspect the folder. Load every masks/*.npy with NumPy and tabulate the number of True entries; read nminus1_definition.json, importer_auxiliary_data.json, static_information_stats.json and action_set.json with pandas. Count actions per bus_group_id and compare each station's count with the upper bound \(2^{d-1} - d\). action_set.json alone will not do: it stores the stations without their actions, which live as diffs in action_set_diffs.hdf5; load both with load_action_set(json, hdf5) and count the expanded actions.
  3. Watch the funnel. Re-run load_grid(DirFileSystem(str(data_folder)), parameters=..., status_update_fn=record) with a callback record(stage, message, *, stats=None) that appends the stage name and stats to a list. Plot n_nodes, n_branches, n_relevant_subs, n_actions and n_disc_branches per stage with matplotlib and name the stage that removes most of each.
  4. Change preprocessing. Repeat step 3 with action_set_filter_bsdf_lodf=False, with action_set_filter_bridge_lookup=False, with action_set_clip=2**3 and with electrical_reassignment_limits=ReassignmentLimits(max_reassignments_per_sub=1). Record n_actions and wall-clock time in a table.
  5. Change import rules. Re-run step 1 with relevant_station_rules=RelevantStationRules(min_busbars=3) and with min_connected_branches=2. Explain why lowering the import threshold below four does not add relevant substations after preprocessing.
  6. A larger grid. Repeat steps 1–3 on create_complex_grid_battery_hvdc_svc_3w_trafo() (generated and imported as in notebooks/example3_e2e_pipeline.ipynb) and compare its stats with those of the node-breaker grid. Then raise cutoff_voltage to 400 kV and reproduce the first item of the "optimizer found nothing" checklist (n_relevant_subs == 0, n_actions == 0, and no error). One might expect ToOp's usual 220 kV cutoff to do it, but this grid's switchable stations are at 380 kV: with 220 kV the importer still keeps 6 relevant substations and preprocessing 5 with 100 actions.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab_toop.ipynb (needs ToOp).

Why is that acceptable for ToOp?

At which current does each branch of the clip become active, and what happens to a border line that is unloaded in the base case?

Finally simulate a topology error by opening a line in the model but not in the measurements, and describe the residual pattern.

docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 22. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: grid_pipeline_toop.py (the Lab, runs with ToOp's interpreter), action_count.py and bridge_lookup.py (Exercise 1), node_reduction.py (Exercise 2), loadflow_limits.py (Exercise 3), se_case14.py (Exercise 4) and dc_state_estimation.py (Exercise 5). Each module's main() prints every number quoted below; the ToOp numbers were produced with ToOp ba1874e on CPU (Windows, outside the container).

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
python grid_pipeline_toop.py <folder> runs the six steps; the functions named below are in that module and lab_toop.ipynb calls them. Running ToOp in place would rewrite data/grid_node_breaker/grid/, so everything happens in a copy.

  1. Import and preprocess. import_grid() copies grid.xiidm (five 225 kV node-breaker voltage levels, nine lines of equal reactance, three generators, two loads, 106 switches), builds prepare_importer_parameters(grid_file, data_folder) with area_settings.cutoff_voltage = 10 and runs convert_file. The importer writes grid.xiidm, importer_auxiliary_data.json, initial_topology/asset_topology_master_data.json and initial_topology/original_gridfile/grid.xiidm, loadflow_parameters.json, the masks/ folder and nminus1_definition.json, in about two seconds. run_preprocessing(importer_parameters, data_folder, PreprocessParameters(), is_pandapower_net=False) (or funnel(), which calls load_grid directly) adds action_set.json, action_set_diffs.hdf5, static_information.hdf5 and static_information_stats.json. During import the log says why six lines leave the reward mask (excluded_branch_ids=['L4', ..., 'L9'] reason=missing_operational_limits: only L1–L3 carry a permanent limit, 90 A) and warns that VLevel5 has no couplers.
  2. Inspect the folder. mask_counts() tabulates the True entries: relevant_subs 2 of 5 buses (VL2_0 and VL3_0, the two voltage levels with at least two busbars and four branches; importer_auxiliary_data.json names them under id_lists.relevant_subs), line_for_nminus1 9, line_for_reward 3, line_disconnectable 9, generator_for_nminus1 3, load_for_nminus1 2, busbar_for_nminus1 8 of 11 busbar sections, switch_for_nminus1 106 (every switch), switch_for_reward 0; the 17 other masks are all False or empty (no transformers, tie lines or boundary lines). nminus1_definition.json has 5 monitored elements (the three lines with limits and the two relevant buses) and 129 contingencies: BASECASE, 9 lines, 3 generators, 2 loads, 8 busbars and 106 switches. static_information_stats.json after preprocessing: n_relevant_subs 1, n_actions 10, n_monitored_branches 3, n_nminus1_cases 11 (8 branch outages, 3 injection outages; the switch and busbar contingencies are not part of the DC solver's N-1), overload_energy_n0 0.0 and overload_energy_n1 61.44 MW. Counting actions per bus_group_id needs both files: action_set.json stores the stations without their actions, which live as diffs in action_set_diffs.hdf5; load_action_set(json, hdf5) expands them (actions_per_station()). The only relevant station, VL2_a, has \(d = 5\) branches (L1, L2, L6, L7, L8) and 10 actions against the bound \(2^{d-1} - d = 11\); the eleventh assignment is removed by the BSDF/LODF filter (step 4). VL3_a has 4 branches (bound 4), VL4_a 3 and VL5_a 1, and none of them is relevant after preprocessing.
  3. Watch the funnel. funnel() passes record(stage, message, *, stats=None) to load_grid and turns the records into a table (28 stages carry stats, 9 more do not). Nothing changes in n_branches (9). The stages that remove the most: assert_network_data for the relevant substations (2 → 1: the log says Removed 1 from relevant nodes. Reason: Less than 4 non-bridge branches connected ... VL3_0; the filter runs in filter_relevant_nodes and the drop shows up in the stats of the next stage), reduce_branch_dimension for the disconnectable branches (9 → 8: L9, the bridge to VL5, left the outage masks one stage earlier and now leaves the disconnectable set), and enumerate_station_realizations for the actions (0 → 10, the only stage that creates them). n_nodes grows, 5 → 6 → 7: combine_phaseshift_and_injection adds the reduced-node column and add_bus_b_columns_to_ptdf the bus-B column of the relevant station. The whole load_grid takes 4 to 5 s here, most of it JAX compilation.

  4. Change preprocessing. variants():

    Parameters n_actions Seconds default 10 4.7 action_set_filter_bsdf_lodf=False 11 4.0 action_set_filter_bridge_lookup=False 10 4.3 action_set_clip=2**3 3 or 4 4.4 electrical_reassignment_limits=ReassignmentLimits(max_reassignments_per_sub=1) 5 4.1

    The BSDF/LODF filter removes exactly one of the eleven assignments of VL2 (a split after which some N-1 case islands the grid); the bridge lookup removes nothing, since no branch at VL2 is a bridge. Clipping to \(2^3\) draws 8 of the 16 patterns with replacement, unseeded, so the count differs between runs (3 in one run, 4 in another), the point made in the worked example. A reassignment limit of one branch keeps the unsplit configuration and the four single-branch moves that survive the other filters. The times are dominated by JAX compilation, not by the filters, on a grid this small. Note that every load_grid run rewrites the artifacts of the folder: after the last variant, action_set.json and action_set_diffs.hdf5 hold five actions. 5. Change import rules. import_rules():

    RelevantStationRules Relevant after import After preprocessing Actions default (2 busbars, 4 branches, 4 elements) VL2_0, VL3_0 1 10 min_busbars=3 VL2_0 1 10 min_connected_branches=2 VL2_0, VL3_0 1 10

    VL3 has two busbars and four branches (L3, L6, L7, L9) but L9 is a bridge to the radial VLevel5, so it has three non-bridge branches and filter_relevant_nodes drops it whatever the import rule said. Lowering the import threshold below four cannot add relevant substations because preprocessing applies its own, stricter rule (four non-bridge branches, an asset topology, no double connections, at least one action left); the import rule can only remove candidates earlier, as min_busbars=3 does with VL3. VL4 (two busbars, three branches) and VL5 (one busbar) never qualify. 6. A larger grid. create_complex_grid_battery_hvdc_svc_3w_trafo() (40 voltage levels at 380, 220, 110, 70 and 63 kV; 44 lines, 10 two-winding and 4 three-winding transformers, 46 buses) imported with cutoff 10 kV has 12 relevant substations after import and the funnel 47 nodes, 67 branches, 51 disconnectable branches, 3 controllable PSTs at compute_bridging_branches; filter_relevant_nodes leaves 9 substations, reduce_branch_dimension 40 and compute_branch_topology_info 24 disconnectable branches, enumerate_station_realizations creates 301 actions and remove_relevant_subs_without_actions keeps 127 (the station VL_NL_380_a with 9 branches has 14 of its 247 possible assignments left; VL_2W_MV_HV_MV_a 11 of 120; VL_3W_HV_a 45 of 57). The final stats: 60 nodes, 67 branches, 9 relevant substations, 127 actions, 24 disconnectable branches, 3 PSTs, 66 N-1 cases, 50 monitored branches, overload_energy_n0 36.7 MW and overload_energy_n1 1 310.9 MW; load_grid takes 11 to 22 s. With cutoff_voltage = 220 the importer keeps 6 relevant substations (the 380 kV ones) and preprocessing 5 with 100 actions: ToOp's usual 220 kV cutoff does not empty the search space of this grid, whose switchable stations are at 380 kV. cutoff_voltage = 400 does: 0 relevant substations after import, n_relevant_subs == 0 and n_actions == 0 after preprocessing, and the run completes without an error, which is exactly why the checklist exists.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text: Enumeration: \(2^{d-1} = 32\) bit patterns for \(d = 6\) (each A/B assignment once, up to swapping the busbars). Isolation removal drops the patterns with one branch alone on a busbar, \(\binom{6}{1} = 6\) of them, leaving \(2^{5} - 6 = 26\): the unsplit configuration, 15 splits of type 2|4 and 10 of type 3|3. The bridge lookup requires at least two non-bridge branches on every busbar in use. With one bridge \(b_0\), the splits that fail are those whose busbar holding \(b_0\) contains exactly one other branch: \(b_0\) paired with each of the five others, 5 assignments (bridge_lookup.funnel() lists them as b0+b1, b0+b2, b0+b3, b0+b4, b0+b5). The 3|3 splits with the bridge keep two non-bridge branches beside it and pass. So 32 → 26 → 21 actions, the unsplit one included (20 splits). The reason: after the outage of a non-bridge branch on that busbar, the bridge would be the busbar's only link, so the LODF of that outage is undefined (the busbar islands); the lookup removes these cases without running a single load flow, and is_valid_bsdf_lodf would otherwise catch them at a much higher price.

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text: node_reduction.py uses a ten-bus ring with two chords (unit reactances), reference injections summing to zero and four significant buses {0, 2, 5, 7}. reduce_ptdf() keeps the four PTDF columns and appends one column, \(\text{PTDF}_{\cdot,\text{insig}}\,p_\text{insig}\), the flow every branch receives from the six collapsed buses at their reference injections; the reduced injection vector is \((p_0, p_2, p_5, p_7, 1)\). At the reference the reduced model reproduces all twelve flows to \(10^{-14}\) MW: the full product \(Hp\) was simply split into two sums and the second one precomputed. After moving 20 MW of load to collapsed bus 3 (balanced by the slack) the reduced model is wrong by up to 11.5 MW on a branch, because the precomputed column still carries bus 3's old injection; a change at significant bus 2 is reproduced exactly. This is acceptable for ToOp because the optimizer never changes injections: per timestep they are inputs, fixed when load_grid builds the static information, and only the topology at relevant substations varies, which touches the kept columns (and their bus-B copies). The reduction trades a column per insignificant bus for one column, which is what makes the PTDF of a continental grid fit on a GPU; the price is that a new timestep needs a new precomputed column, which is why the column is stored per timestep.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text: For \(I_\text{old} = 1\,000\) A, \(f = 1.2\), \(m = 0.05\) the rule \(I_\text{new} = \operatorname{clip}(f I_\text{lf},\ \min(I_\text{old}, I_\text{lf} + m I_\text{old}),\ I_\text{old})\) has three regimes (loadflow_limits.breakpoints()): below \(I_\text{lf} = m I_\text{old}/(f-1) = 250\) A the lower clip is active and \(I_\text{new} = I_\text{lf} + 50\) A; between 250 A and \(I_\text{old}/f = 833.3\) A the factor rules, \(I_\text{new} = 1.2\,I_\text{lf}\); above 833.3 A the upper clip returns the old limit, 1 000 A. With the N-1 factor \(f = 1.4\) the breakpoints move to 125 A and 714.3 A. The plot is a broken line through (0, 50), (250, 300), (833.3, 1000) and flat afterwards, always below the old limit. A border line that is unloaded in the base case gets \(I_\text{new} = m I_\text{old} = 50\) A, 5 % of its rating: ToOp will treat any flow above 50 A on it as an overload, which is the intended behaviour (the neighbouring TSO's lines are not to be loaded by this TSO's remedial actions) but also a trap when a line happens to be out of service or lightly loaded in the forecast. new_limit(100) = 150, new_limit(500) = 600, new_limit(900) = 1000.

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text: se_case14.py builds 82 measurements on case14 after runpp: 14 voltage magnitudes (\(\sigma = 1\,\%\)), p and q at every bus and at the from (hv) side of the 15 lines and 5 transformers (\(\sigma = 2\,\%\) of the value, at least 0.1). Two pandapower conventions matter: bus powers are consumption (res_bus, load positive) and must exclude the shunt at bus 8, which the estimator models as a network element (with the shunt included, even noise-free data give 0.005 pu of voltage error and a failed chi-square test). With exact data the estimate reproduces the power flow to \(10^{-11}\) pu and chi2 is False; with noisy data (seed 14) the largest errors are 0.0015 pu and 0.09°, and chi2_analysis passes. Scaling the active-power measurement of line 0 (measurement 42, from side) by 1.3 makes chi2_analysis return True; the largest normalized residual is that measurement's, \(r_N = 15.2\) (the next one is −3.1), and remove_bad_data(rn_max_threshold=3) drops exactly measurement 42, after which the test passes again. The topology error opens line 8 (buses 5–11) in the model while the measurements still describe it in service: chi2 is True and the six largest normalized residuals all touch the opened line: its own p and q measurements (48.9 and 25.5: the estimator predicts zero flow on a line it believes open, the meters say 7.6 MW), the injections at bus 11 (37.2 and 13.0) and the flows of line 13 (12–13; 30.1 and 11.9), the path that now has to feed bus 11 in the model. A single bad meter produces one dominant residual; a wrong breaker status produces a cluster of residuals around one station, which is how topology errors are told from bad data. The pandapower estimation code emits pandas' SettingWithCopyWarning and, under Python 3.14, a DeprecationWarning for ~bool; quiet_estimation() silences both around the library calls, since the test suite treats warnings as errors.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text: For the three-bus ring of Chapter 16 (\(x = 0.1, 0.1, 0.2\), \(p = (100, 0, -100)\) MW, slack bus 0) the measurement model is \(z = H\theta + e\) with \(\theta = (\theta_1, \theta_2)\), five rows (the flows \(b_k(\theta_f - \theta_t)\) of the three branches and the injections at buses 1 and 2, i.e. rows of \(B_\text{bus}\)) and \(\sigma = 2\) MW for the flow meters, 3 MW for the injection meters. wls() solves the normal equations \(\hat\theta = (H^\top W H)^{-1} H^\top W z\), \(W = \operatorname{diag}(1/\sigma_i^2)\), and returns the residuals \(r = z - H\hat\theta\) and \(J = \sum_i r_i^2/\sigma_i^2\). Noise-free, the true flows (50, 50, 50) and injections (0, −100) are recovered exactly with \(J = 0\). With one noisy sample (seed 16): \(z = (48.8, 51.3, 52.1, 3.1, -94.5)\), \(\hat\theta = (-4.85, -9.86)\) against \((-5, -10)\), residuals \((0.33, 1.17, 2.79, 1.48, 4.83)\) and \(J = 5.16\), below the 95 % chi-square threshold with \(m - n = 3\) degrees of freedom, \(\chi^2_{0.95,3} = 7.815\): the model and the data agree. Adding a 30 MW error to the first flow meter gives \(J = 110.0\), far above the threshold, and the largest normalized residual points at measurement 0. Over 2 000 noisy samples the mean of \(J\) is 3.0, the expected value of \(\chi^2_3\) (test_dc_state_estimation.py), which is the justification of the test: \(J\) is a chi-square sample only when \(H\) is the right model and the \(\sigma_i\) are right.

docs.title: Chapter 23. Optimization modeling: LP, duality, MILP and complexity
docs.text:
Weeks: 2 · Semester: 3 · Prerequisites: Chapter 2

Why it matters for ToOp

Choosing which substations to split and which lines to switch is a combinatorial decision. Written exactly, it is a mixed-integer program, and the problem family is NP-hard. This chapter gives the generic vocabulary you need to read any topology optimization paper and to judge ToOp's design choice:

  • Search-space size. ToOp's exhaustive baseline counts its candidates as a sum of products over substation action sets times a sum of binomial coefficients over disconnectable branches (count_workset_size in optimizer/dc_bruteforce/generator.py). Estimating that number is an exercise in this chapter.
  • Why not a MILP solver. Branch and bound gives optimality certificates but its running time grows exponentially in the worst case; ToOp instead evaluates huge batches of candidates on a GPU with a heuristic search (Chapter 24, Chapter 25).
  • Dual values and relaxations reappear in optimal power flow, nodal prices and convex relaxations.

The power-system formulations (DC-OPF, optimal transmission switching as a MILP and its complexity) are in Chapter 28, after you have seen the heuristics. This chapter stays generic.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Modeling: decision variables, objective, constraints; standard and canonical forms; modeling languages (PuLP, Pyomo) and solvers (HiGHS, GLPK).
  • Linear programming: geometry of polyhedra, vertices and basic feasible solutions, the simplex method, degeneracy and unboundedness.
  • Duality: weak and strong duality, complementary slackness, shadow prices, sensitivity (ranging) analysis.
  • Convex sets and functions; convex vs non-convex problems; why local optima of convex problems are global.
  • Integer and mixed-integer linear programming: logical constraints with binaries, big-M formulations and why a large \(M\) weakens the LP relaxation; branch and bound; cutting planes; optimality gap.
  • Computational complexity: P, NP, NP-completeness and NP-hardness, reductions (knapsack, set cover); exponential search spaces and what "hard in the worst case" does and does not mean in practice.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Formulate a small allocation or location problem as an LP or MILP, solve it with HiGHS (or Octave glpk), and interpret the dual values of the binding constraints.
  • Solve a two-variable LP graphically and explain why an optimum sits at a vertex.
  • Write a big-M formulation of an either-or constraint, compare its LP relaxation bound with the MILP optimum for two values of \(M\), and explain the effect on branch and bound.
  • Estimate the size of a combinatorial search space (for example, ToOp's split and switching candidates) and argue from NP-hardness why exact enumeration does not scale.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A tiny uncapacitated facility location problem shows every modeling idea of the chapter. Open facility \(i \in I\) at fixed cost \(f_i\) (\(y_i \in \{0,1\}\)) and serve customer \(j \in J\) from \(i\) at cost \(c_{ij}\) (\(x_{ij} \ge 0\)):

\[ \min_{x,\,y} \; \sum_{i \in I} f_i y_i + \sum_{i \in I}\sum_{j \in J} c_{ij} x_{ij} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i \in I} x_{ij} = 1 \;\; \forall j, \qquad x_{ij} \le y_i \;\; \forall i,j, \qquad y_i \in \{0,1\}. \]

The linking constraints \(x_{ij} \le y_i\) are the "strong" formulation. The aggregated version \(\sum_j x_{ij} \le |J|\, y_i\) is a big-M constraint with \(M = |J|\): it describes the same integer solutions but a weaker LP relaxation, so branch and bound explores more nodes.

facility_location.py
"""Uncapacitated facility location: strong versus big-M formulation and their LP relaxations (Chapter 23)."""

import pulp

FIXED = {'A': 10, 'B': 12, 'C': 8}  # opening cost per facility
ASSIGN = {  # (facility, customer): assignment cost
    ('A', 1): 2,
    ('A', 2): 4,
    ('A', 3): 5,
    ('A', 4): 7,
    ('B', 1): 6,
    ('B', 2): 3,
    ('B', 3): 2,
    ('B', 4): 4,
    ('C', 1): 7,
    ('C', 2): 6,
    ('C', 3): 5,
    ('C', 4): 2,
}


def build(strong: bool, relax: bool, f: dict = FIXED, c: dict = ASSIGN) -> tuple[pulp.LpProblem, dict]:
    """The PuLP model and its opening variables; ``strong`` picks x_ij <= y_i over the big-M sum constraint."""
    facilities, customers = list(f), sorted({j for _, j in c})
    m = pulp.LpProblem('ufl', pulp.LpMinimize)
    y = m.add_variable_dicts('open', facilities, 0, 1, cat='Continuous' if relax else 'Binary')
    x = m.add_variable_dicts('assign', list(c), lowBound=0)
    m += pulp.lpSum(f[i] * y[i] for i in facilities) + pulp.lpSum(c[k] * x[k] for k in c)
    for j in customers:
        m += pulp.lpSum(x[i, j] for i in facilities) == 1
    if strong:
        for i, j in c:
            m += x[i, j] <= y[i]
    else:  # big-M with M = |J|
        for i in facilities:
            m += pulp.lpSum(x[i, j] for j in customers) <= len(customers) * y[i]
    return m, y


def solve(strong: bool, relax: bool, f: dict = FIXED, c: dict = ASSIGN) -> tuple[float, dict]:
    """Minimum cost and the opening decisions of the chosen formulation, solved with HiGHS."""
    m, y = build(strong, relax, f, c)
    m.solve(pulp.HiGHS(msg=False))
    return pulp.value(m.objective), {i: y[i].value() for i in f}


def main() -> None:
    """Integer optimum and LP relaxation of both formulations."""
    for strong in (True, False):
        print('strong' if strong else 'big-M', solve(strong, relax=False), solve(strong, relax=True))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

Both formulations find the optimum 27 (open only B). The LP relaxation of the strong formulation is already 27, but the big-M relaxation drops to 19.5 with fractional \(y = (0.25, 0.5, 0.25)\): that gap is the work branch and bound has to close, and on larger instances it is the difference between seconds and hours.

docs.text:
Lab: LP geometry, duality and big-M in practice

Tools: GeoGebra (part 1); Jupyter with PuLP + HiGHS, NumPy, pandas and matplotlib (parts 2–3); GNU Octave glpk is an accepted alternative for part 2.

  1. 2-D LP in GeoGebra. Draw the feasible region of \(\max\, 3x_1 + 5x_2\) s.t. \(x_1 \le 4\), \(2x_2 \le 12\), \(3x_1 + 2x_2 \le 18\), \(x \ge 0\). Add a slider for the objective level \(z\) and the line \(3x_1 + 5x_2 = z\); find the last vertex it touches. Add a slider for the right-hand side \(18\) and read the change of the optimum per unit: that is the shadow price. Rotate the objective with a second slider until the optimum jumps to a neighboring vertex (ranging).
  2. Duality check. Solve the same LP in PuLP (or Octave glpk), print the dual values (constraint.pi in PuLP; extra.lambda from [x, fmin, status, extra] = glpk(...) in Octave; mind each tool's sign convention for maximization problems) and verify complementary slackness and strong duality by hand.
  3. MILP and big-M. Generate random uncapacitated facility location instances with NumPy (10–40 sites, 30–120 customers). Solve the strong formulation and the big-M formulation from the worked example; record in a pandas table the LP relaxation value, the MILP optimum, the solve time and, if the HiGHS log shows it, the number of branch-and-bound nodes. Plot time against instance size with matplotlib on a log scale and write three sentences on what the plot says about exact methods for combinatorial problems.

docs.title: Chapter 23 – Solutions
docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 23. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: lp_duality.py and lp_duality.m (Lab steps 1–2 and Exercise 1, PuLP and Octave glpk), facility_location.py and big_m_study.py (Lab step 3), either_or.py, knapsack_bb.py, search_space.py and knapsack_dp.py (Exercises 2–5). Each module's main() prints every number quoted below; the solver is HiGHS through PuLP 3.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. 2-D LP in GeoGebra (the GeoGebra construction itself is not run here; lp_duality.py checks every number you read off the screen). The feasible region of \(\max 3x_1 + 5x_2\) s.t. \(x_1 \le 4\), \(2x_2 \le 12\), \(3x_1 + 2x_2 \le 18\), \(x \ge 0\) is a pentagon with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3), (0, 6) and (2, 6), where the objective takes 0, 12, 27, 30 and 36 (vertices()). Sliding the level line \(3x_1 + 5x_2 = z\) upward, the last vertex it touches is (2, 6) with \(z = 36\): the optimum of an LP sits at a vertex because the objective is linear, so along any edge it is monotone and the best point is an end of the edge. The slider on the right-hand side 18 (rhs_ranging()): \(z = 30, 33, 36, 39, 42\) for \(b_3 = 12, 15, 18, 21, 24\), one unit of objective per unit of \(b_3\), the shadow price \(y_3 = 1\); it holds for \(12 < b_3 < 24\). Below 12 the vertex moves to the \(x_2\) axis and the price becomes 2.5 (\(x_1 = 0\) and \(2x_2 \le b_3\) decides, worth \(5/2\) per unit); above 24 the constraints \(2x_2 \le 12\) and \(x_1 \le 4\) fix the optimum at (4, 6), \(z = 42\), and the price is 0. At the two ends the vertex is degenerate (three constraints meet) and a solver may report either neighbouring price: HiGHS gives 1 at \(b_3 = 12\) and 0 at \(b_3 = 24\). Rotating the objective (objective_ranging(), \(c_2 = 5\) fixed): the optimum stays at (2, 6) for \(0 < c_1 \le 7.5\) and jumps to (4, 3) beyond; at \(c_1 = 7.5\) the level line is parallel to the edge \(3x_1 + 2x_2 = 18\) and every point of that edge is optimal. At \(c_1 = 0\) the optimum is the whole edge from (0, 6) to (2, 6).
  2. Duality check. solve_lab_lp() builds the LP in PuLP and reads constraint.pi. PuLP hands HiGHS a minimization of \(-c^\top x\), so for a maximization the reported pi are the negatives of the textbook shadow prices; with the sign undone, \(y = (0, 1.5, 1)\). Octave's glpk with sense = -1 returns extra.lambda \(= (0, 1.5, 1)\) directly (lp_duality.m, whose test blocks run under tests/test_octave_sources.py). Complementary slackness: slacks \((2, 0, 0)\) and \(y_k \cdot \text{slack}_k = (0, 0, 0)\): constraint 1 has slack, so its price is zero; constraints 2 and 3 bind, so their prices may be positive. Strong duality: \(b^\top y = 4 \cdot 0 + 12 \cdot 1.5 + 18 \cdot 1 = 36 = z\). By hand, the dual is \(\min 4y_1 + 12y_2 + 18y_3\) s.t. \(y_1 + 3y_3 \ge 3\), \(2y_2 + 2y_3 \ge 5\), \(y \ge 0\); with \(y_1 = 0\) (constraint 1 is slack) and both dual constraints tight (\(x_1, x_2 > 0\)) the two equations give \(y_3 = 1\), \(y_2 = 1.5\).

  3. MILP and big-M. big_m_study.study() draws sites and customers in the unit square (assignment cost 10 times the distance, fixed costs between 3 and 8) and solves four models per instance:

    Sites × customers Formulation LP relaxation MILP Gap LP s MILP s B&B nodes 10 × 30 strong 79.78 79.78 0.0 % 0.007 0.017 1 10 × 30 big-M 56.66 79.78 29.0 % 0.003 0.034 1 20 × 60 strong 123.36 123.36 0.0 % 0.019 0.042 1 20 × 60 big-M 79.02 123.36 35.9 % 0.010 0.088 1 30 × 90 strong 175.75 175.75 0.0 % 0.050 0.101 1 30 × 90 big-M 112.92 175.75 35.8 % 0.022 0.267 1 40 × 120 strong 203.10 203.10 0.0 % 0.077 0.182 1 40 × 120 big-M 120.10 203.10 40.9 % 0.039 0.728 1

    Times are from one run on the maintainer's laptop and vary by a few tens of percent. Three sentences for the plot (time against size on a log scale, left to the notebook): the strong formulation's relaxation is integral on every instance, so HiGHS proves optimality at the root and the time grows like that of an LP; the big-M relaxation is 29–41 % below the optimum and the solver needs 2 to 4 times longer, the extra work being cuts and presolve in the root node (HiGHS reports a single branch-and-bound node here, so the exponential tree never materializes on instances this small); the lesson is that the formulation, not the solver, decides whether an exact method is cheap, and that on a problem with a weak relaxation and no strengthening available the tree grows exponentially with the number of binaries, which is the situation of optimal transmission switching (Chapter 28).

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
Standard form: replace the free variable by \(x_2 = x_2^+ - x_2^-\) with \(x_2^\pm \ge 0\) and add slacks \(s_1, s_2 \ge 0\):

\[ \max\ 2x_1 - x_2^+ + x_2^- \quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_1 + x_2^+ - x_2^- + s_1 = 4,\qquad x_1 - x_2^+ + x_2^- + s_2 = 1,\qquad x_1, x_2^\pm, s_1, s_2 \ge 0 . \]

Dual (one variable per primal constraint, \(y_1, y_2 \ge 0\) because the constraints are \(\le\) in a maximization; one constraint per primal variable, an inequality for \(x_1 \ge 0\) and an equation for the free \(x_2\)):

\[ \min\ 4y_1 + y_2 \quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_1 + y_2 \ge 2,\qquad y_1 - y_2 = -1,\qquad y \ge 0 . \]

Graphically (GeoGebra, not run here; exercise_1() solves both with HiGHS): the primal region is the wedge \(x_1 - 1 \le x_2 \le 4 - x_1\), \(x_1 \ge 0\), closed at \(x_1 = 2.5\) where the two lines meet. The objective \(2x_1 - x_2\) prefers small \(x_2\), so along the lower edge \(x_2 = x_1 - 1\) it equals \(x_1 + 1\), largest at the corner (2.5, 1.5): \(z^\ast = 5 - 1.5 = 3.5\). In the dual, \(y_2 = y_1 + 1\) from the equation, the inequality gives \(2y_1 + 1 \ge 2\), i.e. \(y_1 \ge 0.5\), and the objective \(5y_1 + 1\) is smallest at \(y_1 = 0.5\): \(y = (0.5, 1.5)\), value 3.5. The two values agree, as strong duality says, and the two positive dual prices match the two binding primal constraints.

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
With \(y \in \{0, 1\}\): \(x_1 + x_2 \le 4 + M_1 y\) and \(3x_1 + x_2 \le 6 + M_2(1 - y)\); \(y = 0\) enforces the first constraint and relaxes the second, \(y = 1\) the other way round. A big-M is valid when the relaxed constraint excludes no point that the other one allows, so the smallest valid value is the largest violation over the other disjunct, not over the whole box: \(M_1 = \max\{x_1 + x_2 - 4 : 3x_1 + x_2 \le 6,\ 0 \le x \le 10\} = 2\) (at \((0, 6)\)) and \(M_2 = \max\{3x_1 + x_2 - 6 : x_1 + x_2 \le 4,\ 0 \le x \le 10\} = 6\) (at \((4, 0)\)); smallest_valid_m() solves the two small LPs. The box bound alone gives \(M_1 = 20 - 4 = 16\) and \(M_2 = 40 - 6 = 34\), also valid but loose. Smaller values are wrong: \(M_1 = 1\) forbids \((0, 6)\) and \(M_2 = 5\) forbids \((4, 0)\) (test_either_or.py). For \(\max x_1 + x_2\) the integer optimum is 6 at \((0, 6)\), \(y = 1\), for every valid pair. The LP relaxation (\(0 \le y \le 1\)) is where \(M\) matters (solve(..., relax=True)):

\((M_1, M_2)\) Relaxation bound at \(x\), \(y\) (2, 6) 6.00 (0, 6), \(y = 1\) (16, 34) 13.37 (3.37, 10), \(y = 0.585\) (160, 340) 20.00 (10, 10), \(y = 0.100\)

The plot of the relaxation's projection onto the \(x\) plane shows why: with a fractional \(y\) both constraints are shifted outward by \(M_1 y\) and \(M_2(1 - y)\), so the relaxed region is the union of the two disjuncts plus the area between them, and the larger \(M\) the more of the box the shifted lines let in; with \(M \to \infty\) the relaxation is the whole box and the bound is useless. With the smallest valid \(M\) the relaxation here is exact (its hull is the convex hull of the two disjuncts), so branch and bound stops at the root; with the box values it starts from a bound more than twice the optimum and has to branch on \(y\).

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
Bound: the LP relaxation of a knapsack is the greedy fractional solution, items in order of value per unit weight \(c\) (3/1), \(a\) (5/2), \(b\) (4/3). branch_and_bound() prints the tree:

[root]           bound 10.67 = 3 + 5 + 4·(2/3), b fractional -> branch on b
  [b=0]          c = 1, a = 1, weight 3 <= 5: integer, incumbent 8
  [b=1]          capacity left 2: c = 1, a = 1/2 -> bound 9.5 > 8, branch on a
    [b=1, a=0]   c = 1: bound 7 <= 8, pruned by bound
    [b=1, a=1]   weight 5, no room for c: integer, 9 > 8, new incumbent 9

The optimum is 9 with \(a = b = 1\), \(c = 0\); the first incumbent, 8, came from the greedy choice and was beaten by a solution that leaves out the "best" item \(c\). Four nodes were enough for a tree that could have had \(2^3\) leaves; the pruning of \([b=1, a=0]\) used the bound, that of \([b=1, a=1, c=1]\) never arose because the node was already integer. pulp_check() with HiGHS returns 9 and the same solution.

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text: action_counts() draws [52, 39, 32, 18, 20, 5, 7, 3, 13, 50, 40, 55, 32, 38, 59, 45, 39, 34, 35, 57, 19, 50, 41, 3, 25, 52, 35, 4, 47, 45, 52, 13, 8, 53, 4, 34, 7, 20, 30, 27] (sum 1 242). count_workset_size() mirrors ToOp's function: the number of split combinations is \(\sum_{k=0}^{K} \sum_{|S| = k} \prod_{i \in S} n_i\) (the empty set, the unsplit grid, included), and it is multiplied by the number of ways to switch off up to 3 of 200 branches, \(\sum_{d=0}^{3} \binom{200}{d} = 1 + 200 + 19\,900 + 1\,313\,400 = 1\,333\,501\). With at most 2 splits the first factor is \(1 + 1\,242 + \sum_{i<j} n_i n_j = 747\,139\) and the total \(9.96 \times 10^{11}\) candidates: at \(10^5\) evaluations per second, 115 days. With at most 4 splits the product sums reach \(8.1 \times 10^{10}\) and the total \(1.08 \times 10^{17}\): 34 000 years. Even at the \(10^8\) evaluations per second of a GPU batch the four-split enumeration takes 34 years; the space grows with the product of the action counts, i.e. exponentially in the number of simultaneous splits, which is why ToOp samples it (Map-Elites) instead of enumerating it, and why its brute-force generator is a baseline for small cases only.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
In NP. The decision version asks: is there a subset of items with total weight \(\le W\) and total value \(\ge V\)? A certificate is the subset itself, \(n\) bits. The verifier adds the weights and the values of the chosen items and compares them with \(W\) and \(V\): \(O(n)\) additions of numbers of the input's size, polynomial in the input length. A yes-instance has such a certificate and a no-instance has none, so 0-1 knapsack is in NP (verify_certificate() is the verifier).

The dynamic program. \(T[i, w]\) = best value using the first \(i\) items with total weight at most \(w\): \(T[0, w] = 0\) and \(T[i, w] = \max(T[i-1, w],\ T[i-1, w - w_i] + v_i)\) when \(w_i \le w\), else \(T[i-1, w]\). The answer is \(T[n, W]\) and the chosen items are read back by walking from \(T[n, W]\) and checking at each row whether the value changed. The table has \(n(W+1)\) cells, each filled in constant time: \(O(nW)\). knapsack_dp() on the instance of Exercise 3 fills 18 cells and returns 9 with items \(\{a, b\}\); for \(n = 50\) the running time goes from 0.3 ms at \(W = 1\,000\) to 1.2 ms at \(W = 10\,000\) and 20 ms at \(W = 100\,000\), linear in \(W\).

Why this does not contradict NP-completeness. The input writes \(W\) in binary, with \(\log_2 W\) bits (10, 14 and 17 bits in the three runs). A running time of \(O(nW) = O(n\,2^{\text{bits of } W})\) is exponential in the length of the input: doubling the number of bits of \(W\) squares the running time. The algorithm is polynomial only in the numeric value of \(W\), which is what pseudo-polynomial means; a knapsack with weights of 40 bits is beyond this table even for ten items. NP-hardness is a statement about input length, so knapsack is NP-complete and pseudo-polynomially solvable at the same time (it is weakly NP-hard; problems like 3-partition that stay hard with small numbers are strongly NP-hard). The practical reading for topology optimization: an exact method may be fast when the numbers are small or the structure is special, and hopeless on the general case, so one checks the structure before trusting a complexity class in either direction.

docs.title: Chapter 24. Heuristics and evolutionary algorithms
docs.text:
Weeks: 2 · Semester: 4 · Prerequisites: Chapter 5, Chapter 17, Chapter 23

Why it matters for ToOp

The DC optimizer is a genetic algorithm over a discrete genotype: a topology is a set of station actions, disconnected branches and PST setpoints (optimizer/dc/genetic_functions/genotype.py). Unused disconnection slots are padded with a sentinel integer, and duplicate genotypes are removed (deduplicate_genotypes). Crossover samples unique actions from two parents (optimizer/dc/genetic_functions/crossover.py). Mutations (optimizer/dc/genetic_functions/mutation/, defaults in optimizer/interfaces/messages/dc_params.py) are discrete throughout:

  • Substations. The number of substation mutation steps is drawn from a Poisson distribution with \(\lambda = 2\) (n_subs_mutated_lambda) and clipped to the range from 1 to max_num_splits; each step adds, changes or removes a split, or does nothing with the remaining probability (mutate.py, mutate_substations.py). Disconnections are mutated afterwards (mutate_disconnections.py).
  • PST taps (only with enable_nodal_inj_optim=True). Each PST is selected with probability pst_mutation_probability (default 0.2) and moved by an integer step drawn from a discretized Gaussian on \(\{-\lceil 4\sigma \rceil, \dots, \lceil 4\sigma \rceil\}\) with \(\sigma\) = pst_mutation_sigma (default 1), then reset to its starting tap with probability pst_reset_probability (default 0.0) and clipped to the tap range (mutate_nodal_inj.py). A validator requires all three to be zero, or both \(\sigma\) and the mutation probability to be positive.

A brute-force optimizer enumerates every combination of up to max_num_splits split substations and up to max_num_disconnections disconnections lazily with itertools (optimizer/dc_bruteforce/generator.py). On a small grid it gives the exact optimum against which a heuristic can be judged, which is exactly what the lab of this chapter does. Note that line switching is off by default: max_num_disconnections is 0 in optimizer/interfaces/messages/dc_params.py.

docs.text:
• Local search, hill climbing, simulated annealing, tabu search.
  • Genetic algorithms: representation, variation operators, selection, elitism, diversity.
  • Exploration vs exploitation; restarts; the No Free Lunch theorem.
  • Designing a genotype and operators for a constrained discrete problem: fixed-length padded sets, sorted indices, repair vs penalty for infeasible candidates (islanding), deduplication.
  • Exhaustive enumeration as a baseline: counting the search space and knowing when it is still affordable.
  • Randomness in heuristics: seeds, variance between runs (treated rigorously in Chapter 26).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A genotype for "switch off at most \(k\) of \(n\) lines" can be a sorted integer vector of length \(k\) padded with the sentinel \(n\) (ToOp pads with the largest integer instead). Mutation changes one slot, and the candidate is normalized so that equal sets have equal genotypes:

genome_mutation.py
"""A fixed-length genome of substation actions with a sentinel for "no action", and one mutation (Chapter 24)."""

import numpy as np


def normalize(g: np.ndarray, n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Remove duplicates, sort, pad with the sentinel ``n`` (one past the last action index)."""
    u = np.unique(g[g < n])
    return np.concatenate([u, np.full(len(g) - len(u), n)])


def mutate(g: np.ndarray, n: int, rng: np.random.Generator, p_remove: float = 0.2) -> np.ndarray:
    """Overwrite one slot with the sentinel (probability ``p_remove``) or with a random action, then normalize."""
    g = g.copy()
    slot = rng.integers(len(g))
    g[slot] = n if rng.random() < p_remove else rng.integers(n)
    return normalize(g, n)


def main() -> None:
    """Normalize a genome with a duplicate and mutate it once."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)
    n = 41
    g = normalize(np.array([7, 7, 41]), n)  # -> [7, 41, 41]
    print(g, mutate(g, n, rng))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

The fitness function receives the set g[g < n], rebuilds the network without those lines and returns the negated N-1 overload energy, or \(-\infty\) when the switched network is disconnected.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: a genetic algorithm for line switching, checked against brute force

Tools: Jupyter with NumPy, pandas and matplotlib; your DC power flow (Chapter 16) and PTDF/LODF code (Chapter 17).

  1. Fitness evaluator. Load IEEE 30 (MATPOWER case30 includes branch ratings). Scale all loads and generation by a common factor until the base topology has N-1 overloads. For a set \(D\) of switched-off lines, rebuild the PTDF and LODF of the reduced network with your Chapter 17 code and compute the N-1 overload energy

    \[ E(D) = \sum_{c}\sum_{\ell} \max\bigl(0,\ |f_\ell^{(c)}(D)| - \bar f_\ell\bigr), \]

    summing over non-bridge contingencies \(c\) and monitored lines \(\ell\). Return \(-\infty\) if removing \(D\) islands the grid. Validate a few values with a full DC power flow.

  2. Brute force. Enumerate all sets with \(|D| \le 2\) and then \(|D| \le 3\) using itertools.combinations, as ToOp's optimizer/dc_bruteforce/generator.py does. Record the exact optimum, the number of evaluations and the time. Predict the time for \(|D| \le 4\) from the count.

  3. Genetic algorithm. Implement a GA with the genotype of the worked example, tournament selection, elitism, the mutation above and a crossover that samples \(k\) unique indices from the union of the two parents. Use a fixed budget of fitness evaluations (for example 10% of the \(|D| \le 3\) enumeration).
  4. Compare. Run the GA with 10 different seeds. In a pandas table report the best value found, the evaluations needed to first reach the brute-force optimum (or "not reached") and the time. Plot best fitness against evaluations for all seeds in one matplotlib figure. Explain the spread between seeds; you will analyze it statistically in Chapter 26.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.
