docs.title: Chapter 28 – Solutions
docs.text:
Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 28. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: ieee30_ots.py (DC-OPF, optimal transmission switching and lazy N-1 constraints with PuLP and HiGHS; it imports the IEEE 30 network data from Chapter 27's ch27_ieee30.py), braess3.py (the 3-bus case of Exercise 2 and the big-M check of Exercise 1) and acceptance.py (a port of ToOp's AC acceptance rule and the table of a validation run). Each module prints the numbers quoted below when run as a script. The port was checked against ToOp ba1874e with test_acceptance_toop.py (ToOp's interpreter, make test-toop). Lab B uses two fresh runs that lab_b_toop.py made in the course's ToOp container (image toop-course:cpu, ToOp ba1874e, docker run --cpus 4): the run_pipeline call of notebooks/example2_small_grid_toop.ipynb with its settings (30 s of DC search with ToOp's default seed 42, one descriptor split_subs with 4 cells, AC validation of the 5 best topologies), once on the notebook's grid data/grid_node_breaker/grid.xiidm (44 s for the whole pipeline) and once on the complex example grid data/complex_grid/grid.xiidm (65 s). Two settings differ from the notebook: the preprocessing keywords that Pydantic drops are left out, and switching_distance is added to the observed metrics so that dc_info carries it for step 4. The small result files of both runs are in src/lab_b_run/ (res.json, unsplit_ac_metrics.json, and per topology ac_metrics.json, orao_summary.json and the switches.json that lab_b_toop.py adds), and handoff.py reads them anywhere.

The IEEE 30 instance: pandapower's case30 (MATPOWER data: 30 buses, 41 lines with ratings of 16 to 130 MW, 189.2 MW of load). MATPOWER's costs are quadratic, so the LP uses ten times the linear coefficient of each generator: 20 $/MWh at bus 1 (80 MW), 17.5 at bus 2 (80 MW), 10 at bus 22 (50 MW), 32.5 at bus 27 (55 MW), 30 at bus 23 (30 MW) and 30 at bus 13 (40 MW).

docs.title: Lab A
docs.text:
1. DC-OPF and LMPs. The LP of the worked example costs 3101.0 $/h with the dispatch (57.5, 80, 50, 0, 1.7, 0) MW: the 10 $/MWh unit at bus 22 and the 17.5 unit at bus 2 run at their limits, bus 1 (20 $/MWh) is marginal, and 1.7 MW come from the 30 $/MWh unit at bus 23. The LP flows agree with PTDF @ (generation - load) to \(10^{-13}\) MW. One line is at its rating, 22–24 (16 MW): the cheap unit at bus 22 can only leave through 21–22 and 22–24, and 22–24 is full. The duals of the balance constraints range from 11.95 to 38.88 $/MWh. Without congestion every LMP equals the marginal unit's cost (with the ratings relaxed to 10 GW all thirty prices are 20.00); with 22–24 binding, the buses behind it are cheap (bus 22: 11.95, bus 21: 12.60) and those in front of it expensive (bus 24: 38.88, buses 25–26: 32.54, bus 23: 30.00, the 30 $/MWh unit there being marginal for its corner of the grid). An LMP above the dearest running unit is possible: a MW delivered at bus 24 has to come from bus 23 or 27 and back off the cheap unit to keep 22–24 at 16 MW. The difference of the duals across a congested line is its shadow price.

    ieee30_ots.py (data and DC-OPF)
    def data(scale: float = 1.0) -> dict:
    """IEEE 30 for the OPF: the Chapter 27 network dict plus ``load`` (MW per bus) and ``gens`` (bus, MW, $/MWh)."""
    case = ch27_ieee30.load_case(scale)
    net = pn.case30()
    load = np.zeros(case['n_bus'])
    np.add.at(load, net.load.bus.to_numpy(), scale * net.load.p_mw.to_numpy())
    buses = [int(net.ext_grid.bus.iloc[0]), *net.gen.bus.astype(int).tolist()]
    p_max = [float(net.ext_grid.max_p_mw.iloc[0]), *net.gen.max_p_mw.tolist()]
    cost = (10 * net.poly_cost.cp1_eur_per_mw).tolist()  # ext_grid first, then the gens, as in poly_cost
    case.update(load=load, gens=list(zip(buses, p_max, cost, strict=True)), b=1 / case['x'])
    return case


def _base_model(case: dict, name: str) -> tuple[pulp.LpProblem, dict]:
    """Variables and constraints shared by the DC-OPF and the switching MILP; returns the problem and its parts."""
    n_bus, lines = case['n_bus'], case['lines']
    m = pulp.LpProblem(name, pulp.LpMinimize)
    p = [m.add_variable(f'p_{g}', 0, p_max) for g, (_, p_max, _) in enumerate(case['gens'])]
    theta = [m.add_variable(f'theta_{n}', None, None) for n in range(n_bus)]
    f = [m.add_variable(f'f_{k}', -r, r) for k, r in enumerate(case['rating'])]
    m += theta[0] == 0
    balance = []
    for n in range(n_bus):
        generation = pulp.lpSum(p[g] for g, (bus, _, _) in enumerate(case['gens']) if bus == n)
        out_flow = pulp.lpSum(f[k] for k in range(len(lines)) if lines[k][0] == n)
        in_flow = pulp.lpSum(f[k] for k in range(len(lines)) if lines[k][1] == n)
        c = generation - case['load'][n] == out_flow - in_flow
        m += c, f'balance_{n}'
        balance.append(c)
    m += pulp.lpSum(cost * p[g] for g, (_, _, cost) in enumerate(case['gens']))
    return m, {'p': p, 'theta': theta, 'f': f, 'balance': balance}


def dc_opf(case: dict, contingencies: list[int] | None = None) -> dict:
    """DC-OPF as an LP; ``contingencies`` adds the post-outage limits of those lines through the LODF.

    Returns cost ($/h), dispatch ``p`` (MW), flows ``f`` (MW), angles ``theta`` (rad) and the nodal prices ``lmp``
    ($/MWh, the duals of the balance constraints).
    """
    m, v = _base_model(case, 'dc_opf')
    for k, (i, j) in enumerate(case['lines']):
        m += v['f'][k] == case['b'][k] * (v['theta'][i] - v['theta'][j])
    if contingencies:
        lodf = _lodf(case)
        for c in contingencies:
            if np.isnan(lodf[:, c]).any():
                continue  # a bridge: its outage islands the grid and has no LODF, ToOp drops it too
            for k in range(len(case['lines'])):
                if k != c:
                    post = v['f'][k] + lodf[k, c] * v['f'][c]
                    m += post <= case['rating'][k]
                    m += -post <= case['rating'][k]
    m.solve(pulp.HiGHS(msg=False))
    return {
        'status': pulp.LpStatus[m.status],
        'cost': pulp.value(m.objective),
        'p': np.array([x.value() for x in v['p']]),
        'f': np.array([x.value() for x in v['f']]),
        'theta': np.array([x.value() for x in v['theta']]),
        'lmp': np.array([c.pi for c in v['balance']]),
    }

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  2. Switching with big-M. The lines are ranked by their loading in the DC-OPF (22–24 at 100 %, 6–8 at 89 %, 21–22 at 82 %, 2–6, 2–4, ...), and the first 5, 10, 20 or all 41 are switchable. With mode='global' the big-M of line \(\ell\) is \(b_\ell \sum_{k \ne \ell} \bar f_k / b_k\) (520 to 16,037 MW, valid for every connected topology); the cycle bound of Exercise 1 (mode='cycle', 16 to 2,231 MW) is much tighter but valid only while the other lines stay closed. The sweep (HiGHS, 20 s limit):

    switchable \(k\) cost ($/h) switched lines time (s) gap 5 1, 2, 3 3095.5 2–6 0.05–0.10 0 10 1, 2, 3 3095.5 2–6 (plus a no-effect line for \(k \ge 2\)) 0.06–0.20 0 20 1 3084.0 23–24 0.07 0 20 2, 3 3084.0 4–6 + 23–24; 2–4 + 2–6 + 4–6 0.15–0.22 0 41 1 3084.0 6–10 0.11 0 41 2, 3 3084.0 6–7 + 6–10; 1–2 + 2–6 + 4–6 0.09–0.11 0

    Switching saves at most 17 $/h (0.5 %): it reroutes flow around 22–24 so that bus 1 can replace the 1.7 MW of the 30 $/MWh unit, and the dispatch becomes (59.2, 80, 50, 0, 0, 0). The optimum is degenerate (several lines give the same cost, and for \(k \ge 2\) the solver adds lines whose opening changes nothing), so the "switched lines" column should be read as one optimal set among many. Every MILP, 41 binaries included, solves to a zero gap in a fraction of a second: on a 30-bus grid HiGHS's branch and bound sees nothing of the exponential growth, which only shows in the brute-force counts of step 4: with 41 binaries and no N-1 rows the model has a few hundred rows, and the solver's LP bounds prune almost all of the tree. The scaling appears on grids with hundreds of lines and N-1 constraints, where the literature of the chapter reports hours or time-outs; with 20 switchable lines and \(k = 3\) the enumeration already has 1,351 topologies, with 41 lines 11,522.

    ieee30_ots.py (switching MILP and brute force)
    def big_m(case: dict, mode: str = 'global') -> np.ndarray:
    """A bound on |b_l (theta_i - theta_j) - f_l| when line ``l`` is open: ``b_l`` times a bound on the angle gap.

    ``'global'``: the angle gap is at most the sum over every other line of rating / b (a simple path uses each
    line at most once), valid for every connected topology. ``'cycle'``: the shortest path around the line in the
    intact network with weights rating / b, the bound of Exercise 1, valid while every other line stays closed.
    """
    rating_over_b = case['rating'] / case['b']
    if mode == 'global':
        return case['b'] * (rating_over_b.sum() - rating_over_b)
    import networkx as nx  # noqa: PLC0415

    g = nx.Graph()
    for k, (i, j) in enumerate(case['lines']):
        g.add_edge(int(i), int(j), weight=rating_over_b[k], key=k)
    bound = big_m(case, 'global')  # a bridge has no cycle: its opening islands the grid, keep the global bound
    for k, (i, j) in enumerate(case['lines']):
        h = g.copy()
        h.remove_edge(int(i), int(j))
        if nx.has_path(h, int(i), int(j)):
            bound[k] = case['b'][k] * nx.shortest_path_length(h, int(i), int(j), weight='weight')
    return bound


def ots(case: dict, k_max: int, switchable: list[int], time_limit: float = TIME_LIMIT, mode: str = 'global') -> dict:
    """Optimal transmission switching: at most ``k_max`` of the ``switchable`` lines open, big-M formulation."""
    m, v = _base_model(case, 'ots')
    big = big_m(case, mode)
    z = {k: m.add_variable(f'z_{k}', cat='Binary') for k in switchable}
    for k, (i, j) in enumerate(case['lines']):
        gap = case['b'][k] * (v['theta'][i] - v['theta'][j]) - v['f'][k]
        if k in z:
            m += v['f'][k] <= case['rating'][k] * z[k]
            m += -v['f'][k] <= case['rating'][k] * z[k]
            m += gap <= big[k] * (1 - z[k])
            m += -gap <= big[k] * (1 - z[k])
        else:
            m += gap == 0
    m += pulp.lpSum(1 - z[k] for k in switchable) <= k_max
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    m.solve(pulp.HiGHS(msg=False, timeLimit=time_limit))
    info = m.solverModel.getInfo()
    return {
        'status': pulp.LpStatus[m.status],
        'cost': pulp.value(m.objective),
        'switched': sorted(k for k in switchable if z[k].value() is not None and z[k].value() < 0.5),
        'time_s': time.perf_counter() - t0,
        'gap': info.mip_gap,
        'p': np.array([x.value() for x in v['p']]),
    }


def sweep(case: dict, ranked: list[int], time_limit: float = TIME_LIMIT) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Lab A step 2: k = 1, 2, 3 for the 5, 10, 20 and all 41 switchable lines (first entries of ``ranked``)."""
    rows = []
    for n_switchable in (5, 10, 20, 41):
        for k in (1, 2, 3):
            r = ots(case, k, ranked[:n_switchable], time_limit)
            rows.append(
                {'switchable': n_switchable, 'k': k, **{key: r[key] for key in ('cost', 'switched', 'time_s', 'gap')}}
            )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def brute_force(case: dict, k_max: int, switchable: list[int]) -> tuple[float, tuple[int, ...], int, float]:
    """One DC-OPF per set of at most ``k_max`` open lines: best cost, its set, the number of LPs and the time."""
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    best, arg, count = np.inf, (), 0
    for k in range(k_max + 1):
        for subset in itertools.combinations(switchable, k):
            count += 1
            reduced = _without(case, subset)
            if reduced is None:
                continue
            r = dc_opf(reduced)
            if r['status'] == 'Optimal' and r['cost'] < best - 1e-6:
                best, arg = r['cost'], subset
    return best, arg, count, time.perf_counter() - t0


def _without(case: dict, switched: tuple[int, ...]) -> dict | None:
    keep = np.ones(len(case['lines']), dtype=bool)
    keep[list(switched)] = False
    if ch27_ieee30.ptdf(case, keep) is None:
        return None
    return {
        **case,
        'lines': case['lines'][keep],
        'x': case['x'][keep],
        'b': case['b'][keep],
        'rating': case['rating'][keep],
    }

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  3. Lazy N-1 constraints. For a fixed topology the post-outage flow is linear in the base flows, \(f_k^{(c)} = f_k + \mathrm{LODF}_{kc} f_c\), so a contingency adds \(2(n_\ell - 1)\) linear rows to the LP. The DC-OPF dispatch has a worst post-contingency loading of 155 % (22–24 after the outage of 27–28); the five worst contingencies by that measure are 27–28, 21–22, 6–8, 6–28 and 10–20. With those five the SCOPF costs 3357.6 $/h and leaves one violation, 101.8 % on a line after the outage of 22–24 itself (index 30); adding it gives 3369.2 $/h with the dispatch (48.9, 80, 43.0, 17.2, 0, 0) and no violation: two iterations, six contingencies, instead of forty-one. The same LP with every non-bridge contingency at once gives the same 3369.2 $/h, so the lazy loop lost nothing. Security costs 268 $/h here (8.6 %), far more than switching saves, which is why the chapter treats the SCOPF as the yardstick. With switching the LODFs would depend on the topology, so N-1 constraints inside the MILP need the angle formulation per contingency (one copy of the network per outage) or a shift-factor formulation that recomputes the factors per candidate topology (Exercise 3); the lazy loop still applies, with a MILP solve per iteration.

    ieee30_ots.py (LODF constraints and the lazy loop)
    def _lodf(case: dict) -> np.ndarray:
    """LODF matrix (line, outage) of the intact network; a bridge outage gets a column of NaN (its own entry -1)."""
    h = ch27_ieee30.ptdf(case, np.ones(len(case['lines']), dtype=bool))
    hk = h[:, case['lines'][:, 0]] - h[:, case['lines'][:, 1]]
    denominator = 1 - np.diag(hk)
    with np.errstate(divide='ignore', invalid='ignore'):
        lodf = np.where(np.abs(denominator) > 1e-9, hk / denominator, np.nan)
    np.fill_diagonal(lodf, -1.0)
    return lodf


def post_contingency_loading(case: dict, f: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Loading in percent after every single outage, shape (outage, line); a bridge gives a row of NaN."""
    lodf = _lodf(case)
    post = f[None, :] + lodf.T * f[:, None]  # (outage, line)
    return 100 * np.abs(post) / case['rating']


def lazy_scopf(case: dict, n_initial: int = 5) -> tuple[dict, list[dict]]:
    """Lab A step 3: start with the ``n_initial`` worst contingencies, add violated ones until none is left."""
    base = dc_opf(case)
    loading = post_contingency_loading(case, base['f'])
    worst = np.nan_to_num(loading, nan=0).max(axis=1)
    active = list(np.argsort(-worst)[:n_initial])
    history = []
    while True:
        r = dc_opf(case, active)
        loading = post_contingency_loading(case, r['f'])
        worst = np.nan_to_num(loading, nan=0).max(axis=1)
        violated = [int(c) for c in np.flatnonzero(worst > 100 + 1e-6) if c not in active]
        history.append(
            {'constraints': len(active), 'cost': r['cost'], 'worst_loading': worst.max(), 'violated': violated}
        )
        if not violated:
            return r, history
        active.append(violated[int(np.argmax(worst[violated]))])

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  4. Comparison. Brute force over every set of at most two open lines solves 862 LPs in 3.1 s and finds the same 3084.0 $/h (one line, 4–6, is enough; another of the degenerate optima); the MILP with \(k = 2\) and all 41 lines takes 0.1 s. For \(|D| \le 3\) the enumeration needs 11,522 LPs (about 40 s at this rate) and the MILP still a fraction of a second: the exact method wins by three orders of magnitude at this size, and a GA with the same budget as in Chapter 24 cannot beat an exact solver that finishes in 0.1 s. The Chapter 24 brute-force and GA figures of your own run and ToOp's total_branch_combis divided by its run time in res.json were not available here; ToOp's DC solver evaluates batches of thousands of topologies per second on a GPU, but with a different objective (N-1 overload energy of a fixed dispatch, no cost) and without optimality proof, so the comparison is between an exact answer to a small LP-based question and a fast approximate answer to a larger N-1 question.

docs.title: Lab B
docs.text:
1. Reconstruct accept/reject. acceptance.run_table(run) loads every topology_N/ac_metrics.json and the run's unsplit_ac_metrics.json (both Metrics.model_dump(), the first with dc_info added, written by save_ac_metrics_summary), recomputes the three default checks by hand (convergence_ok: non-converging loadflows minus disconnected branches \(\le 1.0 \times\) unsplit; overload_ok: \(\le 0.95 \times\); critical_ok: \(\le 1.1 \times\)), calls the ported rule for the verdict and ranks the rows by dc_info.metrics.fitness (dc_rank 1 is the DC winner). Under ToOp's interpreter, evaluate_acceptance(Metrics(**split), Metrics(**unsplit)) on the same files must return None exactly on the rows whose three checks pass; test_acceptance_toop.py verifies this on a grid of 729 synthetic pairs, and lab_b_toop.toop_verdicts (tested in test_lab_b_toop_toop.py) gives the same verdict as the port for every stored topology. The node-breaker run made 684 epochs and kept 1 topology, the complex one 199 epochs and 4:

    Grid Topology Actions DC fitness DC rank AC overload energy (MW) Critical branches Non-converging Rejected by node-breaker unsplit [] −61.445 – 16.336 2 3 – node-breaker 0 [5] −42.345 1 25.377 1 3 overload-energy complex unsplit [] −1310.860 – 1434.587 31 1 – complex 0 [1, 54, 68] −1160.366 1 1666.565 29 1 overload-energy complex 1 [54, 68] −1169.118 2 1680.170 29 1 overload-energy complex 2 [69] −1184.119 3 1480.865 30 1 overload-energy complex 3 [] −1243.819 4 1434.587 31 1 overload-energy

    The convergence and critical-branch checks pass everywhere; the overload check rejects every candidate, so the DC winner does not survive on either grid. On the node-breaker grid the split that removes 19 MW of DC overload energy adds 9 MW in AC. On the complex grid every split raises the AC overload energy above the unsplit 1434.6 MW, although DC says each lowers it, and the AC order is nearly the reverse of the DC one: the DC winner has the second-highest AC overload, and the best AC result among the splits is the DC's third. Topology 3 is the empty genotype: no split, no disconnection, only pst_setpoints ([-24, -6, -9]; the four elites carry three different settings) that move its DC fitness from −1310.9 to −1243.8. perform_ac_analysis hands the runner only actions and disconnections, and apply_topology_and_save takes no setpoints, so the AC stage validates every topology with the grid's own taps: the AC metrics of this row equal the unsplit ones exactly, the 67 MW of DC improvement from the taps are never checked, and the row fails the threshold of 0.95 times itself. A multiplicative threshold of 0.95 asks for a 5 % improvement, so leaving the grid as it is counts as a rejection.

    acceptance.py (the run table)
    METRICS = ['non_converging_loadflows', 'disconnected_branches', 'overload_energy_n_1', 'critical_branch_count_n_1']


def run_table(run: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Lab B1: one row per ``topology_N/ac_metrics.json`` with the metrics, every check by hand and the verdict."""
    unsplit = json.loads((run / 'unsplit_ac_metrics.json').read_text(encoding='utf-8'))['extra_scores']
    rows = []
    for folder in sorted(run.glob('topology_*'), key=lambda p: int(p.name.split('_')[1])):
        res = json.loads((folder / 'ac_metrics.json').read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
        s = res['extra_scores']
        row = {'topology': folder.name, 'ac_fitness': res['fitness'], **{m: s.get(m, 0) for m in METRICS}}
        row['dc_fitness'] = res.get('dc_info', {}).get('metrics', {}).get('fitness')
        row['convergence_ok'] = s.get('non_converging_loadflows', 0) - s.get(
            'disconnected_branches', 0
        ) <= unsplit.get('non_converging_loadflows', 0)
        row['overload_ok'] = s.get('overload_energy_n_1', 99999) <= 0.95 * unsplit.get('overload_energy_n_1', 0)
        row['critical_ok'] = s.get('critical_branch_count_n_1', 0) <= 1.1 * unsplit.get(
            'critical_branch_count_n_1', 999
        )
        verdict = evaluate_acceptance(s, unsplit)
        row['rejected_by'] = None if verdict is None else verdict['criterion']
        rows.append(row)
    table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    table['dc_rank'] = (
        table['dc_fitness'].rank(ascending=False, method='first') if table['dc_fitness'].notna().any() else None
    )
    return table

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  2. Probe the traps. acceptance.py runs them (ToOp's own function returns the same objects in the test):

    • Zero baseline: unsplit overload_energy_n_1 = 0.0, candidate 0.01 → rejected, overload-energy, value_after = 0.01, value_before = 0.0, threshold 0.95. With an unsplit value of 1.0 MW the same candidate is accepted. A multiplicative threshold on a zero baseline rejects every positive value, so on a worst-k subset where the unsplit grid happens to be clean no candidate can pass.
    • Convergence before overload: unsplit non_converging_loadflows = 1, overload_energy_n_1 = 0.0; candidate 0 non-converging, 5.0 MW → rejected, overload-energy, 5.0 against 0.0. The candidate made the diverging contingency converge and thereby revealed 5 MW of overload the unsplit run never computed; the rule compares that against the unsplit "zero" and rejects an improvement (docs/wall_of_shame.md).
    • The other order: unsplit 1 non-converging and 100 MW; candidate 2 non-converging and 1.0 MW → rejected, convergence, 2 against 1. The convergence check runs first, so a 99 % overload reduction is never looked at when one more case diverges.
    acceptance.py (the rule)
    def evaluate_acceptance(
    split: dict, unsplit: dict, critical_voltage: bool = False, thresholds: dict = THRESHOLDS
) -> dict | None:
    """``None`` when the candidate is accepted, else the first failed check with its values and threshold.

    ``split`` and ``unsplit`` are ``extra_scores`` dicts. The checks run in ToOp's order: non-converging loadflows
    (minus the candidate's disconnected branches), N-1 overload energy, critical branch count and, only with
    ``critical_voltage``, voltage jumps and angle differences. Every threshold multiplies the unsplit value, and
    a metric missing from ``split`` or ``unsplit`` takes ToOp's defaults (99999 for the split overload, 999 for
    the unsplit counts, 0 otherwise).
    """
    checks = [
        (
            'convergence',
            split.get('non_converging_loadflows', 0) - split.get('disconnected_branches', 0),
            unsplit.get('non_converging_loadflows', 0),
        ),
        ('overload-energy', split.get('overload_energy_n_1', 99999), unsplit.get('overload_energy_n_1', 0)),
        (
            'critical-branch-count',
            split.get('critical_branch_count_n_1', 0),
            unsplit.get('critical_branch_count_n_1', 999),
        ),
    ]
    if critical_voltage:
        checks += [
            ('voltage-magnitude', split.get('voltage_jump_count_n_1', 0), unsplit.get('voltage_jump_count_n_1', 999)),
            (
                'voltage-angle',
                split.get('critical_va_diff_count_n_1', 0),
                unsplit.get('critical_va_diff_count_n_1', 999),
            ),
        ]
    for criterion, after, before in checks:
        if not after <= before * thresholds[criterion]:
            return {
                'criterion': criterion,
                'value_after': float(after),
                'value_before': float(before),
                'threshold': thresholds[criterion],
            }
    return None

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  3. Before/after diagrams. lab_b_toop.before_after takes the switches of a topology's orao_summary.json, looks up their voltage-level id in the grid (not the station name: save_slds_of_split_stations passes the id to get_single_line_diagram_custom and names the file after the station), runs an AC load flow on the original and on the modified network, and calls get_single_line_diagram_custom(net, level, highlight_grid_model_ids=switches) on both. Node-breaker topology 0 splits VL2: the coupler VL2_BREAKER goes from closed to open, L12_DISCONNECTOR_4_0 from closed to open and L12_DISCONNECTOR_4_2 from open to closed, so line L12 moves to the second busbar; the two SVGs have 45,735 and 46,475 characters and 3 highlighted elements each. Complex topology 0 splits three voltage levels, VL_2W_MV_HV_MV, VL_3W_HV and VL_MV, with 3, 5 and 4 highlighted switches (12 in all); topology 3 changes no switch and has no diagram. To count the highlighted elements, count the elements whose class contains highlight, which is what ToOp adds to every matching id: the colour #0050fcff appears 7 times in every diagram, highlighted or not, because it sits in the CSS, once per voltage class.

    lab_b_toop.py (ToOp's interpreter)
    """Lab B of Chapter 28 on a fresh ToOp run with AC validation; needs ToOp's interpreter (the course's container).

Run it from this folder::

    python lab_b_toop.py OUT_ROOT [node_breaker] [complex] [--reuse]

For each grid it copies ``grid.xiidm`` of the ToOp checkout (``$TOOP_REPO``, default the ``ToOp`` folder next to
this repository) into ``OUT_ROOT/<grid>`` and makes the ``run_pipeline`` call of
``notebooks/example2_small_grid_toop.ipynb`` with its settings (30 s of DC search with ToOp's default seed 42, one
descriptor ``split_subs`` with 4 cells, AC validation of the 5 best topologies), leaving out the two preprocessing
keywords Pydantic drops and with ``switching_distance`` added to the observed metrics, so that ``dc_info`` carries
it for Lab B4. Then it prints the Lab B1 table (``acceptance.run_table``) next to ToOp's own ``evaluate_acceptance``
verdicts, renders the before/after single-line diagrams of every split station with the
operated switches highlighted (Lab B3, written to ``topology_N/lab_b/``), and stores per topology the kind and voltage
level of every operated switch in ``switches.json`` for the hand-off of Lab B4 (``handoff.py``). With ``--reuse`` the
latest run already in ``OUT_ROOT`` is analysed again instead of running the pipeline.
"""

import datetime
import json
import os
import re
import shutil
import sys
import time
import types
from pathlib import Path

import pypowsybl as pp
import toop_engine_topology_optimizer.dc.main as dc_main
from acceptance import run_table
from omegaconf import DictConfig
from toop_engine_grid_helpers.powsybl.single_line_diagram.get_single_line_diagram_custom import (
    get_single_line_diagram_custom,
)
from toop_engine_interfaces.messages.preprocess.preprocess_commands import PreprocessParameters
from toop_engine_topology_optimizer.ac.scoring_functions import evaluate_acceptance
from toop_engine_topology_optimizer.benchmark.benchmark_utils import (
    PipelineConfig,
    get_paths,
    prepare_importer_parameters,
    run_pipeline,
    suppress_jax_logs,
)
from toop_engine_topology_optimizer.interfaces.messages.results import Metrics

TOOP_REPO = Path(os.environ.get('TOOP_REPO', Path(__file__).resolve().parents[5] / 'ToOp'))
GRIDS = {
    'node_breaker': TOOP_REPO / 'data' / 'grid_node_breaker' / 'grid.xiidm',
    'complex': TOOP_REPO / 'data' / 'complex_grid' / 'grid.xiidm',
}
HIGHLIGHTED = re.compile(r'class="[^"]*\bhighlight\b')  # the class ToOp adds to every highlighted element


class _FileSafeDatetime:
    @staticmethod
    def now() -> str:
        return datetime.datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H-%M-%S')  # noqa: DTZ005


if os.name == 'nt':
    dc_main.datetime = types.SimpleNamespace(datetime=_FileSafeDatetime)


def latest_run(out_root: Path, name: str) -> tuple[Path, Path]:
    """The last run folder of a grid already processed in ``out_root`` and its data folder."""
    data_folder = out_root / name / 'grid'
    runs = sorted((data_folder / 'optimizer_snapshot').glob('run_*'), key=lambda p: int(p.name.split('_')[1]))
    return runs[-1], data_folder


def highlighted(svg: str) -> int:
    """How many SVG elements carry ToOp's ``highlight`` class (the colour itself only appears in the CSS)."""
    return len(HIGHLIGHTED.findall(svg))


def run(out_root: Path, name: str) -> tuple[Path, Path]:
    """The notebook's pipeline on one grid; returns the run folder (``res.json``, ``topology_N/``) and data folder."""
    iteration = out_root / name
    iteration.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    shutil.copy(GRIDS[name], iteration / 'grid.xiidm')
    pipeline_cfg = PipelineConfig(root_path=out_root, iteration_name=name, file_name='grid.xiidm', grid_type='powsybl')
    iteration_path, file_path, data_folder, snapshot_dir = get_paths(pipeline_cfg)
    results = str(iteration_path / 'results' / '{task_name}')
    dc_cfg = DictConfig(
        {
            'task_name': 'test',
            'fixed_files': [str(data_folder / pipeline_cfg.static_info_relpath)],
            'double_precision': None,
            'tensorboard_dir': results,
            'stats_dir': results,
            'summary_frequency': None,
            'checkpoint_frequency': None,
            'stdout': None,
            'double_limits': None,
            'num_cuda_devices': 1,
            'omp_num_threads': 1,
            'xla_force_host_platform_device_count': None,
            'output_json': str(iteration_path / 'results' / 'output.json'),
            'lf_config': {'distributed': False},
            'ga_config': {
                'runtime_seconds': 30,
                'me_descriptors': [{'metric': 'split_subs', 'num_cells': 4}],
                'observed_metrics': ['overload_energy_n_1', 'split_subs', 'switching_distance'],
                'n_worst_contingencies': 2,
            },
        }
    )
    ac_cfg = DictConfig(
        {'n_processes': 1, 'k_best_topos': 5, 'critical_voltage_jump_percent': 5.0, 'critical_va_diff_degree': 20.0}
    )
    importer_parameters = prepare_importer_parameters(file_path, data_folder)
    importer_parameters.area_settings.cutoff_voltage = 10
    paths = run_pipeline(
        pipeline_cfg=pipeline_cfg,
        importer_parameters=importer_parameters,
        preprocessing_parameters=PreprocessParameters(action_set_clip=2**10),
        dc_optim_config=dc_cfg,
        ac_validation_cfg=ac_cfg,
    )
    run_dir = paths[0].parent if paths else sorted(snapshot_dir.glob('run_*'))[-1]
    return run_dir, data_folder


def toop_verdicts(run_dir: Path) -> dict[str, str | None]:
    """ToOp's own ``evaluate_acceptance`` on the stored files: ``None`` (accepted) or the rejecting criterion."""
    unsplit = Metrics.model_validate(json.loads((run_dir / 'unsplit_ac_metrics.json').read_text(encoding='utf-8')))
    out = {}
    for path in sorted(run_dir.glob('topology_*/ac_metrics.json'), key=lambda p: int(p.parent.name.split('_')[1])):
        split = Metrics.model_validate(json.loads(path.read_text(encoding='utf-8')))
        reason = evaluate_acceptance(metrics_split=split, metrics_unsplit=unsplit)
        out[path.parent.name] = None if reason is None else reason.criterion
    return out


def operated_switches(orao_summary: dict) -> list[tuple[str, bool]]:
    """``[(switch id, open?), ...]`` in the order of the ORAO summary."""
    actions = orao_summary['forced-actions']['preventive-actions-list']['actions']
    return [(a['switchId'], a['open']) for a in actions if a['type'] == 'SWITCH']


def before_after(grid_xiidm: Path, topology_dir: Path) -> dict:
    """Lab B3 for one topology: highlighted before/after diagrams per split voltage level, switch kinds and states."""
    orao = json.loads((topology_dir / 'orao_summary.json').read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
    ids = [s for s, _ in operated_switches(orao)]
    before = pp.network.load(str(grid_xiidm))
    after = pp.network.load(str(topology_dir / 'modified_network.xiidm'))
    pp.loadflow.run_ac(before)
    pp.loadflow.run_ac(after)
    sw_before, sw_after = before.get_switches(), after.get_switches()
    switches = {
        s: {
            'kind': sw_before.loc[s, 'kind'],
            'voltage_level_id': sw_before.loc[s, 'voltage_level_id'],
            'open_before': bool(sw_before.loc[s, 'open']),
            'open_after': bool(sw_after.loc[s, 'open']),
        }
        for s in ids
    }
    (topology_dir / 'switches.json').write_text(json.dumps(switches, indent=2), encoding='utf-8')
    out_dir = topology_dir / 'lab_b'
    out_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    levels = {}
    for level in sorted({v['voltage_level_id'] for v in switches.values()}):
        sizes = []
        for tag, net in (('before', before), ('after', after)):
            svg = get_single_line_diagram_custom(net, level, highlight_grid_model_ids=ids)._content
            (out_dir / f'{level}_{tag}.svg').write_text(svg, encoding='utf-8')
            sizes.append((len(svg), highlighted(svg)))
        levels[level] = sizes
    return {'switches': switches, 'diagrams': levels}


def main() -> None:
    """Run the pipeline on the grids named (both by default) and print what Lab B1 and B3 ask for."""
    suppress_jax_logs()
    out_root = Path(sys.argv[1])
    reuse = '--reuse' in sys.argv
    for name in [a for a in sys.argv[2:] if a != '--reuse'] or list(GRIDS):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        run_dir, data_folder = latest_run(out_root, name) if reuse else run(out_root, name)
        print(f'{name}: run folder {run_dir}, pipeline {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s', flush=True)
        res = json.loads((run_dir / 'res.json').read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
        print(f'  DC: {res["iteration"]} epochs, {len(res["best_topos"])} topologies in best_topos')
        table = run_table(run_dir)
        table['toop_rejected_by'] = table['topology'].map(toop_verdicts(run_dir))
        print(table.to_string(index=False))
        for topology_dir in sorted(run_dir.glob('topology_*')):
            if not (topology_dir / 'orao_summary.json').exists():
                continue
            result = before_after(data_folder / 'grid.xiidm', topology_dir)
            print(f'  {topology_dir.name}: diagrams (characters, highlighted elements) {result["diagrams"]}')
            for switch, info in result['switches'].items():
                print(f'    {switch}: {info}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  4. Operator hand-off. orao_summary.json (changing_switches_to_orao_dict) lists the switches to open and to close, station by station, with nothing but SWITCH entries. handoff.instructions adds the kind and voltage level of each switch (switches.json) and writes one line per operation; for the node-breaker topology:

    1. Open breaker VL2_BREAKER in VL2 (can break load current).
    2. Open disconnector L12_DISCONNECTOR_4_0 in VL2 (operate only without current).
    3. Close disconnector L12_DISCONNECTOR_4_2 in VL2 (operate only without current).

    An operator reads more into it than the file says: the disconnectors of L12 may only move while the line carries no current, so its own breaker has to open first and close last, and that breaker is not in the list. handoff.counts compares the counts:

    Grid Topology Actions Operations Breakers Disconnectors AC switching_distance DC switching_distance node-breaker 0 [5] 3 1 2 3 2 complex 0 [1, 54, 68] 12 4 8 12 8 complex 1 [54, 68] 7 3 4 7 4 complex 2 [69] 5 1 4 5 4 complex 3 [] 0 0 0 (not reported) 0

    The number of operations equals the AC switching_distance (counted on the realized topology by extract_switching_distance) for every split, and the DC value (dc_info, a sum of per-action reassignment_distance values computed in preprocessing) equals the number of disconnector operations: it leaves out the coupler breakers that the splits open, one per split station and two in VL_MV (VL_MV_BREAKER and VL_MV_BREAKER#0). docs/topology_optimizer/metrics.md calls the mismatch a bug; for the hand-off, quote the AC number.

    handoff.py
    """The operator hand-off of a ToOp run: ORAO summaries as switching instructions (Chapter 28, Lab B4).

``orao_summary.json`` (``changing_switches_to_orao_dict`` in ``optimizer/ac/summary.py``) lists, per validated
topology, the switches whose state changes; ``switches.json`` (written by ``lab_b_toop.py`` from the grid) adds the
kind and voltage level of each. ``instructions`` turns them into lines an operator can read, and ``counts`` compares
the number of operations with the AC and DC ``switching_distance``; ``run_summary`` and ``acceptance.run_table`` give
the numbers of Lab B1. It reads the runs stored in ``lab_b_run/``::

    python handoff.py [run folder]
"""

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from acceptance import run_table

RUNS = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'lab_b_run'


def load(path: Path) -> dict:
    """A JSON file."""
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding='utf-8'))


def topology_dirs(run_dir: Path) -> list[Path]:
    """The ``topology_N`` folders of a run, in numeric order."""
    return sorted(Path(run_dir).glob('topology_*'), key=lambda p: int(p.name.split('_')[1]))


def operations(orao_summary: dict) -> list[tuple[str, bool]]:
    """``[(switch id, open?), ...]`` in the order of the summary (only ``SWITCH`` entries exist in ToOp ba1874e)."""
    actions = orao_summary['forced-actions']['preventive-actions-list']['actions']
    return [(a['switchId'], a['open']) for a in actions if a['type'] == 'SWITCH']


def instructions(orao_summary: dict, switches: dict) -> list[str]:
    """One line per operation: verb, kind of switch, its id and voltage level, and what the kind allows."""
    lines = []
    for switch, is_open in operations(orao_summary):
        info = switches[switch]
        kind = info['kind'].lower().replace('_', ' ')
        note = 'can break load current' if info['kind'] == 'BREAKER' else 'operate only without current'
        lines.append(f'{"Open" if is_open else "Close"} {kind} {switch} in {info["voltage_level_id"]} ({note})')
    return lines


def counts(run_dir: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Per validated topology: operations in the ORAO summary against the AC and DC switching distances."""
    rows = []
    for folder in topology_dirs(run_dir):
        ac = load(folder / 'ac_metrics.json')
        ops = operations(load(folder / 'orao_summary.json'))
        switches = load(folder / 'switches.json')
        rows.append(
            {
                'topology': folder.name,
                'actions': ac['dc_info']['actions'],
                'operations': len(ops),
                'breakers': sum(switches[s]['kind'] == 'BREAKER' for s, _ in ops),
                'disconnectors': sum(switches[s]['kind'] == 'DISCONNECTOR' for s, _ in ops),
                'ac_switching_distance': ac['extra_scores'].get('switching_distance'),
                'dc_switching_distance': ac['dc_info']['metrics']['extra_scores'].get('switching_distance'),
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def run_summary(run_dir: Path) -> dict:
    """The DC side of a run (epochs, initial fitness, elites with their PST setpoints) and the unsplit AC metrics."""
    res = load(Path(run_dir) / 'res.json')
    unsplit = load(Path(run_dir) / 'unsplit_ac_metrics.json')['extra_scores']
    keys = ('overload_energy_n_1', 'critical_branch_count_n_1', 'non_converging_loadflows')
    return {
        'epochs': res['iteration'],
        'initial_fitness': res['initial_fitness'],
        'elites': [(t['actions'], t['pst_setpoints'], t['metrics']['fitness']) for t in res['best_topos']],
        'unsplit_ac': {k: unsplit[k] for k in keys},
    }


def main() -> None:
    """Print the Lab B1 table, the instructions and the counts of every stored run (or of the run folder given)."""
    pd.set_option('display.width', 200)
    runs = [Path(sys.argv[1])] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else sorted(p for p in RUNS.iterdir() if p.is_dir())
    for run_dir in runs:
        print(run_dir.name, run_summary(run_dir))
        print(run_table(run_dir).to_string(index=False))
        for folder in topology_dirs(run_dir):
            print(f'  {folder.name}:')
            for line in instructions(load(folder / 'orao_summary.json'), load(folder / 'switches.json')):
                print(f'    {line}')
        print(counts(run_dir).to_string(index=False))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
Let line \(\ell = (i, j)\) with susceptance \(b_\ell\) lie on a cycle whose other \(m\) lines \(k = 1, \dots, m\) have ratings \(\bar f_k\) and susceptances \(b_k\). When \(\ell\) is open the two voltage angles are still linked by the rest of the cycle: going from \(i\) to \(j\) along it,

\[ \theta_i - \theta_j = \sum_{k=1}^{m} \pm(\theta_{k}^{+} - \theta_{k}^{-}) = \sum_{k=1}^{m} \pm \frac{f_k}{b_k}, \qquad |\theta_i - \theta_j| \le \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{\bar f_k}{b_k}, \]

because every line of the path respects its rating in any feasible point. The constraint \(-M_\ell(1 - z_\ell) \le b_\ell(\theta_i - \theta_j) - f_\ell \le M_\ell(1 - z_\ell)\) must not cut off any feasible angle pair when \(z_\ell = 0\) (then \(f_\ell = 0\)), so

\[ M_\ell = b_\ell \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{\bar f_k}{b_k} \]

is valid, and it is the smallest valid value when the rest of the cycle is the only path between \(i\) and \(j\). In the 3-bus ring of Exercise 2 (equal reactances 0.1 p.u., ratings 200, 200 and 100 MW) the bound for line 1–3 is \(M = b (200/b + 200/b) = 400\) MW; at the DC-OPF optimum with that line open the angle gap \(b(\theta_1 - \theta_3)\) is 360 MW, inside the bound (braess3.big_m_cycle, gap_when_open). A bound over all topologies is harder because the other lines may be open too: the cycle may not exist, and the angle gap is then set by whichever path survives, so the valid \(M_\ell\) is the maximum over all connected topologies of the shortest weighted path between \(i\) and \(j\) with weights \(\bar f_k / b_k\), a combinatorial quantity. The safe choice is the sum over every other line, \(b_\ell \sum_{k \ne \ell} \bar f_k / b_k\) (a simple path uses each line at most once), which ieee30_ots.big_m(case, 'global') uses and which is 10 to 100 times looser than the cycle bound (520 to 16,037 MW against 16 to 2,231 MW on IEEE 30): a loose \(M\) weakens the LP relaxation and slows the MILP, as in Chapter 23.

braess3.py (big-M check)
def big_m_cycle(line: int) -> float:
    """Exercise 1: b_l times the largest angle gap the rest of the cycle allows, sum of rating / b over its lines."""
    b = 100 / X  # MW per radian
    others = [k for k in range(len(LINES)) if k != line]
    return float(b[line] * sum(RATING[k] / b[k] for k in others))


def gap_when_open(line: int) -> float:
    """|b_l (theta_i - theta_j)| in MW at the DC-OPF optimum with ``line`` open: must stay below ``big_m_cycle``."""
    r = dc_opf((line,))
    i, j = LINES[line]
    return float(abs(100 / X[line] * (r['theta'][i] - r['theta'][j])))

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
Three buses, three lines of equal reactance (1–2, 2–3 and 1–3, ratings 200, 200 and 100 MW), a 10 $/MWh generator at bus 1, a 50 $/MWh generator at bus 3 and 180 MW of load at bus 3. With every line closed, two thirds of a transfer from bus 1 to bus 3 take the direct line 1–3 and one third the path 1–2–3, so line 1–3 reaches its 100 MW rating when bus 1 produces 150 MW; the DC-OPF dispatches (150, 30) MW at 3000 $/h, flows (50, 50, 100) MW. With line 1–3 open, all of bus 1's output takes 1–2–3, each line can carry 200 MW, and the DC-OPF dispatches (180, 0) MW at 1800 $/h: opening a line lowers the cost by 40 %. The dual values explain it. Closed: LMPs (10, 30, 50) $/MWh; the price at bus 3 is the cost of the expensive unit, which is marginal there, and bus 2 sits at 30 because a MW injected at bus 2 reaches bus 3 one third through 2–3 directly and two thirds via 2–1–3, loading the congested line, so its value is a mix of the two generator prices. Open: LMPs (10, 10, 10), one price, the cheap unit marginal everywhere, no congestion rent. The 1200 $/h saved are the 30 MW that the congestion forced onto the expensive unit times the 40 $/MWh price difference. As in Braess's road-network paradox, removing a link helps because flows follow impedances (Kirchhoff), not the cheapest path: the direct line attracts two thirds of the transfer whether or not that is useful, and the DC-OPF has exactly that structure.

braess3.py (DC-OPF)
def dc_opf(open_lines: tuple[int, ...] = ()) -> dict:
    """DC-OPF of the 3-bus case with the lines in ``open_lines`` removed; returns cost, dispatch, flows and LMPs."""
    m = pulp.LpProblem('braess', pulp.LpMinimize)
    p = [m.add_variable(f'p_{g}', 0, p_max) for g, (_, p_max, _) in enumerate(GENS)]
    theta = [m.add_variable(f'theta_{n}', None, None) for n in range(3)]
    f = [m.add_variable(f'f_{k}', -r, r) for k, r in enumerate(RATING)]
    m += theta[0] == 0
    for k, (i, j) in enumerate(LINES):
        if k in open_lines:
            m += f[k] == 0
        else:
            m += f[k] == (theta[i] - theta[j]) / X[k] * 100  # 100 MVA base, flows in MW
    balance = []
    for n in range(3):
        c = pulp.lpSum(p[g] for g, (bus, _, _) in enumerate(GENS) if bus == n) - LOAD[n] == pulp.lpSum(
            f[k] for k, (i, _) in enumerate(LINES) if i == n
        ) - pulp.lpSum(f[k] for k, (_, j) in enumerate(LINES) if j == n)
        m += c, f'balance_{n}'
        balance.append(c)
    m += pulp.lpSum(cost * p[g] for g, (_, _, cost) in enumerate(GENS))
    m.solve(pulp.HiGHS(msg=False))
    return {
        'cost': pulp.value(m.objective),
        'p': np.array([v.value() for v in p]),
        'f': np.array([v.value() for v in f]),
        'theta': np.array([v.value() for v in theta]),
        'lmp': np.array([c.pi for c in balance]),
    }

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
• SOCP / QC / SDP relaxation of the AC equations. Used to validate, a relaxation gives a lower bound on the AC cost or a proof of infeasibility of a candidate topology in seconds, without a Newton solve that may diverge; it would complement the AC stage by rejecting infeasible candidates early rather than compete with the DC stage. Used to seed, the relaxation's angles and voltages are a better starting point than the DC flows, but a relaxation can be inexact (its solution need not correspond to a real operating point), so it cannot replace the AC validation that ToOp runs on the realized topology.
  • Shift-factor (PTDF/LODF) MILP. It would replace ToOp's DC search: the same linear model ToOp evaluates by the million, written as a compact MILP without angle variables, solved to proven optimality for a small number of switching actions. It competes with the DC repertoire directly, with a guarantee instead of a population, and loses when the action set is busbar splits (the factors change per candidate topology and must be regenerated, which is what ToOp's BSDF/LODF updates do inside the solver).
  • Lazy N-1 constraint generation. It would keep the exact method tractable: only the contingencies that actually bind are in the model (six of forty-one in Lab A3). In ToOp the analogue is the worst-k early stopping of the AC stage (n_worst_contingencies), which also looks at a subset first; a lazy exact method would compete with the DC stage for the proposal of candidates and with the early-stopping heuristic for the way contingencies are prioritized.
  • Benders decomposition. The master picks the topology (binaries), the subproblem is the DC-OPF or the N-1 check for that topology, and its duals return a cut to the master; the subproblem is exactly what ToOp's solver evaluates, so Benders would turn ToOp's evaluator into the oracle of an exact search and compete with the evolutionary DC stage. Its cost is one LP per candidate and a master MILP that grows with the cuts, so it scales to hundreds, not millions, of candidates.

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
The question. The day-ahead grid has an N-1 overload (line \(\ell\) after outage \(c\)); the operator wants the switching actions that remove it without creating others, by tomorrow morning.

MILP with lazy N-1 constraints. Formulation: DC-OPF or fixed-dispatch feasibility with binaries per switchable line or busbar coupler, the big-M constraints of the worked example, and the post-contingency flow limits added only for the contingencies found violated (Lab A3). Scalability: exact for tens of switchable elements and a handful of binding contingencies (IEEE 30 solves in a fraction of a second); grows exponentially in the worst case, and node-breaker busbar models multiply the binaries, so real grids need decomposition or a restricted candidate list and still risk time-outs. Guarantees: optimality and infeasibility proofs for the DC model and the contingencies in the set; nothing about contingencies not yet added, nothing about AC. AC feasibility: none; the DC model ignores reactive power, voltages and losses, so every solution needs an AC N-1 check afterwards, like ToOp's. Interpretability: high for the result (a list of switches with a proven cost) and low for the reasoning (duals and cuts are not an operator's language), and a MILP's answer changes abruptly with the data.

Rule-based expert system. Rules of the form "if line \(\ell\) overloads after \(c\), try the splits of the substations adjacent to \(\ell\), then the reconnection of parallel lines", encoded from operating experience and checked by simulation before being proposed. Scalability: linear in the number of rules and simulations; real-time capable; coverage limited to situations someone has written a rule for, and maintenance grows with the grid. Guarantees: none of optimality; what it proposes has been simulated, so it is at least feasible in the model used. AC feasibility: good when the rules are checked with an AC tool, which operators insist on. Interpretability: the best of the three: every proposal comes with its rule, in the operator's vocabulary.

ToOp. A GPU DC solver evaluates millions of topologies, a MAP-Elites repertoire keeps the best per (number of splits, switching distance), and an AC stage re-validates the best cells with an acceptance rule (Lab B). Scalability: the DC stage scales with GPU throughput, not with the number of binaries, and handles busbar splits natively through BSDF/LODF updates; the AC stage is the bottleneck and is throttled by worst-k early stopping. Guarantees: none; an evolutionary search can miss the optimum and its result depends on seed and budget (Chapter 26), and the acceptance rule has the traps of Lab B2. AC feasibility: built in, every proposal that reaches the operator passed a full AC N-1 with PowSyBl; the price is the mismatch between DC and AC metrics (the DC winner can be rejected). Interpretability: medium: the output is a concrete list of switch operations (orao_summary.json) with before/after metrics and diagrams, but why this split works is not explained, and the weighted-sum fitness hides trade-offs (Chapter 27).

Verdict. For a next-day question with a few known overloads and a small candidate list, the MILP gives the defensible answer and the expert system the fastest; ToOp is the tool when the candidate space is large (many substations, splits rather than line switching) and AC feasibility must be part of the search rather than a check afterwards. A reasonable process uses ToOp or the MILP to propose, the AC N-1 to validate, and keeps the rule base as the operator's sanity check and the fallback when the optimizers time out.

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
The checks run in ToOp's order (acceptance.py reproduces it; ToOp's own function returns the same in the test):

  1. Convergence: candidate \(1 - 0 = 1\) non-converging loadflow \(\le 1.0 \times 2\): passes.
  2. Overload energy: \(0.4 \le 0.95 \times 0.0 = 0\): fails. The function returns criterion='overload-energy', value_after=0.4, value_before=0.0, threshold=0.95.
  3. Critical branch count (\(1 \le 1.1 \times 0 = 0\)) would fail too, but is never reached.

This is the zero-baseline trap: the unsplit grid has no N-1 overload (perhaps only on the worst-k subset being evaluated), so any candidate with a positive overload is rejected, however small, even though it also made one diverging contingency converge, which is the improvement the operator would most want. Two changes make the rule robust. First, compare with an absolute tolerance as well: accept when split <= max(threshold * unsplit, absolute) with an absolute allowance in MW and in branches (for instance 1 MW and 1 branch), so that a zero baseline does not become an impossible target. Second, give the convergence improvement credit: when the candidate converges on cases the unsplit grid did not, compare the overload only on the cases both runs computed, or recompute the unsplit baseline on the candidate's converging set; ToOp's docs/wall_of_shame.md records this exact failure. The unused early_stopping_non_convergence_percentage_threshold parameter suggests such a rule was planned.

docs.title: Chapter 29. Learning-based topology control
docs.text:
Weeks: 2 · Semester: 5 · Prerequisites: Chapter 5, Chapter 24, Chapter 28, Chapter 31

Why it matters for ToOp

ToOp is a search-based optimizer: it contains no learned policy, no neural surrogate and no gradients. A search of its packages finds no jax.grad, jax.value_and_grad, jax.jacfwd, jax.jacrev, jax.vjp or jax.jvp; JAX is used for batching, compilation and GPU execution. Yet most of the recent literature on topology control is learning-based, and ToOp shares its vocabulary:

  • ToOp's DC solver documentation introduces its topology encoding through "the topo-vect format as introduced by grid2ops" (docs/dc_solver/quickstart.md), the representation of Grid2Op, the environment of the L2RPN reinforcement learning competitions.
  • The example-grid generator can write Grid2Op-compatible chronics (save_grid2op_compatible in dc_solver/example_grids.py).
  • The DC-screening plus AC-validation design of Chapter 28 is a surrogate-assisted search: a cheap model filters candidates for an expensive one. Neural surrogates and RL policies are alternative ways to propose or rank candidates, and they need the same kind of simulation check before an operator sees them.

This chapter gives you enough reinforcement learning, graph learning and automatic differentiation to read that literature critically, to benchmark a learned agent against search, and to design hybrids.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Reinforcement learning fundamentals: Markov decision processes \((\mathcal S, \mathcal A, P, R, \gamma)\); return \(G_t = \sum_{k \ge 0} \gamma^k R_{t+k+1}\); policies; value functions \(V^\pi\) and \(Q^\pi\) and the Bellman equations; dynamic programming; temporal-difference learning and tabular Q-learning, \(Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha\,[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]\); function approximation and DQN (replay buffer, target network); policy gradient and actor–critic methods; PPO at intuition level (clipped policy updates); exploration (\(\varepsilon\)-greedy, entropy bonus).
  • Topology control as RL: Grid2Op environments, observations (line loadings rho, topo_vect), actions (bus assignments, line status), rewards and game over; the L2RPN competitions; baselines (do-nothing, rule-based "expert" agents); multi-objective RL for topology control (revisits Chapter 27).
  • The action-space size problem: bus assignments grow exponentially with the number of elements per substation; reductions by unitary action sets, action pruning by simulation, hierarchical agents; the connection with ToOp's action enumeration and validity filters (Chapter 22).
  • Graph neural network power-flow surrogates: the grid as a graph, message passing, the graph neural solver of Donon et al., generalization to unseen topologies, accuracy vs speed, physics-based losses.
  • Surrogate-assisted evolutionary search: pre-screening, model management, uncertainty; comparison with ToOp's DC/AC multi-fidelity design.
  • Automatic differentiation: forward and reverse mode, JVPs and VJPs; differentiable DC power flow (the Jacobian of flows with respect to injections is the PTDF of Chapter 17); why discrete switching decisions are not differentiable and what relaxations do about it (awareness).
  • Limits and safety of learned controllers: distribution shift, rare contingencies, no feasibility or optimality guarantees, reward misspecification, interpretability; why TSOs pair learned proposals with simulation checks (Grid2Op's obs.simulate, ToOp's AC validation) and keep a human in the loop.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Formulate grid topology control as an MDP, implement tabular Q-learning for a small Grid2Op environment, and compare it with do-nothing, random and greedy-by-simulation baselines over repeated seeds.
  • Explain why the topology action space defeats naive RL and name three reduction techniques.
  • Train a small neural surrogate of DC flows on NumPy-generated data and report its error and speed-up against the exact solver.
  • Use JAX automatic differentiation to recover the PTDF from a differentiable DC power flow, and argue why ToOp's discrete search does not use gradients.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A DC power flow written in JAX is differentiable. Its Jacobian with respect to the non-slack injections is the PTDF, so automatic differentiation reproduces Chapter 17 without deriving anything:

jax_ptdf.py
"""DC flows of a three-bus ring in JAX, and the PTDF as its automatic derivative (Chapter 29)."""

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

jax.config.update('jax_enable_x64', True)

LINES = jnp.array([[0, 1], [1, 2], [0, 2]])  # 3-bus ring, bus 0 is the slack
B = jnp.array([10.0, 5.0, 8.0])  # line susceptances
A = jnp.zeros((3, 3)).at[jnp.arange(3), LINES[:, 0]].set(1.0).at[jnp.arange(3), LINES[:, 1]].set(-1.0)
B_F = B[:, None] * A  # branch flows = B_F @ theta
B_BUS = A.T @ B_F  # nodal susceptance matrix


def flows(p_noslack: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Branch flows for the injections at buses 1 and 2 (the slack balances them)."""
    theta = jnp.concatenate([jnp.zeros(1), jnp.linalg.solve(B_BUS[1:, 1:], p_noslack)])
    return B_F @ theta


def ptdf() -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Columns of the PTDF for buses 1 and 2: the Jacobian of ``flows``, by forward-mode differentiation."""
    return jax.jacfwd(flows)(jnp.zeros(2))


def main() -> None:
    """Flows for one injection pattern and the PTDF."""
    p = jnp.array([-1.0, 0.5])  # injections at buses 1 and 2
    print(flows(p))  # [ 0.6176 -0.3824 -0.1176]
    print(ptdf())  # [[-0.7647 -0.2941] [0.2353 -0.2941] [-0.2353 -0.7059]]


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

The gradient exists with respect to continuous quantities (injections, susceptances) but not with respect to a switching decision \(z_\ell \in \{0, 1\}\). Relaxing \(z_\ell\) to \([0, 1]\) and scaling \(b_\ell\) by it gives gradients, but the optimum of the relaxation need not be near a good binary topology, which is one reason ToOp searches discrete topologies directly.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: a learned agent against exhaustive one-step search

Tools: Jupyter with NumPy, pandas and matplotlib; Grid2Op with the LightSim2Grid backend (CPU only). Alternative track: NumPy and JAX only.

  1. Environment. Create grid2op.make("l2rpn_case14_sandbox", test=True, backend=LightSimBackend()). List the number of substations and lines, the observation fields you will use (rho, topo_vect, line_status) and the unitary topology actions from env.action_space.get_all_unitary_topologies_set(env.action_space).
  2. Baselines. Run do-nothing, a random topology agent and a greedy agent that, whenever the maximum rho exceeds a threshold, calls obs.simulate(action) for every unitary topology action and plays the one with the lowest simulated maximum loading (an exhaustive one-step search). Use 10 seeds and episodes of 288 steps; record survival time, mean maximum loading and wall-clock time per step.
  3. Tabular Q-learning. Discretize the state (for example the bin of the maximum rho times the index of the most loaded line), restrict the actions to do-nothing plus the 20 actions the greedy agent chose most often, and train with \(\varepsilon\)-greedy exploration. Evaluate the greedy policy of the learned \(Q\) on the same seeds as the baselines and compare with the statistics of Chapter 26. Discuss what the agent cannot know that the exhaustive search checks at every step.
  4. Optional. Replace the table with a small DQN (Stable-Baselines3 through a Gymnasium wrapper of the environment) and compare training cost with the greedy agent's simulation cost.

Alternative track (surrogate). Generate 20,000 random injection vectors for IEEE 30, compute DC flows with your Chapter 16–17 code, train a two-layer MLP in JAX to predict all flows, and report the relative error per line and the speed-up. Then switch off one line not seen in training and measure how the error grows: this is the generalization problem that graph neural solvers address.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb · Steps 1–4 with Grid2Op in the labs container (docker/labs): lab_labs.ipynb.
