The code is in the chapter's src folder: grid_env.py (a five-bus topology-control environment in NumPy with the do-nothing, random, greedy-by-simulation and Q-learning agents), surrogate_mlp.py (the JAX surrogate of the alternative track), value_iteration.py, action_space.py, jax_susceptance.py (which extends the worked example's jax_ptdf.py) and surrogate_ga.py. The IEEE 30 data come from Chapter 27's ch27_ieee30.py. Each module prints the numbers quoted below when run as a script. Grid2Op, LightSim2Grid, Gymnasium and Stable-Baselines3 are not installed in the course environment: the Grid2Op parts of the lab run in the labs container (docker/labs, Grid2Op 1.12.6, LightSim2Grid 1.2.0, Stable-Baselines3 2.9.0 with CPU-only PyTorch 2.14.1) with grid2op_agents_labs.py and dqn_labs.py, on the full l2rpn_case14_sandbox dataset and with the container limited to one CPU core (--cpus=1); the notebook is lab_labs.ipynb. Each step below gives the Grid2Op result first and then the same experiment on the small NumPy environment of the fallback track.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. Environment. With Grid2Op the call is grid2op.make("l2rpn_case14_sandbox", test=True, backend=LightSimBackend()); test=True gives the two chronics that ship with Grid2Op, and without it the full dataset (1,004 chronics, a 294 MB download kept in the container's data volume) is used here. The grid has 14 substations, 20 lines, 6 generators and 11 loads; obs.rho has 20 loadings, obs.topo_vect 57 entries (one per element: the busbar it sits on, −1 if disconnected) and obs.line_status 20. env.action_space.get_all_unitary_topologies_set(env.action_space) returns 178 single-substation reconfigurations, most of them at the big substations: 57 at substation 5, 31 at substation 3, 29 at substation 1, none at substation 7, numbering from 0 as Grid2Op does (compare the 26 of a six-element substation in Exercise 2).

    grid2op_agents_labs.py (environment)
    def make_env(seed: int = 0):
    """The case 14 sandbox on LightSim2Grid: the full dataset when the data volume holds it, else the test chronics."""
    env = grid2op.make(ENV_NAME, test=not DATA_DIR.exists(), backend=LightSimBackend())
    env.seed(seed)
    return env


def describe(env) -> dict:
    """Lab step 1: the sizes of the grid and of the observation, and the unitary topology actions."""
    unitary = env.action_space.get_all_unitary_topologies_set(env.action_space)
    obs = env.reset()
    return {
        'n_sub': env.n_sub,
        'n_line': env.n_line,
        'n_gen': env.n_gen,
        'n_load': env.n_load,
        'rho': obs.rho.shape[0],
        'topo_vect': obs.topo_vect.shape[0],
        'line_status': obs.line_status.shape[0],
        'unitary_topologies': len(unitary),
        'per_substation': np.bincount(
            [int(np.flatnonzero(a.get_topological_impact()[1])[0]) for a in unitary], minlength=env.n_sub
        ).tolist(),
        'chronics': len(env.chronics_handler.real_data.subpaths)
        if hasattr(env.chronics_handler.real_data, 'subpaths')
        else None,
    }


def reset_day(env, chronic: int, seed: int):
    """Start ``chronic`` at its first step with a horizon of one day, seeded (only the random agent uses the seed)."""
    env.seed(seed)
    return env.reset(seed=seed, options={'time serie id': chronic, 'max step': N_STEPS})


def shaped_reward(obs, changed: bool, done: bool, step: int) -> float:
    """The reward of ``grid_env.py``: minus the overload, minus 0.02 per change, minus 5 for an early game over."""
    reward = -float(np.maximum(0.0, obs.rho - 1.0).sum()) - 0.02 * changed
    if done and step < N_STEPS:
        reward -= 5.0
    return reward

    The stand-in grid_env.py of the fallback track has 5 buses, 6 lines of 15 to 130 MW, a slack generator at bus 1 and loads at buses 3, 4 and 5 (35 %, 40 %, 25 % of a daily profile with a 150 MW evening peak, 4 % noise per step); the observation is the vector rho of the six loadings, the topology is one of 7 (every line closed, or one line open: none of the six is a bridge), and the 8 actions are "do nothing" and "switch to topology \(t\)". At the peak the meshed topology loads the weak tie line 2–3 (15 MW) to 114 %, two switches relieve it (open 2–3: 70 %; open 4–5: 80 %) and the other four are destructive (250 % to 583 %), which is the shape of the real action space: most topology actions are harmful. A line above 100 % for more than 2 consecutive steps (Grid2Op's soft-overflow allowance) or above 150 % trips and ends the episode, with a reward of −5.

    grid_env.py (environment)
    def load_profile(step: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Total load in MW: a morning ramp and an evening peak on a day of ``N_STEPS`` steps."""
    t = step / N_STEPS
    return PEAK_MW * (0.45 + 0.25 * np.exp(-(((t - 0.35) / 0.08) ** 2)) + 0.55 * np.exp(-(((t - 0.78) / 0.07) ** 2)))


def topologies() -> list[np.ndarray]:
    """Action set: every line in service, then one line open at a time (bridges excluded, they island the grid)."""
    out = [np.ones(len(LINES), dtype=bool)]
    for k in range(len(LINES)):
        mask = np.ones(len(LINES), dtype=bool)
        mask[k] = False
        if ptdf(mask) is not None:
            out.append(mask)
    return out


def ptdf(in_service: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray | None:
    """PTDF of the lines in service with bus 0 as slack, or ``None`` when the grid is islanded."""
    lines, n_bus = LINES[in_service], len(LOAD_SHARE)
    a = np.zeros((len(lines), n_bus))
    a[np.arange(len(lines)), lines[:, 0]] = 1
    a[np.arange(len(lines)), lines[:, 1]] = -1
    adjacency = np.zeros((n_bus, n_bus))
    adjacency[lines[:, 0], lines[:, 1]] = 1
    if connected_components(adjacency, directed=False)[0] > 1:
        return None
    b = 1 / X[in_service]
    bbus = a.T @ (b[:, None] * a)
    h = np.zeros((len(lines), n_bus))
    h[:, 1:] = (b[:, None] * a[:, 1:]) @ np.linalg.inv(bbus[1:, 1:])
    return h


TOPOLOGIES = topologies()
PTDFS = [ptdf(mask) for mask in TOPOLOGIES]


def rho(topology: int, load_mw: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Loading of every line (0 for an open line) when the total load is ``load_mw``, split by ``LOAD_SHARE``."""
    mask = TOPOLOGIES[topology]
    p = -LOAD_SHARE * load_mw
    p[0] = -p[1:].sum()
    out = np.zeros(len(LINES))
    out[mask] = np.abs(PTDFS[topology] @ p) / RATING[mask]
    return out


class GridEnv:
    """One episode: the state is (step, topology); ``reset`` draws the day's load noise from the seed."""

    n_actions = len(TOPOLOGIES) + 1  # 0 = do nothing, k = switch to topology k - 1

    def __init__(self, seed: int, noise: float = 0.04):
        """``seed`` drives the day's load noise (relative standard deviation ``noise``) and the random agent."""
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.noise = noise

    def reset(self) -> tuple[np.ndarray, int]:
        """Start a day; returns the observation (rho) and the topology index."""
        self.step_index = 0
        self.topology = 0
        self.overflow = np.zeros(len(LINES), dtype=int)  # consecutive steps above 100 % per line
        self.load = load_profile(np.arange(N_STEPS)) * (1 + self.noise * self.rng.standard_normal(N_STEPS))
        return rho(0, self.load[0]), 0

    def simulate(self, action: int) -> np.ndarray:
        """What ``obs.simulate`` does in Grid2Op: the loading after ``action`` at the next step, no state change."""
        topology = self.topology if action == 0 else action - 1
        return rho(topology, self.load[min(self.step_index + 1, N_STEPS - 1)])

    def step(self, action: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, float, bool]:
        """Apply the action and advance one step: reward = -overload - switching cost; done at a trip or day end."""
        changed = action != 0 and action - 1 != self.topology
        if action != 0:
            self.topology = action - 1
        self.step_index += 1
        done = self.step_index >= N_STEPS - 1
        loading = rho(self.topology, self.load[self.step_index])
        overload = np.maximum(0, loading - 1).sum()
        reward = -overload - 0.02 * changed
        self.overflow = np.where(loading > 1, self.overflow + 1, 0)
        if loading.max() > CASCADE_RHO or self.overflow.max() > OVERFLOW_STEPS:
            reward -= 5.0  # a line trips: game over, as in Grid2Op
            done = True
        return loading, reward, done

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  2. Baselines. The reward per step is the same on both tracks: minus the summed overload (in units of rating), minus 0.02 per topology change, minus 5 when a game over ends the day early. With Grid2Op the ten "seeds" are ten days: the first day (288 five-minute steps) of the ten chronics among 0–299 with the highest do-nothing peak loading (chronic_scan, 101 s for the 300 days): 248, 72, 3, 57, 154, 194, 106, 181, 220 and 240. Only four of the 300 first days end in a game over for do-nothing, and all four are among these ten, so the evaluation days are the hard ones by construction. The random and greedy agents act when the maximum loading passes 90 %, over all 178 unitary actions.

    agent (Grid2Op) survival, median (min) of 288 mean max rho reward ms per step do-nothing 288 (3) 0.748 −2.02 0.85 random (acts above 90 %) 3 (1) 0.732 −6.01 0.96 greedy by simulation 288 (288) 0.729 −0.07 4.22

    Do-nothing ends three days at step 3 (days 248, 72 and 3 start with a line above its rating, which trips when Grid2Op's overflow allowance runs out, and the grid does not survive it) and day 57 at step 232 in the evening. The random agent is far worse: it acts as soon as a line passes 90 %, which happens early on these days, plays random topologies and dies within 6 steps on eight of the ten days. The greedy agent survives all ten days with the lowest mean maximum loading; it ran 6,623 simulations (obs.simulate, an AC power flow with LightSim2Grid each), 662 per day, which makes its steps five times as slow as do-nothing's (4.22 against 0.85 ms on one core).

    grid2op_agents_labs.py (agents, Q-learning, comparison)
    class Agents:
    """The lab's agents over the action list ``actions`` (index 0 is do-nothing, the rest unitary topologies)."""

    def __init__(self, env, actions: list, seed: int = 0):
        """``actions[0]`` must be the do-nothing action; ``seed`` drives the random agent."""
        self.env = env
        self.actions = actions
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.simulations = 0  # power flows spent by the greedy agent, to compare with the learned agents

    def do_nothing(self, obs) -> int:
        """Never acts."""
        return 0

    def random(self, obs) -> int:
        """Plays a random topology action when a line passes the threshold."""
        return int(self.rng.integers(1, len(self.actions))) if obs.rho.max() > THRESHOLD else 0

    def greedy(self, obs) -> int:
        """Simulates every action when a line passes the threshold and plays the one with the lowest maximum loading.

        A simulation that ends the game (``done``) or is illegal counts as infinitely bad; do-nothing is candidate 0,
        so the agent acts only when some topology beats staying put.
        """
        if obs.rho.max() <= THRESHOLD:
            return 0
        worst = np.full(len(self.actions), np.inf)
        for i, action in enumerate(self.actions):
            sim_obs, _, sim_done, sim_info = obs.simulate(action)
            self.simulations += 1
            if not sim_done and not sim_info['is_illegal'] and not sim_info['is_ambiguous']:
                worst[i] = sim_obs.rho.max()
        return int(np.argmin(worst))


def run_episode(env, agent, chronic: int, seed: int, actions: list, trace: list | None = None) -> dict:
    """One day of ``chronic`` played by ``agent(obs) -> action index``: survival, mean max loading, reward, ms/step."""
    obs = reset_day(env, chronic, seed)
    total, maxima, done, step = 0.0, [], False, 0
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    while not done:
        index = agent(obs)
        obs, _, done, info = env.step(actions[index])
        step += 1
        changed = index != 0 and not info['is_illegal']
        total += shaped_reward(obs, changed, done, step)
        maxima.append(float(obs.rho.max()))
        if trace is not None:
            trace.append(index)
    return {
        'survival': step,
        'mean_max_rho': float(np.mean(maxima)),
        'reward': total,
        'ms_per_step': 1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / step,
    }


def state_index(obs, in_reference: bool) -> int:
    """Discrete state: bin of the maximum loading, most loaded line, whether the grid is in its reference topology."""
    bin_index = int(np.searchsorted(RHO_BINS, obs.rho.max()))
    return (bin_index * len(obs.rho) + int(obs.rho.argmax())) * 2 + int(in_reference)


def n_states(env) -> int:
    """Size of the Q table's first axis."""
    return (len(RHO_BINS) + 1) * env.n_line * 2


def frequent_actions(env, unitary: list, chronics=TRAIN_CHRONICS, n_top: int = 20) -> tuple[list[int], dict]:
    """Lab step 3: the ``n_top`` unitary actions the greedy agent plays most often on the training chronics.

    Returns the indices into ``unitary`` (most frequent first), the play counts and the greedy agent's episode
    statistics on those days (with the number of simulations it spent).
    """
    actions = [env.action_space({}), *unitary]
    counts = np.zeros(len(actions), dtype=int)
    stats = []
    for chronic in chronics:
        agents = Agents(env, actions, seed=chronic)
        trace: list[int] = []
        stats.append(run_episode(env, agents.greedy, chronic, chronic, actions, trace))
        stats[-1]['simulations'] = agents.simulations
        counts += np.bincount(trace, minlength=len(actions))
    counts[0] = 0
    top = [int(i) - 1 for i in np.argsort(-counts, kind='stable')[:n_top] if counts[i] > 0]
    return top, {'counts': counts[1:], 'stats': stats}


def q_learning(
    env,
    actions: list,
    chronics=TRAIN_CHRONICS,
    episodes: int = 200,
    seed: int = 100,
    alpha: float = 0.2,
    gamma: float = 0.95,
    eps: float = 0.3,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Tabular Q-learning over ``actions`` on the days ``chronics`` in turn; epsilon decays linearly to 0.01."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q = np.zeros((n_states(env), len(actions)))
    for episode in range(episodes):
        epsilon = max(0.01, eps * (1 - episode / episodes))
        chronic = int(chronics[episode % len(chronics)])
        obs = reset_day(env, chronic, seed + episode)
        in_reference, done, step = True, False, 0
        s = state_index(obs, in_reference)
        while not done:
            i = int(rng.integers(len(actions))) if rng.random() < epsilon else int(np.argmax(q[s]))
            obs, _, done, info = env.step(actions[i])
            step += 1
            changed = i != 0 and not info['is_illegal']
            in_reference = in_reference and not changed
            reward = shaped_reward(obs, changed, done, step)
            s_next = state_index(obs, in_reference)
            target = reward if (done and step < N_STEPS) else reward + gamma * q[s_next].max()
            q[s, i] += alpha * (target - q[s, i])
            s = s_next
    return q


class QPolicy:
    """The greedy policy of a Q table in the signature of the other agents (tracks the reference-topology flag)."""

    def __init__(self, q: np.ndarray):
        """A fresh policy starts in the reference topology."""
        self.q = q
        self.in_reference = True

    def __call__(self, obs) -> int:
        """The action with the highest Q value in the observed state."""
        i = int(np.argmax(self.q[state_index(obs, self.in_reference)]))
        if i != 0:
            self.in_reference = False
        return i


def compare(env, actions: list, chronics=CHRONICS) -> dict:
    """Do-nothing, random and greedy agents over ``actions`` on the same chronics and seeds."""
    out: dict[str, list[dict]] = {'do-nothing': [], 'random': [], 'greedy (simulate)': []}
    for chronic in chronics:
        agents = Agents(env, actions, seed=chronic)
        out['do-nothing'].append(run_episode(env, agents.do_nothing, chronic, chronic, actions))
        out['random'].append(run_episode(env, agents.random, chronic, chronic, actions))
        out['greedy (simulate)'].append(run_episode(env, agents.greedy, chronic, chronic, actions))
        out['greedy (simulate)'][-1]['simulations'] = agents.simulations
    return out


def evaluate_q(env, q: np.ndarray, actions: list, chronics=CHRONICS) -> list[dict]:
    """The greedy policy of the Q table on the evaluation chronics."""
    return [run_episode(env, QPolicy(q), chronic, chronic, actions) for chronic in chronics]


def summary_table(results: dict) -> str:
    """The table of the solutions: survival (median, min), mean maximum loading, reward and ms per step."""
    lines = [f'{"agent":18s} {"survival (median, min)":>24s} {"mean max rho":>13s} {"reward":>9s} {"ms/step":>8s}']
    for name, runs in results.items():
        surv = np.array([r['survival'] for r in runs])
        lines.append(
            f'{name:18s} {np.median(surv):10.0f} {surv.min():12d} '
            f'{np.mean([r["mean_max_rho"] for r in runs]):13.3f} '
            f'{np.mean([r["reward"] for r in runs]):9.2f} '
            f'{np.mean([r["ms_per_step"] for r in runs]):8.2f}'
        )
    return '\n'.join(lines)

    On the stand-in of the fallback track: ten seeds (one noisy day each), episodes of 288 steps.

    agent survival, median (min) of 287 mean max rho reward ms per step do-nothing 217 (216) 0.597 −5.14 0.02 random (acts above 90 %) 212 (210) 0.595 −6.65 0.02 greedy by simulation 287 (287) 0.552 −0.02 0.02

    Do-nothing loses line 2–3 around step 217 on every seed, three consecutive steps above 100 % into the evening peak. The random agent acts when a line passes 90 %, mostly with one of the four destructive topologies, and dies a few steps earlier. The greedy agent simulates all 8 actions when the loading passes 90 % and plays the one with the lowest simulated maximum (env.simulate, the counterpart of Grid2Op's obs.simulate): it opens line 2–3 once, in the evening, and finishes the day with a mean maximum loading of 0.55. Wall-clock time is 0.02 ms per step for every agent on this grid; the greedy agent's 8 simulations per decision cost nothing here, but they are 8 power flows per step on a real grid (hundreds of actions on case 14, each an AC solve in Grid2Op), which is the cost the learned agent is meant to avoid.

  3. Tabular Q-learning. With Grid2Op the state is the bin of the maximum loading (6 bins with edges 0.6, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1), the index of the most loaded line and whether the grid is still in its reference topology: \(6 \times 20 \times 2 = 240\) states. The training days are kept apart from the evaluation days: the twenty first days of chronics 300–1003 with the highest do-nothing peak loading (212 s to scan; 20 of those 704 days end in a game over for do-nothing, 6 of them at step 3). On them the greedy agent ran 14,857 simulations in 38 s and played only 18 distinct actions (action 137 of the unitary list 21 times, 89 13 times, 132 8 times, the rest 6 times or fewer), so the reduced action set is do-nothing plus those 18, two short of the 20 the lab asks. Training: 200 days (ten passes over the twenty), \(\alpha = 0.2\), \(\gamma = 0.95\), \(\varepsilon\) decaying from 0.3 to 0.01, 28 s; the table visits 56 of its 240 states.

    agent (Grid2Op) survival, median (min) of 288 mean max rho reward ms per step do-nothing 288 (3) 0.748 −2.02 0.85 greedy by simulation 288 (288) 0.729 −0.07 4.22 Q-learning 288 (138) 0.781 −1.82 0.79

    Day by day, Q-learning survives 288, 288, 288, 237, 153, 138, 288, 288, 288 and 288 steps against do-nothing's 3, 3, 3, 232 and six full days. It learned what the training days taught: an overloaded line at the start of the day is relieved by a switch, so it survives the three step-3 crises. But it also switches on days 154 and 194, where doing nothing was safe, and loses them at steps 153 and 138. Paired against do-nothing (Chapter 26) it is better on 4 days, worse on 2 and equal on 4: a sign test gives \(p = 0.69\), no evidence either way with ten days, although the mean reward is higher (−1.82 against −2.02). Against the greedy agent it is never better. It runs at the cost of do-nothing (0.79 ms per step), with no simulations.

    On the stand-in of the fallback track the state is the bin of the maximum loading (6 bins with edges 0.6, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1), the index of the most loaded line and the current topology: \(6 \times 6 \times 7 = 252\) states. The action set is reduced as the lab asks: do-nothing plus the actions the greedy agent played most often on ten training days, which is a single one here (action 4, open line 2–3; the greedy agent never needed another), so the table has \(252 \times 2\) entries. Training: 500 days drawn from one seed, \(\alpha = 0.2\), \(\gamma = 0.95\), \(\varepsilon\)-greedy with \(\varepsilon\) decaying from 0.3 to 0.01, about 4 s. The decay matters: with a constant \(\varepsilon\) the agent explores the switch at some point of the morning on almost every day, stays in the safe topology, and never visits the meshed grid at the peak, so the states that matter are never learned and the greedy policy of the table is do-nothing (this was the first attempt). The learned policy, evaluated on the ten baseline seeds: survival 287 (287), mean maximum loading 0.557, reward −0.04, 0.03 ms per step. It survives every day with a single switch, like the greedy agent, but later: the greedy agent acts when line 2–3 passes 90 % (steps 209–212 of the ten days), the table only once the loading is in the bin above 1.0 (steps 213–216), so the Q agent tolerates one or two steps of a few percent overload (0.002 to 0.07 units of rating per day) that cost it the 0.02 of reward and the slightly higher mean loading. With ten paired seeds (Chapter 26) the difference is 0 in survival and 0.02 in reward on every day: real, but a consequence of the state discretization, not of the learning. What the agent does not know: the table maps a coarse state to an action with no model of the grid; it has never seen a load pattern outside its training days, a second line at risk, or a day where opening 2–3 is the wrong move, while the exhaustive search re-checks every action against the actual next state at every step. The agent's advantage is that it does not need those simulations at run time; its risk is that it cannot tell when its table is wrong. The Grid2Op table shows the same risk at full size: it plays a switch it learned on a crisis day on a day that did not need one, and nothing in its 240 states tells it the difference.

    grid_env.py (agents and Q-learning)
    def do_nothing(env: GridEnv, loading: np.ndarray) -> int:
    """Never acts."""
    return 0


def random_agent(env: GridEnv, loading: np.ndarray) -> int:
    """Acts at random when a line is above 90 %, as a baseline for the value of information."""
    return int(env.rng.integers(env.n_actions)) if loading.max() > 0.9 else 0


def greedy_agent(env: GridEnv, loading: np.ndarray, threshold: float = 0.9) -> int:
    """Simulates every action when the loading passes ``threshold`` and plays the one with the lowest maximum."""
    if loading.max() <= threshold:
        return 0
    worst = [env.simulate(a).max() for a in range(env.n_actions)]
    return int(np.argmin(worst))


def state_index(loading: np.ndarray, topology: int) -> int:
    """Discrete state: bin of the maximum loading, index of the most loaded line, current topology."""
    bin_index = int(np.searchsorted(RHO_BINS, loading.max()))
    return (bin_index * len(LINES) + int(loading.argmax())) * len(TOPOLOGIES) + topology


N_STATES = (len(RHO_BINS) + 1) * len(LINES) * len(TOPOLOGIES)


def run_episode(env: GridEnv, policy) -> dict:
    """Survival steps, mean maximum loading, total reward and wall-clock seconds per step of one episode."""
    loading, _ = env.reset()
    total, maxima, done = 0.0, [], False
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    while not done:
        loading, reward, done = env.step(policy(env, loading))
        total += reward
        maxima.append(loading.max())
    return {
        'survival': env.step_index,
        'mean_max_rho': float(np.mean(maxima)),
        'reward': total,
        'ms_per_step': 1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(maxima),
    }


def frequent_actions(n_top: int = 2, seeds: range = range(100, 110)) -> list[int]:
    """Lab step 3: do-nothing plus the ``n_top`` actions the greedy agent played most often on training days."""
    counts = np.zeros(GridEnv.n_actions, dtype=int)
    for seed in seeds:
        env = GridEnv(seed)
        loading, _ = env.reset()
        done = False
        while not done:
            a = greedy_agent(env, loading)
            counts[a] += 1
            loading, _, done = env.step(a)
    counts[0] = 0
    return [0, *[int(a) for a in np.argsort(-counts)[:n_top] if counts[a] > 0]]


def q_learning(
    actions: list[int], episodes: int = 500, seed: int = 100, alpha: float = 0.2, gamma: float = 0.95, eps: float = 0.3
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Tabular Q-learning over the reduced action list on days drawn from ``seed``; returns the Q table.

    Exploration is epsilon-greedy with epsilon decaying linearly from ``eps`` to 0.01: with a constant epsilon the
    agent switches somewhere during the morning on almost every training day and never sees the meshed grid at
    the peak, so the states that matter are never learned.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q = np.zeros((N_STATES, len(actions)))
    for episode in range(episodes):
        epsilon = max(0.01, eps * (1 - episode / episodes))
        env = GridEnv(int(rng.integers(1 << 31)))
        loading, topology = env.reset()
        s, done = state_index(loading, topology), False
        while not done:
            i = int(rng.integers(len(actions))) if rng.random() < epsilon else int(np.argmax(q[s]))
            loading, reward, done = env.step(actions[i])
            s_next = state_index(loading, env.topology)
            tripped = done and env.step_index < N_STEPS - 1
            target = reward if tripped else reward + gamma * q[s_next].max()
            q[s, i] += alpha * (target - q[s, i])
            s = s_next
    return q


def q_policy(q: np.ndarray, actions: list[int]):
    """The greedy policy of a Q table over the reduced action list, in the signature of the other agents."""

    def policy(env: GridEnv, loading: np.ndarray) -> int:
        return actions[int(np.argmax(q[state_index(loading, env.topology)]))]

    return policy


def compare(
    seeds: range = range(10), q: np.ndarray | None = None, actions: list[int] | None = None
) -> dict[str, list[dict]]:
    """Every agent on the same seeds; the Q policy is included when a table and its action list are given."""
    agents = {'do-nothing': do_nothing, 'random': random_agent, 'greedy (simulate)': greedy_agent}
    if q is not None and actions is not None:
        agents['Q-learning'] = q_policy(q, actions)
    return {name: [run_episode(GridEnv(seed), policy) for seed in seeds] for name, policy in agents.items()}

  4. Optional DQN. Case14Gym wraps the Grid2Op day in a gymnasium.Env: the observation is the 20 loadings (clipped at 10) plus the reference-topology flag, the action space Discrete(19) (the reduced set of step 3), the reward that of step 2, and a game over before step 288 terminates the episode. Stable-Baselines3's DQN('MlpPolicy') with two hidden layers of 64, learning from step 1,000, \(\gamma = 0.95\), exploration decaying over the first half of the budget, trains for 20,000 environment steps (about 70 days of experience) cycling over the training days of step 3: 384 s on one core, 19.2 ms per step, most of it the network updates (an environment step costs about 0.8 ms). Exploration ends most training days early: the 20,000 steps make 797 episodes, 25 steps each on average.

    agent (Grid2Op) survival, median (min) of 288 mean max rho reward ms per step do-nothing 288 (3) 0.748 −2.02 0.78 greedy by simulation 288 (288) 0.729 −0.07 4.05 DQN, 20,000 steps 58 (3) 0.731 −6.13 1.21

    (This run was separate from the one of step 2, hence slightly different times.) The trained network survives 3, 3, 3, 288, 3, 112, 288, 288, 3 and 288 steps: it fixes day 57 but none of the step-3 crises, and it causes game overs on days 154, 194 and 220, which do-nothing survives. With this budget the training cost is paid and buys nothing; the table of step 3, 28 s of training over a coarse state and the same actions, does better. The comparison the lab asks for: the greedy agent spends 6,623 simulations on the ten evaluation days (662 per day, every day, at run time) and no training; the DQN spends 20,000 training steps once (6.4 min) and then 1.2 ms per step. The trade pays only when the network is good, which takes far more than 70 days of experience on this grid, and only while the deployment days look like the training days.

    dqn_labs.py
    class Case14Gym(gym.Env):
    """Gymnasium view of the Grid2Op day: discrete reduced actions, loadings as observation, the lab's reward."""

    metadata = {'render_modes': []}

    def __init__(self, env, actions: list, chronics=lab.TRAIN_CHRONICS, seed: int = 0):
        """``actions[0]`` is do-nothing; each ``reset`` takes the next training chronic in turn."""
        super().__init__()
        self.env, self.actions, self.chronics = env, actions, list(chronics)
        self.base_seed, self.episode = seed, 0
        self.observation_space = gym.spaces.Box(0.0, 10.0, (env.n_line + 1,), dtype=np.float32)
        self.action_space = gym.spaces.Discrete(len(actions))
        self.in_reference, self.step_count = True, 0

    def _observe(self, obs) -> np.ndarray:
        return np.append(np.minimum(obs.rho, 10.0), float(self.in_reference)).astype(np.float32)

    def reset(self, *, seed=None, options=None):
        """Start the next chronic (or ``options['chronic']``) at its first step, one day long."""
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        chronic = (
            options['chronic']
            if options and 'chronic' in options
            else self.chronics[self.episode % len(self.chronics)]
        )
        self.episode += 1
        self.in_reference, self.step_count = True, 0
        obs = lab.reset_day(self.env, int(chronic), self.base_seed + self.episode)
        self.last_obs = obs
        return self._observe(obs), {}

    def step(self, action: int):
        """Grid2Op step with the lab's reward; a game over before the end of the day terminates the episode."""
        obs, _, done, info = self.env.step(self.actions[int(action)])
        self.step_count += 1
        changed = int(action) != 0 and not info['is_illegal']
        self.in_reference = self.in_reference and not changed
        reward = lab.shaped_reward(obs, changed, done, self.step_count)
        self.last_obs = obs
        terminated = done and self.step_count < lab.N_STEPS
        truncated = done and not terminated
        return self._observe(obs), reward, terminated, truncated, info


def train(gym_env: Case14Gym, steps: int = TRAIN_STEPS, seed: int = SEED) -> DQN:
    """DQN with a small MLP, exploration decaying over the first half of the budget, learning from step 1000."""
    model = DQN(
        'MlpPolicy',
        gym_env,
        learning_rate=1e-3,
        buffer_size=50_000,
        learning_starts=1_000,
        batch_size=64,
        gamma=0.95,
        train_freq=4,
        target_update_interval=500,
        exploration_fraction=0.5,
        exploration_final_eps=0.02,
        policy_kwargs={'net_arch': [64, 64]},
        seed=seed,
        verbose=0,
        device='cpu',
    )
    model.learn(total_timesteps=steps)
    return model


class DQNPolicy:
    """The trained network as an agent in the signature of ``grid2op_agents_labs`` (deterministic action)."""

    def __init__(self, model: DQN):
        """A fresh policy starts in the reference topology."""
        self.model = model
        self.in_reference = True

    def __call__(self, obs) -> int:
        """The network's greedy action for the observed loadings."""
        x = np.append(np.minimum(obs.rho, 10.0), float(self.in_reference)).astype(np.float32)
        i = int(self.model.predict(x, deterministic=True)[0])
        if i != 0:
            self.in_reference = False
        return i


def evaluate(env, model: DQN, actions: list, chronics=lab.CHRONICS) -> list[dict]:
    """The DQN's greedy policy on the baseline chronics, same statistics as the other agents."""
    return [lab.run_episode(env, DQNPolicy(model), chronic, chronic, actions) for chronic in chronics]

    On the stand-in of the fallback track the same wrapper is a gymnasium.Env around GridEnv with observation_space = Box(0, 10, (6,)) (the loadings) and action_space = Discrete(8); it was not trained. The table of step 3 already plays the single useful switch there, so a network could at best match it after \(10^4\)–\(10^5\) environment steps (35 to 350 days), against zero training for the greedy agent, whose cost is 8 simulations per decision instead.

  5. Alternative track (surrogate). IEEE 30 with pandapower's case30 injections scaled per bus by a uniform factor in \([0.5, 1.5]\) (slack balancing): 20,000 training samples, flows from the PTDF. A two-layer MLP (29 inputs, 64 tanh units, 41 outputs, full-batch Adam, 1,500 steps, 14 s on CPU) reaches a test error of 0.19 % of the rating on average and 0.43 % at worst (line index 9) on 2,000 unseen injections: the map is linear, so a small network learns it almost exactly. Speed: the exact flows are one matrix product with the PTDF, 0.11 ms for 2,000 cases, the MLP 0.95 ms, a speed-up of 0.12, that is a slow-down. A surrogate of a linear DC power flow cannot beat the PTDF, which is already the cheapest possible evaluator; surrogates pay off against AC power flows (Newton iterations, convergence failures) and against repeated topology changes, where the PTDF must be rebuilt. Generalization: with line 25–27 switched off (never seen in training) the error grows to 6.5 % of the rating on average and 47.8 % on line index 32 (24–25, the line that takes over the flow), 35 times the intact error. The network learned one PTDF; a topology change is a different linear map, and nothing in the input tells the network that the grid changed. That is the generalization problem graph neural solvers address by putting the topology into the input (messages along the lines that exist), and the reason ToOp's AC validation recomputes rather than predicts.

    surrogate_mlp.py (data)
    def dataset(case: dict, n: int, seed: int, in_service: np.ndarray | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Random injections (loads and generation scaled by 0.5 to 1.5 per bus, slack balancing) and their DC flows.

    Flows of an open line are zero, so the output always has one value per line of the intact network.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mask = np.ones(len(case['lines']), dtype=bool) if in_service is None else in_service
    h = ch27_ieee30.ptdf(case, mask)
    p = case['p'][None, :] * rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5, (n, case['n_bus']))
    p[:, 0] = -p[:, 1:].sum(axis=1)
    flows = np.zeros((n, len(case['lines'])))
    flows[:, mask] = p @ h.T
    return p[:, 1:], flows  # the slack injection is implied
    surrogate_mlp.py (model)
    def init_params(n_in: int, n_out: int, hidden: int, key) -> dict:
    """Two dense layers with tanh in between, Glorot-style scaling."""
    k1, k2 = jax.random.split(key)
    return {
        'w1': jax.random.normal(k1, (n_in, hidden)) * jnp.sqrt(2 / (n_in + hidden)),
        'b1': jnp.zeros(hidden),
        'w2': jax.random.normal(k2, (hidden, n_out)) * jnp.sqrt(2 / (hidden + n_out)),
        'b2': jnp.zeros(n_out),
    }


def predict(params: dict, x: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Normalized injections in, normalized flows out."""
    return jnp.tanh(x @ params['w1'] + params['b1']) @ params['w2'] + params['b2']


def train(
    x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, steps: int = STEPS, hidden: int = HIDDEN, seed: int = 0, lr: float = 3e-3
) -> dict:
    """Full-batch Adam on the mean squared error of the normalized targets; returns params and the scalers."""
    x_mean, x_std = x.mean(axis=0), x.std(axis=0) + 1e-9
    y_mean, y_std = y.mean(axis=0), y.std(axis=0) + 1e-9
    xn, yn = jnp.asarray((x - x_mean) / x_std), jnp.asarray((y - y_mean) / y_std)
    params = init_params(x.shape[1], y.shape[1], hidden, jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    opt = {k: (jnp.zeros_like(v), jnp.zeros_like(v)) for k, v in params.items()}

    def loss(p):
        return jnp.mean((predict(p, xn) - yn) ** 2)

    @jax.jit
    def step(p, m_v, t):
        g = jax.grad(loss)(p)
        new_p, new_mv = {}, {}
        for k in p:
            m = 0.9 * m_v[k][0] + 0.1 * g[k]
            v = 0.999 * m_v[k][1] + 0.001 * g[k] ** 2
            m_hat, v_hat = m / (1 - 0.9**t), v / (1 - 0.999**t)
            new_p[k] = p[k] - lr * m_hat / (jnp.sqrt(v_hat) + 1e-8)
            new_mv[k] = (m, v)
        return new_p, new_mv

    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        params, opt = step(params, opt, t)
    return {'params': params, 'x_mean': x_mean, 'x_std': x_std, 'y_mean': y_mean, 'y_std': y_std}


def surrogate_flows(model: dict, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Flows in MW from raw injections."""
    xn = (x - model['x_mean']) / model['x_std']
    return np.asarray(predict(model['params'], jnp.asarray(xn))) * model['y_std'] + model['y_mean']


def relative_error(pred: np.ndarray, true: np.ndarray, rating: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Mean absolute error per line divided by the line's rating, in percent."""
    return 100 * np.abs(pred - true).mean(axis=0) / rating

Take the states \(s_0\) = "secure" and \(s_1\) = "overloaded", the actions \(a_0\) = wait and \(a_1\) = switch, and the model of value_iteration.py: waiting keeps a secure grid secure with probability 0.9 and an overloaded one overloaded with probability 0.7; switching lands in the secure state with probability 0.8 from either state; the rewards are \(R(s_0, a_0) = 0\), \(R(s_1, a_0) = -1\) (one unit per overloaded step) and \(R(s, a_1) = -0.1\) (the switching cost). The Bellman optimality equation is

\[ V^*(s) = \max_{a} \Bigl[ R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, V^*(s') \Bigr], \]

that is, with \(\gamma = 0.9\),

\[ \begin{aligned} V^*(s_0) &= \max\bigl\{\, 0.9\,[0.9\,V^*(s_0) + 0.1\,V^*(s_1)],\;\; -0.1 + 0.9\,[0.8\,V^*(s_0) + 0.2\,V^*(s_1)] \,\bigr\}, \\ V^*(s_1) &= \max\bigl\{\, -1 + 0.9\,[0.3\,V^*(s_0) + 0.7\,V^*(s_1)],\;\; -0.1 + 0.9\,[0.8\,V^*(s_0) + 0.2\,V^*(s_1)] \,\bigr\}. \end{aligned} \]

Value iteration from \(V_0 = (0, 0)\): \(V_1 = (\max\{0, -0.1\}, \max\{-1, -0.1\}) = (0, -0.1)\); \(V_2 = (\max\{0.9 \cdot 0.1 \cdot (-0.1),\; -0.1 + 0.9 \cdot 0.2 \cdot (-0.1)\}, \max\{-1 + 0.9 \cdot 0.7 \cdot (-0.1),\; -0.1 + 0.9 \cdot 0.2 \cdot (-0.1)\}) = (-0.009, -0.118)\); \(V_3 = (-0.0179, -0.1277)\), and so on. The operator is a \(\gamma\)-contraction, so the error shrinks by at least 0.9 per step and the iteration converges, after 177 steps for a tolerance of \(10^{-10}\), to \(V^* = (-0.0989, -0.2088)\) with the policy "wait when secure, switch when overloaded". The check: solving \((I - \gamma P_\pi) V = R_\pi\) for that policy gives the same values, and the three other deterministic policies are worse: always wait \((-1.96, -4.13)\), always switch \((-1, -1)\), switch when secure and wait when overloaded \((-3.95, -5.58)\). The lesson for topology control is the structure of the answer: a small switching cost is worth paying as soon as the grid is overloaded, and not before.

value_iteration.py
def bellman_update(v: np.ndarray, gamma: float = GAMMA) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """One Bellman optimality step: Q(s, a) = R(a, s) + gamma sum_s' P(a, s, s') V(s'); returns max and argmax."""
    q = R + gamma * P @ v  # shape (action, state)
    return q.max(axis=0), q.argmax(axis=0)


def value_iteration(
    gamma: float = GAMMA, tol: float = 1e-10, max_iter: int = 10_000
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, list]:
    """Iterate from V = 0 until the largest change is below ``tol``; returns V*, the greedy policy and the history."""
    v = np.zeros(len(R[0]))
    history = [v.copy()]
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        v_new, policy = bellman_update(v, gamma)
        history.append(v_new.copy())
        if np.abs(v_new - v).max() < tol:
            return v_new, policy, history
        v = v_new
    raise RuntimeError('value iteration did not converge')


def policy_value(policy: np.ndarray, gamma: float = GAMMA) -> np.ndarray:
    """Exact value of a deterministic policy: solve (I - gamma P_pi) V = R_pi."""
    p_pi = np.array([P[a, s] for s, a in enumerate(policy)])
    r_pi = np.array([R[a, s] for s, a in enumerate(policy)])
    return np.linalg.solve(np.eye(len(policy)) - gamma * p_pi, r_pi)

docs.text:
Each of the 6 elements goes to busbar A or B: \(2^6 = 64\) labelled assignments. Swapping the two busbars gives the same electrical topology, so there are \(2^5 = 32\) distinct ones (every assignment and its mirror image, and no assignment is its own mirror). Not all are useful: an assignment that leaves one element alone on a busbar is a disconnection in disguise, and one that leaves a busbar empty is the unsplit configuration. ToOp's rule (both busbars keep at least two branches) leaves \(2^{5} - 6 - 1 = 25\) splits (Chapter 19, Exercise 8), 26 configurations with the unsplit one; Grid2Op's get_all_unitary_topologies_set applies the same "no busbar with a single element" rule and the enumeration in action_space.py gives 26 as well. For 14 such substations acting independently the joint space is \(64^{14} = 2^{84} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{25}\) labelled, \(32^{14} = 2^{70} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{21}\) up to symmetry and \(26^{14} \approx 6.5 \times 10^{19}\) with the validity rule: no table, no neural network output layer and no enumeration can cover it, which is the action-space problem of the chapter. The reductions: unitary actions change one substation per step (\(14 \times 25 = 350\) actions, a few hundred on case 14, the set the lab's greedy agent searches); per-station action sets with validity filters, which is what ToOp enumerates in preprocessing (n_actions_per_sub, with the bridge and isolation filters of Chapter 22) and then combines by evolution rather than enumeration; pruning by simulation, keeping the actions that ever helped (Lab step 3 kept one of eight); and hierarchical agents that first choose the substation, then the configuration.

action_space.py
def assignments(elements: int, busbars: int = 2) -> int:
    """Every assignment of ``elements`` to labelled ``busbars``."""
    return busbars**elements


def assignments_up_to_symmetry(elements: int) -> int:
    """Two busbars whose swap gives the same topology: half of the labelled assignments."""
    return 2 ** (elements - 1)


def toop_splits(elements: int) -> int:
    """ToOp's valid splits of a substation with ``elements`` branches: both busbars keep at least two branches.

    Choosing the branches of the second busbar with 2 <= |B| <= d - 2 gives 2^d - 2 - 2d labelled assignments, each
    split counted twice (B and its complement), so 2^(d-1) - d - 1 splits; the unsplit configuration is one more.
    """
    return 2 ** (elements - 1) - elements - 1


def unitary_topologies(elements: int) -> int:
    """Grid2Op's ``get_all_unitary_topologies_set`` for one substation, counted by enumeration.

    Every assignment up to the busbar swap in which no busbar holds exactly one element, the unsplit one included;
    equals ``toop_splits + 1`` because both rules drop the same configurations.
    """
    configurations = set()
    for code in range(2**elements):
        second = frozenset(i for i in range(elements) if code >> i & 1)
        if len(second) in (1, elements - 1):
            continue
        configurations.add(frozenset([frozenset(range(elements)) - second, second]))
    return len(configurations)


def joint(per_substation: int, substations: int = 14) -> int:
    """Joint action space of independent choices at every substation."""
    return per_substation**substations

flows_b(p, b) rebuilds \(B_f = \mathrm{diag}(b) A\) and \(B_{bus} = A^\top B_f\) from the susceptance vector, so jax.jacfwd(flows_b, argnums=1) is the \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\partial f_\ell / \partial b_k\). For the injections of the worked example (\(p = (-1, 0.5)\) at buses 1 and 2, flows \((0.6176, -0.3824, -0.1176)\) on lines 0–1, 1–2, 0–2):

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial b} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.0145 & -0.0360 & 0.0043 \\ 0.0145 & -0.0360 & 0.0043 \\ -0.0145 & 0.0360 & -0.0043 \end{pmatrix}. \]

The central difference \((f(b + h e_2) - f(b - h e_2)) / 2h\) with \(h = 10^{-6}\) reproduces the third column to \(2 \times 10^{-11}\). Two structural facts are visible. The rows of lines 0–1 and 1–2 are equal and the row of 0–2 is their negative: in a single loop a change of any susceptance only moves flow between the two paths from bus 0 to bus 2 (through bus 1, or direct), so the nodal balances are untouched, \(A^\top\, \partial f / \partial b_k = 0\). And \(\sum_k b_k\, \partial f_\ell / \partial b_k = 0\): the flows are homogeneous of degree zero in \(b\), scaling every reactance by the same factor changes nothing. For an operator the gradient says how the flows move when a line's reactance changes: a series reactor or a phase-shifting transformer on line 1–2 (making \(b_1\) smaller) pushes flow from the path through bus 1 to the direct line at 0.036 MW per unit of susceptance, and the sign tells which way. It is the continuous relaxation of switching: \(b_k \to 0\) opens the line, and the derivative at the current \(b\) is the first-order estimate of the effect, exact for the linear DC model only along the path, since the map \(b \mapsto f\) is nonlinear (a rational function). It does not give the gradient with respect to a binary status, and the linear extrapolation to \(b_k = 0\) is wrong when the line carries much flow, which is why ToOp evaluates discrete topologies exactly (LODF, BSDF) instead of following this gradient.

jax_susceptance.py
def flows_b(p_noslack: jnp.ndarray, b: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Branch flows for the injections ``p_noslack`` when the lines have susceptances ``b``."""
    b_f = b[:, None] * A
    b_bus = A.T @ b_f
    theta = jnp.concatenate([jnp.zeros(1), jnp.linalg.solve(b_bus[1:, 1:], p_noslack)])
    return b_f @ theta


def dflows_db(p_noslack: jnp.ndarray = P, b: jnp.ndarray = B) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Jacobian of the flows with respect to the susceptances, shape (line, line), forward mode."""
    return jax.jacfwd(flows_b, argnums=1)(p_noslack, b)


def finite_difference_column(k: int, h: float = 1e-6, p_noslack: jnp.ndarray = P, b: jnp.ndarray = B) -> np.ndarray:
    """Central difference of the flows with respect to ``b[k]``: one column of the Jacobian."""
    e = jnp.zeros(len(b)).at[k].set(h)
    return np.asarray((flows_b(p_noslack, b + e) - flows_b(p_noslack, b - e)) / (2 * h))

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
The GA is the Chapter 24 one: genomes of at most \(K = 2\) switched lines of IEEE 30 (loads scaled by 1.5 as in Chapter 27, exact fitness ch27_ieee30.overload_energy, islanding penalized), population 20, tournament of two, crossover by sampling from the union of the parents, mutation of one slot, elitist survival, 400 exact evaluations per run. The target is the exact optimum with two lines, 44.6 MW (lines 24–25 and 6–28, Chapter 27). The assisted variant generates five times as many offspring, scores them with a linear surrogate (one weight per line plus a bias, least squares on every genome evaluated so far) and evaluates exactly only the best 20 %. Over ten seeds:

GA runs reaching 44.7 MW exact evaluations to target (median, min, max) best value, median plain 6 of 10 75 (10, 313) 44.6 MW assisted 3 of 10 23 (10, 25) 155.8 MW

The surrogate does what it is supposed to when it is right: the three successful assisted runs reach the target in 23 exact evaluations against a median of 75. But it fails in seven runs out of ten, and those runs end far from the optimum (median best value 155.8 MW): the linear model assumes that switching effects are additive, and Chapter 24's Exercise 3 shows they are not (the pair 24–25 + 6–28 is much better than the sum of the two single switches would suggest). The surrogate therefore ranks the offspring by the single-line effects it has seen, steers the exact budget to combinations of individually good lines, and the population converges prematurely. This is the model-management problem of surrogate-assisted evolution (Jin 2011): a pre-screening model needs either a form that can represent interactions (pairwise terms, a Gaussian process, a GNN) or a fraction of the exact budget spent on offspring the surrogate ranks low, to keep correcting it. ToOp's two-stage design is the same idea with a physics model instead of a learned one: the DC solver is the cheap screen, exact for its own objective, and the AC stage the expensive evaluation; a learned surrogate would sit in front of the DC stage and inherit exactly this failure mode. A sign test on the ten paired runs gives no significant difference in evaluations-to-target because the assisted GA has only three successes; the honest summary is "faster when it works, and it works less often".

surrogate_ga.py
def features(genome: np.ndarray, n_line: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """One-hot of the switched lines plus a bias: the linear surrogate assumes additive switching effects."""
    f = np.zeros(n_line + 1)
    f[genome[genome < n_line]] = 1
    f[-1] = 1
    return f


def exact(case: dict, genome: np.ndarray, n_line: int) -> float:
    """N-1 overload energy of the switched lines of a genome, islanding capped at ``PENALTY``."""
    return min(ch27_ieee30.overload_energy(case, tuple(int(g) for g in genome if g < n_line)), PENALTY)


def random_genome(rng: np.random.Generator, n_line: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """One to ``K_MAX`` distinct lines, sorted and padded with the sentinel ``n_line``."""
    k = rng.integers(1, K_MAX + 1)
    g = np.full(K_MAX, n_line)
    g[:k] = rng.choice(n_line, k, replace=False)
    return np.sort(g)


def offspring(rng: np.random.Generator, parents: np.ndarray, n_line: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Tournament of two, crossover by sampling from the union of the parents, mutation of one slot."""
    a, b = parents[rng.integers(len(parents))], parents[rng.integers(len(parents))]
    pool = np.unique(np.concatenate([a[a < n_line], b[b < n_line]]))
    k = min(len(pool), rng.integers(1, K_MAX + 1)) if len(pool) else 0
    g = np.full(K_MAX, n_line)
    if k:
        g[:k] = rng.choice(pool, k, replace=False)
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        g[rng.integers(K_MAX)] = n_line if rng.random() < 0.3 else rng.integers(n_line)
    g = np.unique(g[g < n_line])
    return np.concatenate([g, np.full(K_MAX - len(g), n_line)])


def run(case: dict, seed: int, assisted: bool, budget: int = BUDGET, pop: int = POP) -> dict:
    """One GA run: best value, exact evaluations spent and the evaluation at which ``TARGET`` was first reached."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_line = len(case['lines'])
    genomes = np.array([random_genome(rng, n_line) for _ in range(pop)])
    values = np.array([exact(case, g, n_line) for g in genomes])
    archive_x, archive_y = [features(g, n_line) for g in genomes], list(values)
    used, reached = pop, None
    best = values.min()
    if best <= TARGET:
        reached = int(np.argmax(values <= TARGET)) + 1
    while used < budget:
        order = np.argsort(values)
        parents = genomes[order[: pop // 2]]
        if assisted:
            candidates = np.array([offspring(rng, parents, n_line) for _ in range(5 * pop)])
            w, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(np.array(archive_x), np.array(archive_y), rcond=None)
            scores = np.array([features(g, n_line) for g in candidates]) @ w
            children = candidates[np.argsort(scores)[:pop]]
        else:
            children = np.array([offspring(rng, parents, n_line) for _ in range(pop)])
        child_values = np.array([exact(case, g, n_line) for g in children])
        for g, v in zip(children, child_values, strict=True):
            used += 1
            archive_x.append(features(g, n_line))
            archive_y.append(v)
            if reached is None and v <= TARGET:
                reached = used
        genomes = np.vstack([genomes, children])
        values = np.concatenate([values, child_values])
        keep = np.argsort(values)[:pop]
        genomes, values = genomes[keep], values[keep]
        best = min(best, values.min())
    return {'best': float(best), 'evaluations': used, 'reached_at': reached}


def compare(case: dict, seeds: range = range(10)) -> dict[str, list[dict]]:
    """Plain against assisted GA on the same seeds."""
    return {'plain': [run(case, s, False) for s in seeds], 'assisted': [run(case, s, True) for s in seeds]}

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
Brief: should the TSO deploy a reinforcement-learning topology agent?

Recommendation. Not as a controller. Deploy it, if at all, as a proposal generator whose every suggestion is simulated before a human sees it, and measure it against the exhaustive one-step search and the rule base for a year before giving it more.

What it offers. A trained policy answers in milliseconds without simulating hundreds of actions (Lab step 2: the greedy search costs one power flow per candidate action per step; the agent costs a table lookup or a forward pass), and the L2RPN results show agents that keep case-14 and case-118 grids alive through days the do-nothing baseline does not survive.

Distribution shift. The policy is only as good as the days it has seen. Training uses historical or synthetic chronics; the next heat wave, a new wind farm, a different maintenance pattern or a market change produces states outside that distribution, and a table or network gives a confident answer there with no warning (Lab step 3: the agent cannot tell when its table is wrong). Retraining lags the grid; the lag is where the risk lives.

Rare contingencies. Reinforcement learning optimizes expected return. An N-1 event that happens once a year is a negligible part of the return unless the reward is shaped to make it dominant, and then the agent learns a different, more conservative behaviour that costs every day. ToOp's overload_energy_n_1 is an N-1 metric by construction; an RL reward that is not will leave contingency security to luck.

Guarantees. None: no feasibility guarantee (the proposed topology may island the grid, as four of the eight actions of the small environment do), no optimality, no bound on how far the policy is from the best action, and no explanation. A MILP gives bounds, ToOp gives a validated metric per proposal, the agent gives a number.

Simulation checks. The non-negotiable element. Every proposal is run through obs.simulate or an AC N-1 analysis before it reaches the operator, and rejected when it does not improve the validated metrics. This turns the agent into a candidate generator, which is a role it can fill well, and removes the only failure mode that matters, a wrong action executed. The cost is one or a few simulations per step, which the agent was supposed to save; the saving is then the difference between simulating hundreds of actions and simulating one.

How ToOp validates the proposals. ToOp's AC stage is exactly this check: the agent's topology is applied to the grid model, the AC N-1 is run, and evaluate_acceptance compares non-convergence, overload energy and critical branches with the unsplit grid (Chapter 28; mind its zero-baseline trap). An agent's proposal can also seed ToOp's DC repertoire, where it competes with the evolutionary candidates and is kept only if its cell has nothing better; the operator then reads one orao_summary.json whatever the source of the topology.

Interpretability and the human in the loop. Operators act on proposals they can explain to the next shift. Present the agent's output as "topology X, validated: overload −40 %, no new critical branch, 3 switch operations", never as "the agent says X". Keep the rule base as the sanity check and the exhaustive search as the reference the agent must beat on the same seeds (Chapter 26) before any scope is widened.

docs.title: Chapter 30. Scientific Python
docs.text:
Weeks: 3.5 · Semester: 1 · Prerequisites: none

Why it matters for ToOp

Every lab in this plan is in Python, and ToOp's preprocessing, backends and data handling use NumPy, SciPy sparse, NetworkX, pandas and Polars with full type annotations.

  • Grid backends. ToOp reads grids through two open-source power system libraries behind one abstract class: BackendInterface (interfaces/backend.py) with PandaPowerBackend (dc_solver/preprocess/pandapower/pandapower_backend.py) and PowsyblBackend (dc_solver/preprocess/powsybl/powsybl_backend.py). The AC stage calls pandapower or pypowsybl and returns Polars or pandas frames (contingency/ac_loadflow_service/ac_loadflow_service.py).
  • Tests. Six packages under packages/, each with a pytest suite and a 90% coverage gate (.coveragerc). Notebooks in notebooks/ are executed as tests.
  • Git workflow. Trunk-based development with squash merges; pull request titles must follow Conventional Commits (.github/workflows/validate_pr_title.yaml), and local checks run through pre-commit (.pre-commit-config.yaml). See docs/contribution_guide.md.
  • Environments. Dependencies are managed by uv (uv.lock); on Windows ToOp runs in a Linux container (Chapter 0).

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Python: functions, classes, dataclasses, type hints, modules and packages.
  • NumPy: arrays, broadcasting, fancy indexing, einsum; SciPy sparse matrices and solvers.
  • NetworkX graphs; pandas and Polars data frames (the same table in both; lazy vs eager evaluation in Polars).
  • matplotlib: line plots, histograms, heat maps of a matrix, saving figures for a report.
  • Jupyter: notebooks vs scripts, kernels, restart-and-run-all as a reproducibility check, clearing outputs before a commit.
  • Power system libraries as black boxes: load a test grid in pandapower and pypowsybl, inspect element tables (buses, lines, transformers, generators, loads) as data frames, run an AC and a DC power flow, read the result tables. The theory comes later (Chapter 15, Chapter 16).
  • git: commits, branches, merges, remotes, forks and pull requests; Conventional Commits messages; pre-commit hooks.
  • Virtual environments and uv (uv sync, uv run, lock files); testing with pytest (fixtures, parametrization, markers, coverage).
  • Containers: image vs container, bind mounts and named volumes, docker compose, and why ToOp's Windows path is a Linux container (revisits Chapter 0).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Both libraries ship test grids and store every element type as a data frame. Treat the solvers as black boxes for now; only the data handling matters here (checked with pandapower 3.1 and pypowsybl 1.15, the versions in ToOp's lock file, and with pandapower 3.5 and pypowsybl 1.16, the versions of the course environment).

two_libraries.py
"""The same two operations in pandapower and pypowsybl: load a case, run a power flow, read a result table."""

import pandapower as pp
import pandapower.networks as pn
import pypowsybl as pypo


def pandapower_case57():
    """IEEE 57-bus case: element counts, then AC and DC from-end active flows per line (pandas Series)."""
    net = pn.case57()  # element tables are pandas DataFrames
    counts = (len(net.bus), len(net.line), len(net.trafo))
    pp.runpp(net)  # AC power flow; results land in net.res_line, net.res_bus, ...
    ac_p = net.res_line.p_from_mw.copy()
    pp.rundcpp(net)  # DC power flow overwrites the same result tables
    dc_p = net.res_line.p_from_mw
    return counts, ac_p, dc_p


def pypowsybl_ieee14():
    """IEEE 14-bus case in pypowsybl: the load flow status and the line results p1, i1."""
    n = pypo.network.create_ieee14()
    result = pypo.loadflow.run_ac(n)
    lines = n.get_lines()[['p1', 'i1']]  # results are columns of the element tables
    return result[0].status, lines


def main() -> None:
    """Run both and print the headline numbers."""
    counts, ac_p, dc_p = pandapower_case57()
    print(counts)
    print((ac_p - dc_p).abs().max())  # largest AC-DC difference of a line flow, MW
    status, lines = pypowsybl_ieee14()
    print(status)  # ComponentStatus.CONVERGED
    print(lines.head())


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

Note the two different styles: pandapower writes results into res_* tables of a mutable net object, while pypowsybl updates the network and exposes results as columns of get_lines(), get_buses() and so on.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: install ToOp, run a package's tests, read a reference implementation

Tools: the ToOp container from Chapter 0 (or, on Linux, macOS or WSL, a host install with uv sync --all-groups); pytest; git; Jupyter + NumPy + pandas + matplotlib; pandapower and pypowsybl.

  1. Environment. Use the Chapter 0 container, or install on a host with uv sync --all-groups. Explain in two sentences where the code (/app, a bind mount of your checkout) and the environment (/opt/venv, a named volume) live in the container, and why the image keeps them apart ("Why the virtualenv is not in the repository folder" in the course fork's docker/README.md).

  2. Tests. Run one package's suite, uv run pytest packages/interfaces_pkg/tests -q, then the CI-style run with coverage (one command):

    UV_PROJECT=packages/interfaces_pkg uv run pytest packages/interfaces_pkg/tests \
  --cov=packages/interfaces_pkg/src --cov-config=.coveragerc

    Find the coverage threshold in .coveragerc and the three least-covered modules in the report.

  3. Reference implementation. Read packages/dc_solver_pkg/tests/numpy_reference.py end to end as a piece of Python, not yet as mathematics: list the functions, the jaxtyping shape annotations (Float[np.ndarray, " n_branches n_nodes"]), the numpy-style docstrings, where fancy indexing and broadcasting are used, and which errors are raised. Find one test that imports it (packages/dc_solver_pkg/tests/jax/test_lodf.py). You will return to its mathematics in Chapter 17.

  4. Black-box power flow. In a notebook, load pandapower's case57, run AC and DC power flows, put the two p_from_mw columns side by side in a pandas and a Polars frame, and plot a histogram of their difference with matplotlib. Save the notebook with outputs cleared, and commit it on a branch of your own course repository with a Conventional Commits message.

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

Known discrepancy: the reference implementation's docstrings have drifted

In packages/dc_solver_pkg/tests/numpy_reference.py (lab step 3) the module docstring cites a bsdf_check_split function "also used to pre-filter the action set" that no longer exists in the file, and the comments of calc_lodf describe shapes (M,) and (E, M) while its signature takes a single int, a trace of an earlier vectorized version. Read the code, not the docstrings, when the two disagree.

docs.title: Chapter 30 – Solutions
docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 30. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: two_libraries.py (the worked example), incidence.py, sparse_vs_dense.py, ieee14_flows.py, case57_ac_dc.py and loading_query.py, each with a test_*.py next to it. Every script prints the numbers quoted below when run from the src folder (python incidence.py, and so on). The numbers come from the course environment (pandapower 3.5, pypowsybl 1.16, NumPy 2.4, SciPy 1.18, Python 3.14 on Windows); the Polars parts were run with ToOp's environment (Polars 1.42, ToOp commit ba1874e), which is the one that has Polars. Lab steps 1–2 and Exercise 6 quote the output of commands run in the ToOp container, given with each solution.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. Environment. The code lives in /app, a bind mount of your checkout on the host, so a file edited on Windows is the file the container imports, with no copy and no rebuild (the six packages/* are installed editable). The environment lives in /opt/venv, on the named volume toop-venv, because the Dockerfile sets UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv (and puts /opt/venv/bin first on PATH). They are kept apart because a Linux virtual environment under /app/.venv would collide with a .venv created natively on Windows and would push thousands of small files across the WSL2 file-system bridge on every import; on the named volume it stays on the Linux side and survives docker compose down (docker compose down -v deletes it, which is the documented repair when it gets into a bad state). The facts are from the course fork's docker/README.md ("Why the virtualenv is not in the repository folder") and docker/Dockerfile, and the container confirms them (see Exercise 6): /opt/venv/bin/python is a symbolic link to the image's /usr/local/bin/python3.11, so the environment holds the packages and borrows the interpreter, and the environment's 3.0 GB (du -sh /opt/venv) never touch the Windows side.

  2. Tests. The threshold is in the [report] section of .coveragerc: fail_under = 90, with show_missing = true (the report lists the uncovered line numbers) and sort = cover (the report is sorted by coverage, so the least-covered modules are at the top of the table and the three you are asked for are its first three rows). The plain run is uv run pytest packages/interfaces_pkg/tests -q; the CI-style run adds --cov=packages/interfaces_pkg/src --cov-config=.coveragerc, with UV_PROJECT=packages/interfaces_pkg so that uv run resolves the package's own project.

    Both runs were made in the course image toop-course:cpu (built from the course fork's docker/Dockerfile), with a checkout of ToOp commit ba1874e bind-mounted read-only at /app, JAX on the CPU, and Docker Desktop's VM at 16 CPUs and 13.6 GB, shared with other ToOp containers during the runs. From Git Bash:

    cd ToOp
MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 docker run --rm --shm-size=2gb -e COVERAGE_FILE=/tmp/.coverage \
  -v "$(pwd -W):/app:ro" -w /app toop-course:cpu \

    case57_ac_dc.py
    """AC and DC from-end flows of pandapower's case57 side by side, in pandas and Polars, with a histogram (Lab 4)."""

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from two_libraries import pandapower_case57


def side_by_side() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per line of case57: AC flow, DC flow and their difference, all in MW at the from end."""
    _, ac_p, dc_p = pandapower_case57()
    df = pd.DataFrame({'ac_p_from_mw': ac_p, 'dc_p_from_mw': dc_p})
    df['difference_mw'] = df['ac_p_from_mw'] - df['dc_p_from_mw']
    return df


def to_polars(df: pd.DataFrame):
    """The same table as a Polars frame (Polars is in ToOp's environment, not in the course one)."""
    import polars as pl

    return pl.from_pandas(df.reset_index(names='line'))


def histogram(df: pd.DataFrame, bins: int = 20) -> plt.Figure:
    """Histogram of the AC - DC difference of the from-end flows."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.hist(df['difference_mw'], bins=bins)
    ax.set_xlabel('AC - DC from-end flow [MW]')
    ax.set_ylabel('lines')
    ax.set_title('case57: where the DC approximation is off')
    return fig


def main() -> None:
    """Print the summary of the difference and the histogram counts that the figure shows."""
    df = side_by_side()
    print(df.round(2).head())
    print(df['difference_mw'].describe().round(2))
    worst = df['difference_mw'].abs().idxmax()
    print(f'largest gap: line {worst}, AC {df.ac_p_from_mw[worst]:.1f} MW, DC {df.dc_p_from_mw[worst]:.1f} MW')
    counts, edges = np.histogram(df['difference_mw'], bins=10)
    print('histogram counts:', counts.tolist())
    print('bin edges [MW]:', np.round(edges, 1).tolist())
    try:
        print(to_polars(df).head(3))
    except ImportError:
        print("Polars is not installed in this environment; run the script with ToOp's interpreter to see it")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text:
Two fancy-indexed assignments build the whole matrix: a[rows, from_bus] = 1.0 and a[rows, to_bus] = -1.0, with rows = np.arange(n_branch). Each row has exactly one \(+1\) and one \(-1\), so it sums to zero, and \(A^\top A\) is the Laplacian (Chapter 2): for the four-bus, five-branch grid of the Chapter 31 worked example its diagonal is the degree sequence \((2, 3, 3, 2)\). The test is parametrized over a three-bus path, a triangle and that four-bus grid, and also checks the Laplacian of the triangle and the two ValueErrors. uv run pytest docs/part-5-computing/ch30-scientific-python/src/test_incidence.py reports 5 passed (three parametrized cases plus two tests).

incidence.py
"""Branch-bus incidence matrix of a graph as a type-annotated NumPy function (Chapter 30, Exercise 1)."""

import numpy as np


def incidence_matrix(from_bus: np.ndarray, to_bus: np.ndarray, n_bus: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Dense incidence matrix with one row per branch: +1 at the from bus, -1 at the to bus.

    Args:
        from_bus: Integer array with the from bus of every branch.
        to_bus: Integer array with the to bus of every branch, same length.
        n_bus: Number of buses, which fixes the number of columns.

    Returns:
        Float array of shape (n_branch, n_bus). Every row sums to zero because each branch leaves one bus and
        enters another; A.T @ A is the graph Laplacian (Chapter 2).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the two bus arrays differ in length or a branch connects a bus to itself.
    """
    from_bus, to_bus = np.asarray(from_bus, dtype=int), np.asarray(to_bus, dtype=int)
    if from_bus.shape != to_bus.shape:
        raise ValueError('from_bus and to_bus must have the same length')
    if np.any(from_bus == to_bus):
        raise ValueError('a branch cannot start and end at the same bus')
    rows = np.arange(len(from_bus))
    a = np.zeros((len(from_bus), n_bus))
    a[rows, from_bus] = 1.0
    a[rows, to_bus] = -1.0  # fancy indexing: one assignment per branch, no Python loop
    return a


def main() -> None:
    """The four-bus, five-branch grid of the Chapter 31 worked example and its Laplacian."""
    a = incidence_matrix([0, 0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 2, 2, 3, 3], 4)
    print(a)
    print('row sums:', a.sum(axis=1))
    print('Laplacian A.T @ A:')
    print(a.T @ a)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
test_incidence.py
import numpy as np
import pytest
from incidence import incidence_matrix

GRAPHS = [
    ([0, 1], [1, 2], 3),  # a path of three buses
    ([0, 1, 2], [1, 2, 0], 3),  # a triangle
    ([0, 0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 2, 2, 3, 3], 4),  # the four-bus grid of Chapter 31
]


@pytest.mark.parametrize(('from_bus', 'to_bus', 'n_bus'), GRAPHS)
def test_every_row_sums_to_zero(from_bus, to_bus, n_bus):
    a = incidence_matrix(from_bus, to_bus, n_bus)
    assert a.shape == (len(from_bus), n_bus)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(a.sum(axis=1), np.zeros(len(from_bus)))


def test_triangle_laplacian():
    a = incidence_matrix([0, 1, 2], [1, 2, 0], 3)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(a.T @ a, [[2, -1, -1], [-1, 2, -1], [-1, -1, 2]])


def test_bad_input_raises():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match='same length'):
        incidence_matrix([0, 1], [1], 2)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match='same bus'):
        incidence_matrix([0, 1], [1, 1], 2)

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
random_symmetric(n) draws scipy.sparse.random(n, n, density=0.02), symmetrizes it with \(M + M^\top\) and adds \(2n I\) so the matrix is strictly diagonally dominant, hence never singular; at \(n = 200\) it has 1 766 nonzeros of 40 000. The two solvers agree to \(3.9 \times 10^{-18}\). timings() takes the best of three timeit runs of spsolve and of np.linalg.solve(a.toarray(), b) (the conversion is part of the dense route). On the machine that wrote this (CPU timings, two runs, so you see how much they move):

\(n\) spsolve [ms] dense solve [ms] dense / sparse 200 1.0–1.1 36–66 34–67 400 5.7–6.5 162–192 25–33 800 33–36 362–533 10–16 1600 276–296 542–988 2.0–3.3 3200 2 077–2 093 935–1 076 0.5

On log-log axes the dense curve is a line of slope about 3 (\(n^3\) flops) once \(n\) is large enough for the BLAS overhead to be negligible, while the sparse curve is steeper, close to slope 3 as well between 800 and 3200: the LU factors of a random sparse matrix fill in almost completely, so the sparse solver ends up doing dense work with sparse bookkeeping and the dense solver overtakes it near \(n \approx 2000\)–3000. Grid matrices are different: a power system's \(B\) matrix is close to planar, and a fill-reducing ordering keeps its factors sparse, which is why SciPy sparse (and ToOp's preprocessing) stay far ahead on real grids. The lesson of the plot is that "sparse" is a property of the pattern, not of the count of zeros.

sparse_vs_dense.py
"""Sparse against dense linear solves on random symmetric matrices, timed with timeit (Chapter 30, Exercise 2)."""

import timeit
from functools import partial

import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve


def random_symmetric(n: int, density: float = 0.02, seed: int = 0) -> sp.csc_matrix:
    """Random sparse symmetric matrix, made strictly diagonally dominant so that it is never singular.

    Args:
        n: Matrix size.
        density: Fraction of nonzero entries of the random part before symmetrization.
        seed: Seed of the NumPy generator.

    Returns:
        The matrix M + M.T + 2 n I in CSC format, the format spsolve prefers.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    m = sp.random(n, n, density=density, format='csc', random_state=rng)
    return (m + m.T + 2 * n * sp.identity(n, format='csc')).tocsc()


def dense_solve(a: sp.csc_matrix, b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Solve a x = b with the dense LAPACK solver of NumPy, conversion to a dense array included."""
    return np.linalg.solve(a.toarray(), b)


def solve_both(a: sp.csc_matrix, b: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Solve a x = b with the sparse LU of spsolve and with the dense solver."""
    return spsolve(a, b), dense_solve(a, b)


def timings(sizes: tuple[int, ...], density: float = 0.02, repeat: int = 3) -> list[tuple[int, float, float]]:
    """Best-of-repeat run time in seconds of spsolve and of numpy.linalg.solve for each size.

    The dense timing includes the conversion to a dense array, since that is what the dense route costs when the
    matrix arrives sparse. The sparse run time grows roughly with the fill-in of the LU factors; the dense one
    grows as n**3.
    """
    out = []
    for n in sizes:
        a = random_symmetric(n, density)
        b = np.ones(n)
        t_sparse = min(timeit.repeat(partial(spsolve, a, b), number=1, repeat=repeat))
        t_dense = min(timeit.repeat(partial(dense_solve, a, b), number=1, repeat=repeat))
        out.append((n, t_sparse, t_dense))
    return out


def main() -> None:
    """Check the two solutions agree at n = 200, then print the timing table for the plot."""
    a = random_symmetric(200)
    x_sparse, x_dense = solve_both(a, np.ones(200))
    print(
        f'n = 200: {a.nnz} nonzeros of {200 * 200}, max |x_sparse - x_dense| = {np.abs(x_sparse - x_dense).max():.2e}'
    )
    print(f'{"n":>6s} {"spsolve [ms]":>14s} {"dense solve [ms]":>18s} {"dense/sparse":>13s}')
    for n, t_sparse, t_dense in timings((200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200)):
        print(f'{n:6d} {1e3 * t_sparse:14.2f} {1e3 * t_dense:18.2f} {t_dense / t_sparse:13.1f}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

ieee14_flows.py
"""AC and DC active line flows of pypowsybl's IEEE 14 case, sorted by magnitude (Chapter 30, Exercise 3)."""

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import pypowsybl as pypo


def _converged(results) -> None:
    """Stop if the load flow of the main synchronous component did not converge."""
    if results[0].status != pypo.loadflow.ComponentStatus.CONVERGED:
        raise RuntimeError(f'load flow did not converge: {results[0].status}')


def line_flows() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Active power at the from end of every line after an AC and after a DC load flow.

    Returns:
        Frame indexed by line id with the columns ``p1_ac`` and ``p1_dc`` (MW), sorted by decreasing |p1_ac|.
        The DC run overwrites the same ``p1`` column of ``get_lines()``, which is why the AC values are copied
        first.
    """
    n = pypo.network.create_ieee14()
    _converged(pypo.loadflow.run_ac(n))
    p1_ac = n.get_lines()['p1'].copy()
    _converged(pypo.loadflow.run_dc(n))
    p1_dc = n.get_lines()['p1']
    df = pd.DataFrame({'p1_ac': p1_ac, 'p1_dc': p1_dc})
    return df.reindex(df['p1_ac'].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)


def bar_chart(df: pd.DataFrame) -> plt.Figure:
    """Two bar series side by side, one line per group of bars, in the order of the frame."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
    pos = range(len(df))
    ax.bar([p - 0.2 for p in pos], df['p1_ac'], width=0.4, label='AC')
    ax.bar([p + 0.2 for p in pos], df['p1_dc'], width=0.4, label='DC')
    ax.set_xticks(list(pos), df.index, rotation=90)
    ax.set_ylabel('p1 [MW]')
    ax.set_title('IEEE 14: active power at the from end of every line')
    ax.legend()
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig


def main() -> None:
    """Print the sorted table and the largest AC-DC gap."""
    df = line_flows()
    print(df.round(2).to_string())
    gap = (df['p1_ac'] - df['p1_dc']).abs()
    print(f'largest |AC - DC| gap: {gap.max():.2f} MW on {gap.idxmax()}; mean gap {gap.mean():.2f} MW')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
