docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
res_line_case57() joins from_bus and to_bus from net.line onto net.res_line (63 lines). The pandas version is eager, two statements: a boolean mask with the median, then groupby('from_bus')['loading_percent'].mean(). The Polars version is one lazy expression chain: pl.from_pandas(...).lazy().filter(pl.col('loading_percent') > pl.col('loading_percent').median()).group_by('from_bus').agg(pl.col('loading_percent').mean()).sort('from_bus').collect(). Nothing is computed until collect(), the median is an expression inside the filter rather than a value computed beforehand, and group_by does not sort its output (pandas does), hence the explicit sort. Results: the median loading is 0.17 %, 31 of the 63 lines are above it, they leave from 23 distinct buses, and the five highest means are from bus 7 (1.78 %), 0 (1.13 %), 1 (0.99 %), 6 (0.84 %) and 13 (0.67 %). The Polars frame holds the same 23 rows to floating-point precision (test_loading_query.py, run with ToOp's interpreter; the from_bus column comes back as u32, pandas keeps it as int64). The percentages are tiny because the MATPOWER case57 ships no line ratings and pandapower fills max_i_ka with a very large value: the exercise is about the query, and the ranking is what the numbers mean.

loading_query.py
"""The same query on pandapower's case57 line results in pandas and in Polars (Chapter 30, Exercise 4).

Keep the lines whose loading is above the median, then average the loading per from bus.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

import pandapower as pp
import pandapower.networks as pn

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    import pandas as pd


def res_line_case57() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """``net.res_line`` of case57 after an AC power flow, with the ``from_bus`` of every line joined in."""
    net = pn.case57()
    pp.runpp(net)
    return net.res_line.join(net.line[['from_bus', 'to_bus']])


def pandas_query(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Mean loading per from bus of the lines above the median loading, eager pandas style."""
    above = df[df['loading_percent'] > df['loading_percent'].median()]
    return above.groupby('from_bus')['loading_percent'].mean()


def polars_query(df: pd.DataFrame):
    """The same result with a Polars LazyFrame: nothing runs until ``collect()``."""
    import polars as pl

    query = (
        pl.from_pandas(df.reset_index(names='line'))
        .lazy()
        .filter(pl.col('loading_percent') > pl.col('loading_percent').median())
        .group_by('from_bus')
        .agg(pl.col('loading_percent').mean())
        .sort('from_bus')
    )
    return query.collect()


def main() -> None:
    """Print the median, the pandas result and, when Polars is installed, the Polars result."""
    df = res_line_case57()
    print(f'{len(df)} lines, median loading {df["loading_percent"].median():.2f} %')
    result = pandas_query(df)
    print(f'{len(result)} from buses with at least one line above the median; the five most loaded:')
    print(result.sort_values(ascending=False).head().round(2).to_string())
    try:
        print(polars_query(df).head())
    except ImportError:
        print("Polars is not installed in this environment; run the script with ToOp's interpreter to see it")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

pre-commit install
printf 'x = 1   \n' > bad.py && git add bad.py .pre-commit-config.yaml && git commit -m "feat: add bad file"
# trailing-whitespace....Failed  -  hook id: trailing-whitespace  -  files were modified by this hook

The hook strips the spaces and fails the commit; git add bad.py and commit again to get it through. ToOp's validate_pr_title.yaml installs commitizen and runs cz check --message "$PR_TITLE", and the course environment has the same tool, so the question can be settled without a pull request:

Title python -m commitizen check --message ... Fix/some slug rejected: does not match the pattern (build|bump|chore|ci|docs|feat|fix|perf|refactor|revert|style|test)(\(\S+\))?!?: ... fix: handle empty action set Commit validation: successful! update docs rejected, same pattern (no type, no colon)

Fix/some slug is what GitHub proposes for a branch named fix/some-slug with more than one commit (type capitalised, colon dropped), so a branch of several commits needs its title typed by hand, or the squash merge lands a subject the convention rejects.

docs.title: Exercise 6
docs.text:
Run in the course image toop-course:cpu (built from the course fork's docker/Dockerfile) with ToOp commit ba1874e mounted at /app. Both commands print /opt/venv/bin/python: the Dockerfile sets UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv and puts /opt/venv/bin first on PATH, so the shell's python and uv run's interpreter are the same file. which -a python also lists /usr/local/bin/python, the image's own interpreter, which is what a stock python:3.11-slim image without that PATH change would answer; and readlink -f /opt/venv/bin/python gives /usr/local/bin/python3.11: the environment is a folder of packages around the image's interpreter.

To see what a restart keeps without touching the compose project, the same experiment can be made with two docker run --rm containers (each one deleted on exit, as docker compose down deletes its container) that share a named volume at /opt/venv, as the compose file mounts toop-venv. From Git Bash, in the ToOp checkout:

docker volume create try-venv
for i in 1 2; do
  MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 docker run --rm -v "$(pwd -W):/app:ro" -v try-venv:/opt/venv -w /app toop-course:cpu \
    bash -c 'ls /opt/venv/marker.txt /root/marker.txt; date > /opt/venv/marker.txt; date > /root/marker.txt'
done
docker volume rm try-venv

The first container starts with an empty volume, which Docker seeds from the image's /opt/venv; its entrypoint's uv sync rebuilds the seven editable ToOp packages (Prepared 7 packages in 29.85s) and ls finds neither marker. The second container prints Checked 312 packages in 60ms (the rebuilt packages are on the volume) and finds /opt/venv/marker.txt but not /root/marker.txt. So, after docker compose down and docker compose up -d:

  • /opt/venv survives: it is the named volume toop-venv, which down leaves alone (only down -v removes volumes). The entrypoint still runs uv sync at every start, but it finds nothing to do (60 ms above).
  • /app survives for a different reason: it is a bind mount, the files live on the host.
  • Everything written elsewhere in the container's file system (a pip install into the image's Python, a file under /root or /tmp, an apt-get install) lives in the container's writable layer, which down deletes together with the container; up -d starts a fresh container from the image, so that state is gone.

The rule: state you want to keep goes in a volume or a bind mount, and the image is rebuilt, never patched in place.

docs.title: Chapter 31. JAX and GPU computing fundamentals
docs.text:
Weeks: 2 · Semester: 3 · Prerequisites: Chapter 30

Why it matters for ToOp

The solver and the optimizer are JAX programs, and every JAX idea in this chapter appears in them:

  • jax.jit with static and traced arguments (dc_solver/jax/topology_looper.py).
  • jax.vmap to batch over topologies, injections and outages (dc_solver/jax/compute_batch.py).
  • lax.scan, lax.cond, lax.fori_loop and jnp.where instead of Python control flow, and fixed shapes with padding sentinels so variable-size topologies fit one compiled program (dc_solver/jax/batching.py).
  • Equinox pytrees, jaxtyping shape annotations on every array, explicit PRNG keys in the genetic operators (optimizer/dc/genetic_functions/), forced float64, and pmap for multiple GPUs.

This chapter teaches these tools on small, self-contained programs. How ToOp uses them, and the traps specific to its data structures, are the subject of Chapter 32.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Functional programming: pure functions, immutability, functional array updates (x.at[i].set(v)).
  • Tracing and compilation with XLA: abstract values (shape and dtype), jaxprs, the compilation cache; static vs traced arguments (static_argnums, static_argnames); what triggers recompilation (new shapes or dtypes, new static values, a new function object such as a fresh lambda); jax.no_tracing() as a guard in tests.
  • Automatic vectorization with vmap (in_axes, out_axes); writing the single-case function first.
  • Control flow under jit: jnp.where, lax.cond, lax.scan, lax.while_loop, lax.fori_loop with a traced bound; fixed shapes, padding and out-of-bounds sentinels read with x.at[idx].get(mode="fill", fill_value=...); why Python if on a traced value raises ConcretizationTypeError (in recent JAX, its subclass TracerBoolConversionError).
  • Pseudo-random numbers: explicit keys, jax.random.split, reproducibility.
  • Pytrees; Equinox modules (eqx.Module, eqx.field(static=True)); jaxtyping shape annotations and runtime checking with beartype.
  • Numerics: float32 by default vs jax_enable_x64 (revisits Chapter 4 with a GPU cost attached); integer widths.
  • GPU concepts: data parallelism, host–device transfer, asynchronous dispatch and how to time it, memory preallocation, batch sizing and out-of-memory errors, float32 vs float64 speed on consumer cards; pmap over several devices (overview).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Predict, for a given sequence of calls, which calls of a jitted function compile and which hit the cache, and confirm the prediction with jax.no_tracing().
  • Rewrite a NumPy routine that uses Python loops and branches as a jitted, vmapped JAX function with fixed shapes.
  • Measure compile time and steady-state run time separately on CPU and GPU, and explain when a GPU pays off.
  • Annotate arrays with jaxtyping and catch a shape or dtype error at runtime.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
N-1 screening with line outage distribution factors (Chapter 17): for the outage of branch \(b\) from bus \(f_b\) to bus \(t_b\),

\[ \mathrm{LODF}_{a,b} = \frac{\mathrm{PTDF}_{a,f_b}-\mathrm{PTDF}_{a,t_b}}{1-\left(\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,f_b}-\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,t_b}\right)}, \qquad \mathrm{LODF}_{b,b} = -1, \qquad f^{(b)} = f^{0} + \mathrm{LODF}_{\cdot,b}\, f^{0}_{b}. \]

Write the function for one outage, with no Python branching on array values, then let vmap add the batch axis and jit compile the whole batch:

n1_screen.py
"""N-1 screening of every branch outage at once with jit and vmap, with no exceptions inside (Chapter 31)."""

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

jax.config.update('jax_enable_x64', True)  # before creating any array


def ptdf_matrix(from_bus: jnp.ndarray, to_bus: jnp.ndarray, x: jnp.ndarray, n_bus: int, slack: int = 0):
    """PTDF (branches x buses) with the slack column at zero."""
    m = len(from_bus)
    a = jnp.zeros((m, n_bus)).at[jnp.arange(m), from_bus].set(1.0).at[jnp.arange(m), to_bus].set(-1.0)
    bf = a / x[:, None]
    bbus = a.T @ bf
    keep = jnp.arange(n_bus) != slack
    sol = jnp.linalg.solve(bbus[1:, 1:], bf[:, 1:].T).T  # slack 0 is the first bus
    return jnp.where(keep[None, :], jnp.concatenate([jnp.zeros((m, 1)), sol], axis=1), 0.0)


def n1_flows(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, outage):
    """Flows after the outage of one branch, plus a flag that is False when the outage islands the grid."""
    f0 = ptdf @ p
    col = ptdf[:, from_bus[outage]] - ptdf[:, to_bus[outage]]
    denom = 1.0 - col[outage]  # zero exactly for a bridge
    lodf = jnp.where(jnp.arange(ptdf.shape[0]) == outage, -1.0, col / denom)
    return f0 + lodf * f0[outage], jnp.abs(denom) > 1e-11  # flows and a success flag, no exception


screen = jax.jit(jax.vmap(n1_flows, in_axes=(None, None, None, None, 0)))


def main() -> None:
    """Screen a four-bus grid: the N-1 flow matrix has one row per outage."""
    from_bus, to_bus = jnp.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 2]), jnp.array([1, 2, 2, 3, 3])
    x = jnp.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.1, 0.2, 0.1])
    p = jnp.array([100.0, 0.0, 0.0, -100.0])
    ptdf = ptdf_matrix(from_bus, to_bus, x, 4)
    flows, ok = screen(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, jnp.arange(len(from_bus)))  # shape (n_branch, n_branch)
    print(jnp.round(flows, 1))
    print(ok)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

Three habits to notice. The bridge case returns a flag instead of raising, because a compiled batch cannot stop halfway. The outage index is a traced array, so a new outage set of the same length reuses the compiled program; passing it as a Python tuple in static_argnums would compile once per distinct tuple. And GPU timings must wait for the result (jax.block_until_ready or converting to NumPy) and must exclude the first call, which includes compilation.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
Lab: port N-1 screening from NumPy to JAX

Tools: Jupyter + NumPy + JAX + matplotlib, in the ToOp container (Chapter 0), which already has JAX, pandapower, jaxtyping and beartype; the toop-gpu service if an NVIDIA GPU is available.

  1. Port. Take your NumPy PTDF/LODF code from the Chapter 17 lab. Write n1_flows for a single outage as in the worked example, vmap it over all branches, and jit it. Check that the result matches your NumPy screening to 1e-9 on IEEE 14 and 118.
  2. Second batch axis. On IEEE 118, vmap again over a batch of 100 random injection vectors (generated with jax.random.split keys), so one call returns an array of shape (100, n_branch, n_branch).
  3. Timing. Build PTDFs for pandapower's case118, case300, case1354pegase and case2869pegase. For each, time the single-injection screening of step 1 (the \(n_{branch}^2\) output of case2869pegase already takes about 170 MB in float64): the first call and the median of the next ten calls, on CPU (JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu) and, if available, on GPU, in float64 and in float32. Plot time against number of branches on log-log axes. Where does the GPU start to win, if at all? How large is the float64 penalty on your card?
  4. Accidental recompilation. Make the outage set a Python tuple and mark it static (static_argnums); call the function with ten different outage sets of the same length and count compilations (for example with a Python counter inside the function, which only runs while tracing). Then pass a fresh lambda post-processing function on every call. Fix both, and prove the fix with jax.no_tracing().

Solutions: Lab · Notebook: lab.ipynb.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
All statements are also in exercises.ipynb; the worked examples run in examples.ipynb.

  1. For g = jax.jit(f, static_argnums=1), predict how many times f is traced for the calls g(x3, 2), g(y3, 2), g(x4, 2), g(x3, 3), g(x3.astype(jnp.float32), 2), where x3, y3 are float64 arrays of length 3 and x4 of length 4. Then check your answer in a notebook. (Jupyter: JAX)

    Solution: Exercise 1.

  2. (Jupyter: JAX) Write clip_negative(x) with if x.sum() > 0: and call it under jit. Read the error, then fix it twice, with jnp.where and with lax.cond. Which version evaluates both branches, and when does that matter?

    Solution: Exercise 2.

  3. (Jupyter: JAX + NumPy) Pad a list of variable-length index arrays to a fixed length with a sentinel equal to the array length, and gather with x.at[idx].get(mode="fill", fill_value=0.0). What happens if the sentinel is -1 instead? Relate the answer to why production code chooses a large out-of-bounds sentinel.

    Solution: Exercise 3.

  4. (Jupyter: JAX + matplotlib) Compute the LODF matrix of IEEE 118 in float32 and float64, and plot the absolute difference against \(|1-(\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,f_b}-\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,t_b})|\). Which outages lose the most accuracy in float32, and what does that say about near-bridges (Chapter 4)?

    Solution: Exercise 4.

  5. (Octave) Implement N-1 screening of IEEE 118 twice in Octave: a for loop over outages, and one vectorized matrix expression. Compare run times. Which JAX transformation plays the role of your vectorized rewrite, and what does jit add on top?

    Solution: Exercise 5.

    Known discrepancy: MATPOWER's bridge masking fails on case118

    If you take the LODF from MATPOWER 8.1, makeLODF(mpc, H, true) (bridge masking) stops on case118 with br(197): out of bound 186 inside find_bridges, which trips over the parallel branches of that case; it works on case14. Call makeLODF(mpc, H) without the option and mask the bridges yourself, as in Chapter 17.

  6. (Jupyter: JAX + jaxtyping) Annotate n1_flows with Float[Array, " n_branch n_bus"]-style shapes, decorate it with @jaxtyped(typechecker=beartype), and call it with a PTDF whose number of columns does not match the injection vector. What error do you get, and at which moment (tracing or execution)?

    Solution: Exercise 6.

docs.title: Chapter 31 – Solutions
docs.text: Solutions of the Lab and the Exercises of Chapter 31. Try each task before reading its solution. The code is in the chapter's src folder: n1_screen.py (the worked example), grid_data.py, n1_batch.py, timing_sweep.py, compile_count.py, control_flow.py, lodf_precision.py, shape_check.py and n1_loop_vs_vec.m, each with a test next to it. Every script prints the numbers quoted below when run from the src folder. The JAX numbers are CPU numbers (JAX 0.11 on the course environment, Python 3.14, Windows), with jax_enable_x64 on, except the CPU against GPU comparison of Lab step 3, which ran on an NVIDIA GPU and a CPU in ToOp's GPU container (JAX 0.5.3; details there). The jaxtyping exercise ran with ToOp's environment (jaxtyping 0.2.38, beartype 0.22, JAX 0.5.3, ToOp commit ba1874e), which is the one that has those libraries. Elsewhere, GPU behaviour is described, not measured.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text:
1. Port. n1_flows in n1_screen.py is the single-outage function: the LODF column \((\mathrm{PTDF}_{\cdot,f_b}-\mathrm{PTDF}_{\cdot,t_b})/(1-(\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,f_b}-\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,t_b}))\), the diagonal entry forced to \(-1\) with jnp.where, the post-contingency flows \(f^0 + \mathrm{LODF}_{\cdot,b} f^0_b\), and a boolean flag |denom| > 1e-11 in place of the ValueError the NumPy loop raises for a bridge. screen = jax.jit(jax.vmap(n1_flows, in_axes=(None, None, None, None, 0))) adds the outage axis. grid_data.branch_data pulls from_bus, to_bus, x and the injections out of pandapower through its MATPOWER converter (bus numbers consecutive from zero, lines and transformers both branches), and grid_data.numpy_ptdf/numpy_screen are the Chapter 17 loop. On IEEE 14 (20 branches, 1 bridge) and IEEE 118 (186 branches, 9 bridges) the JAX flows match the NumPy flows to 1e-9 on every non-bridge outage, the two PTDFs match to 1e-9, and the flags match the bridges the loop skipped (test_grid_data.py).
  2. Second batch axis. n1_batch.screen_injections = jax.jit(jax.vmap(screen, in_axes=(None, None, None, 0, None))): a vmap of the already jitted, already vmapped screening, with the batch on the injection argument only. random_injections splits one key into 100 subkeys and perturbs the base injection by 10 % Gaussian noise. One call on IEEE 118 returns flows of shape (100, 186, 186) in float64 and ok of shape (100, 186); the 9 bridges are flagged in every one of the 100 injections (900 False flags in all, since a bridge is a property of the topology, not of the injection); the largest post-contingency flow of a batch member ranges from 362.2 to 624.0 MW; the same key gives the same batch (True).

  3. Timing. timing_sweep.time_screen clears the compilation cache, times the first call (compilation included) and the median of the next ten, every call wrapped in jax.block_until_ready. The PTDF is built in float64 and cast, so the float32 rows time the screening itself in float32. CPU, one run:

    Grid Branches Output float64 first [s] float64 steady float32 first [s] float32 steady case118 186 0.3 MB 0.119 0.1 ms 0.090 0.1 ms case300 411 1.4 MB 0.108 0.7 ms 0.099 0.4 ms case1354pegase 1 991 31.7 MB 0.696 26.9 ms 0.104 8.9 ms case2869pegase 4 582 168 MB 1.126 156 ms 0.194 104 ms

    On log-log axes the steady-state line has slope close to 2 between 411 and 4 582 branches (the output is \(n_{branch}^2\) numbers, and the work is a rank-one update per outage), and the first call is almost flat at 0.1 s for the small grids: that is compilation, which does not depend on the data, plus the one-time backend start-up in the first row. The float64 penalty on this CPU is 1.5–3× in the steady state (26.9 vs 8.9 ms, 156 vs 104 ms), mostly memory traffic: the float64 output of case2869pegase is 168 MB, twice the float32 one.

    CPU against GPU. The same timing_sweep.py runs in the ToOp GPU environment of Chapter 32 (its solutions describe it), which has JAX, the CUDA plugin and pandapower: image toop-toop-gpu:latest, ToOp ba1874e's uv.lock, JAX 0.5.3 with jax-cuda12-plugin 0.5.3 (CUDA runtime 12.9), Python 3.11, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Laptop GPU (4 096 MiB, 35 W, driver 617.42), docker run --cpus 4, on an otherwise idle machine. Only JAX_PLATFORMS changes: cpu for the CPU, cuda,cpu for the GPU. python timing_sweep.py repeat 3 runs one discarded warm-up sweep and then three sweeps, and prints the medians:

    Grid Branches CPU first [s] CPU float64 CPU float32 GPU first [s] GPU float64 GPU float32 case118 186 0.064 0.241 ms 0.123 ms 0.150 0.224 ms 0.188 ms case300 411 0.052 0.470 ms 0.391 ms 0.133 1.560 ms 1.501 ms case1354pegase 1 991 0.654 33.9 ms 14.1 ms 0.154 5.04 ms 3.89 ms case2869pegase 4 582 2.657 227 ms 161 ms 0.186 31.9 ms 25.9 ms

    The "first" columns are the float64 first calls; the float32 first calls are 0.06–0.20 s on the CPU and 0.12–0.28 s on the GPU. The CPU of this container (JAX 0.5.3, four cores) is slower than the course environment of the table above (JAX 0.11, Windows, all cores), so compare devices only within one table. On log-log axes the GPU's steady-state line is flat at 0.2–1.6 ms for the two small grids, where the time is kernel launches and not arithmetic. From case1354pegase to case2869pegase it rises with a slope close to 2, like the CPU's, but six to seven times lower. The GPU starts to win between 411 and 1 991 branches. On case118 the two devices tie (0.22 against 0.24 ms), and on case300 the CPU is 3.3 times faster. On case1354pegase the GPU is 6.7 times faster in float64 and 3.6 times in float32, and on case2869pegase 7.1 and 6.2 times. The GPU's first call is a flat 0.13–0.19 s: compilation plus copying the PTDF to the device. On the CPU the first float64 call of the two Pegase grids is much slower than its float32 call (0.65 against 0.08 s, 2.66 against 0.20 s). That float64 call is the first to write a 32 or 168 MB output in the process. Fresh memory pages are the likely cost, since the float32 call that follows can reuse them.

    The float64 penalty on this card is small, 1.0–1.3 times (31.9 against 25.9 ms on case2869pegase). The 1/32 float64 arithmetic rate of a GeForce card never shows, because the screening is a rank-one update per outage, which reads and writes \(n_{branch}^2\) numbers and does almost no arithmetic per number. It is bound by memory bandwidth, and float64 only doubles the bytes. On the CPU the penalty is 1.2–2.4 times.

    The results agree. python timing_sweep.py agree screens each grid on the GPU and on the CPU, each device building its own PTDF, and compares the flows of the outages both flag as valid. In float64 the largest difference is 1.5e-14 of the largest flow on case118, 7.5e-14 on case300, 6.6e-13 on case1354pegase (1.4e-9 MW) and 1.3e-13 on case2869pegase, with identical bridge flags. Float32 against float64 on the GPU differs by 2.9e-7, 1.1e-6, 1.2e-6 and 1.0e-3 of the largest flow: 2.25 MW on case2869pegase, where the float32 rounding of a few near-bridge outages is amplified as in Exercise 4. All bridges are still flagged, because the PTDF is built in float64 and only then cast, so a bridge's denominator is cast from an exact zero. When the whole computation is in float32, as in Chapter 32's ToOp runs, some bridges are not flagged.

    timing_sweep.py
    """Compile time against steady-state time of the N-1 screening, per grid size and precision (Chapter 31, Lab 3).

Run as ``python timing_sweep.py`` for the four grids of the lab (a few minutes on a laptop CPU). Set
``JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu`` for the CPU, or leave JAX to pick the GPU when it has one (a JAX with the CUDA plugin). Two
more modes::

    python timing_sweep.py repeat 3   # one warm-up sweep, then the median of three sweeps
    python timing_sweep.py agree      # the same screening on the GPU and on the CPU, compared entry by entry
"""

import statistics
import sys
import time

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from grid_data import branch_data
from n1_screen import ptdf_matrix, screen

CASES = ('case118', 'case300', 'case1354pegase', 'case2869pegase')


def time_screen(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, repeats: int = 10) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Seconds of the first call (compilation included) and the median of the next ``repeats`` calls.

    Every call waits for its result with ``block_until_ready``; without that, JAX's asynchronous dispatch
    returns before the device has finished and the timer measures nothing. The cache is cleared first so that
    the first call always compiles, even when the same shapes were seen earlier in the process.
    """
    jax.clear_caches()
    outages = jnp.arange(ptdf.shape[0])
    start = time.perf_counter()
    jax.block_until_ready(screen(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, outages))
    first = time.perf_counter() - start
    later = []
    for _ in range(repeats):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        jax.block_until_ready(screen(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, outages))
        later.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
    return first, statistics.median(later)


def sweep(cases: tuple[str, ...] = CASES, repeats: int = 10) -> list[dict]:
    """One row per grid and precision: branch count, output size, first-call and steady-state seconds.

    The PTDF is built once in float64 and cast, so the float32 rows measure the screening itself in float32.
    """
    rows = []
    for case in cases:
        from_bus, to_bus, x, p = (jnp.array(v) for v in branch_data(case))
        ptdf64 = ptdf_matrix(from_bus, to_bus, x, len(p))
        for dtype in (jnp.float64, jnp.float32):
            ptdf, inj = ptdf64.astype(dtype), p.astype(dtype)
            first, steady = time_screen(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, inj, repeats)
            n_branch = ptdf.shape[0]
            rows.append(
                {
                    'case': case,
                    'n_branch': n_branch,
                    'dtype': jnp.dtype(dtype).name,
                    'output_mb': n_branch * n_branch * jnp.dtype(dtype).itemsize / 1e6,
                    'first_s': first,
                    'steady_s': steady,
                }
            )
    return rows


def repeated_sweep(cases: tuple[str, ...] = CASES, repeats: int = 10, runs: int = 3) -> list[dict]:
    """``sweep`` once as a warm-up (backend start-up, file caches, GPU clocks), then ``runs`` times; the medians.

    Every run clears the compilation cache per row, so each ``first_s`` is a full compilation again.
    """
    sweep(cases, repeats)
    results = [sweep(cases, repeats) for _ in range(runs)]
    return [
        {**rows[0], **{k: statistics.median(r[k] for r in rows) for k in ('first_s', 'steady_s')}}
        for rows in zip(*results, strict=True)
    ]


def agreement(case: str) -> dict:
    """The screening of ``case`` on the default device (the GPU, if any) against the CPU, and float32 against float64.

    Each device builds its own PTDF and screens every outage. Flows are compared on the outages that both runs
    flag as valid; ``missed_bridges`` counts the bridges the float32 run does not flag (its denominator is
    rounding noise instead of zero, far above the ``1e-11`` threshold), whose flows look valid and are not.
    """
    data = branch_data(case)
    out = {'case': case, 'devices': (str(jax.devices()[0]), str(jax.devices('cpu')[0]))}
    runs = {}
    for name, device, dtype in (
        ('default64', jax.devices()[0], jnp.float64),
        ('cpu64', jax.devices('cpu')[0], jnp.float64),
        ('default32', jax.devices()[0], jnp.float32),
    ):
        with jax.default_device(device):
            from_bus, to_bus, x, p = (jax.device_put(jnp.array(v), device) for v in data)
            ptdf = ptdf_matrix(from_bus, to_bus, x, len(p)).astype(dtype)
            flows, ok = screen(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p.astype(dtype), jnp.arange(ptdf.shape[0]))
            runs[name] = (np.asarray(flows, dtype=np.float64), np.asarray(ok))
    for label, (a, b) in {
        'device_vs_cpu_float64': ('default64', 'cpu64'),
        'float32_vs_float64': ('default32', 'default64'),
    }.items():
        (fa, oka), (fb, okb) = runs[a], runs[b]
        both = oka & okb
        diff = np.abs(fa[both] - fb[both]).max()
        out[label] = {
            'max_abs_mw': float(diff),
            'max_rel': float(diff / np.abs(fb[both]).max()),
            'flags_equal': bool((oka == okb).all()),
            'missed_bridges': int((oka & ~okb).sum()),
            'missed_max_flow_mw': float(np.abs(fa[oka & ~okb]).max()) if (oka & ~okb).any() else None,
        }
    return out


def main() -> None:
    """Print the table the log-log plot is drawn from (time against number of branches, one line per dtype)."""
    mode = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 'once'
    print('backend:', jax.default_backend(), '-', jax.devices()[0].device_kind, '- JAX', jax.__version__)
    if mode == 'agree':
        for case in CASES:
            print(agreement(case))
        return
    rows = repeated_sweep(runs=int(sys.argv[2])) if mode == 'repeat' else sweep()
    print(f'{"case":15s} {"branches":>8s} {"dtype":>8s} {"output MB":>10s} {"first [s]":>10s} {"steady [ms]":>11s}')
    for r in rows:
        print(
            f'{r["case"]:15s} {r["n_branch"]:8d} {r["dtype"]:>8s} {r["output_mb"]:10.1f} '
            f'{r["first_s"]:10.3f} {r["steady_s"] * 1e3:11.3f}'
        )


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

    Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

  4. Accidental recompilation. compile_count.counting wraps a function so that a Python counter runs on every Python-level call; under jit the Python body only runs while tracing, so the counter counts compilations. With the outage set as a Python tuple marked static (screen_static), every distinct tuple is a new cache key: on the four-bus grid, 4 calls with 4 distinct pairs give 4 traces, and in general ten different outage sets give ten compilations, even though all have the same length (the test checks that the count equals the number of distinct tuples, and that a second round of the same tuples adds none). With a fresh lambda passed as the static post argument (screen_then), 10 calls give 10 traces: every lambda expression evaluates to a new function object, and function objects hash by identity. The fixes: pass the outages as a jnp array, so only its shape and dtype matter (screen in the worked example), and define the post-processing function once at module level (worst_flow): 10 calls, 1 trace. The proof: after one warm-up call per shape, the fixed versions run inside with jax.no_tracing(): without error, while a call with a new outage length inside that block raises RuntimeError (test_compile_count.py). Build the index arrays before entering the block: creating an array is itself a dispatch that no_tracing flags the first time it sees that shape and dtype.

    compile_count.py (the static tuple)
    def _screen_static(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, outages: tuple):
    """The outage set as a Python tuple marked static: one compilation per distinct tuple."""
    return jax.vmap(n1_flows, in_axes=(None, None, None, None, 0))(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, jnp.array(outages))


screen_static_counted, static_traces = counting(_screen_static)
screen_static = jax.jit(screen_static_counted, static_argnums=4)
    compile_count.py (the fresh lambda and the fix)
    def _screen_then(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, outages, post):
    """Screen, then apply a post-processing function passed as a static argument."""
    flows, ok = screen(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus, p, outages)
    return post(flows), ok


screen_then_counted, then_traces = counting(_screen_then)
screen_then = jax.jit(screen_then_counted, static_argnames='post')


def worst_flow(flows):
    """Largest absolute flow per outage. Defined once at module level: one function object, one compilation."""
    return jnp.abs(flows).max(axis=1)

docs.title: Exercise 2
docs.text:
Eagerly, clip_negative_python works ([0, 2, 0, 5] for x = [-1, 2, -3, 5]). Under jit the if asks bool() of a tracer and raises TracerBoolConversionError (a ConcretizationTypeError): while tracing, JAX knows the shape and dtype of x.sum() > 0 but not its value, so it cannot pick a branch. Both fixes give the same result under jit:

control_flow.py (the three versions)
def clip_negative_python(x):
    """Python ``if`` on a traced value: fine eagerly, TracerBoolConversionError under jit."""
    if x.sum() > 0:
        return jnp.maximum(x, 0.0)
    return x


def clip_negative_where(x):
    """Both branches are computed on every call; ``where`` picks per element."""
    return jnp.where(x.sum() > 0, jnp.maximum(x, 0.0), x)


def clip_negative_cond(x):
    """One branch is executed at run time (outside vmap); the predicate is a scalar."""
    return lax.cond(x.sum() > 0, lambda v: jnp.maximum(v, 0.0), lambda v: v, x)

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

jnp.where evaluates both branches on every call and selects per element; lax.cond compiles both but executes only the taken one (its predicate must be a scalar). It matters when a branch is expensive (you pay for both with where), when the untaken branch produces inf or NaN that leak through gradients, and when a branch has side effects (jax.debug.print). The gradient shows it: for safe_sqrt_where(x) = where(x > 0, sqrt(x), 0), jax.grad at \(x=-1\) is nan, because the derivative of sqrt is evaluated at \(-1\) and \(0 \times \text{NaN}\) is NaN; with lax.cond it is 0.0. Under vmap, however, cond is lowered to a select_n over both branches (jax.make_jaxpr(jax.vmap(clip_negative_cond)) contains select_n), because different batch members may take different branches: inside a vmapped, jitted solver like ToOp's, cond buys nothing over where, and the code uses jnp.where and masks throughout.

docs.title: Exercise 3
docs.text:
pad_indices([[0, 1, 2], [3], [1, 3]], sentinel=4) gives [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 4], [1, 3, 4]] and x.at[idx].get(mode="fill", fill_value=0.0) on x = [10, 20, 30, 40] returns [[10, 20, 30], [40, 0, 0], [20, 40, 0]]: index 4 is out of bounds, so the slot reads the fill value and the row sums [60, 40, 60] are the sums of the real members. With sentinel=-1 the gather returns [[10, 20, 30], [40, 40, 40], [20, 40, 40]] and the row sums become [60, 120, 100]: JAX normalizes negative indices like NumPy does, so -1 is the last element, in bounds, and every padding slot silently adds x[-1]. Nothing fails; the numbers are just wrong. That is why production code pads with a large positive sentinel (ToOp's int_max(), Chapter 32): it is out of bounds for every array the code will ever index, so mode="fill" drops it, and if it ever shows up in a result it is an obviously impossible index rather than a plausible one. The same reasoning says why an int64 sentinel stored in an int32 array is dangerous: it wraps to -1, which is this exercise's bad case.

control_flow.py (padding and gathering)
def pad_indices(groups: list[list[int]], sentinel: int) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Variable-length index lists as one rectangular int array, unused slots filled with ``sentinel``."""
    width = max(len(g) for g in groups)
    return jnp.array([list(g) + [sentinel] * (width - len(g)) for g in groups])


def gather_fill(x, idx):
    """Gather with out-of-bounds slots replaced by 0.0; valid sentinels are >= len(x), never negative."""
    return x.at[idx].get(mode='fill', fill_value=0.0)

docs.title: Exercise 4
docs.text:
lodf_precision.lodf_matrix computes the whole LODF matrix at once, in the dtype of the PTDF it is given; the study builds the PTDF of IEEE 118 in float64 and casts it to float32 for the second run, so the difference measures what the LODF formula itself does to float32 round-off (a float32 PTDF solve would add its own error of order \(10^{-6}\) relative on top). IEEE 118 has 9 bridges, with \(|1-(\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,f_b}-\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,t_b})| < 10^{-11}\); their columns are infinite in both precisions and are excluded. Over the 177 other outages the largest float32 error of a column has median \(1.1 \times 10^{-7}\) and maximum \(5.5 \times 10^{-7}\), and it grows as the denominator shrinks: median \(2.5 \times 10^{-7}\) for \(|\text{denom}| < 0.2\) against \(5.7 \times 10^{-8}\) for \(|\text{denom}| \ge 0.5\), with a correlation of \(-0.79\) between \(\log_{10}\) error and \(\log_{10} |\text{denom}|\). The five smallest denominators among non-bridges are the outages of branches 114–115 (0.053), 70–71 (0.059), 108–109 (0.069), 4–5 (0.072) and 65–68 (0.080), with errors between \(1.6 \times 10^{-7}\) and \(5.1 \times 10^{-7}\). On the plot (error against \(|\text{denom}|\), both axes logarithmic) the cloud slopes down to the right: these are the near-bridges. A branch whose outage leaves only a weak parallel path has \(\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,f_b}-\mathrm{PTDF}_{b,t_b}\) close to 1, so the division by \(1-(\cdot)\) amplifies the round-off of the numerator by \(1/|\text{denom}|\): a condition number, in the sense of Chapter 4, that is set by the topology, not by the solver. In float64 the same amplification acts on \(10^{-16}\) and is harmless; in float32 it eats a quarter of the seven significant digits for the worst outages here, and all of them on a grid with a denominator of \(10^{-4}\). This is why ToOp forces float64 even on GPUs that pay for it.

lodf_precision.py
"""LODF of IEEE 118 in float32 and float64: which outages lose accuracy, and why (Chapter 31, Exercise 4)."""

import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from grid_data import branch_data
from n1_screen import ptdf_matrix


def lodf_matrix(ptdf, from_bus, to_bus):
    """LODF (monitored branch x outaged branch) in the dtype of ``ptdf``, plus the LODF denominators.

    LODF[a, b] = (PTDF[a, f_b] - PTDF[a, t_b]) / (1 - (PTDF[b, f_b] - PTDF[b, t_b])), LODF[b, b] = -1.
    Bridges have a zero denominator and an infinite column; the caller masks them with ``abs(denom) > 1e-11``.
    """
    col = ptdf[:, from_bus] - ptdf[:, to_bus]  # (n_branch, n_outage)
    denom = 1.0 - jnp.diagonal(col)
    lodf = col / denom[None, :]
    eye = jnp.eye(ptdf.shape[0], dtype=bool)
    return jnp.where(eye, -1.0, lodf), denom


def precision_study(case: str = 'case118') -> dict:
    """Per outage: |denominator| and the largest |LODF32 - LODF64| in its column (bridges excluded)."""
    from_bus, to_bus, x, p = (jnp.array(v) for v in branch_data(case))
    ptdf64 = ptdf_matrix(from_bus, to_bus, x, len(p))
    lodf64, denom = lodf_matrix(ptdf64, from_bus, to_bus)
    lodf32, _ = lodf_matrix(ptdf64.astype(jnp.float32), from_bus, to_bus)
    ok = np.abs(np.asarray(denom)) > 1e-11
    error = np.full(len(ok), np.nan)  # bridge columns are infinite in both precisions: no error to compare
    error[ok] = np.abs(np.asarray(lodf32, dtype=np.float64)[:, ok] - np.asarray(lodf64)[:, ok]).max(axis=0)
    return {
        'from_bus': np.asarray(from_bus),
        'to_bus': np.asarray(to_bus),
        'abs_denom': np.abs(np.asarray(denom)),
        'error': error,
        'ok': ok,
    }


def main() -> None:
    """Print the bridges, the five outages with the smallest denominators and the error trend."""
    study = precision_study()
    ok, denom, error = study['ok'], study['abs_denom'], study['error']
    print(f'{int((~ok).sum())} bridges (|1 - (PTDF_b,fb - PTDF_b,tb)| < 1e-11), excluded from the comparison')
    order = np.argsort(denom + np.where(ok, 0.0, np.inf))[:5]
    print('smallest denominators among non-bridges:')
    for b in order:
        print(
            f'  outage {b:3d} (bus {study["from_bus"][b] + 1:3d}-{study["to_bus"][b] + 1:3d}): '
            f'|denom| = {denom[b]:.4f}, max |LODF32 - LODF64| = {error[b]:.2e}'
        )
    print(f'float32 error over all non-bridge outages: median {np.median(error[ok]):.1e}, max {error[ok].max():.1e}')
    small, large = np.median(error[ok][denom[ok] < 0.2]), np.median(error[ok][denom[ok] >= 0.5])
    print(f'median error, |denom| < 0.2: {small:.1e}; |denom| >= 0.5: {large:.1e}')
    rho = np.corrcoef(np.log10(denom[ok]), np.log10(error[ok]))[0, 1]
    print(f'correlation of log10 error with log10 |denom|: {rho:.2f}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Exercise 5
docs.text:
Both versions start from MATPOWER's makePTDF and the base-case flows \(f^0 = H P\). The loop takes one outage at a time: one PTDF column difference, one scalar denominator, one rank-one update. The vectorized version forms all column differences at once, col = H(:, f) - H(:, t) (an \(n_l \times n_l\) matrix whose column \(k\) belongs to outage \(k\)), divides every column by its own denominator with broadcasting, sets the diagonal to \(-1\), blanks the bridge columns, and builds every post-contingency flow vector in one expression F = f0' + L' .* f0. On IEEE 118 (Octave 11.3, MATPOWER 8.1, CPU) the two give identical matrices (largest difference exactly 0, the same 9 bridge rows) and take 3.2–3.7 ms for the loop against 0.4–0.5 ms vectorized, a factor of about 8. The vectorized rewrite is what jax.vmap does for you: it takes the one-outage function and adds the batch axis mechanically, with no hand-written broadcasting. jit adds what no array language can: it compiles the whole batched program into one fused XLA executable, so the intermediate \(n_l \times n_l\) matrices (col, L, L') need not all be materialized, Python and interpreter overhead disappear from the steady state, and the same program runs unchanged on a GPU. One finding on the way: makeLODF(mpc, H, true) (bridge masking) of MATPOWER 8.1 stops with br(197): out of bound 186 inside find_bridges on case118, so the file masks the bridges itself.

n1_loop_vs_vec.m
function [F_loop, F_vec, t_loop, t_vec] = n1_loop_vs_vec(casename)
  % N-1 flows of every single branch outage of a MATPOWER case, computed twice: a for loop over the
  % outages and one vectorized matrix expression, each timed (Chapter 31, Exercise 5).
  % Row k of F is the flow vector after the outage of branch k; bridge rows are NaN in both versions.
  define_constants;
  mpc = ext2int(loadcase(casename));
  H  = makePTDF(mpc);                                   % PTDF, slack = reference bus
  Pbus = real(makeSbus(mpc.baseMVA, mpc.bus, mpc.gen)) * mpc.baseMVA;   % net injections, MW
  f0 = H * Pbus;                                        % base-case flows
  f = mpc.branch(:, F_BUS);
  t = mpc.branch(:, T_BUS);
  nl = size(mpc.branch, 1);

  tic;
  F_loop = nan(nl, nl);
  for k = 1:nl                                          % one outage at a time, as a Python loop would
    col = H(:, f(k)) - H(:, t(k));
    denom = 1 - col(k);
    if abs(denom) < 1e-11
      continue;                                         % bridge: islands the grid, row stays NaN
    end
    lodf = col / denom;
    lodf(k) = -1;
    F_loop(k, :) = (f0 + lodf * f0(k))';
  end
  t_loop = toc;

  tic;
  col = H(:, f) - H(:, t);                              % column k: PTDF difference of outage k, all at once
  denom = 1 - diag(col)';                               % 1 - (H(k, f_k) - H(k, t_k)) as a row vector
  L = col ./ denom;                                     % broadcasting divides each column by its denominator
  L(1:nl + 1:end) = -1;                                 % the outaged branch loses its flow
  L(:, abs(denom) < 1e-11) = NaN;                       % bridges (makeLODF(mpc, H, true) fails on case118 in 8.1)
  F_vec = f0' + L' .* f0;                               % F(k, a) = f0(a) + L(a, k) f0(k), by broadcasting
  t_vec = toc;
end

%!test
%! if isempty(which('loadcase')), disp('MATPOWER not on the path, test skipped'); return; end
%! [Fl, Fv, tl, tv] = n1_loop_vs_vec('case118');
%! assert(size(Fl), [186 186]); assert(size(Fv), [186 186])
%! ok = all(isfinite(Fl), 2);
%! assert(sum(~ok) >= 1)                                % IEEE 118 has bridges
%! assert(isequal(ok, all(isfinite(Fv), 2)))            % both versions flag the same outages
%! assert(Fv(ok, :), Fl(ok, :), 1e-8)
%! assert(tl > 0 && tv > 0)
%! fprintf('case118: loop %.4f s, vectorized %.4f s, ratio %.1f\n', tl, tv, tl / tv)

docs.text:
shape_check.py (the annotated function)
# ruff reads the shape strings as forward references and reports F722; ToOp ignores that rule repository-wide
@jaxtyped(typechecker=beartype)
def n1_flows_checked(
    ptdf: Float[Array, ' n_branch n_bus'],  # noqa: F722
    from_bus: Int[Array, ' n_branch'],  # noqa: F722
    to_bus: Int[Array, ' n_branch'],  # noqa: F722
    p: Float[Array, ' n_bus'],  # noqa: F722
    outage: Int[Array, ''],  # noqa: F722
) -> tuple[Float[Array, ' n_branch'], Bool[Array, '']]:  # noqa: F722
    """The worked example's ``n1_flows`` with every shape named; the same name must mean the same size."""
    f0 = ptdf @ p
    col = ptdf[:, from_bus[outage]] - ptdf[:, to_bus[outage]]
    denom = 1.0 - col[outage]
    lodf = jnp.where(jnp.arange(ptdf.shape[0]) == outage, -1.0, col / denom)
    return f0 + lodf * f0[outage], jnp.abs(denom) > 1e-11

Open the src/ folder on GitHub to see or download all the files of this chapter.

A valid call gives the worked example's first row, [0, 100, -25, 25, 75] with the flag True. Called with a PTDF of 4 columns and an injection vector of 5 entries, the function raises jaxtyping.TypeCheckError (a TypeError subclass) whose message names the mismatch: "The problem arose whilst typechecking parameter 'p'. Actual value: f64[5]. Expected type: Float[Array, 'n_bus']", followed by the shapes of every argument and the current bindings n_branch=5, n_bus=4 (set by ptdf, which was checked first). Eagerly it happens at call time, before any arithmetic. Under jit it happens while tracing: the tracers that stand for the arguments carry concrete shapes and dtypes, which is all jaxtyping checks, so the error appears on the first call for a given set of shapes, with the same message, and never at execution. The flip side is that a cached call does not run the Python body at all, so it is not checked again, which is fine, since its shapes are by definition the ones that passed. This is also why ToOp can leave ENABLE_BEARTYPE on in its test configuration at no run-time cost: the checks run once per compilation, not once per batch. The course environment does not ship jaxtyping and beartype; test_shape_check.py skips there and passes with ToOp's interpreter.

docs.title: Chapter 32. JAX in ToOp: internals and GPU tuning
docs.text:
Weeks: 1.5 · Semester: 4 · Prerequisites: Chapter 18, Chapter 31

Why it matters for ToOp

ToOp's speed depends on compiling the solver once and feeding it millions of topologies; its correctness depends on the compiled program seeing the data you think it sees. Both are governed by a few design choices:

  • What is static. StaticInformation (dc_solver/jax/types.py) holds a traced dynamic_information: DynamicInformation and a static field solver_config: Static[SolverConfig] = eqx.field(static=True). The jitted core iterate_symmetric_sequential (dc_solver/jax/topology_looper.py) is declared with static_argnames=("solver_config", "aggregate_output_fn"): those two arguments select the compiled program, while DynamicInformation (PTDF, injections, limits, action set) is traced. The recompilation trigger is SolverConfig plus the aggregation function, not StaticInformation as a whole (ToOp's packages/dc_solver_pkg/README.md states the coarser version).
  • How static values are compared. SolverConfig.__hash__ and StaticInformation.__hash__ both return id(self), and __eq__ is self is other. The compile cache is keyed on object identity, not on values.
  • Fixed shapes. Padding with the int_max() sentinel, read through .at[idx].get(mode="fill") (dc_solver/jax/batching.py, dc_solver/jax/lodf.py), and loops with traced bounds (lax.fori_loop in optimizer/dc/genetic_functions/mutation/mutate.py).
  • Memory and devices. batch_size, batch_size_bsdf and batch_size_injection trade memory for throughput; jax.pmap with buffer donation spreads batches over GPUs (dc_solver/jax/topology_looper.py, optimizer/dc/worker/optimizer.py).

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• The static/dynamic split in ToOp: what SolverConfig holds (batch_size_bsdf, batch_size_injection, slack, n_stat, number_most_affected, contingency_ids, enable_bb_outages, distributed, ...) and what DynamicInformation holds (ptdf, nodal_injections, branch_limits, action_set, unsplit_flow, branches_to_fail, ...); functional updates with jax_dataclasses.replace.
  • Identity hashing and its consequences: replace(solver_config) with unchanged values still recompiles; mutating a field in place (solver_config.number_most_affected = 20) reuses the old compiled program; a fresh lambda as aggregate_output_fn recompiles every call (you measure the first, cached and fresh-lambda call times on IEEE 57 in the Lab); every static field (for example number_most_affected) recompiles when changed.
  • Hidden constants: run_solver builds a DefaultAggregateOutputFn whose hash is hash(solver_config) and which stores max_mw_flow and branches_to_fail as Python attributes (dc_solver/jax/topology_looper.py). Those arrays are baked into the compiled program as constants (see the Lab).
  • The optimizer loop: run_single_device_epoch is jitted with iterations_per_epoch and update_fn static, and runs lax.fori_loop over run_single_iteration, which donates jax_data (optimizer/dc/worker/optimizer.py). packages/topology_optimizer_pkg/tests/test_jax_compilation.py uses jax.no_tracing() to prove that later epochs do not retrace and that changing iterations_per_epoch or the batch size does.
  • Data-dependent loop counts without recompiling: the number of substation mutations is a Poisson draw clipped to [1, max_num_splits] and used as the traced upper bound of jax.lax.fori_loop (mutate.py); fori_loop over batches in topology_looper.py.
  • Sentinels and integer widths: int_max() (dc_solver/jax/types.py) as an out-of-bounds pad value, dropped by get(mode="fill", fill_value=...); why a sentinel that wraps to -1 corrupts data instead of being ignored; the int_dtype() helper introduced on the course fork's feat/add-docker-compose branch (not in upstream main), whose docstring attributes Windows-only failures to dtype=int following the platform's C long (Exercise 4).
  • Multiple devices: lf_config.distributed=True → jax.pmap with static_broadcasted_argnums=(6, 7) and donate_argnums=(3,) (the result storage) in topology_looper.py, and jax.pmap of the epoch with donate_argnums=(0,) in optimizer/dc/worker/optimizer.py; faking several CPU devices with XLA_FLAGS=--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=N (optimizer/benchmark/benchmark_utils.py, dc_solver/jax/benchmarks/runner.py).
  • Memory and throughput knobs, in the order to cut on out-of-memory: lf_config.batch_size ("the largest value that fits in your VRAM" in notebooks/example3_e2e_pipeline.ipynb; the DC optimizer copies it into batch_size_bsdf in optimizer/dc/genetic_functions/initialization.py), then, for direct solver calls, solver_config.batch_size_bsdf, then batch_size_injection (both named for out-of-memory errors in "Debugging Tips" of .github/copilot-instructions.md). BSDF work is proportional to max_num_splits, and disconnection work to max_num_disconnections, even when the slots are unused (packages/dc_solver_pkg/README.md). The README calls the latter "a LODF computation for every slot"; in the batch path apply_disconnections (dc_solver/jax/disconnections.py, called from dc_solver/jax/compute_batch.py) applies all slots as one joint multi-outage (MODF) update of size max_num_disconnections, and a failed solve marks the whole topology unsuccessful. The batch-size search notebook dc_solver/jax/parse_batch_size_finder.ipynb plots mean time over a grid of (batch_size_bsdf, batch_size_injection) benchmark runs.
  • Precision and environment: jax_enable_x64 forced in optimizer/dc/main.py and dc_solver/preprocess/convert_to_jax.py; runner.py sets JAX_ENABLE_X64, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, OMP_NUM_THREADS and XLA_FLAGS per benchmark and runs each benchmark in a spawned process, because these variables only take effect before JAX initializes; float64 on consumer GeForce cards reported at about 1/32 of float32 speed (the GPU banner of the course fork's docker/device_banner.py); XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false on small GPUs.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Given a change to a ToOp input (a SolverConfig field, a DynamicInformation array, the batch size, the aggregation function), predict whether the solver recompiles, reuses the compiled program correctly, or reuses it incorrectly, and prove it with timings and the compile cache of the jitted core.
  • Measure compile time, steady-state throughput and peak memory of run_solver as a function of the batch sizes, and choose settings for a given device.
  • Explain how padding sentinels, traced loop bounds and buffer donation keep ToOp's shapes fixed and its memory bounded.

docs.text:
• ToOp sources, read in this order: dc_solver/jax/types.py (SolverConfig, DynamicInformation, StaticInformation), dc_solver/jax/topology_looper.py (run_solver, DefaultAggregateOutputFn, run_solver_symmetric, iterate_symmetric_sequential), dc_solver/jax/batching.py, optimizer/dc/worker/optimizer.py, packages/topology_optimizer_pkg/tests/test_jax_compilation.py.
